docs.title: Automated Security Helper
docs.text: ASH runs open-source security scanners and aggregates their findings. AWS Labs project. Apache 2.0 license.

docs.title: Scanning
docs.text:
• Application code, infrastructure, secrets, and dependencies
  • Severity thresholds and suppressions
  • SARIF, HTML, JSON, Markdown, and CSV reports

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Install ASH with Python 3.10+ and pipx:

pipx install git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0

From your project directory, choose an execution mode:

# Linux/macOS
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
alias ash="uvx git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0"

# Windows PowerShell
irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex
function ash { uvx git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0 $args }

docs.title: Using pip
docs.text: pip install git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0

docs.title: Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git --branch v3.7.0
cd automated-security-helper
pip install .

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
# Run a scan in local mode (the scanner tools installed on this machine)
ash --mode local

# Run a scan in container mode (all tools)
ash --mode container
ash --mode local
ash --mode precommit
Mode Requirements container OCI-compatible runtime local Local scanner dependencies precommit Dependencies for the enabled subset

Installation · Quickstart

docs.title: Scanners
docs.text:
• Code: Bandit, Semgrep, Opengrep
  • Infrastructure: Checkov, CDK-Nag, CFN-Nag
  • Secrets: detect-secrets
  • Dependencies and software inventory: Grype, npm audit, Syft

A scan ends by printing the exit codes and the one it exits with:

=== ASH Exit Codes ===
  0: success
  1: scan errors / scanner failures
  2: actionable findings at or above threshold (fail_on_findings is true; default true)
  3: invalid config or refused input
  4: workspace definition or policy error
  5: usage error
ERROR (2) Exiting due to 122 actionable findings found in ASH scan

docs.title: Help
docs.text:
pre-commit run ash --all-files

The ash hook runs bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag and npm-audit. It needs pre-commit running on Python 3.10 to 3.14, and Node.js and npm on PATH for cdk-nag and npm-audit. ash-simple-scan is the same hook under its earlier id. See Using ASH with pre-commit for running without Node.js and for the container hook, ash-full-scan.

docs.title: Output Files
docs.text:
ASH v3 produces several output files in the .ash/ash_output/ directory:

  • ash_aggregated_results.json: Complete machine-readable results
  • reports/ash.summary.txt: Human-readable text summary
  • reports/ash.summary.md: Markdown summary for GitHub PRs and other platforms
  • reports/ash.html: Interactive HTML report
  • reports/ash.csv: CSV report for filtering and sorting findings

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: How do I run ASH on Windows?  ASH v3 can run directly on Windows in local mode with Python 3.10+. Simply install ASH using pip, pipx, or uvx and run with `--mode local`. For container mode, you'll need WSL2 and a container runtime like Docker Desktop, Rancher Desktop, or Podman Desktop.  How do I run ASH in CI/CD pipelines?  ASH can be run in container mode in any CI/CD environment that supports containers. See the [tutorials](getting-started/ci.md) for examples.  How do I exclude files from scanning?  ASH leaves out of its scan set every file a `.gitignore` or `.ignore` file in the scanned tree matches. You can also configure ignore paths in your `.ash/.ash.yaml` configuration file. The summaries record how many files the ignore files excluded, and `--no-honor-ignore-files` (or `honor_ignore_files: false` in a config file outside the scanned tree) scans those files too. See [Ignore files and the scan set](reference/coverage.md#what-decides-the-files).  Does ASH scan its own output, or the templates in cdk.out?  ASH leaves its own output out of the scan, whether or not `.gitignore` lists it: the output directory of the current scan, and `.ash/ash_output` under the scanned directory and under the directory ASH runs from. In a git checkout, regular files committed to one of those directories are still scanned (a committed link is not), and ASH warns that its output directory holds committed files. Outside a git checkout, or when git cannot list the repository, only the current scan's output directory is left out: an earlier run's `.ash/ash_output` is scanned like the rest of the tree, and ASH warns once per scan while the scan set still holds files in it, naming it and saying how to leave it out: delete it, or list it in an ignore file such as `.gitignore`. Adding it to `global_settings.ignore_paths` leaves its findings out, but the scan still reads it, so the warning repeats until the directory is deleted or an ignore file lists it. The output directory is recognized when it or the scanned directory is given through a link above the tree, as `/var` is on macOS. A scan does not delete or overwrite a committed file: when git tracks one where a scan writes its output (`ash_aggregated_results.json`, `ash-ignore-report.txt`, `ash-scan-set-files-list.txt`, `ash-scan-set-run.json`, `ash.log`, `ash.log.jsonl`, `.ash_previous_results_restored`, or anything under `analysis/`, `reports/`, `scanners/`, `converted/`, `.ash_previous_results/` or `.ash_previous_results.partial/`), the scan exits 3 before it deletes or writes anything, in every mode and from the MCP server. When git cannot list the repository the output directory is in (git is not installed, or it fails on the repository), any file at one of those paths stops the scan the same way, and the message names git's error and says to let git read the repository or remove the old results. A report over existing results (`--use-existing`) is stopped only where it writes: the results file, the logs, `reports/`, and `analysis/` with `--inspect` or `converted/` with `--cleanup`. A `.ash/ash_output` that is a link, or that a link inside the scanned directory leads to, is not taken as ASH's output, however the path to it is spelled, and a scan into an output directory git tracks as a link exits 3. The trivy-repo plugin still reads those directories, and ASH drops the findings it reports there, except in committed files. Any other directory is scanned, even one holding an earlier run's or another shard's results; ASH warns when a directory holds `ash_aggregated_results.json`, or both `ash-ignore-report.txt` and `ash-scan-set-files-list.txt`. Write shard output outside the scanned directory, or list it in `.gitignore`. CloudFormation templates that `cdk synth` writes (`*.template.json`) are scanned even when `.gitignore` excludes `cdk.out`, so cdk-nag and cfn-nag check them; the rest of the `cdk.out` directory stays excluded.  How do I run ASH in an offline/air-gapped environment?  Build an offline image with `ash --mode container --offline --offline-semgrep-rulesets p/ci --no-run`, push to your private registry, then use `ash --mode container --offline --no-build` in your air-gapped environment.  I am trying to scan a CDK application, but ASH does not show CDK Nag scan results -- why is that?  ASH uses CDK Nag underneath to apply NagPack rules to *CloudFormation templates* via the `CfnInclude` CDK construct. This is purely a mechanism to ingest a bare CloudFormation template and apply CDK NagPacks to it; doing this against a template emitted by another CDK application causes a collision in the `CfnInclude` construct due to the presence of the `BootstrapVersion` parameter on the template added by CDK. For CDK applications, we recommend integrating CDK Nag directly in your CDK code. ASH will still apply other CloudFormation scanners (cfn-nag, checkov) against templates synthesized via CDK, but the CDK Nag scanner will not scan those templates.

docs.title: Frequently asked questions
docs.text: Short answers, each with a link to the page that has the details. The config examples are keys to add to your ASH config file. ash config init writes one, .ashrc.yaml, in the current directory.

docs.title: Why does my first scan exit 1?
docs.text:
At least one scanner is MISSING: its tool is not installed, or ASH found the tool only inside the scanned directory, such as in the project's .venv, and did not run it (see Tools inside the scanned directory). A scan with a MISSING scanner is incomplete, and an incomplete scan exits 1 even when it also found something. Run ash dependencies install to install the tools it can install. A scanner with nothing to scan shows as SKIPPED whether or not its tool is installed, so npm-audit and cdk-nag need Node.js, and cfn-nag needs Ruby with a C compiler, only in a project they have something to scan in: CloudFormation templates for cdk-nag and cfn-nag, and a lockfile beside a package.json for npm-audit. To scan without a tool you cannot install, leave its scanner out with ash --exclude-scanners cdk-nag,npm-audit. See A scanner shows MISSING and Exit codes.

In a project without CloudFormation templates, cdk-nag shows as SKIPPED in this scan, with or without Node.js, so the exit code is detect-secrets' verdict alone:

ash --scanners cdk-nag,detect-secrets --no-progress

docs.title: How do I install ASH, and which version should I pin?
docs.text: Install from GitHub, with a git URL or with Homebrew from the repository's tap; Install ASH shows each method. ASH is not published on PyPI. The PyPI project named automated-security-helper is not published by this project, so do not install ASH by that name. Pin an exact release tag or a commit. The floating v3 tag moves to every new 3.x release, including releases with breaking changes. A pin fixes ASH's own code, not every dependency: uv, pipx, and pip resolve ASH's dependencies again when they install it. Homebrew installs the release its formula names, the latest one, with the dependency versions locked in that release's uv.lock.

docs.title: Is there a container image?
docs.text: ASH publishes no image. ash build-image builds one from a release tag, and ash --mode container builds one and runs the scan in it. ASH uses the first of finch, docker, nerdctl, and podman that it finds on your PATH, or the one you name with --oci-runner. The default image runs as a non-root user whose UID and GID you can set; --build-target ci builds the image that runs as root, which a job running as root needs. See Run ASH in a container.

docs.title: Which scanners run on my code?
docs.text: In local and container mode, every enabled scanner runs on every scan. A scanner that finds nothing of its kind to check, such as actionlint in a repository without GitHub Actions workflows, shows as SKIPPED, whether or not its tool is installed. Scanner coverage lists the languages and file types each scanner checks, and the scanners reference lists each scanner's options.

docs.title: Does ASH scan my CDK app?
docs.text:
It scans the CloudFormation templates the app synthesizes, not the CDK source. Run cdk synth before the scan, so that the templates exist under cdk.out. ASH scans the *.template.json files there even when a .gitignore excludes cdk.out, at the root of the scanned directory or inside your CDK app's directory, and the rest of cdk.out stays out of the scan. The same holds for an assembly that cdk synth -o writes to another directory. cdk-nag, cfn-nag, cfn-lint, and the other CloudFormation scanners then evaluate the templates. To check, look for a template in the list of files the scan read:

mkdir -p cdk.out
echo '{"Resources": {"Bucket": {"Type": "AWS::S3::Bucket"}}}' > cdk.out/App.template.json
echo cdk.out >> .gitignore
ash --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

grep cdk.out/App.template.json .ash/ash_output/ash-scan-set-files-list.txt

docs.title: A scanner hangs. What can I do?
docs.text: ASH stops a scanner's tool after its scan_timeout, 1800 seconds by default. Set a lower value under that scanner's options, scanners.<name>.options.scan_timeout, and see A scanner hangs for common causes.

docs.title: How do I suppress a finding?
docs.text:
Add a suppression with the finding's rule ID, its path, and your reason:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: B602
      path: src/build.py
      reason: The command is a constant string; no user input reaches it.

ash report shows each finding's rule ID. You can add expiration with a date in quotes, such as "2027-06-30"; from that date the suppression stops applying, and ash config lint reports it as expired. ASH also honors inline ash-ignore comments, and scanners honor their own, such as bandit's # nosec. See Suppress findings.

docs.title: How do I keep files or directories out of the results?
docs.text:
Add them to global_settings.ignore_paths, each with a reason:

global_settings:
  ignore_paths:
    - path: tests/fixtures/**
      reason: Test data with deliberate findings.

ASH passes the ignore paths to every scanner. Some scanners skip those files and others scan them, and either way ASH drops every finding located in an ignored path. ASH also reads .gitignore, so directories it excludes, such as .venv/ and node_modules/ in most projects, are not scanned. If they are not in .gitignore, add them to ignore_paths. See Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions.

docs.title: How do I scan files that a .gitignore excludes?
docs.text: Pass --no-honor-ignore-files, or set honor_ignore_files: false in a config file outside the scanned tree. A config file inside the repository being scanned cannot change this setting. See Ignore files and the scan set.

docs.title: How do I fail only on high-severity findings, or never fail on findings?
docs.text:
Set the threshold under global_settings, and fail_on_findings at the top level of the file, not under global_settings:

fail_on_findings: true
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: HIGH

With fail_on_findings: false, or --no-fail-on-findings on the command line, findings never fail the scan. An incomplete scan, or one with a vulnerability database or offline ruleset past its age bound, still exits 1. See Set the gate.

docs.title: Why do two scanners report the same problem?
docs.text: ASH runs scanners whose checks overlap and does not deduplicate their findings: semgrep and opengrep run the same ruleset, grype and trivy both check dependencies, and detect-secrets and gitleaks both look for secrets. Each finding carries its scanner's own rule ID, so a suppression for one does not cover the other. To keep one of a pair, turn the other off by setting scanners.opengrep.enabled to false in the config or by passing --exclude-scanners opengrep. See Choose scanners.

docs.title: Does ASH work on Windows?
docs.text: Local mode installs and runs on Windows, but semgrep and opengrep are off there and show as SKIPPED, and there is no scanner sandbox. If another program named ash comes first on your PATH (Git for Windows and MSYS2 ship a shell by that name), run ASH as ashv3, which is the same command. Container mode is not tested on Windows. See Install ASH.

docs.title: Which GitHub Actions permissions does ASH need?
docs.text: The job that calls the reusable workflow run-ash-security-scan.yml must grant contents: read, checks: write for its JUnit check, and pull-requests: write for its pull request comment. GitHub refuses to start a call that grants fewer. Uploading results to code scanning outside same-repository pull requests needs security-events: write, granted to a separate job that calls upload-ash-sarif.yml. See Run ASH in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Can ASH run offline or in an air-gapped network?
docs.text:
Yes. With --offline, ASH runs every scanner in its offline mode and installs nothing, except npm-audit, which does not run offline. Some scanners still make requests; only the scanner sandbox, or container mode with --offline, removes the network itself. The rules and vulnerability databases must be in place first; an image built with ash build-image --offline contains them. Each database has an age bound, from a day to a month, and by default a scan fails when one is past it (an image built with OFFLINE=YES only warns for trivy's database), so plan to rebuild offline images often. See Run ASH offline and Content databases.

npm, yarn, and pnpm audit a lockfile by asking the registry, so in an offline scan npm-audit is MISSING, and the scan exits 1, for a project with a lockfile beside a package.json. For a project without one it is SKIPPED. To scan such a project offline, add --exclude-scanners npm-audit:

echo '{"name": "demo", "version": "1.0.0"}' > package.json
echo '{"name": "demo", "version": "1.0.0", "lockfileVersion": 3, "packages": {}}' > package-lock.json
ash --offline --scanners npm-audit,detect-secrets --no-progress

docs.title: What does a scan send over the network?
docs.text: ASH itself sends no telemetry. The scanners download rules and vulnerability databases, and some send data to their own services: for example, semgrep sends usage metrics to Semgrep when it uses registry rules, and npm-audit sends your dependency tree to the npm registry. See what leaves the machine during a scan.

docs.title: Can I use ASH programmatically?
docs.text:
Yes. run_ash_scan runs a scan from Python:

from automated_security_helper.core.enums import RunMode
from automated_security_helper.interactions.run_ash_scan import run_ash_scan

results = run_ash_scan(
    source_dir="/path/to/code",
    output_dir="/path/to/output",
    mode=RunMode.local,
    # Return the results even when there are actionable findings
    fail_on_findings=False,
)
print(f"{results.metadata.summary_stats.actionable} actionable findings")

It returns the results only when the scan's exit code is 0. Otherwise it raises SystemExit with that code, as ash scan exits with it, which is why the example passes fail_on_findings=False. An incomplete scan still raises. A keyword that run_ash_scan does not take raises TypeError. See Python API.

docs.title: Connect an AI assistant
docs.text:
Use stdio for a local MCP client, or Streamable HTTP when your client needs an HTTP transport. Follow the editor and agent guidance to add ASH to an existing coding workflow.

The MCP tool reference explains each tool's inputs and outputs. For a running scan, poll its status before fetching results; review coverage as well as findings.

docs.title: Reporting destinations
docs.text:
Destination Guide Output GitHub or another SARIF consumer Report formats Code scanning annotations and portable finding data AWS Security Hub Security Hub reporter Centralized security findings Amazon S3 S3 reporter Stored scan artifacts Amazon CloudWatch Logs CloudWatch Logs reporter Scan logs in an existing operational workflow Amazon Bedrock Bedrock summary reporter Executive and technical summaries with traceable finding references A custom destination Build a reporter plugin A delivery format that fits your environment

Configure enabled reporters in your ASH configuration. AWS reporters need the permissions and regional settings described in their guides. A scan's exit status reflects its configured thresholds and execution state; a report's filters change only the view.

docs.title: Ask a question or report a bug
docs.text:
Questions, bug reports, and feature requests all go to GitHub issues. Search the open and closed issues first, then open a new issue with the bug report or feature request form.

For a bug, include:

  • the output of ash --version, and how you installed ASH
  • your operating system, and the mode you ran in (local, container, precommit, or nix)
  • the exact command, and the console output from its first line
  • what you expected to happen

ASH's reports can contain secret values that the scanners found, copied from your code, and the reports and the log show paths on your machine. Do not attach them to an issue. Paste only the lines that show the problem, with any secrets removed.

Troubleshoot covers common problems by symptom, and the FAQ has short answers to the questions people ask most.

docs.title: Report a security issue
docs.text:
If you find a security issue in ASH itself, do not report it in a public GitHub issue. Email aws-security@amazon.com, as SECURITY.md describes. Include a description of the issue and its impact, the steps to reproduce it, and the ASH versions affected.

SECURITY.md also says what is in scope. A false positive from a scanner is not a security issue: suppress it in your config, as Suppress findings shows. A bug in a scanner that ASH runs, such as semgrep or cfn-lint, belongs with that scanner's project.

Security fixes go to the 3.x releases. ASH 2.x is no longer supported.

docs.title: Content databases
docs.text: Some scanners compare your code against data they download: vulnerability advisories, or a set of rules. ASH calls that data a content database. A scan can only find what its databases know about, so after every scanner that reads one, ASH checks how old the database is and, by default, fails the scan when it is older than its bound.

docs.title: Which scanners use one
docs.text:
Database Read by Age bound Where the bound comes from Age read from grype-db grype 5 days (120 hours) grype's own default for db.max-allowed-built-age built in grype db status -o json trivy-db trivy, trivy-repo 24 hours trivy's own rule for its official database: current until the next scheduled update, 24 hours after it was built VulnerabilityDB.UpdatedAt in trivy version --format json semgrep-offline-rules semgrep, offline only 30 days ASH's choice the time in .ash-rules-fetched-at in the rules cache, else the oldest rules file's modification time opengrep-offline-rules opengrep, offline only 30 days ASH's choice the same

The bounds are fixed: no config key, variable, or flag changes them. Online, semgrep and opengrep download their ruleset at scan time, so there is no local copy to age. checkov, npm-audit, and syft are declared as having no content database: checkov's policies ship inside the checkov package ASH installs, npm-audit asks the npm registry at scan time and so does not run offline (Run ASH offline), and syft only catalogs packages. trivy's Java database is never downloaded (ASH tells trivy to skip it), and trivy's misconfiguration checks bundle is refreshed but not age-checked.

docs.title: Why a stale database fails the scan
docs.text:
A clean result from an old database is not evidence that the code is clean: every advisory or rule published since the database was built is missing from the scan. An offline scan makes this worse, because the tools themselves stop checking. ASH runs grype offline with grype's age validation turned off, and trivy with database updates skipped, so that an air-gapped host can scan at all. ASH's check after the scan is then the only limit on the database's age.

A database whose age cannot be read counts as stale, for example when the probe fails or the cache holds no database. A scanner that did not run at all (MISSING) has no database reading; it fails the scan as incomplete instead.

docs.title: What happens when a database is stale
docs.text:
With content_db_staleness: fail, the default, ASH keeps the scan's findings, logs an error that names the database, its age, and how to refresh it, adds an ASH-CONTENT-DB-STALE notification at level error to the SARIF, and exits 1. That happens whatever fail_on_findings says. A scanner that found nothing against the stale database is recorded ERROR, with the database named, because its clean result is no verdict; one that reported findings stays FAILED. The exit message reports the stale database once, with its refresh advice, rather than also listing the scanner as incomplete.

With content_db_staleness: warn, ASH logs a warning, adds the same notification at level warning, and lets the scan pass or fail on its findings. The reports carry the notification, so a reader can see the scan ran against an old database.

There are three ways to change the default:

  • content_db_staleness: warn for every database;
  • a content_db_staleness_overrides entry for one database, which needs an expiration date and a reason and stops applying at 00:00 UTC on that date;
  • --allow-stale-content-db or --no-allow-stale-content-db on the command line. Either one wins over the config file and clears every per-database override: the first sets warn, the second fail.

An image built with ash build-image --offline holds trivy-db to warn instead of fail by default, because trivy's 24-hour bound would otherwise fail every trivy scan in the image from a day after the build. A stale trivy-db then does not fail the scan, and the reports say the database was stale and that the offline image's default let the scan go on. grype-db and the offline rulesets still fail the scan. To hold trivy-db to content_db_staleness in the image too, set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false or pass --no-allow-stale-content-db; a content_db_staleness_overrides entry for trivy-db also takes precedence over this default. The default applies wherever ASH_OFFLINE_AT_BUILD_TIME is YES, which the image sets when it is built with OFFLINE=YES; a config can turn it off but not on.

Every reading, fresh or stale, is recorded in the results. A config file inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, such as a repository's own, cannot relax the check: a warn from it that differs from the operator's policy is replaced, and a policy: warn entry the operator did not set is dropped, with a warning. A fail from it is kept. A config an MCP client delivers may not change either setting under the default policy. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Where the databases are cached
docs.text:
ASH resolves one cache directory per tool and passes the same directory to the scan, the refresh, and the age check. It always names that directory to the tool (GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR for grype, trivy --cache-dir for trivy), so a db.cache-dir in a grype config is ignored with a warning, and a cache.dir in a trivy config is overridden.

Tool Linux macOS Windows grype $GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/grype/db, else ~/.cache/grype/db $GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/grype/db, else ~/Library/Caches/grype/db %GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR%, else %XDG_CACHE_HOME%\grype\db, else %LOCALAPPDATA%\cache\grype\db trivy $TRIVY_CACHE_DIR, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/trivy, else ~/.cache/trivy $TRIVY_CACHE_DIR, else ~/Library/Caches/trivy %TRIVY_CACHE_DIR%, else %LOCALAPPDATA%\trivy

trivy and trivy-repo run with trivy --cache-backend=memory, so a scan only reads trivy's cache directory. An offline scan can therefore use a cache it may only read, such as one shared between CI jobs or built into an image. An online scan needs the cache writable when trivy's database is due an update, because ASH updates it there before every online scan, sandboxed or not.

XDG_CACHE_HOME counts only when it is an absolute path. For trivy on Linux, a relative value sends the cache to $TMPDIR/trivy. The ASH container image sets GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR=/deps/.grype and TRIVY_CACHE_DIR=/deps/.trivy. The offline semgrep and opengrep rules are read from the directories SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR and OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR name; the image sets them to /deps/.semgrep and /deps/.opengrep.

docs.title: When ASH refreshes a database
docs.text:
ASH has no command that refreshes a database on its own. Refreshes happen inside online scans:

  • trivy and trivy-repo: before every online scan, ASH downloads trivy's database (and, when the scan includes misconfiguration checks, the checks bundle), once per scan, then tells trivy not to update during the scan.
  • grype: under the sandbox, ASH runs grype db update before the scan. Without the sandbox, grype updates its own database when it is older than the 120-hour bound, which ASH passes to it.

When ASH runs a refresh itself (trivy's before every online scan, grype's under the sandbox), it runs outside the scanner sandbox, with network, from a working directory outside the scanned tree, and with ASH's empty tool configuration. For trivy, a trivy.yaml that the operator names in the trivy or trivy-repo scanner's config_file option, outside the scanned tree, is used instead, so a database mirror set there applies. A refresh holds a lock in the cache directory, so two scanners, or on Linux and macOS two scans, do not run ASH's refresh at once, and it times out after 900 seconds. A failed refresh fails that scanner. For a repository you do not trust, scan in local mode with the sandbox on, as in Scan a repository you do not trust.

The age checks are protected the same way: each probe runs with ASH's empty tool configuration from outside the scanned tree, so a configuration file in the repository cannot point the probe at a different database from the one the scan read.

Offline, nothing is refreshed. The databases must already be in the cache: ash build-image --offline builds an image with current grype and trivy databases and the semgrep and opengrep rulesets (p/ci by default), in which every scan runs offline. On a host you can run grype db update and trivy image --download-db-only while online. Because each bound counts from when the database itself was built, an offline image reports trivy's database stale within a day of the image build, as a warning by default, and starts failing grype scans within five days, unless you rebuild it or relax the policy. Run ASH offline covers seeding the caches and choosing a rebuild cadence.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used across these docs, in alphabetical order. Each entry links to the page that explains it.

docs.title: Actionable finding
docs.text: An unsuppressed finding at or above the severity threshold that applies to its scanner. Actionable findings are what fail_on_findings counts: any actionable finding makes the scan exit 2. See Set the gate.

docs.title: Age bound
docs.text: The age past which ASH treats a content database as too old to trust: 120 hours for grype's database, 24 hours for trivy's, and 30 days for the offline rulesets. See Content databases.

docs.title: Aggregated results
docs.text: ash_aggregated_results.json, the file ASH writes at the root of the output directory. It holds the resolved configuration, with each value read from the environment recorded as its reference, a status row per scanner and converter, and the aggregated SARIF, and every reporter renders it. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Aggregated SARIF
docs.text: The single SARIF run that every scanner's results are merged into, written as reports/ash.sarif. Findings are appended, not deduplicated. See How ASH works.

docs.title: AWS plugins
docs.text: The ash_aws_plugins package, which ships with ASH and holds reporters that send results to AWS services. It loads only when the operator names it in a plugin module list; a repository config cannot. See AWS reporters.

docs.title: Client-supplied
docs.text: The mark ASH puts on a suppression or ignore path set by a config file an MCP client delivered, rather than by the operator. A client-supplied ignore path keeps the finding in the results as a suppressed finding instead of dropping it. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Community plugin
docs.text: A plugin package that ships with ASH but is not built in, such as the trivy-repo, snyk-code, and ferret-scan scanners. ash scan loads it only when a plugin module list names it; for the MCP server, see What a plugin can do. See Community plugins.

docs.title: Content database
docs.text: Data a scanner downloads and matches code against: grype's and trivy's vulnerability databases, and the rulesets semgrep and opengrep use offline. Each has an age bound, and by default a scan fails when one is older than its bound. See Content databases.

docs.title: Converter
docs.text: A plugin that runs in the convert phase and turns files scanners cannot read, such as archives and Jupyter notebooks, into files they can. Its output is scanned as the converted target. See How ASH works and the converter reference.

docs.title: Delivered tree
docs.text: Source code an MCP client sent to an ASH MCP server, as a git URL or a zip upload. The server keeps it under the MCP workspace root, and its config files belong to the MCP-client tier. See Run the MCP server.

docs.title: Event subscriber
docs.text: A plugin that runs code when a scan event happens, such as a phase starting or a scanner finishing. See Subscribe to scan events.

docs.title: Exit code
docs.text: The number ash scan returns: 0 for success, 1 for an incomplete or failed scan, 2 for actionable findings, 3 for a configuration it cannot use or an input it refuses before scanning, such as a linked output directory, 4 for a workspace error, and 5 for a usage error, such as an unknown option. See Exit codes.

docs.title: Finding
docs.text: One result a scanner reported, which is one result in the SARIF. Two scanners reporting the same problem produce two findings.

docs.title: Gate
docs.text: The rules that turn a scan's results into its exit code: fail_on_incomplete_scanners, content_db_staleness, fail_on_findings, and the severity thresholds. See Set the gate.

docs.title: Ignore path
docs.text: An entry in global_settings.ignore_paths. Findings located in matching files are dropped from the results. When it has an expiration date, it stops applying on that date, as a suppression does. See Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions.

docs.title: In-tree tool
docs.text: A program found inside the scanned directory, for example in an in-repo .venv/bin or node_modules/.bin. ASH does not run in-tree tools unless the operator passes --allow-in-tree-tools, sets ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS, or sets allow_in_tree_tools in the --cli-json-input document. ash mcp never runs them. See Manage scanner tools.

docs.title: Incomplete scan
docs.text: A scan in which a selected scanner is MISSING or ERROR, no scanner ran, or a converter could not convert all of its inputs. With the default fail_on_incomplete_scanners, an incomplete scan exits 1 whatever it found. See Set the gate.

docs.title: Inline suppression
docs.text: A comment in the source that suppresses a finding on its line: ASH's ash-ignore and ash-ignore-next-line, or a scanner's own syntax such as bandit's # nosec. See Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions.

docs.title: MCP client
docs.text: A program that uses the ASH MCP server, such as an AI coding agent or an IDE. Files it delivers to the server form the MCP-client trust tier. See Run the MCP server and Configuration trust model.

docs.title: MCP workspace root
docs.text: The directory where the ASH MCP server keeps each session's delivered source and config: ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/ash-mcp, else ~/.cache/ash-mcp. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: MISSING
docs.text: The status of a scanner that was selected but did not run, because its tool was not found or was found only inside the scanned directory, or because it cannot run offline, as npm-audit cannot. The reason is in the scanner's missing_reason. A MISSING scanner makes the scan incomplete. See Troubleshoot.

docs.title: Offline mode
docs.text: A scan with --offline or ASH_OFFLINE set: every scanner runs in its offline mode, except npm-audit, which does not run offline, and ASH downloads and installs nothing. Content databases must already be in the cache. See Run ASH offline.

docs.title: Operator
docs.text: The person or pipeline running ASH. The operator owns the command line, the environment, and config files outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, and is the only tier that may grant sandbox access or choose where ASH's AWS reporters send results. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Output directory
docs.text: The directory ASH writes its results, reports, and logs to: --output-dir, else .ash/ash_output inside the scanned directory. ASH leaves it out of every scan, apart from the files git tracks in it. See Output files and How ASH works.

docs.title: Phase
docs.text: One stage of a scan: convert, scan, or report, run in that order, plus the optional inspect phase. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Plugin module
docs.text: A Python module that ASH imports to register plugins, named in ash_plugin_modules, --config-overrides, --ash-plugin-modules, ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES, or the Python API's ash_plugin_modules argument. It runs inside ASH's own process, outside the scanner sandbox. See Plugins.

docs.title: Reporter
docs.text: A plugin that renders the aggregated results in one format and writes it to the reports/ directory. See the reporter reference.

docs.title: Repository config
docs.text: An ASH config file inside a git checkout or inside the scanned directory, such as the .ash/.ash.yaml ASH discovers in the repository, or a config kept in an ops repository of its own. It cannot grant sandbox access, load ASH's off-host plugin packages, or choose where ASH's AWS reporters send results. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Run mode
docs.text: Where a scan runs: local (the default), container, nix, or precommit, chosen with --mode. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Sandbox grant
docs.text: A setting that gives sandboxed scanners more than the default policy: sandbox.network_scanners, sandbox.extra_read_paths, sandbox.read_path_scanners, or sandbox.env_scanners. Only the operator may grant. See Scanner sandbox.

docs.title: Scanned directory
docs.text: The directory a scan runs over: --source-dir, the working directory, or a workspace's root. A config file inside it is a repository config, and for the tool files you name ASH also looks at the scanned tree around it.

docs.title: Scanned tree
docs.text: The outermost git checkout at or above the scanned directory, or the scanned directory itself when it is not in a checkout. ASH treats every file inside it as written by the repository being scanned, so a tool file you name there is refused for the scanners that do not allow one. For every restricted setting a config file makes, a config file inside any git checkout, the scanned one or a separate one such as an ops repository, is a repository config. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Scanner
docs.text: A plugin that runs a security tool against a target and returns its results as SARIF. See the scanner reference.

docs.title: Scanner exclusion
docs.text: A scanner's own option that keeps files away from it, such as bandit's excluded_paths or checkov's skip_path. The scanner never sees the files, so nothing about them reaches the results. See Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions.

docs.title: Scanner sandbox
docs.text: An operating-system confinement around the processes a scanner starts through ASH, with limited reads and writes, a filtered environment, and no network unless the scanner needs one; how strict it is depends on the backend. Off by default. See Scanner sandbox.

docs.title: Scanner status
docs.text: The result ASH records for each scanner and target. PASSED: it ran and found nothing actionable. FAILED: it ran and found actionable findings. ERROR: ASH tried to run it and it failed, or its tool could not start as asked. MISSING: it was selected but could not run. SKIPPED: it was not selected or was excluded, --python-only left it out, it does not support this platform, or it had nothing to scan. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Severity threshold
docs.text: The least severe level that counts as actionable: global_settings.severity_threshold, MEDIUM by default, or a scanner's own severity_threshold option, which replaces it for that scanner. See Set the gate.

docs.title: Shard
docs.text: One of several scans of the same repository that each run a share of the scanners, combined afterward with ash merge. See Scale to large repositories.

docs.title: Suppression
docs.text: An entry in global_settings.suppressions, or an ash-ignore comment, that keeps a finding in the results but marks it suppressed, with a reason. Suppressed findings do not count toward the gate. See Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions.

docs.title: Target
docs.text: What a scanner scans: source, the scanned directory, or converted, the files the converters produced. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Trust tier
docs.text: The owner ASH assigns to a piece of configuration: operator, repository, or MCP client. The tier decides which settings the configuration may make. See Configuration trust model.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text: A set of projects scanned together in one run, defined by a VS Code .code-workspace file, from the CLI or over MCP. See Scale to large repositories.

docs.title: How ASH works
docs.text: ASH runs a set of third-party security scanners over one directory, collects what they report into one results model, writes that model out in several report formats, and returns one exit code. This page explains each of those steps and the rules that connect them.

docs.title: Phases
docs.text:
A scan runs up to three phases, always in this order: convert, scan, and report. --phases runs a subset of them, and ash report renders reports again from an existing results file without scanning.

flowchart LR
    src[Source directory] --> convert[Convert phase<br/>archive, jupyter]
    convert --> conv[converted/ target]
    src --> scan
    conv --> scan[Scan phase<br/>scanners in parallel]
    scan --> sarif[Per-scanner SARIF<br/>paths, severity, suppressions]
    sarif --> merged[Aggregated results<br/>one SARIF run]
    merged --> report[Report phase<br/>final suppression pass, reporters]
    report --> out[reports/ash.*]
    report --> code[Exit code]

In the convert phase, converters turn files that scanners cannot read into files they can. The archive converter extracts the scannable members of zip and tar archives (.zip, .tar, and .gz), and the jupyter converter turns notebooks into scripts with nbconvert. Their output goes to converted/ in the output directory and becomes a second scan target, converted, next to the source target. A converter that crashes, or that cannot convert one of its inputs, makes the scan incomplete.

In the scan phase, each selected scanner runs its tool against each target and produces SARIF. ASH rewrites the paths in that SARIF relative to the source directory, maps each result to a severity, applies suppressions and ignore paths, and merges the result into the aggregated SARIF.

In the report phase, ASH applies suppressions once more to the merged SARIF, recomputes the counts, and runs every enabled reporter. Each reporter writes its file under reports/, named ash.<extension>. A reporter that fails logs an error and writes nothing; it does not change the exit code.

Where the scan runs is a separate choice, the run mode. local (the default) runs the scanners installed on the host. container builds an image and runs the same scan inside it. nix runs it inside nix develop, which supplies pinned scanner binaries, and always scans offline. precommit is a local scan of a fixed set of fast scanners (bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag, and npm-audit, plus any you name with --scanners) with simplified output. It scans the whole source directory, not only the staged files, and in workspace mode it changes only the output. See Run ASH in a container and Run ASH with pre-commit.

docs.title: How scanners are selected
docs.text:
ASH ships 16 built-in scanners, all enabled by default except semgrep and opengrep on Windows. For each scanner it knows about, ASH asks these questions in order and records the first answer that stops the scanner:

  1. Is it enabled? scanners.<name>.enabled: false in the config turns a scanner off. --scanners cannot turn it back on; ash scan --config-overrides scanners.<name>.enabled=true can.
  2. Was it selected? --scanners is an allowlist and --exclude-scanners removes names from it. A scanner that is not selected is recorded SKIPPED.
  3. Does it need only Python, when --python-only is set? A scanner that runs a tool of its own is recorded SKIPPED.
  4. Does it support this platform? A scanner that declares the operating system unsupported (semgrep on Windows) is recorded SKIPPED.
  5. Are its dependencies there? A scanner whose tool cannot be found, or is found only inside the scanned directory, is recorded MISSING. A scanner that the scan has nothing for is recorded SKIPPED instead, for example cdk-nag and cfn-nag with no CloudFormation template, or npm-audit with no lockfile beside a package.json.

ASH asks the first four before it looks for the scanner's tool, so a scanner they leave out is SKIPPED whether or not its tool is installed.

Scanners outside the built-in set, such as the community scanners, are considered only when their plugin module is loaded; for the MCP server, see What a plugin can do. The scanner reference lists every scanner, its tool, and its defaults; Choose scanners covers turning them on and off.

docs.title: How scanners run
docs.text:
With the default --strategy parallel, ASH runs scanners in a thread pool of min(32, CPUs + 4) workers. Each worker runs one scanner against the source target and then against the converted target when there is one. --strategy sequential runs them one at a time.

A scanner receives a directory, not a file list. Most scanners walk that directory themselves. ASH passes the configured ignore paths to every scanner. Some scanners use them to skip files, and ASH applies them again to the results. Each scanner's tool runs as a subprocess. When the sandbox is on, the processes a scanner starts through ASH run inside it; ASH's own process does not.

ASH leaves its own output out of every scan, whether or not .gitignore lists it: the output directory of the scan in progress, and .ash/ash_output under the scanned directory and under the directory ASH runs from. A .ash/ash_output that is a link, or that a link inside the scanned directory leads to, is not taken as ASH's output. In a git checkout, the files git tracks in those directories are scanned like any other file, in the scan's own output directory too, and ASH logs a warning that its output directory holds committed files. Outside git, ASH leaves those directories out whole. ASH tells each scanner that can skip a directory to skip the ones that hold no committed file, and drops what a scanner reports in ASH's own files there, other than the converted files, even with --ignore-suppressions. Any other directory is scanned, even one that holds an earlier run's or another shard's results. CloudFormation templates that cdk synth writes (*.template.json) are scanned even when the root .gitignore lists cdk.out, so cdk-nag and cfn-nag check them; the rest of the cloud assembly stays out.

docs.title: The results model
docs.text:
The engine writes everything a scan produced to ash_aggregated_results.json at the root of the output directory. It holds:

  • the resolved configuration the scan used, with each value a config file read from the environment recorded as the reference the file wrote (Read values from the environment);
  • one row per scanner and target, with a status (PASSED, FAILED, ERROR, MISSING, or SKIPPED) and counts by severity, plus the reason a MISSING scanner did not run (missing_reason) or a SKIPPED one was left out (skipped_reason);
  • one row per converter, with the inputs it could not convert;
  • the aggregated SARIF;
  • an SBOM in CycloneDX form when an SBOM scanner ran.

Each scanner's own output is also kept under scanners/<name>/<target>/. Every reporter renders this same model. The scan's own reports, such as ash.html, are built with the values a config read from the environment, where the file records the references. The layout of the output directory is in Output files.

The aggregated SARIF has a single run. Each scanner's results are appended to it, and each scanner's tool description and rules are added to tool.extensions. Every result carries scanner_name in its properties, so you can tell which scanner reported it. A result's severity comes from the scanner's own severity when it reports one, and otherwise from the SARIF level: error counts as critical, warning as medium, note as low, and none as info. A result with no level is read as warning, SARIF's own default. Every report and the gate use the same mapping.

docs.title: Findings are merged, not deduplicated
docs.text:
ASH does not deduplicate findings, within a scan or across shards. When two scanners report the same problem, the results contain two findings, each with its own scanner name and rule ID. The default scanner set overlaps in several places:

  • semgrep and opengrep both run the p/ci ruleset;
  • grype and trivy both match dependency manifests against vulnerability advisories;
  • detect-secrets and gitleaks both look for secrets;
  • several scanners evaluate CloudFormation templates.

This has three consequences. Finding counts are counts of scanner results, not of distinct problems. A suppression that names a rule_id matches the rule IDs of whichever scanner uses that ID, so the same problem reported by another scanner under another ID stays unsuppressed; a suppression without rule_id covers every rule in its path. And the gate counts every unsuppressed duplicate. If two scanners overlap more than you want, turn one of them off; see Choose scanners. Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions explains how suppressions match.

Sharding splits a scan by scanner, not by file, so ash merge of the shards does not count any finding twice. See Scale to large repositories.

docs.title: Where the exit code comes from
docs.text: ASH decides the exit code after the report phase, from the scanner rows and the unsuppressed findings in the aggregated SARIF. It checks the conditions in a fixed order and stops at the first that holds, so an incomplete scan (exit 1) wins over findings (exit 2), and a stale content database fails the scan even with fail_on_findings off. An invalid configuration stops the scan before it starts (exit 3), exit 4 is a workspace error, and a usage error, such as an unknown option or an invalid --min-severity, exits 5 before anything runs. Exit codes lists the order, and Set the gate shows how to choose what fails a build.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text: Scanners, reporters, and converters are all plugins, and so are event subscribers, which run code on scan events such as a phase starting or a scanner finishing. The built-in plugins live in one package that every scan loads. Other plugin packages, including the community scanners and the AWS reporters that ship with ASH, load in ash scan only when a plugin module list names them: ash_plugin_modules in the config, --config-overrides, --ash-plugin-modules, ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES, or the Python API's ash_plugin_modules argument. For the MCP server, see What a plugin can do. A plugin module is imported into ASH's own process and runs with ASH's access, outside the scanner sandbox; only the subprocesses a scanner starts through ASH are sandboxed. Which config files may name which modules is part of the trust model. Plugins explains the plugin model and how to write one.

docs.title: Scanner sandbox
docs.text: Every scanner reads files the scanned repository wrote, and a scanner is a large program with its own parsers and plugins. The scanner sandbox runs each scanner's processes under an operating-system confinement, so that a repository that makes a scanner misbehave reaches less of the host. The sandbox is off by default. To turn it on and set it up on each platform, see Enable the scanner sandbox.

docs.title: What it wraps
docs.text:
When the sandbox mode is anything other than off, ASH wraps every process a scanner starts through ASH's process helpers while that scanner runs. That includes the probes ASH runs to check each scanner's tool, and the detect-secrets and cdk-nag scans, which ASH runs in child processes so that the sandbox can wrap them.

It does not wrap:

  • ASH's own process: configuration loading, the converters' own code, parsing of scanner output, the reporters, and the Python code of every plugin module. A tool a converter starts (nbconvert for notebooks) is not ASH's own process: it is held to the sandbox like a scanner's tool;
  • git, which ASH runs to list changed files;
  • the content database refresh that ASH runs itself before an online scan, outside the sandbox and with network, from a working directory outside the scanned tree and with an empty tool configuration (see Content databases);
  • any process a third-party plugin starts without ASH's helpers.

ASH refuses shell commands under the sandbox instead of wrapping them, and a sandboxed scan does not install missing scanner tools. Install them first with ash dependencies install, which also installs the notebook converter's nbconvert.

docs.title: What it enforces
docs.text:
The policy is the same for every backend:

  • Reads are granted for the system directories (/usr, /etc, /opt, and the like), the directories on PATH, ASH's own installation, uv's tool, interpreter, and cache directories, the scanner tool's own installation, the paths the scanner declares, sandbox.extra_read_paths, and the source, output, target, and working directories. Your home directory and /tmp are hidden, apart from the tool directories the policy grants. bwrap and Landlock give the scanner a private home and private temporary directories, and firejail a private home and /tmp. Under sandbox-exec the scanner gets a private temporary directory, and HOME points at your home, which it cannot read. On firejail and sandbox-exec, /var/tmp stays readable. How much else stays readable depends on the backend (table below).
  • With bwrap, the only host directory a scanner can write to is its own results directory. Landlock isolates less (see the table); use it only where bwrap cannot run. Cache directories a scanner declares are available, but writes to them never reach the host.
  • The environment is reduced to an allowlist (PATH, TZ, locale, terminal, and color settings, certificate bundle paths, VIRTUAL_ENV, JAVA_HOME, GEM_HOME, GEM_PATH, SYSTEMROOT, and names starting with ASH_, UV_, PYTHON, or LC_) plus the prefixes each scanner declares. Any name containing TOKEN, PASSWORD, SECRET, CREDENTIAL, AUTH, API_KEY, SESSION, or a similar marker is dropped unless the scanner names it exactly. Variables under the allowed prefixes reach every sandboxed scanner, so do not put credentials in their values; use a credential helper, or a variable whose name marks it as a credential. Proxy settings are passed only to scanners that have a network.
  • A scanner gets a network only if it needs one (next section). On Linux, a seccomp filter also refuses Unix-domain sockets on every backend.
  • After each sandboxed process, and again after the scanner finishes, ASH removes symbolic links and special files the scanner left in its results directory.

How each backend implements that policy differs, and so does what it can hold:

Backend Platform Reads outside the granted paths Network when none is granted Running programs from the scanned tree Notes bwrap Linux Not visible Separate network namespace Allowed The strictest Linux backend. Needs unprivileged user namespaces. Cache writes go to a throwaway overlay where bwrap and the kernel support one. firejail Linux Everything outside the home and temporary directories stays readable firejail --net=none Allowed Hides the Docker, Podman, and containerd sockets and the SSH agent. Refuses to run inside a container that has its own PID namespace. landlock Linux Denied seccomp refuses every socket Allowed Needs Landlock ABI 3 (Linux 6.2) or later; on an older kernel it counts as unavailable. No namespaces: the scanner sees the host's processes and their command lines, and shares the host's /dev/shm. Below Landlock ABI 6, signals to processes outside the sandbox are not restricted. sandbox-exec macOS Everything outside the home and temporary directories stays readable Denied Denied in the scanned tree, the writable directories, and the caches The only backend that restricts which programs run.

auto tries bwrap, then firejail, then landlock on Linux, and sandbox-exec on macOS, and uses the first one whose probe can start a real sandbox. Windows has no backend; run ASH under WSL2 with bwrap, or use container mode. The Linux socket filter exists only for x86_64 and aarch64, so on other Linux architectures every Linux backend fails its probe.

No backend limits CPU, memory, disk use, or the number of processes. The scan timeout is the only bound on a runaway scanner.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
Under the sandbox, a scanner has a network only when it declares that it needs one, or when sandbox.network_scanners names it. These scanners declare a need: semgrep and opengrep (registry rules), grype, trivy, and trivy-repo (vulnerability data), npm-audit (the registry's audit endpoint), and snyk-code (Snyk's service). detect-secrets needs a network only when its verification filter is on, and gets one only when sandbox.network_scanners names it. Every other scanner runs with no network. --offline removes the network from every scanner, whatever the grants say.

When sandbox.network_scanners is set, the list replaces the declarations: a scanner it names gets a network on every online scan, and a scanner it does not name gets none. Naming detect-secrets therefore gives it a network whether or not its verification filter is on.

A scanner that has a network shares the host's network. There is no egress filter: it can reach any address the host can reach, including services on localhost and on the local network, and it can send anything it can read.

docs.title: Grants, and who may make them
docs.text:
Four settings grant a sandboxed scanner more than the policy above: sandbox.network_scanners, sandbox.extra_read_paths, sandbox.read_path_scanners, and sandbox.env_scanners. Give a scanner more access says what each one grants.

Only the operator may grant. A grant counts when it comes from --config-overrides; from a config file outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory, named with --config or ASH_CONFIG; in workspace mode, from the --config file given to the workspace scan, under the same rule with the workspace root as the scanned directory; or from the MCP server's own configuration, under the same rule. When such a file extends a base that cannot grant, only the grants it writes in its own sandbox section count, not what it inherits from any base or changes with patch. --sandbox sets the mode and grants nothing.

A config file inside any git checkout, the scanned one or a separate one such as an ops or dotfiles repository, or inside the scanned directory, cannot grant, whether it is the file you name or a base it extends. Nor can, under ash mcp, one an MCP client delivered. ASH drops the grants of a file that cannot grant and logs a warning that names the file and the settings and says how to grant instead. Its network_scanners list still counts as a limit, so a repository can take the network away from its own scan but cannot add one. Its sandbox.mode applies only when no operator source turns the sandbox on; it cannot turn off, or change, a mode you set. Under the MCP server's default policy, a delivered file whose own sandbox section gives a scanner a network or an extra_read_paths entry the server's settings do not, or changes a sandbox mode other than off that the server sets, is refused instead (What a delivered config cannot set); its other grants are dropped the same way. Configuration trust model explains how ASH decides where a config file belongs.

docs.title: What fails closed
docs.text:
A scanner that cannot be sandboxed the way the configuration asks is never run unsandboxed. Its tool cannot start as asked, so each scan is recorded ERROR with the start-failure code 127 as the scanner's exit_code in ash_aggregated_results.json, and the default fail_on_incomplete_scanners makes the scan exit 1; 127 is the scanner's recorded code, not the exit status. The reason is in the scan output and ash.log, as a line such as detect-secrets could not start its tool on source: sandbox-exec is not available: sandbox-exec is not available on Linux. That covers:

  • an explicit backend that is not installed or cannot start a sandbox on this host;
  • auto when no backend works, with a reason that lists why each one failed;
  • a Linux architecture for which bwrap cannot apply the Unix-socket filter;
  • turning the sandbox on at all on Windows;
  • a scanner that the config file names under a different name than its own, because grants follow a scanner's own name.

A converter's tool is held to the same rule. When the sandbox cannot be provided, nbconvert does not run: each notebook is listed in the converter's refused_inputs with the reason, the row's failure reads jupyter could not start its tool: <reason>, and its dependencies_satisfied stays true, since nothing was found missing. A tree with no notebooks loses nothing.

ASH also refuses, rather than runs unsandboxed, a shell command that a scanner tries to start, and a scanner whose results directory is reached through a symbolic link. ASH looks up the sandbox programs themselves (bwrap, firejail) the way it looks up scanner tools: never through the working directory or from inside the scanned tree, unless you allow in-tree tools. Which backend a scan used is written to ash.log; the results record only the requested mode, in ash_config.sandbox.mode.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not filter the traffic of a scanner that has a network.
  • It does not confine ASH's own process, the converters' own code, the reporters, plugin code, or the content database refresh. The tools a converter starts are confined like a scanner's.
  • On firejail and sandbox-exec, files outside your home and temporary directories stay readable.
  • On the Linux backends, a scanner can run programs from the scanned tree inside its sandbox.
  • It shares the host's kernel and sets no resource limits.
  • It does not apply in container mode. ash scan --mode container turns the sandbox off for the scan inside the container, and logs a warning when the sandbox was asked for; the container is the boundary there. See Run ASH in a container.
  • It does not make a scanner's results trustworthy. A scanner still reads every file in the source tree, and a hostile file can still change what it reports.

One setting to plan for: an offline semgrep or opengrep scan reads its rules from the directory SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR or OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR names, and under the sandbox it can read only directories the sandbox mounts. Keep the rules cache under a system directory such as /opt, or add it to sandbox.extra_read_paths.

docs.title: Scanning untrusted code
docs.text: Sometimes the repository you scan is not one you trust: a pull request from a fork, a third-party dependency you are vetting, or code an agent fetched. That repository controls every file ASH and the scanners read. It can ship a config file for ASH to discover, configuration files the scanners pick up by name, programs placed where a tool lookup might find them, symbolic links, and files written to make a parser misbehave. This page lists the defenses ASH has, which of them are on by default, and what leaves your machine during a scan.

docs.title: Defenses, and which are on by default
docs.text:
Defense What it does On by default Configuration trust tiers A config file inside any git checkout, an operations or dotfiles repository included, or inside the scanned directory cannot grant sandbox access, load ASH's plugin packages that send data off the host, or choose where the AWS reporters send findings. Scanner options and scanner config files in the tree can still change what a scanner reports; see what the trust model does not protect. Yes In-tree tool refusal ASH does not start a scanner, or a tool it looks up for a scan such as git, node, or a sandbox program, when it finds that program only inside the scanned directory (an in-repo .venv/bin, node_modules/.bin) or through the working directory. A scanner whose tool exists only there is MISSING. Yes. --allow-in-tree-tools or ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS turns it off; ash mcp never does. Output directory link refusal ASH stops with exit 3, before writing anything, when the output directory, or one of the directories or fixed-name files ASH clears or writes in it, is a symbolic link; a report file that is a link stops the run with exit 1 before any reporter writes. Keep the output directory outside the repository. Yes Archive member checks The archive converter does not read an archive that is a link, and does not extract members that are links or special files, have absolute names or .. in them, or would land outside its output. The converters do not read an input file that is a link or a special file. Yes Scanner sandbox Runs each scanner's processes with limited reads and writes, a filtered environment, and no network unless the scanner needs one. How strict it is depends on the backend. No. Turn it on with --sandbox or sandbox.mode. Container mode Runs the whole scan inside a container that sees only the source and output directories. No. ash scan --mode container. Offline mode ASH runs every scanner in its offline mode and installs nothing. Some scanners still make requests; the network itself is removed only under the sandbox or in container mode. No. --offline or ASH_OFFLINE.

The content database refreshes that ASH runs itself, and its database age checks, run from a working directory outside the scanned tree with ASH's own empty tool configuration; see Content databases.

Three points about these defaults. The sandbox is not on unless you turn it on, so a default local scan runs every scanner with your environment, your home directory, and your network. In a scan of one directory, the repository's own config still controls the verdict on the CLI unless you pass your own with --config, and the repository's inline suppression comments apply either way (see the trust model's list of what it does not protect). And the tiers, the tool refusal, and the link checks decide what ASH does with the repository's files; they do not stop a file in the repository from making a scanner misbehave, which is what the sandbox and container mode are for.

docs.title: What leaves the machine during a scan
docs.text:
ASH itself sends no telemetry. The scanners it runs, and some of its own steps, use the network when the scan is online. --offline turns most of this off; only the sandbox, or container mode with --offline, removes the network itself.

Source What it sends or fetches How to stop it Scanner installs A missing Python tool (bandit, checkov, semgrep, and nbconvert for the notebook converter) is installed at scan time with uv tool install, from PyPI unless uv is configured otherwise. Online, uv may also ask the package index about a tool's version range when it runs one that is installed. ash dependencies install checks the SHA-256 digest of each binary tool it downloads from a GitHub release. The Python tools come from the package index uv is configured with, PyPI by default, within each tool's version range, and cfn-nag's gem is the version ASH pins, from the gem sources Ruby is configured with; ASH checks no digest for either. Install the tools before the scan with ash dependencies install, which also installs nbconvert. Offline scans install nothing. Content databases grype and trivy download their vulnerability databases, and trivy downloads its checks bundle for scans that include misconfiguration checks. --offline, with the databases already in the cache. See Content databases. semgrep, opengrep Download the configured registry ruleset (p/ci by default). semgrep is run with semgrep --metrics auto, which sends usage metrics to Semgrep when the rules come from its registry; see Semgrep's metrics documentation. scanners.semgrep.options.metrics: "off", a local ruleset, or --offline. checkov Uses Prisma Cloud's API to add guideline links to its results, as checkov's README describes. ASH passes checkov --skip-download, which turns that off, only in offline mode. --offline. detect-secrets When its settings include detect-secrets' verification filter, sends each candidate secret to the service that issued it, to check whether it is live. A repository's .secrets.baseline can turn this on. Turn the sandbox on and leave detect-secrets out of sandbox.network_scanners. npm-audit Sends the dependency tree of each lockfile to the npm registry's audit endpoint. --offline (npm-audit then audits nothing and reports no findings). grype, syft May check for a newer release of themselves. ASH turns these checks off in offline mode. --offline. trivy Checks for a newer trivy release; ASH passes trivy --disable-telemetry. The sandbox with --offline, or container mode with --offline. zizmor Calls the GitHub API for its online audits, with the token in GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, only when the operator sets online_audits. Under the sandbox it gets a network only when sandbox.network_scanners names zizmor, and never those token variables. Leave online_audits off. snyk-code Uploads the scanned source to Snyk with the Snyk CLI's credentials. It runs only when ash_snyk_plugins is loaded. Do not load it, and do not install or authenticate the Snyk CLI on a host that runs ASH unless every scan there may send source to Snyk. AWS reporters Send results to AWS services, only when the operator loads ash_aws_plugins. AWS reporters lists what each one sends. Do not load them. Container mode Building the image downloads the base image and every tool, and clones ASH from GitHub unless you build from a local checkout. Build the image ahead of time with ash build-image --no-run, run from outside any repository, and scan with ash scan --mode container --no-build.

Under the sandbox, the scanners that keep a network (semgrep, opengrep, grype, trivy, trivy-repo, npm-audit, and snyk-code) share the host's network with no egress filter. If a file in the repository makes one of them misbehave, that scanner can send anything it can read to any address the host can reach. --offline, or a sandbox.network_scanners list that leaves a scanner out, is the only way to remove that.

docs.title: Putting the defenses together
docs.text:
For a hostile repository the defenses work together. Your own config, kept outside every git checkout and passed with --config in a scan of one directory, keeps the gate, the enabled scanners, and the grants yours, though the repository's inline suppression comments still apply. The sandbox limits what a scanner can reach if a file makes it misbehave, and --offline or a short sandbox.network_scanners list takes its network away. An output directory outside the repository keeps the repository from shaping where ASH writes. Plugin modules are the exception: they run in ASH's own process, so name only modules you trust. Scan a repository you do not trust has the setup step by step.

The default fail_on_incomplete_scanners matters here. If a backend cannot sandbox a scanner, its scans are ERROR with the start-failure code 127 and its tool never runs unsandboxed; a scanner whose tool exists only inside the repository is MISSING. Either way the scan exits 1, rather than passing on fewer scanners than you asked for. The sandbox also needs an absolute HOME, because it gives each scanner the home directory as HOME and grants paths under it. With an empty or relative HOME, a scanner it would run is not run and is ERROR, with HOME is not an absolute path in its error.

On Windows there is no sandbox backend. Run ASH under WSL2 with --sandbox bwrap, or use container mode with --offline, which gives the container no network. Keep the source and the output in separate directory trees, such as C:\work\src\pr-1234 and C:\work\ash-output\pr-1234. Container mode mounts your --config file read-only for the scan inside the container (The config file). The sandbox is off inside the container, so every scanner in it shares the container's access.

When an AI agent or another MCP client delivers the code to an ASH MCP server, the delivered tree's config files are MCP-client files and get the stricter rules in the trust model. Run the MCP server describes how to run that server.

docs.title: Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions
docs.text: ASH has three ways to keep a finding from failing a scan, and they differ in what they leave behind. A suppression keeps the finding in the results and marks it suppressed, with your reason. An ignore path removes the finding from the results. A scanner's own exclusion keeps the scanner from looking at the file, so there is no finding at all. This page explains how each one works and how it shows up in the gate and the reports. To write them, see Suppress findings.

docs.title: How they differ
docs.text:
Suppression Ignore path Scanner exclusion Set in global_settings.suppressions, or an inline ash-ignore comment global_settings.ignore_paths the scanner's options, such as bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, semgrep and opengrep exclude, and syft exclude Matches a path, optionally narrowed by rule ID, line range, package, or symbol a path what the scanner's tool matches Is the file scanned? Yes Passed to every scanner; some skip the files, others scan them No Is the finding in the results? Yes, marked suppressed with the reason No No, it never existed Counts toward the gate? No No No Expiration Enforced Enforced Enforced for bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, and syft exclude; none for the others

A scanner's own inline suppression comment works one of two ways, depending on the tool. bandit (# nosec) and detect-secrets (# pragma: allowlist secret) drop the finding, so ASH never sees it, as with a scanner exclusion. semgrep and opengrep (# nosemgrep) and checkov (checkov:skip=<check>:<reason>) report the finding with a SARIF suppression, and ASH keeps it in the results as a suppressed finding with the tool's justification, which can be empty. Either way the finding does not count toward the gate. For other scanners, see the tool's own documentation.

docs.title: How a suppression matches
docs.text:
Paths are matched relative to the scanned directory and case-sensitively, so tests/** does not match Tests/, and a path that starts with ./ matches nothing. In a pattern without **, * also matches across directory separators, so src/*.py matches src/sub/deep/app.py. ** matches any depth. A trailing slash is literal, unlike in an ignore path, so tests/ matches no finding, and neither does a bare directory name such as tests; tests/**/* matches the files below the directory.

A suppression with a rule_id matches only findings with that rule ID. The rule ID is a case-insensitive pattern with no scanner prefix, so it matches whichever scanner reports that ID. A suppression without rule_id matches every rule in its path. With line_start and line_end, a finding matches when its lines overlap the range; line_start alone runs to the end of the file, and a finding with no line never matches a line-scoped suppression. A finding gets only the first suppression that matches it.

Because ASH does not deduplicate findings, the same problem reported by two scanners is two findings with two rule IDs. A suppression written for one scanner's rule ID leaves the other one in place. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Order of application
docs.text:
ASH applies these rules to each scanner's SARIF as it arrives, and again to the merged SARIF before the reporters run:

  1. Findings located in ASH's own output directory are dropped, except in its converted/ work directory and in files git tracks there. The rest are ASH's reports, not part of the code.
  2. Ignore paths are checked against every location of a finding. A match drops the finding. ASH adds no ignore paths of its own here, so a dependency finding located in node_modules/ stays unless you ignore that path. bandit and checkov skip .venv/, venv/, and node_modules/ themselves.
  3. Configured suppressions are checked against the finding's first location.
  4. Inline ash-ignore comments are checked: ash-ignore on the finding's line, or ash-ignore-next-line on the line above it.
  5. An npm-audit finding about a package that is only reachable through other findings is suppressed when every one of those findings is suppressed.

docs.title: Expiration
docs.text:
A suppression's expiration is a date. On that date, by the host's local clock, the suppression stops matching, and the finding counts toward the gate again on the next scan. The config stays valid: the scan fails on the finding, and a warning at the start of the scan lists every suppression and ignore path that has expired. ASH also logs a warning at the start of a scan for the entries that expire within the next 30 days, and ash config lint reports suppressions and ignore paths that have already expired.

An ignore path's expiration works the same way: on that date it stops applying, and the findings it dropped come back on the next scan. The entries of bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, and syft exclude expire the same way, and stop excluding their files. An expired entry stays in the config file and in the results; only its effect stops.

Results written by another ASH version can hold an entry that this version refuses in a config file, such as one with an unknown key or a date in another format. ash report, ash merge, and the other commands that read results still load them, with a warning that names the problem, and never apply that entry.

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
Only unsuppressed findings at or above the severity threshold count toward fail_on_findings. Suppressed findings, findings under an ignore path, and findings a scanner never reported do not count, whatever their severity. Set the gate covers thresholds.

--ignore-suppressions turns ASH's whole suppression step off. Configured suppressions, ignore paths, and inline ash-ignore comments stop applying, so their findings come back and count toward the gate. So do client-supplied entries, scanner exclusions from an MCP client's config included: ASH applies those itself, so the findings they would have marked are ordinary findings. For ignore paths this goes back to the files: ASH gives the scanners and converters no ignore paths, so every scanner reads the files under one and the converters convert the archives and notebooks there. It does not touch what the scanners did themselves: files a scanner skipped through its own exclusion options, and findings its inline comments hid, stay unreported, and findings a scanner reported as suppressed stay suppressed. The repository's .gitignore and .ignore files still remove files from the set ASH hands several scanners (Coverage), and findings in ASH's own output directory stay out of the results. In container mode the flag reaches the scan inside the container and works there as in a local scan.

docs.title: In the reports
docs.text:
Output A suppressed finding ash.sarif and ash_aggregated_results.json Kept, with a suppressions entry: kind: inSource and a justification that starts with (ASH) for a configured suppression or (ASH inline) for an ash-ignore comment.
