A suppression the scanner reported keeps the scanner's own justification. ash.flat.json, ash.csv Kept, with is_suppressed and the justification ash.html Listed in a separate table of suppressed findings, with the justification ash.junit.xml A <skipped type="suppression"> test case with the justification ash.ocsf.json Kept, with a suppressed status ash.gl-sast-report.json Kept at severity Info, unless exclude_suppressed is set ash.ghas.sarif Left out, unless exclude_suppressed is turned off ash.summary.md, ash.summary.txt Counted in the suppressed column only

Findings under an ignore path appear in none of these. The unused-suppressions reporter writes ash.unused-suppressions.json and .md, which list the configured suppressions that matched no finding.

docs.title: Client-supplied entries
docs.text:
When a scan's config includes a file an MCP client delivered, each suppression and ignore path that file sets is marked client_supplied, unless it matches an entry from an operator source, and so are scanner exclusions from that file. A marked ignore path or exclusion does not keep files from being scanned: the files are scanned, and each finding it covers is kept as a suppressed finding with a (ASH, client-supplied config) justification and clientSupplied: true in the SARIF. Marked findings do not count toward the gate, like other suppressed findings. Configuration trust model explains when entries are marked and where the mark appears.

ASH marks entries only in configs an MCP client delivered. In a CLI scan, a repository's own suppressions, ignore paths, and inline suppressions apply the same way yours do, which matters when the repository is not yours; see Scanning untrusted code.

docs.title: Configuration trust model
docs.text: ASH reads its configuration from places with different owners. You, the person or pipeline running ASH, control the command line, the environment, and the files outside the repository. The repository being scanned controls every file inside it, including the .ash/.ash.yaml that ASH discovers without being asked. A client of the ASH MCP server controls the files it delivers to the server. ASH sorts configuration into three tiers by owner, and limits what the repository and MCP clients can set for a short list of settings: the ones that grant access, send data off the host, or choose code for a tool to run.

docs.title: The three tiers
docs.text:
Tier Where the configuration comes from Operator Command-line flags, including --config-overrides, --ash-plugin-modules, and --sandbox; the environment, including ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES; a config file outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory, named with --config or ASH_CONFIG. Repository Any config file inside a git checkout or inside the scanned directory: the discovered .ash/.ash.yaml and its siblings, a --config or ASH_CONFIG that points into the repository being scanned, and a config file kept in a checkout of its own, such as an ops or dotfiles repository. MCP client Any file under the MCP server's workspace root, where delivered source trees and uploads are stored, except each session's config/ directory, which only the server writes. Also any other config file a client names as a tool's config_path, wherever it is, unless it is in a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names or in its session's config/ directory, which only the server writes.

The MCP workspace root is ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT when set, read against the current directory when it is relative; else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/ash-mcp when XDG_CACHE_HOME is an absolute path, since a relative one is ignored; else ~/.cache/ash-mcp when HOME is an absolute path. A file there is an MCP-client file whether or not a server is running, so a CLI scan of a delivered tree, with that tree as --source-dir, gets the same treatment. With an empty or relative HOME and neither variable, or with an ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT under ~, there is no workspace root, and no file is an MCP-client file because of where it is. ash mcp still starts, with a warning that ASH uses nothing under ~.

docs.title: How a file's tier is decided
docs.text:
The tier depends on where a file is, not on who names it. Passing a repository's file with --config does not make it an operator file.

The repository tier exists because the scanned target is untrusted relative to the operator. Nothing the target ships, whether committed or only present in its checkout, may grant itself reads, tool options, or sandbox exceptions. A config file inside any git checkout, the scanned one or a separate one such as an ops or dotfiles repository, may have been written by someone other than the operator, so it is repository-tier, and so is a config file inside the scanned directory when that directory is in no checkout. When ASH ignores a setting from such a file, it names the file in a warning that says how to keep the setting: pass it with --config-overrides, or move it to a config file outside every git checkout and outside the scanned directory.

A file is inside a git checkout when it, or any directory above it, holds a .git entry: a directory, or the .git file of a submodule or linked worktree. ASH checks the path as you named it, its resolved path, and every symbolic link it passes through on the way, so a symbolic link into or out of a checkout counts either way. For a scanned directory that is not in a checkout, a file inside it counts under any of the directory's names: as given, resolved, or as the shell's $PWD names it.

In this example the scanned directory, ../app, is a checkout of its own, and your config is in ../ops, a separate checkout. ASH ignores its sandbox grant, names the setting in a warning, and leaves the grant out of the configuration it uses:

git init --quiet ../app
git init --quiet ../ops
printf 'project_name: app\nsandbox:\n  extra_read_paths:\n    - /opt/shared-rules\n' > ../ops/ash.yaml
ash config get --source-dir ../app --config ../ops/ash.yaml > ../ops-config.txt 2>&1
grep -F 'sandbox.extra_read_paths' ../ops-config.txt
! grep -F -- '- /opt/shared-rules' ../ops-config.txt

The same file outside every git checkout is the operator's, and the grant is kept:

mkdir -p ../plain
cp ../ops/ash.yaml ../plain/ash.yaml
ash config get --source-dir ../app --config ../plain/ash.yaml | grep -F -- '- /opt/shared-rules'

The rule applies to every file a config is built from, which means the root file and every base it extends, each judged by the path its extends entry names as well as by the file it resolves to. If any of them is inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, the whole config is treated as repository-tier for the restricted settings, and ASH names those files in the warning. An operator file outside every checkout that extends a base inside one keeps the sandbox settings it writes in its own sandbox section, and for some scanners the tool file paths it writes itself, but nothing it inherits from a base. Its other restricted settings come from the trusted base described below, so set them with --config-overrides. A base reached through a symbolic link that leaves the config file's own directory is refused before anything is granted.

ASH reads one config file per scan, plus the files it extends. When you pass --config to a scan of one directory, ASH does not read the repository's own config file. In workspace mode, the file --config (or ASH_CONFIG) names is layered over each project's own config: every setting your file makes is final for every project, and a project's own config fills only the settings yours leaves out (Scan a multi-project workspace). --dry-run shows it in an operator: line under each project. Here the project's config sets LOW and yours sets HIGH, which wins:

mkdir -p ../ws/api
printf 'global_settings:\n  severity_threshold: LOW\n' > ../ws/api/.ash.yaml
printf '{"folders": [{"path": "api"}]}\n' > ../ws/project.code-workspace
printf 'global_settings:\n  severity_threshold: HIGH\n' > ../operator.yaml
ash scan --workspace ../ws/project.code-workspace --config ../operator.yaml --dry-run > ../plan.txt
grep -F '(the fields it sets are final)' ../plan.txt
grep -E 'threshold: +HIGH' ../plan.txt

When a config is repository-tier, ASH takes the restricted settings from a trusted base instead: the file ASH_CONFIG names, if it is outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, otherwise the defaults, with your --config-overrides applied on top. In workspace mode, the scanned tree is the checkout that holds the workspace root, or the root itself, and the --config file given to the workspace scan is the trusted base when it is outside every git checkout. That file, and every base it extends, must be outside that tree: one inside it, or under the MCP workspace root, is refused with exit code 3, naming the file, before any project is resolved. Under the MCP server, the trusted base is the server's own configuration, the file ASH_CONFIG names, under the same rule: when that file is inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, the restricted settings come from the defaults. An ASH_CONFIG that is unset or empty means the defaults. One that names a path that is not a file, a file that cannot be read, or a config that does not load stops a scan with exit code 3, and stops ash mcp from starting, with exit code 3.

Two setups surprise people. A config you trust but keep in a git checkout of its own, such as an ops repository, cannot make the restricted settings below, because it is in a checkout. If your home directory is itself a git checkout (a common dotfiles setup), the outermost checkout above a project under it is your home directory, so a scan of that project counts your whole home directory as the scanned tree. Every config file under your home directory, yours included, is then repository-tier for that scan. Keep your operator config outside it, for example under /etc/ash.

docs.title: The scanned tree
docs.text:
One rule looks only at the scanned tree: where a tool file the operator names may be. The scanned tree is the git checkout that holds the scanned directory: the outermost directory at or above it that holds a .git entry. When the scanned directory is not in a checkout, the scanned tree is the scanned directory itself. ASH finds the tree from the scanned directory as you named it, from its resolved path, and, when you scan the working directory or one below it, from the shell's $PWD. A file is inside the tree when it or a directory above it is the tree's directory, compared by file identity rather than by name, and a symbolic link inside the tree counts as inside it wherever it points.

A tool file you name as the operator, with --config-overrides, in a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, or in an environment variable, is used unless it is inside the scanned tree and the scanner does not allow one there, so it may be in a checkout of your own, such as an ops repository. A tool file that any other config file names, one in an ops checkout included, or that ASH finds by name, is used only from outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. To keep such a path, move the config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, or pass the option with --config-overrides. Options only the operator can set lists the scanners this covers. ASH names each refused path in a warning of this form, where <option> is the option or the file it looked for, and <reason> says where the file is, such as it is inside the git checkout at /home/me/ops:

Ignoring <option> (<path>): <reason>. A file that a config file inside a git checkout or the scanned directory names, or that ASH finds in the scanned directory, is passed to the tool only from outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. To keep a setting, move the file outside every git checkout, or pass the setting with --config-overrides. A file inside the scanned directory has to move out of it as well.

For a path you named, the warning ends instead: "A file inside the scanned tree, or one an MCP client delivered, is not passed to the tool; name one outside it."

docs.title: What each tier may set
docs.text:
Settings not listed here can be set from any tier. The repository tier's limits also apply to MCP-client files, which have further limits of their own (next section).

Kind of setting From the operator From a repository file Sandbox grants: sandbox.network_scanners, sandbox.extra_read_paths, sandbox.read_path_scanners, and sandbox.env_scanners Honored Ignored. A network_scanners list is kept as a limit: scanners it does not name get no network. The sandbox mode, sandbox.mode Honored. A mode in ASH_CONFIG's file, or in the --config file of a workspace scan, counts even when that file is inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, because a mode other than off grants nothing. Applies only when no operator source turns the sandbox on. It cannot turn off, or switch away from, a mode the operator chose. In workspace mode this includes a project's own config file. Plugin module lists, ash_plugin_modules Honored Only ASH's own plugin modules and modules installed outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. A third-party package in a virtual environment inside a checkout counts as inside it. Never ash_aws_plugins or ash_snyk_plugins, or any module inside either, whose plugins send findings or source off the host. Where the AWS reporters send results, and with which credentials: the region, profile, and account of aws-security-hub; the region, profile, model, and output files of bedrock-summary-reporter; the region, log group, and stream of cloudwatch-logs; the region, profile, bucket, and key prefix of s3; and whether each of these reporters runs Honored Replaced by the trusted value. Whether the scanned repository's own .gitignore and .ignore files decide what is scanned, honor_ignore_files Honored Replaced by the trusted value. Letting trivy send anonymous usage data to its vendor on an online trivy-repo scan, scanners.trivy-repo.options.disable_telemetry: false Honored Replaced by the trusted value: the default true, which passes trivy repository --disable-telemetry, unless the operator set false. A file may set true. The archive extraction limits, max_members, max_member_bytes, max_total_bytes, and max_compression_ratio under converters.archive.options Honored A value at or below the trusted one is kept; a higher one is replaced by the trusted value. detect-secrets' verification filter, which sends each candidate secret to the service that issued it, and plugins or filters it loads from a file:// path Honored, except from a baseline inside the scanned tree Removed, unless the trusted settings name the same filter or file. A baseline's own copies of these count only when the baseline is outside the scanned tree and any checkout that holds it, and an operator source names the same baseline_file. Which release of a scanner's or converter's tool runs, tool_version, in every scanner and converter section Honored Replaced by the trusted value, or by the tool's default constraint where the trusted settings set none. Relaxing the stale content database check: content_db_staleness: warn, and content_db_staleness_overrides entries with policy: warn Honored, as is --allow-stale-content-db A value equal to the trusted one, or one that makes the check stricter (fail), is kept. Any other policy is replaced by the trusted value, and any other entry is dropped. Scanner options that name a tool config file, ignore file, rules or plugin directory, or a program for a tool to run, or that choose which part of a tool's own config applies Honored. For some scanners the file may not be inside the scanned tree. Limited for some scanners only: some ignore the repository's value, and the others accept only a path outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. Set these options from an operator source, and pass your config with --config so the repository's config is not read.

Options only the operator can set lists the scanners that limit the options in the last row. The reporter limits apply to a reporter's section under any spelling ASH reads as that reporter, so a repository's reporter section spelled BedrockSummary is limited like bedrock-summary-reporter. The table is how a scan reads the reporter settings. ash report and ash merge read stored results, which do not record which tree was scanned, so any config file they read, even one outside every git checkout, is held to the repository column for whether each AWS reporter runs and where it sends: those come only from --config-overrides (Rendering a reporter from saved results). Two rules apply from every tier: reporters.<name>.extension must be a plain filename suffix, and report files are written only inside the reports directory.

docs.title: When a lower tier sets something it may not
docs.text:
From a repository file, ASH ignores the value, uses the trusted one, logs a warning that names the settings and the file and says how to keep them, and runs the scan. For example:

Ignoring sandbox.network_scanners, sandbox.extra_read_paths from /work/repo/.ash/.ash.yaml: that config is inside a git checkout or the scanned tree, or was delivered by an MCP client. A network_scanners list there still removes network from scanners it does not name, and a sandbox mode there still applies when nothing else turns the sandbox on. To keep a setting, move the file outside every git checkout, or pass the setting with --config-overrides. A file inside the scanned directory has to move out of it as well.

Here the repository's config gave grype a network and a read path. To give grype a network yourself, pass --config-overrides 'sandbox.network_scanners=[grype]'.

An MCP-client file is also checked against the server's runtime-override policy, the denied_paths and denied_value_patterns of global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides, whether or not runtime_overrides.enabled is set. The policy comes from the server's own configuration: the file ASH_CONFIG names when the server starts, or the built-in defaults when ASH_CONFIG is unset or empty. An ASH_CONFIG that names a path that is not a file, or a file that does not load, stops ash mcp from starting, with exit code 3. By default the list covers the gate settings (fail_on_findings, fail_on_incomplete_scanners, content_db_staleness and its overrides, and content_db_staleness_offline_image_default), the scanner options that drop findings by rule ID, by a baseline, or by a whole category, options that limit how much a scanner reads or that turn on its own network calls, each scanner's offline option, each scanner's own config file, which version of a tool runs, every setting of the reporters that send findings off the host (aws-security-hub, bedrock-summary-reporter, cloudwatch-logs, and s3), their enabled included, and the gitlab-sast reporter's exclude_suppressed; What a delivered config cannot set lists them. If a delivered file sets any of them to a value other than the trusted one, ASH refuses the whole file rather than trimming it. The error names each field, the MCP tools report it with error_type: config_field_denied, and on the CLI it is a configuration error (exit 3). If the policy itself cannot be read, because the file ASH_CONFIG names exists but does not load, or has two sections that ASH reads as the same plugin, a config with an MCP-client file is refused with config_policy_unreadable. The server meets that case only when the file changed after it started.

The check follows where the file is, not whether a server is running. In this example the parent directory is the workspace root, so the scanned directory is a delivered tree, and its config turns off fail_on_findings:

project_name: delivered
fail_on_findings: false

The CLI refuses the config with exit code 3:

ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT="$(dirname "$PWD")" ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

Outside the workspace root the same file is a repository file, which may turn the gate off, so the same scan exits 0 although detect-secrets reports a finding:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

The default list also names sandbox, ash_plugin_modules, global_settings.mcp, suppressions, and ignore paths, and delivered files are checked differently for those. Sandbox settings and plugin modules may restrict the server's own but not widen them: a delivered file whose own sandbox section gives a scanner a network or an extra_read_paths entry the server's config does not, or sets a sandbox mode other than the server's when the server's mode is not off, or whose own ash_plugin_modules list loads a module the table above keeps out, is refused the same way. Any other sandbox grant or module a delivered file asks for is dropped, as for a repository file. A delivered file's global_settings.mcp section has no effect, and suppressions and ignore paths are honored and marked, as described next. Under the default policy a delivered config can still disable scanners, turn the reporters that write only local files on or off and set their options, apart from gitlab-sast's exclude_suppressed, and raise severity thresholds. It cannot turn a reporter that sends findings off the host on or off: its enabled: false for one of them is not refused, but it has no effect, and each runs as the server's config says, or by the reporter's own default where that config sets nothing. Run the MCP server covers running the server.

docs.title: Client-supplied suppressions and ignore paths
docs.text:
In a scan whose config includes an MCP-client file, each suppression and ignore path that file sets is marked client_supplied: true, unless it matches an entry from an operator source. Per-scanner path exclusions that file sets (bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, semgrep and opengrep exclude, syft exclude, and ferret-scan exclude_patterns) are taken out of the scanner's options and handled the same way. Each is matched the way its scanner reads it: a bandit entry as the **/<path>/** glob ASH passes bandit, against the file's absolute path; a checkov entry as a regular expression found in, or a substring of, the absolute path of the file or of a directory above it; and the others as globs that match the path or any directory in it. A finding the matching misses is reported unsuppressed, never hidden. A delivered scanners.trivy-repo.options.ignore_file is not passed to trivy. When it is a regular file inside the scanned tree, each unexpired ID in it suppresses and marks the trivy-repo findings with that rule ID; any other file, including a symbolic link, is not read.

The mark changes what the entry does. A client-supplied ignore path or exclusion does not keep files from being scanned or converted. The files are scanned, and each finding the entry would have hidden is kept in the results as a suppressed finding. Like every suppressed finding, it does not count toward fail_on_findings.

The mark shows up in:

  • ash_aggregated_results.json, on each entry of ash_config.global_settings.suppressions and ignore_paths;
  • the SARIF, where the suppression's justification starts with (ASH, client-supplied config) and, for a scanner exclusion, names the entry it came from, such as scanners.bandit.options.excluded_paths entry 'tests', and its properties carry clientSupplied: true. A suppression entry has kind: inSource; an ignore path or scanner exclusion has kind: external;
  • the reports that show suppression justifications: CSV and flat JSON, HTML, JUnit (<skipped>), OCSF, and GitLab SAST (which keeps suppressed findings at severity Info unless exclude_suppressed is set).

The GitHub code scanning SARIF leaves suppressed findings out by default, and the Markdown and text summaries show only counts, so the mark is not visible there. Syft's SBOM components get an ash:clientSuppliedExclusion property instead. Each exclusion taken out of a scanner's options is also logged as a warning and recorded in the results as a config_warning validation checkpoint.

ASH marks entries only in MCP-client files and, in an ash --workspace scan, in a workspace policy file under the MCP workspace root, whose entries are also checked against the runtime-override policy as each project gets them. The MCP workspace tools do not use such a policy file at all (Workspace scans over MCP). Only ASH sets the mark: a client_supplied value written in a config file, or set with --config-overrides, is ignored. In a CLI scan, a repository's own suppressions look the same as yours.

docs.title: What the trust model does not protect against
docs.text:
The tiers decide who may change the settings above. They do not make every setting the operator's, and they do not make scanning a hostile repository safe on their own.

  • A repository-tier config on the CLI can still turn off fail_on_findings and fail_on_incomplete_scanners, raise severity thresholds, disable scanners and reporters, and add suppressions, ignore paths, and per-scanner exclusions. None of this is marked. To keep these choices yours in a scan of one directory, pass your own config with --config, so that the repository's config is not read. You can also override the repository's values on the command line: --config-overrides replaces any setting (for example scanners.bandit.enabled=true or global_settings.suppressions=[]), flags such as --fail-on-findings, --fail-on-incomplete-scanners, and --no-allow-stale-content-db take precedence over a config file, and --ignore-suppressions stops the repository's suppressions and ignore paths from applying. In workspace mode every setting your --config makes is final for every project, and a project's own config fills only the settings yours leaves out.

    With --ignore-suppressions, every scanner reads the files under the repository's ignore paths, and their findings come back. It does not lift a scanner's own exclusion options, such as bandit's excluded_paths, or the repository's .gitignore and .ignore files (See every finding). In a repository where detect-secrets reports a password in app.py, a repository config that ignores app.py keeps the scan passing:

    global_settings:
  ignore_paths:
    - path: app.py
      reason: Fixture value, not a real password


    ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

    --ignore-suppressions brings the finding back, and the scan fails:

    ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress --ignore-suppressions

    To drop only the repository's ignore paths and keep its suppressions, replace the ignore paths with --config-overrides, and the finding fails the scan too:

    ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress \
  --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths=[]'

    A suppression of the same finding is lifted the same way, and the scan fails:

    global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - path: app.py
      rule_id: SECRET-SECRET-KEYWORD
      reason: Fixture value, not a real password


    ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress --ignore-suppressions

  • Some scanners read configuration files from the scanned directory by name. For actionlint, bandit, cfn-lint, checkov, ferret-scan, gitleaks, grype, opengrep, semgrep, syft, trivy, trivy-repo, and zizmor, ASH gives the tool its own configuration instead, or keeps the repository's file from being read, a .semgrepignore included. detect-secrets reads a .secrets.baseline or .ash/.secrets.baseline in the source directory and uses the plugins and filters it lists, unless your config sets plugins_used in detect-secrets' scan_settings. The table above says which of the baseline's settings ASH drops. Apart from those settings, ASH does not limit or mark these files, or any other file a tool reads from the scanned directory on its own.

  • Inline suppression comments in the source, ASH's ash-ignore and each scanner's own (for example bandit's # nosec), are written by the repository and honored in every tier.
  • Only ASH's own AWS reporters and off-host plugin packages are covered. A third-party reporter declares its destination options in the class attribute destination_options; ASH reads the declaration from the class and admits a destination only from the trusted base: the defaults, an operator config outside the tree, and --config-overrides. A third-party plugin package installed outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, named in a repository config, is imported and runs with ASH's access.
  • Once you load ash_aws_plugins, a repository config still sets the Bedrock reporter's content options, such as include_code_snippets and custom_prompt. A config an MCP client delivers can also turn the reporters that write only local files on or off and set their options. Once you load ash_snyk_plugins, a repository config can switch snyk-code off and set its options.
  • The MCP-client tier limits what a delivered config can change in a scan. It is not a boundary between MCP clients; see Run the MCP server for the deployment it supports.

Scanning untrusted code covers the other defenses.

docs.title: Contribute to ASH
docs.text:
This page covers a development checkout, the layout of the repository, and what a pull request goes through before it merges. The other contributor pages are Test your change, Test the documentation, and Releases and versions.

To report a bug or ask for a feature, open an issue on GitHub. To report a security issue, do not open a public issue: follow SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Set up a development checkout
docs.text:
You need git, uv, and Python 3.10 to 3.14. uv downloads a Python in that range if none is installed.

  1. Fork the repository on GitHub, then clone your fork:

    git clone https://github.com/<your-account>/automated-security-helper.git
cd automated-security-helper

    Replace <your-account> with your GitHub user name.

    Work in a git clone, not in an unpacked source archive. The unit suite, the docs checks, and the snapshot checks list files with git ls-files, so they fail outside a git work tree, and git must be on your PATH.

  2. Install the project, its development tools, and both optional extras:

    uv sync --extra cdk --extra symbols

    This creates .venv with ASH installed in editable mode, the dev dependency group (pytest, ruff, mypy, pre-commit, mkdocs, and the rest), and the two extras that CI installs: cdk (aws-cdk-lib and cdk-nag, which the cdk-nag scanner needs) and symbols (the tree-sitter grammars that symbol: suppressions use). A plain uv sync leaves both extras out, and the tests that need them then skip; the skip reason names the extra.

    The repository has no .python-version file, so uv uses the newest installed Python in the supported range. To develop against a particular version, name it: uv sync --python 3.12 --extra cdk --extra symbols.

    The scanners are not project dependencies. A scan runs the Python-based ones, such as bandit, checkov, and semgrep, with uv tool run, and finds binary ones such as grype or trivy on your PATH or in ~/.ash/bin, where ash dependencies install puts them. See Manage scanner tools.

  3. Check that the ASH in your checkout runs:

    uv run ash --version

    It prints the version in pyproject.toml.

docs.title: Operating system notes
docs.text:
• Windows: some test data paths are long. Enable long paths in git before you clone:

    git config --global core.longpaths true

    Git for Windows and MSYS2 ship a shell named ash. uv run ash finds the project's ASH first, because uv run puts the project's environment at the front of PATH; outside uv run, the ashv3 alias runs the same entry point. - CI runs the unit suite on Linux (x86_64 and arm64), macOS on Apple silicon, and Windows, each with Python 3.10 to 3.14, so any of these works for development. - Some tests need programs that are not Python packages, such as a container runtime, a sandbox backend, or Nix. Test your change says which, and how they are selected.

docs.title: Devfile environments
docs.text: An IDE that reads devfiles can use devfile.yaml at the root. Its install command installs uv into ~/.local/bin and runs uv sync, build runs uv build, and test runs uv run pytest. Each command puts ~/.local/bin on PATH itself, so it also runs under a POSIX sh. That uv sync installs neither extra. To run the commands by hand, copy them from devfile.yaml or DEVELOPMENT.md.

docs.title: Run ASH from your checkout
docs.text:
uv run runs a command in the checkout's environment, so uv run ash is the ASH you are editing. With no arguments, ash scans the current directory, which inside the checkout is the ASH repository itself. To scan another project with your checkout's code, run from that project and point uv at the checkout with uv run --project:

cd ~/src/my-project
uv run --project ~/src/automated-security-helper ash --source-dir . --output-dir .ash/ash_output

uv run --project keeps your working directory. uv run --directory also uses the checkout's environment but first changes into the checkout, so relative paths then resolve inside the checkout. To run the MCP server from your checkout, see Test an MCP change locally. Every command and option is in the CLI reference.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text: Directory What it holds automated_security_helper/ The package: the CLI and MCP server (cli/), configuration models (config/), the scan phases (core/), plugin base classes (base/), built-in and community plugins (plugin_modules/), result models (models/), JSON schemas (schemas/), and shared utilities (utils/) tests/ Unit, integration, and snapshot tests, test data, and test helpers; see Test your change docs/ docs/content/ is this site, built with mkdocs from mkdocs.yml scripts/ Generators for the reference pages, the docs checks, the version template manager, and the verification scripts some CI jobs run .github/ Workflows, composite actions (actions/), the gate scripts CI runs (scripts/), the changelog template, and curated release notes ash-agent-plugins/ The agent and IDE plugins: the shared sources in agentic-coding/transpiler/_base/, the transpiler that renders them, and the generated per-platform plugin trees skills/ The ash-mcp agent skill, generated by the transpiler deploy/ The CDK app, CDK constructs, and Terraform for running ASH on AWS examples/ Example CI configurations and an example plugin package .ash/ The ASH configuration that CI uses to scan this repository Formula/ The Homebrew formula nix/ Nix packages for the scanners nixpkgs does not carry; flake.nix at the root defines the development shell utils/ ash_helpers.sh, which you source from a shell profile to get an invoke-ash command that runs this checkout's ./ash from any directory; ash_helpers.ps1, which defines Invoke-ASH, the container wrapper for PowerShell; and older per-scanner scripts that ASH does not run

docs.title: Open a pull request
docs.text:
1. For anything beyond a small fix, open an issue first so the change can be discussed before you spend time on it.
  2. Create a branch in your fork from the latest main, and keep the change to one purpose. A reformat of unrelated code makes the change hard to review.
  3. Add or update tests for the change, and run them as described in Test your change.
  4. Update the docs the change affects. Docs are checked against the code, so a page that names an option that no longer exists fails CI; see Test the documentation. If users will see different behavior, describe it under ## Unreleased in CHANGELOG.md (see Releases and versions).
  5. Open the pull request against main with a title in the commit message format below, and fill in the template's checklist.

A pull request merges when it has one approving review, every review conversation is resolved, and the required checks pass (see the table below). The "Protect main" ruleset also requires the branch to be up to date with main, and it includes a code quality rule set to every severity. A push after an approval dismisses it. Merging goes through GitHub's merge queue, which squashes the pull request into one commit and runs the required checks again on the result.

Pull requests from forks run with a read-only token and without repository secrets, so a few steps that need them, such as the scan's comment on the pull request, are skipped. GitHub can also hold the workflow runs of a first-time contributor until a maintainer approves them.

docs.title: Commit messages and pull request titles
docs.text:
Commit messages and pull request titles follow Conventional Commits, as checked by commitizen:

<type>(<optional scope>)<optional !>: <description>

The type is one of build, bump, chore, ci, docs, feat, fix, perf, refactor, revert, style, and test. A scope cannot contain whitespace, and ! marks a breaking change. For example:

feat(reporters): add a JUnit reporter option for suite names
fix(sandbox): keep the scanner cache writable under bwrap
docs: rewrite the contributor pages
feat!: drop the v2 configuration format

The Validate PR title check runs cz check on the pull request title. The squash merge takes its subject from the pull request title when the pull request has several commits, and from the commit itself when it has one, and the title check does not see that commit. So give a single commit a conventional subject too; the commit-msg hook below checks it for you. The squash commit's body keeps every commit message, so trailers such as Snapshot-Update: survive the merge.

The type of the subject that lands on main decides what the release does with it:

Subject on main Changelog Version bump feat listed under Feat minor fix, refactor, perf listed under Fix, Refactor, or Perf patch any type with !, or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer listed major, capped to minor on the 3.x line build, bump, chore, ci, docs, revert, style, test not listed none

So a change to CI only is ci: .... Written as fix(ci): ..., it is listed under Fix and makes the next release a patch release. Releases and versions has the details.

docs.title: What CI runs on a pull request
docs.text:
Three checks are required to merge: "ash / SAST, SCA, and IaC Scan", Validate PR title, and required-checks. required-checks stands for every job in the "ASH - Unified CI" workflow, so all of those have to pass too. The repository also requires the code scanning results that the ASH scan uploads, so a pull request that introduces an alert does not merge.

Check What it checks Required ash / SAST, SCA, and IaC Scan ASH scans this repository with the configuration in .ash/, fails on actionable findings, and posts a summary on the pull request; the sarif job uploads the SARIF report to code scanning yes Validate PR title the pull request title passes cz check yes lint the JSON schemas match a regeneration; the docs checks pass; every CI artifact upload and cache is allowlisted; every cached content database is time-bounded; and ruff check, ruff format --check, and mypy pass. ty runs for information only through required-checks actionlint actionlint and shellcheck over every workflow through required-checks snapshot-trailers every changed golden file has a Snapshot-Update: trailer, and every snapshot belongs to a test module through required-checks unit-test (<os>, py<version>) the unit and snapshot suite with both extras, on five runners and Python 3.10 to 3.14, plus the cdk-nag integration tests. A test that cannot find an extra fails rather than skipping, and the leg fails when total coverage of automated_security_helper/ is under 80% through required-checks integration-test (ubuntu-latest) the integration suite with pytest --run-integration --run-slow, and the examples in the docs through required-checks build-docs mkdocs build --strict, and scripts/docs_versions.py check on the versioned site through required-checks converter-integration (<os>) the converter integration tests on macOS and Windows through required-checks scan (<method>, <os>) real scans by every way of running ASH: local, the Python container launcher, ./ash, PowerShell, each container runtime, offline, and with the community plugins through required-checks external-target scan (<os>), multi-project attribution (<os>) a scan of a directory outside the repository; a workspace scan that keeps findings with their projects through required-checks sandbox escape (<os>), sandbox scanner parity (<sandbox>, <os>) the sandbox backends contain a scanner; each scanner gives the same results with and without a sandbox through required-checks deploy-tree AWS helpers (moto server) the helper scripts in deploy/, against a local moto server through required-checks <method> (<os>, py<version>) each install method (the pip, pipx, uvx, pre-commit, and MCP bundle, Homebrew, and the container runtimes) on each runner and Python it supports. The bundle runs ASH's pre-commit hooks against fixture repositories on one leg per operating system. The Homebrew legs, on Linux x86_64 and macOS with Python 3.12, install the formula built from the pull request's commit, run brew test, and scan with the installed ASH through required-checks required-checks fails when any Unified CI job failed or was canceled; when all of them pass it is skipped, which GitHub counts as passing yes Build wheel and sdist, and assert their contents the package builds and contains what it should no upgrade (<from>) the tree installs into a clean environment, over the latest release, and over the previous commit no dependency-review no new dependency with a high-severity advisory no Assert every action is pinned to a commit sha, Assert no boolean workflow input is treated as a string workflow hygiene no cdk template drift, generated buildspec drift, terraform hygiene, cdk-nag the committed IaC in deploy/ matches a fresh synth, and passes its own checks no TypeScript CI, Agent Plugins Drift, CDK Extra Drift, Install Method Validation, Docs CI Runners the TypeScript packages in deploy/, the generated agent plugins, the cdk extra fallback, the Nix install, and the CI examples in the docs, each under its CI system's own runner (see Run the CI examples with their runners); each runs only when a pull request changes its files no

A check that is not required does not block the merge when it fails, but the failure still shows on the pull request.

docs.title: Scheduled checks
docs.text:
The "ASH - Pinned Tool Versions" workflow runs every Monday and can be started by hand. It runs scripts/check_pinned_tool_versions.py --fail-on-outdated --markdown and writes the report to the job summary. The script compares:

  • each version pinned in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py (the release binaries, the Python scanners the container image installs, the license-only entries, and the cfn-nag gem) with its upstream's latest release on GitHub, PyPI, or RubyGems;
  • each package=version pin on an apt-get install line in the Dockerfile with the Debian and NodeSource package indexes, for amd64 and arm64.

The script fetches only HTTPS URLs on api.github.com, pypi.org, rubygems.org, deb.debian.org, and deb.nodesource.com, and checks every redirect hop against the same rule before it follows it. With GITHUB_TOKEN or GH_TOKEN set, it sends the token to the GitHub API only, carries it across a redirect only to the same scheme, host, and port, and retries a GitHub lookup that gets 403 once without the token. It exits 2 when a lookup fails, the pins cannot be read, an apt-get install line names a package without a version, or an apt-get install line pins a package to a different version than another stage does, and 1 when no package index carries an apt pin's version. A pin that is behind makes it exit 1 only with check_pinned_tool_versions.py --fail-on-outdated, as the workflow runs it; otherwise it exits 0. To run it locally, from a checkout:

python scripts/check_pinned_tool_versions.py

The workflow opens no issue or pull request. A bump changes every digest, the license files, and the source commit in tool_downloads.py, so a person makes it; the report lists each value a bump has to change.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
CI runs these, and so can you:

uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format --check .
uv run --group dev --extra cdk mypy automated_security_helper/

uv run ruff format . and uv run ruff check --fix . fix what they can. The ruff settings, including the line length of 88, are in [tool.ruff] in pyproject.toml, which also requires ruff 0.16.10 or later: an older ruff exits with code 2 rather than lint with different rules. tests/test_data/ is excluded, because those files are scanner input. mypy checks the package, not the tests or scripts. Its per-module overrides in pyproject.toml are a baseline that only shrinks: fix a new type error rather than adding the module to the overrides.

docs.title: Pre-commit hooks
docs.text:
The repository's .pre-commit-config.yaml runs ruff, formats JSON files, regenerates the JSON schemas, and keeps the cdk extra fallback in sync on each commit. The fallback sync runs its script on Python 3.13 outside the project environment (uv run --no-project), so it leaves your .venv and its extras as they are. The config also checks the commit message with commitizen. pre-commit install on its own installs only the pre-commit stage, not the commit message check. Install both, then run the hooks over the whole tree:

uv run pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit --hook-type commit-msg
uv run pre-commit run --all-files

Run pre-commit through uv run, so it uses the project's Python; the pinned commitizen hook needs Python 3.10 or later. The first commit takes longer while pre-commit builds the hook environments, and the schema regeneration runs on every commit.

On a clean checkout, pre-commit run --all-files passes and changes nothing. The JSON formatter skips the files that a tool writes or a check compares byte for byte: the generated agent plugin trees, _base/mcp.json that they copy, and the vendored schemas under ash-agent-plugins/, the synthesized CDK templates, the npm manifests in deploy/, and the snapshot files. Change those with the tool that owns them. It also skips the editor settings under .vscode/, and deploy/cdk/tsconfig.json, which has comments. CI runs ruff and the other checks directly rather than through these hooks, because the ruff and JSON hooks fix what they find instead of reporting it.

The config also has a manual hook that scans the repository with your checkout's ASH:

uv run pre-commit run --hook-stage manual ash

These hooks are for developing ASH. To run ASH as a pre-commit hook in your own repository, see Run ASH with pre-commit.

docs.title: Test the documentation
docs.text:
Every command, config file, environment variable, link, and page in these docs is checked against the code. A docs change that names an option ASH does not have, a config key ASH ignores, or a page that no longer exists fails CI. This page explains how the checks decide what a code block is, how to mark a block that cannot be checked the usual way, how to run the checks yourself, and what each failure means.

There are three layers:

  • Static checks, in the lint job. They read every Markdown file in the repository and compare it with the code: the CLI, the config models, the environment variables ASH reads, the navigation, and the link targets. They also check the docs URLs and paths that ASH's own source names. They run in about ten seconds.
  • The docs-example runner, in the integration-test job. It runs every runnable shell and Python block, page by page, and fails when a block exits with the wrong code.
  • The site build, in the build-docs job. It runs mkdocs build --strict with link and anchor validation, then publishes the site as versions to a throwaway branch with the network blocked, and checks what readers of each version would see (see Versioned docs).

All three jobs are in the Unified CI workflow and run on every pull request and merge queue entry. The required-checks gate depends on each of them, so a failure in any layer blocks the merge. The "Docs Deploy" workflow, ash-repo-docs.yml, only publishes the site, after a push to main and when someone runs it by hand on a release tag.

docs.title: How blocks are classified
docs.text:
A fenced code block is checked according to its language. A fence with no language is an error, because a command in it would escape every check. Use text for output samples.

Language Unmarked, it is Checked bash, sh, shell, console run executed by the runner; every ash line parsed zsh, fish, powershell, pwsh, ps1, cmd, bat an error must be marked illustrative yaml, yml, json, jsonc, toml config kind=ash parsed, and validated as an ASH config python, py run executed by the runner; must parse; imports must resolve dockerfile not executed ash in RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT lines parsed groovy an error must be marked config kind=jenkinsfile (see CI pipelines); ash in its sh steps parsed jenkinsfile, Jenkinsfile an error, marked or not nothing; fence a Jenkinsfile as groovy anything else (text, mermaid, diff, ...) not executed nothing

In a console block, only the lines that start with a $ prompt (and their continuation lines) are commands. Everything else is output.

docs.title: Markers
docs.text:
A marker is an HTML comment on the line directly above the opening fence. It does not render on the site.

<!-- doctest: illustrative reason="needs Docker" -->
```bash
ash --mode container --source-dir .
```

A blank line between the marker and the fence is an error, as is a marker with no block after it, so a marker cannot end up governing a different block after an edit. Values with spaces go in double quotes. Unknown modes and keys are errors.

docs.title: Shell and Python blocks
docs.text:
run is the default. Use the marker only to change how the block runs.

Marker Meaning <!-- doctest: run expect-exit=2 --> the block must exit with code 2 <!-- doctest: run expect-exit=nonzero --> the block must fail, with a code other than 126 or 127 (a command not executable or not found) <!-- doctest: run expect-exit=any --> the exit code is not checked, so an output sample must directly follow the block <!-- doctest: run timeout=300 --> allow 300 seconds instead of 60 <!-- doctest: run env="ASH_OFFLINE=YES,LANG=C" --> set these variables for this block only <!-- doctest: run fixture=empty --> start a new session in another fixture project <!-- doctest: run fresh --> start a new session in the default fixture <!-- doctest: illustrative reason="needs AWS credentials" --> do not run the block

illustrative needs a reason a reader would accept, such as "needs Docker", "installs from the network", "needs AWS credentials", "Windows only", or "runs in CI". "TODO", "TBD", and "n/a" are rejected, and so is a reason that names no cause, such as "example" or "illustrative example only". An illustrative block is still checked statically: its ash lines must parse, and a Python block must still parse and import.

The runner treats a page as one session, the way a reader follows a tutorial:

  • Blocks run in order, in one copy of a fixture project. The default fixture is sample-project, a small git repository with a hardcoded password that detect-secrets reports without network access. Fixtures live in tests/test_data/docs_fixtures.
  • Files, the working directory, and shell variables carry from one shell block to the next. Shell blocks run under set -e, so a block stops at its first failing command.
  • A Python block runs in a fresh interpreter in the session's directory and environment, with that directory on its import path. It cannot change the session, except through save-as (below).
  • HOME is private to the session, ash is the one in the project's virtual environment, and downloads fail at once: every proxy variable points at a port that refuses connections, and uv, pip, and npm run offline. A block that needs the network must be illustrative. This is not a sandbox: a program that ignores the proxy variables can still connect, and blocks run as you, so run the examples only on docs you trust.

This block runs in CI. The default fixture has one finding, so the scan exits with 2:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

docs.title: Output samples
docs.text:
A text block marked output directly after a block the runner runs is a sample of that block's output. Prose may sit between the two:

```bash
ls .ash/ash_output/reports
```

The scan wrote one report:

<!-- doctest: output -->
```text
ash.sarif
```

The runner compares the sample with what the block printed, stdout and stderr together, whatever exit code the block expects. The CLI check does not read the sample's ash lines as commands. Both texts are normalized first:

  • ANSI escape codes are removed, and Rich's box-drawing characters become spaces, so a table row reads as its cells;
  • durations (46ms, 1.23s, 3 seconds), clock times (0:00:03), and timestamps (2026-10-11T12:00:01Z) become <time>;
  • the session's project directory reads as ., with the paths under it relative, and its HOME as ~;
  • each run of whitespace becomes one space, and blank lines are dropped.

Then every line of the sample, other than a line that is only ..., must appear in a line of the output, in order, starting and ending at word boundaries. ... inside a line stands for any text there, so detect-secrets ... PASSED matches a table row. The output is rendered 100 columns wide, the way Rich lays out a table in the runner.

A block marked output anywhere else is an error: as the first block on a page, after an illustrative block, after a block that is only saved, after a config block, or after another sample. Nothing printed it there, so the marker would only hide its ash lines from the CLI check. tests/unit/test_docs_corpus_census.py counts the samples the runner compares, so a sample it stops comparing fails the unit suite.

docs.title: Config blocks
docs.text:
An unmarked config block must be a complete ASH config. Mark any other file with its kind.

Marker The block is <!-- doctest: config kind=ash-fragment at=scanners.bandit --> the value of one key of an ASH config <!-- doctest: config kind=pyproject --> a pyproject.toml whose [tool.ash] table is an ASH config <!-- doctest: config kind=ash-invalid reason="severity is uppercase" --> a config ASH must reject <!-- doctest: config kind=github-actions --> a GitHub Actions workflow <!-- doctest: config kind=gitlab-ci --> a GitLab CI file <!-- doctest: config kind=buildspec --> an AWS CodeBuild buildspec <!-- doctest: config kind=azure-pipelines --> an Azure Pipelines file <!-- doctest: config kind=jenkins --> a YAML Jenkins definition <!-- doctest: config kind=jenkinsfile --> a declarative Jenkinsfile, on a groovy block <!-- doctest: config kind=circleci --> a CircleCI config.yml <!-- doctest: config kind=docker-compose --> a Compose file <!-- doctest: config kind=pre-commit --> a .pre-commit-config.yaml <!-- doctest: config kind=mcp-client --> an MCP client configuration <!-- doctest: config kind=ash-output model=automated_security_helper.models.asharp_model.AshAggregatedResults.scanner_results --> part of a file ASH writes; model= names its output model as <module>.<Model>, then any fields below it <!-- doctest: config kind=mcp-response of=mcp.run_ash_scan --> an example of an MCP tool's response, in a json block or a text block with placeholders <!-- doctest: config kind=other reason="an IAM policy" --> any other file

Every kind must parse in its language. ASH configs are read with ASH's own reader and validated by its models, which refuse an option a plugin does not declare. Any key ASH would accept and never read is an error too: a scan ignores an unknown top-level key, so a reader who copied one would see it do nothing. Commands in the run, command, script, and commands keys of CI files, in the sh steps of a Jenkinsfile, and the command of an MCP server entry, get the same checks as a shell block. A pre-commit block must use hook IDs that .pre-commit-hooks.yaml defines. An mcp-response example must be one response the tool named by of returns: every key it shows, nested ones included where the code spells the value out, must be a key of one dict the tool's return statements build. A key written as a placeholder, such as "<scanner_name>", stands for any key.

An ash-output block is validated against the model model= names, which must be one of ASH's own. Every key the block shows must be a field the model declares, even where the model accepts extra keys, because a renamed key in a sample is a key ASH does not write. SARIF's property bags are the exception: they take any key.

docs.title: Saving a block as a file
docs.text:
A tutorial often shows a file and then a command that uses it. With save-as=<path>, the runner writes the block, exactly as shown, to that path in the page's project before the blocks after it run. Missing directories are created. save-as works on any block: Python, shell, config, Dockerfile, or text.

<!-- doctest: save-as=my_plugins/greeting.py -->
```python
def hello():
    return "hi"
```

```python
from my_plugins.greeting import hello

print(hello())
```
Marker What the runner does <!-- doctest: save-as=my_plugins/greeting.py --> saves the block and does not run it <!-- doctest: run save-as=tools/check.py --> saves the block, then runs it; a Python block runs from the saved file, so __file__ is that path <!-- doctest: config kind=github-actions save-as=.github/workflows/ash.yml --> saves the block, which is still validated as its kind <!-- doctest: save-as=.ash/.ash.yaml --> on a YAML block saves the block, which is still validated as a complete ASH config

The path is relative to the root of the page's fixture project, whatever directory earlier blocks changed to. An absolute path, a path containing .., and a path that goes through a symbolic link are refused, and the block fails; the static check reports the first two before CI runs. A marker without a mode may carry nothing but save-as. An illustrative block is never run or saved, so illustrative with save-as is an error: use a marker without a mode to save a block that must not run, such as a PowerShell script.

The python check knows which modules a page saves. save-as=my_plugins/scanner.py makes my_plugins and my_plugins.scanner importable by every Python block of the page, a name imported from a saved module must be defined in it, and a relative import in a saved package resolves within that package.

docs.title: CI pipelines
docs.text:
A block of kind github-actions, gitlab-ci, buildspec, jenkinsfile, or circleci is a pipeline, which the Docs CI Runners workflow runs under its CI system's own runner (see Run the CI examples with their runners). Its marker says how:

Marker The block is <!-- doctest: config kind=github-actions --> a complete pipeline; its runner runs it, and ASH must exit 2 in it <!-- doctest: config kind=github-actions save-as=.github/workflows/ash.yml --> a complete pipeline that later blocks on the page may extend; it still runs on its own <!-- doctest: config kind=github-actions extends=.github/workflows/ash.yml --> a fragment, run merged into the pipeline that the nearest block above it saved at that path <!-- doctest: config kind=gitlab-ci extends=.gitlab-ci.yml event=merge_request --> a pipeline run for the event it names <!-- doctest: config kind=circleci runner=none reason="uses a private orb" --> a pipeline no runner runs; the static checks still read it

The keys follow these rules:

  • extends= is valid on github-actions and gitlab-ci blocks, the kinds with a merge rule. It must name a block above it on the page, saved with save-as= at that path, of the same kind, and a fragment cannot also carry save-as=.
  • event= takes pull_request or push on a github-actions block, and push or merge_request on a gitlab-ci block; the other kinds take no event. Without it, a GitHub workflow runs for pull_request when its on: lists that event, and for push otherwise, and a GitLab pipeline runs for push.
  • runner= takes only none, and then needs a reason= that follows the illustrative rules. reason= goes with runner=none only.
  • azure-pipelines blocks and YAML jenkins blocks have no runner. They take none of these keys and get the static checks only.
  • A groovy block must be marked config kind=jenkinsfile, with runner=none and a reason when no runner can run it. An unmarked groovy block, or one marked only with save-as=, is an error, so a Jenkinsfile cannot drop out of the runs. So is a block fenced jenkinsfile or Jenkinsfile, whatever its marker: fence it as groovy.

A fragment is merged into the pipeline it extends by its kind's rule:

  • gitlab-ci: as GitLab merges an included file, with the fragment as the including file. Mappings merge at any depth and the fragment's value wins; anything else, such as a script: or rules: list, is replaced by the fragment's.
  • github-actions, a mapping of jobs: the jobs are added to the saved workflow, and a job with the ID of a saved one replaces it whole.
  • github-actions, a list of steps: a named step replaces the saved job's step with the same name, and an unnamed one the step that uses the same action, whatever its @ ref. A step with no counterpart goes right before the next fragment step that replaces one, or right after the last replaced step.

The static checks merge each fragment the same way and report one that does not merge, such as a list of steps none of which replaces a saved step, or one whose steps match steps in more than one job. Whether a block scans only the changed files is read from the pipeline, not the marker: an ash command with --changed-files-only, or a call of run-ash-security-scan.yml with its changed-files-only input set to true. tests/unit/test_docs_ci_runner_census.py compares the blocks each runner leg runs with an exact list, and checks that every CI block is run by a leg, marked runner=none, or of a kind with no runner, so a block that stops running fails the unit suite.

docs.title: Option tables
docs.text:
A table that documents options, keys, or parameters carries a marker naming the section it documents, on the line directly above its header row:

<!-- doctest: options of=scanners.bandit -->
| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `confidence_level` | string | `all` | Lowest confidence bandit reports |

Every row's first code span must be a key of that section, and its Default cell must state the default the code has. A column headed Defaults to, If not passed, If not set, or If unset is a Default column too. Any other column whose header says it holds defaults is an error, because nothing compares it.

A table without a marker is an error, so a new table cannot skip the check, when both of these hold:

  • its first header cell is Option, Key, Field, Setting, Argument, Param, Parameter, or Prop, or it has a column of defaults;
  • most of its rows name a key: of the ASH config model, of an ash command, of an MCP tool, or of a section in the code tree (a Python function's parameters, a Terraform module's variables, an action's or workflow's inputs, the Dockerfile's build arguments, a CloudFormation template's parameters, or a TypeScript interface's properties). A name close to a key counts, so a table of misspelled keys still needs its marker.

A table of other things, such as a list of defenses that are on or off by default, needs no marker. A table headed Variable or Environment variable whose rows are mostly upper-case names is checked as environment variables instead: each name must be one ASH reads, and each Default cell must say what the environment variable reference says.

A row can name several keys when its first cell is only a list of code spans (`quiet`, `simple`, and `debug`). Its Default cell then holds one value for all of them, or one code span per key in the same order (`False`, `"origin/main"`). A key written with a value (`--build-target ci`) is checked as the key alone.

Add complete to the marker when the table lists every key of its section, as in <!-- doctest: options of=scanners complete --> above a table of every scanner ASH ships. Each key of the section that no row names is then an error. --help, a hidden option, and the options ASH reads from every scanner need no row.

of= The rows are scanners.bandit, reporters.sarif, converters.archive that plugin's options (the same as adding .options) scanners.* the keys every scanner entry has (name, enabled, options) scanners, reporters, converters the plugins of that section, by name, built-in and community ones; a column headed Enabled by default or On by default is compared with each plugin's enabled default config the top-level keys of an ASH config global_settings, sandbox, global_settings.suppressions, ... the keys under that config path; a path through a list means one item of it workspace-policy, workspace-policy.workspace, ... keys of the workspace policy file cli, cli.scan, cli.config.get, ... the options and arguments of that ash command mcp.run_ash_scan, ... the parameters of that MCP tool, from the input schema the server lists python.automated_security_helper.interactions.run_ash_scan.run_ash_scan the parameters of a Python function, a class's __init__ (python.<module>.<Class>) or a method (python.<module>.<Class>.<method>), read from the source without importing it dockerfile the build arguments of the shipped Dockerfile, with the defaults its ARG lines give cloudformation:deploy/cdk/templates the Parameters of one CloudFormation template, or of every template in a directory github-inputs:.github/workflows/run-ash-security-scan.yml the inputs of a GitHub Action (its action.yml or the directory holding one) or of a workflow (workflow_call and workflow_dispatch) typescript:deploy/cdk-constructs/src/ash-scan-step.ts:ASHScanStepProps the properties of a TypeScript interface; one without ? is required, and the default is its JSDoc @default (an @default - words default is prose and is not compared) terraform:deploy/terraform/modules/fargate the variables of a Terraform module: every variable block in the directory's .tf files; one without a default is required, and one whose default is not a literal has no default to compare

Python, Dockerfile, CloudFormation, GitHub, TypeScript, and Terraform sections are read from the code tree, the checkout of the installed ASH (see Check docs against another checkout's code).

A Default cell is one of:

  • a value in one code span, read as YAML: `true`, `1800`, `[]`, `null`, `ash-scan`, or `">=1.7.0,<2.0.0"` for a string that YAML would read as something else. A path under the repository or home directory starts <repository>/ or ~/;
  • from `ENV_NAME`, else `VALUE` (one or more from parts) for a default ASH reads from the environment; VALUE is the default when the variable is unset;
  • `VALUE` on Linux and macOS; `VALUE` on Windows for a default that depends on the platform;
  • one of the phrases required, see the section (the key is a nested section), computed at run time, or depends on the platform, and for ash options off, on, or not set. empty means an empty string or list. A phrase may be set in emphasis (*required*).

A bare word such as true or None is read the same way; anything else is reported.

Defaults of a python. section are read as Python, not YAML: write `None`, `False`, `"low"`, or `ExecutionStrategy.PARALLEL`. A literal is compared by value and anything else by its source text, and a string may also be written without quotes (`t3.medium`). Dockerfile, CloudFormation, GitHub, and TypeScript defaults are compared as written, so `NO` is the string NO, not false. A default that is a member of an enum or class may be written by the member alone: `PIP` for ASHInstallMode.PIP, `PARALLEL` for ExecutionStrategy.PARALLEL.

docs.title: Commands, options, and variables in prose
docs.text:
An inline code span that starts with ash, or with a wrapper that runs it (uvx, pipx run, uv run, docker run), is checked like a command. A span that is only an option must be an option of some ash command, so write another program's option with the program: pytest --run-integration, not the bare option. On a generated reference page, a row a plugin's code wrote names the program even for an option ASH also has, because there a bare --config could be either. That covers the rows of a plugin's options table and the environment variables whose purpose is quoted from a plugin module. Write zizmor --config, and ash --config for ASH's own.

Every ASH_* name anywhere on a page must be a variable ASH reads. So must every name in the first column of a table headed "Variable" or "Environment variable". Write a family as ASH_MCP_*; at least one variable ASH reads must start with the prefix.

An inline code span that is a dotted config path starting with a top-level config key (scanners.bandit.options.severity_threshold, global_settings.suppressions, sandbox.mode, also with a value after it, as in scanners.bandit.enabled=false) must resolve in ASH's config models, community plugins included when this ASH has them. Use * or <name> for a plugin name that is not fixed: scanners.<name>.enabled.

Two more kinds of name are accepted. A build argument, declared with ARG in the Dockerfile ASH ships or passed by ASH as --build-arg NAME=... (as it passes the image name to a custom Containerfile), is documented like any variable. A variable only the test suite reads or CI sets (in tests/, or in an env: block under .github/) is accepted on contributor pages (the pages under docs/content/contributing/, the repository's CONTRIBUTING.md, and its DEVELOPMENT.md) and reported anywhere else, because a user cannot use it. Running the checks with scripts/verify_docs_freshness.py --verbose prints which of these sets each accepted name matched.

One kind of read is not in the read set: a config value that starts with a reference such as ${NAME:default} or ${NAME}, which ASH's config loader replaces with the environment variable for any name its rule allows (every ASH_* name, and three AWS ones). When the variable is not set, ${NAME:default} becomes default, and a scan refuses a config whose ${NAME} has no default, with exit 3. A name that one of the page's ASH config blocks references either way counts as read everywhere on the page, so the page can set the variable its own config uses.

docs.title: File and scanner names
docs.text:
An inline code span that names a file ash.<name>, alone or at the end of a path, or reports/<name>, must name a file ASH writes. That is the report of a registered reporter (ash.<extension>), a file a reporter's code writes beside its report (the S3 reporter's reports/s3-report.json), a file name a reporter's options default to, a file name held by a constant in ASH's package whose name says it is one (ending in _FILE, _FILES, _FILENAME, and the like), or a file the repository ships (Formula/ash.rb). The report of a reporter a Python block on the same page declares counts on that page. So does the report of a plugin package in this repository, such as the example plugin package, on a page in the package's project directory or a page that names the package. A placeholder, as in reports/ash.<extension>, is not checked.

In a table, every item of a column headed Scanner, Scanners, Built-in scanners, Community plugins, or Community scanners must be one scanner ASH ships, built in or a community plugin as the header says. A note in parentheses after a name is ignored. Any other item of several words is an error, because nothing can check it: write semgrep, opengrep (as far as their rules cover the language), and put longer notes in another column.

docs.title: Links and pages
docs.text:
• A relative link must reach an existing file, and its #anchor an existing heading or id. On site pages, anchors are computed the way mkdocs computes them; in files GitHub renders (README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md), the way GitHub does.
  • A page under docs/content may only link to files under docs/content, because mkdocs cannot publish anything else. Link to other repository files with their GitHub URL, https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/blob/main/<path>; the path must exist.
  • Every page is reachable from a .nav.yml, or matches a pattern in not_in_nav in mkdocs.yml with a comment saying why. A .nav.yml entry may be a page, a directory (which then uses its own .nav.yml, or lists everything in it), or a glob such as docs/plugins/community/*.md. The check runs awesome-nav's own resolver, so a glob means what it means in the build, including that it only picks up pages no other entry already took. A glob that matches nothing is an error. A glob with options is written - glob: "<pattern>" with at least one option beside it; on its own, - glob: "<pattern>" is a titled link to a page named by the pattern.
  • When you move or rename a page, add the old path to docs/redirects.yml. The site build writes a page at the old URL that forwards readers to the new one, keeping the #anchor they followed, so that anchor must exist on the new page.

docs.title: Docs links in the ASH source
docs.text:
ASH itself names docs pages: help text and error messages point at the site, ash get-genai-guide fetches a docs file from GitHub by path, and some messages name a heading. The static checks read every string in the package source (docstrings excepted) and require that:

  • a URL on the site reaches a page, directly or through a redirect, and its #anchor exists on the page it ends at;
  • a raw or blob GitHub URL to a docs file names a file that exists. A redirect does not help here, because fetching the file does not follow it; when a page moves, the code must change too;
  • a GitHub URL to any other repository file names a file that exists;
  • a docs path (docs/content/...md) exists, and a heading the text quotes beside it ('Some heading' in docs/content/page.md) is a heading on that page.

An f-string is read with each placeholder replaced by the constant it names. A URL whose path depends on anything else cannot be checked, and is reported as such.

docs.title: Run the checks locally
docs.text:
Run these from a checkout of the repository.

# Every static check, as the lint job runs them
uv run python scripts/verify_docs_freshness.py

# The examples of one page, through the runner
uv run pytest tests/integration/docs/test_docs_examples.py --run-integration -n 0 -k getting-started

# The site, as the docs job builds it
uv run mkdocs build --clean --strict

verify_docs_freshness.py prints PASS or FAIL for each check, with the findings under each failing one, and exits 1 when any check fails. A check that raises did not run: it prints ERROR with the error, and the script exits 2. Several checks list files with git, so run the script in a git checkout rather than an extracted copy of one. The expression in pytest -k getting-started selects pages by path, so it runs every page whose path contains getting-started. To check that the runner and the checks themselves still catch what they should:

uv run pytest tests/unit/test_docs_checks_can_fail.py tests/unit/test_docs_freshness_gate_can_fail.py
uv run pytest tests/integration/docs/test_docs_runner_can_fail.py --run-integration -n 0

docs.title: Check docs against another checkout's code
docs.text:
Docs written for code that is not on main yet are checked against a checkout that has it, while the pages stay in their own checkout. Run the checks with the code checkout's interpreter and name the docs checkout. Every ASH import, the CLI, the config models, and the environment variables come from the interpreter's ASH; every page, the nav, mkdocs.yml, the redirect map, and the fixtures come from the docs checkout. Both commands print which package and which docs root they used.

CODE=../code-checkout
DOCS=$PWD

"$CODE/.venv/bin/python" "$DOCS/scripts/verify_docs_freshness.py" --docs-root "$DOCS"

"$CODE/.venv/bin/pytest" "$DOCS/tests/integration/docs" --run-integration -n 0 --docs-root="$DOCS"

Use the code checkout's pytest rather than python -m pytest from the docs checkout: python -m puts the current directory first on the import path, and the docs checkout's copy of the package would then be the one imported. Pass the option to pytest as one word, pytest --docs-root=<checkout>: pytest reads a separate value as a test path before the option is registered, and when the tests and the docs come from different checkouts it then loads both checkouts' tests/conftest.py and stops with "option names {'--run-slow'} already added".

The reference page generators take the same two checkouts: each documents the ASH its interpreter imports, and compares its page in the docs checkout with what it generates (generate_cli_docs.py --docs-root "$DOCS" --check). Run them from any directory; each prints the package it documents.

CODE=../code-checkout
DOCS=$PWD

for page in cli_docs config_reference converter_reference env_var_reference \
    mcp_tool_reference reporter_docs scanner_reference; do
  "$CODE/.venv/bin/python" "$DOCS/scripts/generate_$page.py" --docs-root "$DOCS" --check
done

Without the check option, each rewrites its page instead. The MCP tools generator also writes the agent plugins' tool reference, so after rewriting it, copy that into every plugin from the docs checkout:

cd "$DOCS/ash-agent-plugins"
uv run --project agentic-coding/transpiler agentic-plugins build

A generator's run is offline and leaves the home directory alone: uv and pip may not reach an index, every proxy variable points at a local port that refuses connections, and uv's and the XDG cache, data, and config directories are temporary ones that are removed when it exits. Building the scanner plugins asks each tool for its version, and online that used to install the tools into the home directory.

docs.title: Run the CI examples with their runners
docs.text:
The pipelines on the CI pages also run, each under its CI system's own local runner, in the Docs CI Runners workflow, ash-docs-ci-runners.yml. It runs on a pull request that changes a path its paths filter lists, such as a CI page or its template, the harness and its pins, the fixture, or the install, scan, and report code the runs check. It also runs from the Actions tab, for every leg, or the legs of the runner its legs input names. A required check that does not run blocks the merge, so this path-filtered workflow is not a required check, and required-checks, which stands for the jobs of the "ASH - Unified CI" workflow, does not cover it.

Each leg of its matrix is one runner on one page, and runs every block of that page the runner can run:

Kind Runner Legs github-actions nektos/act, which runs each job on the hosted runner itself act, one for each page whose GitHub Actions blocks it runs gitlab-ci gitlab-ci-local, which runs each job in its image: gitlab-ci-local jenkinsfile Jenkinsfile Runner jenkinsfile-runner-lts, on the LTS core of Jenkins pinned in runners.toml, and jenkinsfile-runner-bundled, on the core the Jenkinsfile Runner release is built against buildspec the AWS CodeBuild local agent codebuild-agent circleci the CircleCI CLI: circleci config validate and circleci config process, then circleci local execute circleci azure-pipelines, YAML jenkins none; these blocks get the static checks only none

The core that Jenkinsfile Runner's release is built against is past its upstream support period. Its leg runs only on a GitHub-hosted runner's throwaway VM, with no listener and no credentials.

docs.title: How a run is set up
docs.text:
Each block a leg runs is one test of tests/integration/docs/test_docs_ci_runners.py, from the census in scripts/docs_checks.py. For each one:
