  • The block, merged into the pipeline it extends if it is a fragment, is committed as the pipeline file of a new git repository made from the default fixture, sample-project, with a bare repository holding main as its origin. For a pull request or merge request event, a branch adds one commit with changed.py, whose one finding is a subprocess.call with shell=True (bandit B602).
  • The leg checks out the pull request's head commit, not the merge commit (on a dispatch, the commit it was dispatched on), and builds its wheel. In the block's install line, the release becomes that wheel, which gitlab-ci-local and circleci local execute mount into the job's container. The CodeBuild agent cannot mount it, and a wheel in the source would be scanned, so there the install line names the head commit, which pip installs with git. A call of ASH's reusable workflows becomes a call of the pull request's own copy in the fixture, with ash-version set to the head commit. A GitLab job on ASH's own image, registry.example.com/security/automated-security-helper:ci, runs on the image the run builds under that name from the checkout's Dockerfile (the ci target).
  • Each rewrite is an exact replacement, or an insertion at a place read from the pipeline (its parsed YAML, or a Jenkinsfile's sh script), whose count is recorded. A block the rewrites cannot follow fails its test: one with none of the install forms they know, or one that could still get ASH from somewhere else, such as another install of Python packages, another reference to ASH's repository, or an image of ASH the run does not build. So an edit to an install line cannot quietly test the release. The install checks read the pipeline's commands as written, so a command assembled at run time from variables is not seen.
  • After each install, the rewrite adds a command that prints the installed distribution's direct_url.json. In a job on the image the run builds, it adds one right before the first command that runs ASH, which prints from inside the image a one-line record of the installed ASH: its version, its direct_url.json if it has one, the number of its package files and one SHA256 of their paths and SHA256s, and the SHA256 of its METADATA and entry_points.txt. The fixture's copy of run-ash-security-scan.yml gets one counted step, right after its one uvx --reinstall step (the scan), that prints the record of the ASH the scan ran, even when the scan failed; the repository's own workflow is not changed.
  • Each runner starts with an environment built from nothing: a new, empty home directory, a PATH of the directory that holds the runner, then a fixed system PATH, LANG, the tool download cache of its pytest session (the runs and the controls each have their own), and only the variables that runner needs. An ash that records that it ran is first on the test process's own PATH, and the session fails if any pipeline reached it.
  • Each launch has a time limit, the matrix row's launch_timeout. While the runner runs, the test process is the child subreaper of what it starts, so a process whose parent ends stays below the test process, and the runner's environment holds a marker of that launch's own, which the processes it starts inherit unless they clear their environment. When the runner ends, or runs out of time, the processes in its process group, those the launch started below the test process, and those whose environment holds the marker get SIGTERM, and those still running after a short grace SIGKILL. Then the containers the Docker daemon gained while the runner ran are removed, before the next block runs. If any of them is left, the test fails. A process that another service starts for the run, and that gets neither the marker nor a new container, is not found.
  • Each Jenkins home stays in pytest's work directory, outside the output directory the workflow uploads; only the build's log, build.xml, JUnit record, and archive are copied out.
  • The runners and tools are pinned by SHA256 and the images by digest, in tests/integration/docs/ci_runners/runners.toml and the Jenkins plugin lists beside it, and every image the leg pulls is checked against those digests and the images the run builds.

docs.title: What a run checks
docs.text:
Every runnable block expects ASH to exit 2 on the fixture's findings. A test passes only when its run shows all of these:

  • the runner's own result: the jobs that gate on findings fail under act, gitlab-ci-local exits non-zero and the exit code its gate job reads is 2, the build fails under Jenkinsfile Runner and circleci local execute, and the BUILD phase fails under the CodeBuild agent;
  • ASH's verdict line in the log, such as ERROR (2) Exiting due to 3 actionable findings found in ASH scan, with the count the fixture plants: two findings in app.py, one more in changed.py on a pull request or merge request branch, and only that one for a scan of the changed files;
  • the reports where the page says the pipeline keeps them: act's artifact store, the GitLab job's artifacts, the Jenkins build's archive and JUnit record, the CodeBuild agent's artifact and report directories, and for CircleCI a copy that the rewrite adds as the job's last step, because circleci local execute discards the project directory when the job ends;
  • the actionable findings by file in ash_aggregated_results.json;
  • under act, what the stubs recorded: the SARIF file each upload was given (on the sharded example only the last upload's, which must be the SARIF the merge step wrote), the check run the reusable scan workflow publishes, with one failed test per actionable finding, and, for a pull request, its comment; and each step that stops workflow commands printing its resume token;
  • which ASH ran. Each printed direct_url.json must name the wheel the leg built, with its SHA256, or the head commit of the base repository, one for each print in each run of its job, and the wheel file must still have that SHA256 after the run. No line of the log may show ASH downloaded from a package index: a pypi.org or files.pythonhosted.org URL that names it, a Downloading line for it, or uv's + automated-security-helper== line for a copy that came from neither a file nor a git URL. The job on the image the run builds is checked by its own record instead: its version, its package files (less bytecode and the revision file that each build writes for itself), its METADATA, and its entry points must match those of the wheel built from the same checkout, a direct_url.json in it must name a local file with that wheel's name, and the runner's log must name the image the run built, as its build recorded it.

After the runs, tests/integration/docs/ci_runners/check_junit.py checks that the leg ran one test for each block the census gives it, and skipped none. The negative controls in tests/integration/docs/test_docs_ci_runners_can_fail.py run the first block of each leg, page, and install mechanism, the wheel or a git commit, with an install that cannot succeed: a wheel path that does not exist, or a commit no repository has. In each, the job's script must start, a line it prints must name the broken input with the installer's refusal of it, and the run must fail with no verdict line, so a pipeline that fails for another reason is not taken for one that ran the ASH under test. The job on the image the run builds installs nothing, so it has no control. One more control checks that the outer ash never ran, and check_junit.py --controls checks that every control ran.

The runs start containers that are given the Docker socket, as the CodeBuild agent and circleci local execute do, so the tests refuse to run anywhere but a GitHub-hosted runner unless DOCTEST_CI_RUNNERS_ANYWHERE=1 is set. The refusal is an error, not a skip. Set the variable only on a machine you can throw away, whose Docker daemon nothing else uses: each launch removes every container the daemon gained while it ran. A launch also needs Linux's child subreaper and /proc, and is refused before it starts on a host without them. Unless pytest is started with pytest --run-ci-runners, it deselects these tests, so the unit and integration jobs never run them. Listing the tests starts no runner, and shows which blocks each leg runs:

uv run pytest tests/integration/docs/test_docs_ci_runners.py --run-integration --run-ci-runners --collect-only -q -n 0

docs.title: What the runs do not check
docs.text:
• Job permissions and GitHub's services. act gets no token, and the actions that write to GitHub (code scanning uploads, pull request comments, and check runs) are replaced by stubs that record what they were given.
  • What GitLab, GitHub, and CodeBuild do with the reports, such as GitLab's merge request widget or a CodeBuild report group. The runs read the files the jobs keep.
  • Other Jenkins agents. The Jenkinsfile runs on Jenkinsfile Runner's built-in node, which an init hook labels linux, on the hosted runner itself.
  • Other CodeBuild images and container mode. The agent runs the pinned aws/codebuild/amazonlinux-x86_64-standard:5.0 build image, and is given neither the host's AWS credentials nor privileged mode.
  • CircleCI's cache and its uploads. The runs check nothing about restore_cache, save_cache, store_test_results, or store_artifacts.

docs.title: Versioned docs
docs.text:
The site is published as versions with mike. Each version is a directory of the gh-pages branch, and versions.json at the root of the branch lists them for the version selector in the site header.

  • Every push to main publishes the version main, titled "main (unreleased)". Its pages say that they describe unreleased code, and link to the latest release. Its version-pinned pages are built from their templates with main for the version, so their install commands install main (@main, git clone --branch main, rev: main), and the notice says so. Where a template needs the release number itself, as in a sample of ash --version output, it writes {{RELEASE}}, which stays the current release number. The static checks report {{RELEASE}} written as the ref of an install command anywhere but a table row or a text block, so the main version cannot install a release.
  • Running the docs workflow by hand on a release tag vX.Y.Z publishes the version X.Y.Z (see Releases and versions). The newest release also gets the latest alias. latest/ is a full copy of it rather than a redirect, and every version names its latest/ page as the canonical one for search engines. A patch release for an older line is published without moving latest.
  • A page of a release that is not the latest shows a notice saying so, with a link to the latest release.
  • Any other tag, such as the floating v3 or a prerelease, publishes nothing.

The deploy also manages the root of the branch. The root index.html redirects to latest/, or to main/ until a release has been published, and every page path of that version has a redirect at the root that keeps the #anchor. So /how-to/install/#install-from-main still works, and so does an old page path that docs/redirects.yml maps, through the redirect the build writes for it. Everything else at the root is removed on each deploy, except .nojekyll, CNAME, and versions.json. To keep another file there, add it to ROOT_KEEP in scripts/docs_versions.py.

That script does all of the publishing. The workflows never run mkdocs gh-deploy, which replaces the whole branch with one unversioned build and so would delete every version; the site check in the lint job fails if one does. strict: true in mkdocs.yml makes every build strict, including the ones mike runs. To preview a page that still has warnings, use mkdocs serve --no-strict.

docs.title: Previewing the versions
docs.text:
mkdocs serve shows one version. To see the version selector and the notices, publish to a local branch and serve that. Unless it is told to push, the deploy only commits to the branch it is given, and a branch other than gh-pages keeps the preview apart from the real site:

uv run python scripts/docs_versions.py deploy --ref refs/tags/v0.0.1 --branch docs-preview
uv run python scripts/docs_versions.py deploy --ref refs/heads/main --branch docs-preview
uv run mike serve --branch docs-preview   # http://localhost:8000/, stop with Ctrl+C
git branch -D docs-preview

The ref only names the version: both commands publish the docs in your working tree.

docs.title: What the versions check does
docs.text:
The build-docs job runs uv run python scripts/docs_versions.py check. It publishes 0.0.1, then 0.0.0, then main to a throwaway branch of the checkout, with every proxy pointing at a port that refuses connections, so a build that needs the network fails. Before publishing it puts stand-ins for an unversioned site at the root of the branch: a stylesheet, a sitemap, a page no version has, and an old page from docs/redirects.yml. The check fails unless:

  • mike list and versions.json show the three versions, with latest on 0.0.1 only, because 0.0.0 is older;
  • every page of every version configures the version selector and loads the theme script that reads versions.json;
  • every page of a release carries the outdated notice, every page of main carries the unreleased one, and no page carries the other;
  • latest/ is a copy of 0.0.1, and the other versions name latest/ as canonical;
  • the version-pinned pages of each release pin that release and no other. On main, outside tables and text blocks, they pin no release, and every install-command form that a page uses in 0.0.1 names main on that page, from @main to refs/heads/main. The committed pages pin the current version, which is neither 0.0.1 nor 0.0.0, so this fails unless every build rendered the pages from their templates;
  • the root redirects every page of latest/, the old page redirects to its place under latest/, and the stand-ins are gone.

It deletes the branch afterwards and never pushes. It prints how many versions, pages, and redirects it checked. tests/unit/test_docs_versions.py plants each defect the check exists for (a missing setting in mkdocs.yml, a template without the notices, aliases that are not copies, a root left unversioned, an older release that takes latest, pinned pages left as committed) on a small site, and requires the check to report it.

docs.title: What a failure means
docs.text: Each static finding is one line: the file and line, the check in brackets, and the problem. Runner failures name the page, the line of the block, the command, the exit code, and the end of the output. A refused save-as reports save-as refused and the reason instead of an exit code. An output sample that does not match reports the first sample line the output lacks, as '<line>' is not in the output of the block at line <N>, with the end of the output.

docs.title: Add a generated reference page
docs.text:
A reference page that restates the code (a list of options, variables, scanners, or tools) is generated, never written by hand. To add one:

  1. Write scripts/generate_<name>.py. It renders the page from the code (the click tree, a pydantic model, or the plugin registry) and writes it under docs/content/reference/. Run as generate_<name>.py --check, it writes nothing, compares what it would write with the committed file, prints a diff, and exits non-zero if they differ. scripts/generate_reporter_docs.py is a complete example: it writes the whole page, accepts generate_reporter_docs.py --check --docs-root <dir>, and keeps its hand-written columns in a table, REPORTER_DOCS, that it requires to cover every registered reporter.
  2. Start the page with a banner that says Generated by scripts/generate_<name>.py and gives the command that regenerates it, uv run python scripts/generate_<name>.py, so a reader who wants to change it knows not to edit it.
  3. Add the script and its page to REFERENCE_PAGES in tests/unit/test_generated_docs_freshness.py. That one entry runs generate_<name>.py --check in the unit suite, so the suite fails when the code changes and the page does not, and checks the banner in the page's first 600 characters.
  4. Add the page to GOLDEN in .github/scripts/check-snapshot-trailers.py, so a commit that changes it needs a Snapshot-Update: trailer.
  5. Add the page to .nav.yml. The static checks then cover it like any other page.

The implementation of all of this is in scripts/docs_checks.py and tests/integration/docs/docs_runner.py. Page paths the checks depend on are constants at the top of docs_checks.py.

docs.title: Releases and versions
docs.text: ASH versions come from commit messages. commitizen reads the subjects on main since the last tag, picks the next version, writes the changelog entry, and rewrites the files that pin the version. A release is a git tag and a GitHub Release: nothing is published to PyPI or to a container registry, so users install ASH from a git URL at a tag (see Install ASH). This page explains each piece, for contributors who need to know what their commit message does and for maintainers who cut releases.

docs.title: Where the version is kept
docs.text:
The version is version in the [tool.commitizen] table of pyproject.toml. [project] version holds the same value: commitizen rewrites both, and tests/unit/test_agent_plugin_ash_version.py fails if they differ. To print it:

uv run cz version --project

An installed ASH reports the version in its package metadata with ash --version.

Other files pin an ASH tag that users install from: the Homebrew formula, the sources of the agent plugins, the install commands in the README and in these docs, the ASH version that each deployment target in deploy/ installs when none is given, and the CodeBuild example in examples/. Each is kept current in one of two ways:

  • It is listed in version_files under [tool.commitizen], and cz bump rewrites the version in it. The release runs cz bump --check-consistency, so a listed file that does not contain the current version fails the release before anything is tagged. After the rewrite, a pre_bump_hooks entry rebuilds the generated agent plugin trees so they land in the same commit.
  • It is a template. See Version-pinned pages.

tests/unit/test_agent_plugin_ash_version.py also walks the whole tree for install references to this repository, such as automated-security-helper.git@v<version>, and fails when one names a version other than the current one. So a new page that pins a release has to be a template or be listed in version_files, or the unit suite fails at the next release. A floating @v3 and a {{VERSION}} placeholder are not version pins and pass.

docs.title: How the next version is chosen
docs.text:
commitizen reads the subject of each commit on main since the last release tag, and the BREAKING CHANGE: footers in their bodies. Pull requests are squash-merged, so each pull request is one commit (see Commit messages and pull request titles). The largest increment wins:

Commit Increment a ! before the colon, or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer major feat minor fix, refactor, perf patch any other type none

If every commit since the last tag has a type with no increment, there is nothing to release: cz bump exits with code 21, and the release job fails.

docs.title: The release line
docs.text:
main carries breaking commits that ship in 3.x, because 4.0.0 is reserved for later packaging work. The RELEASE_LINE value at the top of .github/workflows/ash-create-release.yml controls this. It is committed in the file rather than offered as an input when the workflow runs, so the line a release lands on is decided in reviewed history.

  • 3.x, the current value: when commitizen detects a major increment, the workflow bumps the minor version instead, and its log and run summary name every breaking commit it overrode. Patch and minor increments pass through unchanged. The workflow refuses to run if the current version is not 3.x, and fails if the bump would leave 3.x.
  • auto: commitizen's own choice, so a breaking change produces a major version. To release 4.0.0, the change that lands v4 sets RELEASE_LINE to auto. Once the version is 4.x, 3.x refuses to run, so a value left at 3.x fails rather than capping 4.x.

The commits themselves are not rewritten, so their breaking-change notes still appear in the changelog. A release whose version understates what it changes carries hand-written notes in .github/release-notes/<tag>.md. For example, .github/release-notes/v3.8.0.md lists the behavior changes that 3.8.0 ships as a minor release, with their opt-outs.

To preview a bump locally, without changing anything:

uv run cz bump --dry-run --changelog --increment MINOR   # what RELEASE_LINE 3.x does when it caps a major
uv run cz bump --dry-run --changelog                     # what RELEASE_LINE auto does

The preview shows the curated notes for the next tag, but not the hand-written ## Unreleased notes: the release workflow moves those into the release notes file only when it runs, as described below.

docs.title: What the changelog contains
docs.text:
Each release's entry in CHANGELOG.md has three parts, in this order:

  1. The curated notes from .github/release-notes/<tag>.md, when that file exists. The changelog template, .github/changelog/CHANGELOG.md.j2, includes it under the version heading.
  2. Hand-written notes. Contributors describe user-visible changes under ## Unreleased at the top of CHANGELOG.md. commitizen would replace that section with the generated entry, so before it bumps, the release workflow moves the section's text into .github/release-notes/<next tag>.md, after any curated notes, and removes the section. That file is read as a Jinja template, so the release fails if the section contains {{, {%, or {#.
  3. The generated sections: BREAKING CHANGE, with the text of each BREAKING CHANGE: footer, then Feat, Fix, Refactor, and Perf, with one line per commit and its scope in bold. A commit marked with ! is listed under its own type, or with no heading when its type has none.

Commits of every other type are left out unless they are marked breaking. That includes dependency updates, which Dependabot titles build: or ci:, and changes to CI and tests.

docs.title: How a release is cut
docs.text:
A maintainer runs Actions > ASH - Create Release > Run workflow. The workflow:

  1. applies the release line, and folds the ## Unreleased notes into the release notes;
  2. runs cz bump --changelog --check-consistency, which sets the new version, rewrites the version_files, rebuilds the agent plugin trees, writes the changelog entry, and commits all of it as bump: version <old> → <new>;
  3. renders the version-pinned pages from their templates and regenerates the JSON schemas;
  4. smoke-tests the result (ash --help, ash config validate, and one unit test file);
  5. commits the rest as chore(release): <old> -> <new> on the branch release/v<new>, pushes it, and opens a pull request with that title.

The release pull request goes through the same checks and review as any other. When it merges, the "ASH - Tag and Publish Release" workflow, which reacts to a merged pull request whose title starts with chore(release):, does the rest:

  • It checks that the curated release notes, if any, are in the changelog entry, and refuses to publish otherwise.
  • It creates the tag v<version> and a GitHub Release at the head of main, with the version's changelog entry followed by GitHub's generated notes.
  • It moves the floating major tag (see Tags).

It does not start the docs workflow. See The documentation site for how a release's docs version is published.

docs.title: The release App
docs.text:
A pull request opened with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN does not start its own required checks ("ash / SAST, SCA, and IaC Scan", Validate PR title, required-checks): GitHub creates the runs in an approval-required state, and a maintainer with write access has to select Approve workflows to run in the pull request's merge box. The release pull request says so in its description when that happens. To have the checks start on their own, the workflow opens the pull request with a GitHub App token instead. A repository admin sets that up once:

  • A GitHub App owned by the organization, with no webhook and no callback URL.
  • Its only repository permission is Pull requests: Read and write; GitHub adds metadata read. No Contents permission: the branch push stays on GITHUB_TOKEN, and the App only opens the pull request. The workflow requests exactly pull-requests: write when it mints the token, so the mint fails if the App lacks it.
  • The App installed on this repository only.
  • Two repository secrets under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions: RELEASE_APP_CLIENT_ID, the App's Client ID (not the numeric App ID), and RELEASE_APP_PRIVATE_KEY, the full contents of a private key's .pem file.

The workflow uses the App only when both secrets are set. With one or neither, it logs a warning and falls back to GITHUB_TOKEN. With both set, a misconfigured App (not installed, wrong permission, or bad key) fails the job at the token step, before anything is bumped or pushed, rather than falling back. A working setup shows the Mint a GitHub App token step running, the App as the pull request's author, and the checks starting without an approval banner.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
Every release has an exact tag, v<version>, which the release workflows create once and never move. To install the same ASH every time, pin a git URL or a GitHub Actions reference to an exact tag, or to a commit SHA, which cannot move at all.

The floating major tag, v3 for the 3.x releases, points at the newest release of that major version. The tag workflow moves it with the GitHub API to the commit it tagged, creating it if it does not exist yet. A reference to @v3 therefore picks up every 3.x release, including the minor releases that carry breaking changes under the release line above.

The tag workflow only tags main. A patch release for an older version is built on a branch from that version's tag, outside the workflow: 3.7.1, for example, is built on 3.7.0, is not in main's history, and has no entry in main's CHANGELOG.md. When such a release is the newest one, v3 points at it, so v3 can name a commit that is not on main, and the version that main reports can be lower than the newest tag.

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The site is versioned. Each push to main publishes the version main. A release tag does not publish anything by itself. The docs workflow, run by hand on a release tag, publishes a version named after the release: v3.8.0 publishes 3.8.0. The newest release also moves the latest alias, which is where the site root and search engines send readers, so a release changes what most readers see. A patch release for an older line, built outside the workflow as described under Tags, publishes its version when the docs workflow is run on its tag and leaves latest where it is. The floating major tag publishes nothing. How the versions are built and checked is in Testing the documentation.

A tag that the tag workflow creates is created with GITHUB_TOKEN, and a push made with that token starts no workflow, so the docs workflow never runs on it, and the tag workflow does not start it. To publish a release's docs version, or to publish it again if the version is missing, run the docs workflow from Actions > Docs Deploy > Run workflow, choosing the release tag as the ref. Running it on main publishes main again.

A tag pushed by hand runs the docs workflow as it is at the tagged commit. For a tag on a commit from before the site was versioned, that is the old workflow, whose mkdocs gh-deploy --force force-pushes a single unversioned build as a commit with no parent, so every published version disappears from gh-pages along with its history. That applies to pushing the floating v3 by hand while it points at such a commit, and to a patch release built on a release from before versioning. A ruleset on gh-pages that blocks force pushes stops it; the versioned deploy only ever fast-forwards the branch. Without one, recover by running the docs workflow again on main and on each release tag whose version should exist, in any order: whichever release is newest takes latest.

docs.title: Version-pinned pages
docs.text:
A page that shows an install command pinned to the current release is generated from a template. The template has the same name plus .template (for example README.md.template), and the rendered page is committed beside it. A template has two placeholders:

  • {{VERSION}} is the ref an install command uses, written after a v where the command names a tag: @v{{VERSION}}, rev: v{{VERSION}}.
  • {{RELEASE}} is the current release number, for text that needs the number itself: what ash --version prints, the release that this repository's generated files pin, a release named in a table.

Both render as the release version at a release, so the committed page shows the same number in both places. They differ only on the docs site's main version, described below.

scripts/version_template_manager.py generate renders the template of each file listed in its target_files over that file. The release workflow runs it after the bump. Run it with uv run, which reinstalls the project after a version change: the script takes the version from the installed package's metadata before it looks at pyproject.toml.

uv run python scripts/version_template_manager.py list       # the templates it renders
uv run python scripts/version_template_manager.py generate   # render them over their pages

The docs site renders these templates as well, through the mkdocs hook docs/hooks/install_refs.py. When it builds a release's docs it renders them with that release's version, which gives the committed page. When it builds the main version it renders them with main: v{{VERSION}} becomes main, so @v{{VERSION}} becomes @main, git clone --branch v{{VERSION}} becomes git clone --branch main and rev: v{{VERSION}} becomes rev: main; refs/tags/v{{VERSION}} becomes refs/heads/main; and a bare {{VERSION}} becomes main. {{RELEASE}} becomes the current release number, which is what an install of main reports. Any other build, such as mkdocs serve, shows the committed pages.

So write every sentence around {{VERSION}} to read correctly with either a release or main in its place ("installs ASH v{{VERSION}}", not "installs the v{{VERSION}} release"), and use {{RELEASE}} only where the number has to stay a release number. Never write {{RELEASE}} as the ref of an install command, in any of the forms scripts/version_template_manager.py lists in INSTALL_REF_FORMS (@v, --branch v, rev: v, refs/tags/v, a flake ref, --ash-revision-to-install v, ash-version: v): the main version would then install a release. The docs checks report one anywhere except a table row or a text block, which may name the release because neither is a command a reader runs.

Edit the template, not the rendered page: generate overwrites the page, so an edit made only to the page is lost at the next release. tests/unit/test_version_template_round_trip.py renders every template with the current version on each pull request and fails when the result differs from the committed page, so the two cannot drift in the meantime. To add a templated page, add it to target_files, write its .template file with {{VERSION}} and, where it needs one, {{RELEASE}}, render it with generate, and commit both files. The round-trip test also fails when a rendered template still contains something shaped like a placeholder, such as a misspelled {{RELASE}}. Avoid the script's convert action: it rewrites the template of every file in target_files from its rendered page, and turns every version reference it finds into the placeholder, including deliberately older ones.

scripts/version_bump.py and scripts/build_integration.py are not part of the release process. version_bump.py changes only the first version = line of pyproject.toml, so using it leaves [tool.commitizen] version behind; bump with commitizen instead.

docs.title: Test your change
docs.text: This page covers running the tests in a development checkout, the integration and snapshot tests, the rules the test suite enforces on new tests, and how to try an MCP change before you open a pull request. It assumes the setup in Contribute to ASH, with both extras installed.

docs.title: Run the test suite
docs.text:
uv run pytest

This runs every test under tests/, spread across one pytest-xdist worker per logical CPU (-n auto in pytest.ini), and writes a JUnit report to test-results/. It does not measure coverage: pytest.ini carries no coverage options, so a run passes or fails on its tests alone. Integration tests are skipped; see Integration tests.

To run in one process, which pytest --pdb and ordered print output need, pass pytest -n 0.

docs.title: Run part of the suite
docs.text:
Name a directory, a file, or a test:

uv run pytest tests/unit/config
uv run pytest tests/unit/cli/mcp/test_progress_monitor.py -n 0

tests/utils/selection.py chooses tests by marker, by keyword, or by what changed, and runs pytest on them with the Python that runs it. Run it from the repository root; --help lists its options, and it passes any option it does not know to pytest:

uv run python -m tests.utils.selection --keyword suppression --exclude-marker slow tests/unit/config
uv run python -m tests.utils.selection --changed --base-branch main

python -m tests.utils.selection --changed --base-branch <branch> runs the test files that differ from that branch (main when the option is left out), and the whole suite when no test file differs. Its functions can also be imported, for example from tests.utils.selection import get_changed_files, run_selected_tests.

docs.title: Measure coverage
docs.text:
CI's unit-test job splits each operating system and Python version into eight shards. A shard runs every eighth test file and measures coverage of automated_security_helper/ without a threshold. The unit-coverage job then combines the eight shards of each operating system family at Python 3.12 and fails when total coverage is under 80%. The unit-test step passes the options itself (.github/actions/run-unit-tests/action.yml); .coveragerc says what to measure and where to write the reports, and sets no threshold. To run the whole suite with the same options and the threshold:

ASH_REQUIRE_CDK_EXTRA=1 ASH_REQUIRE_SYMBOLS_EXTRA=1 uv run pytest \
  --cov=automated_security_helper --cov-config=.coveragerc \
  --cov-report=term-missing --cov-fail-under=80

ASH_REQUIRE_CDK_EXTRA and ASH_REQUIRE_SYMBOLS_EXTRA make a test that needs a missing extra fail instead of skipping. The threshold is for the full suite. To see the coverage of a partial run, pass the pytest --cov options without pytest --cov-fail-under, which would fail the run on the code it did not exercise. pytest --cov-report=html writes an HTML report to test-results/coverage_html.

docs.title: Where tests live
docs.text:
Directory What it holds tests/unit/ Unit tests, laid out like the package tests/integration/ Tests that run real scanners, real ash processes, sandboxes, or other host features; skipped unless you pass pytest --run-integration tests/snapshot/ Snapshot tests of what ASH prints and writes tests/test_data/ Scanner input and sample results. It is test input, so ruff does not lint it tests/utils/ Test helpers, including iter_repo_files and the walk guard described below, and the test-selection tools selection.py and optimization.py tests/infrastructure/ A CDK stack for testing offline mode by hand in an isolated AWS VPC; it needs an AWS account and is not part of any test run

tests/conftest.py provides the shared fixtures. Use pytest's tmp_path or the ash_temp_path fixture for files a test writes; ash_temp_path is a fresh directory under tests/pytest-temp/, which is gitignored and removed after the test. The test_plugin_context fixture builds a PluginContext with the default configuration and source, output, and work directories under ash_temp_path. Set environment variables with pytest's monkeypatch.setenv, which restores them after the test, or with the temp_env_vars fixture, a wrapper over it: temp_env_vars(NAME="value") sets each variable to str(value), and after the test each one is back to its previous value, or unset if it had none.

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
A test is an integration test when its path is under tests/integration/ or it carries the integration marker. A test marked slow is skipped unless you pass pytest --run-slow. Both flags only lift the skip; they do not collect anything the default run does not. To run the suite the way the integration-test CI job does:

uv run pytest tests/integration tests/unit/cli/mcp/test_source_delivery_scan_e2e.py \
  --ignore=tests/integration/docs --run-integration --run-slow -n 0

The job runs tests/integration/docs, the docs examples, as a separate step; see Test the documentation.

Some integration tests run a scanner binary and skip when it is not installed. CI installs them first, and turns a missing one into a failure:

uv run ash dependencies install --tool actionlint --tool cfn-lint --tool cfn-guard

Binary tools go to ~/.ash/bin, where ASH looks for them.

Other tests need something on the host, and run in their own CI jobs:

  • tests/integration/sandbox/ needs a sandbox backend: bubblewrap, firejail, or Landlock on Linux, sandbox-exec on macOS. Each test skips when its backend cannot run (the sandbox escape job requires them).
  • tests/integration/converters/ runs on macOS and Windows in the converter-integration job, as well as in integration-test.
  • Snapshot tests of output that only a real container runtime or Nix can produce live in tests/snapshot/container/runtime/. They are deselected, not skipped, unless you pass pytest --run-container-snapshots or pytest --run-nix-snapshots; the scan jobs that have the runtime pass them. To update them, build the image (or install Nix) and run the module with its flag plus pytest -n 0 --snapshot-update; each module's docstring lists the environment variables it reads.

docs.title: Snapshot tests
docs.text:
What ASH prints and writes is pinned by snapshot tests, so a change to user-visible output fails CI until someone has looked at it and recorded why it changed. The tests are under tests/snapshot/ and use syrupy. Each test module's snapshots are in the __snapshots__/ directory next to it.

Snapshots must be identical on every machine. The snapshot and text_snapshot fixtures pass output through one normalizer, SnapshotNormalizer in tests/snapshot/support/normalize.py, which masks values that change from run to run (temporary paths, the repository root, the home directory, IDs, and versions). The fixtures also pin the terminal (100 columns, no color, and no TTY) and unset the CI variables that change ASH's output. Do not normalize inside a test. If a test produces a value that varies, register it with the normalizer (add_root, add_literal) or extend the normalizer, with a test in tests/snapshot/test_snapshot_normalizer.py that shows what it masks.

Time is not masked. When output contains the wall clock, pin it with the pinned_clock fixture, or pin_clock in tests/snapshot/support/fixture_model.py for a module that fixture does not cover. Only when the time cannot be pinned, and the test has been shown to differ between runs or time zones (run it several times, and with TZ set to Pacific/Kiritimati and to America/Adak), turn masking on for that test or module with the snapshot_masking marker. tests/snapshot/conftest.py describes what each of its switches masks:

import pytest

pytestmark = pytest.mark.snapshot_masking(mask_instants=True, mask_durations=True)

When output really differs by platform, render every variant on every operating system and snapshot each under its own name, for example text_snapshot("md")(name="windows"). Do not skip a snapshot test on some platforms: a skipped variant is never compared, and its snapshot looks unused to the runs that skip it.

docs.title: Update a snapshot
docs.text:
1. Run the snapshot tests and read the diff that syrupy prints:

    uv run pytest tests/snapshot

  2. Decide whether the new output is what you intended. If it is not, fix the code.

  3. If it is, rewrite the snapshots of the tests you changed, in one process:

    uv run pytest tests/snapshot/cli/test_snapshot_cli_help.py -n 0 --snapshot-update

    Under xdist, several workers rewrite the same snapshot file at once and the last one drops the others' snapshots without an error, so always pass pytest -n 0 here. 4. Review the change file by file with git diff -- '**/__snapshots__/**'. 5. Commit the code change and its snapshots together, with a trailer that says why the output changed:

    git commit --trailer "Snapshot-Update: the summary table now shows suppressed findings"

The snapshot-trailers job fails when a golden file changed in a commit that has no non-empty Snapshot-Update: trailer. Golden files are the snapshot files, the MCP tool-surface golden, the generated JSON schemas, the generated reference pages, and the generated MCP tool reference; the full list, with the reason for each entry, is the GOLDEN table in .github/scripts/check-snapshot-trailers.py. The trailer has to be on a commit that changed the file, so a follow-up commit that only adds it does not count. If the change is in your latest commit, run git commit --amend --no-edit --trailer "Snapshot-Update: <why>". If it is in an earlier commit, run the git rebase command that the failing job prints, which amends only the commits that touched the file. Then push with git push --force-with-lease.

CI never updates snapshots: tests/snapshot/conftest.py refuses pytest --snapshot-update when CI or GITHUB_ACTIONS is exactly true, and tests/snapshot/test_snapshot_policy.py fails if any workflow, action, script, or pytest configuration passes it. A missing snapshot fails, and so does a snapshot that no test asserts any more. syrupy cannot see the snapshots of a test module you deleted or renamed, so check-snapshot-trailers.py --orphans checks that every file under a __snapshots__/ directory belongs to a test module next to it, and that no __snapshots__/ directory is empty. When you rename a module, move its snapshots; when you delete one, delete its snapshots, with a trailer either way. The orphan check reads the file list from git, so it needs a git checkout, and it does not look at directories git ignores.

docs.title: Rules the suite enforces on new tests
docs.text: The unit suite runs under xdist on 25 CI legs, so a test that depends on what another test left behind fails on some legs and not others. No marker takes a test out of the parallel run, so every test has to be safe beside the others; to debug one in a single process, pass pytest -n 0. The suite guards against two such dependencies, keeps the install receipts that tests write out of your home directory, refuses test modules that hold no test, and needs a git checkout.

docs.title: Tests that walk a directory
docs.text:
tests/unit/test_repo_walkers_skip_scratch.py reads every module under tests/, and every function in scripts/ and .github/scripts/ that a test reaches, and fails on any directory walk (rglob, a glob with **, os.walk, os.fwalk, Path.walk, or shutil.copytree) that can enter a directory other runs create and delete: tests/pytest-temp, .ash/ash_output, .venv, or a node_modules next to a tracked package.json. It also fails on a walk whose directory it cannot work out. Other workers create and remove directories under tests/pytest-temp all the time, so a walk there races them.

To list the repository's files, use git ls-files. To walk a tree, use iter_repo_files from tests/utils/helpers.py: it prunes tests/pytest-temp before os.walk descends, and takes skip_dirs for other directories to leave out. Walks under tmp_path, ash_temp_path, or a tempfile directory are private to the test and pass. A walk the guard cannot resolve but that is safe goes in the _EXEMPT table in that test file, keyed by file, function, and the walked expression, with the reason; an entry that no longer matches a flagged walk fails the suite too.

docs.title: State that outlives a test
docs.text:
Some objects are process-wide: the uv tool runner, the memos of tool-version and executable lookups, and the plugin registry. A test that changes them changes them for every later test on the same worker. Autouse fixtures in tests/conftest.py restore them after each test:

  • _restore_process_wide_tool_state restores the uv tool runner, the lookup memos, and the plugin manager's registrations and event handlers. It keeps a successful tool version answer, because those probes are slow.
  • _no_scanned_tree_scope_outlives_its_test fails a test that leaves a scanned-tree scope active.
  • _restore_ash_logger_switches restores the ash logger's level, propagation, and disabled flag, which any logging.config.dictConfig call can change.

The fixtures limit the damage; they do not make every patch safe. Build the object under test before you patch, and patch the module's own reference, for example monkeypatch.setattr(module_under_test, "subprocess", fake_subprocess), rather than subprocess.run, which every caller in the process shares, including the uv runner's own probes. To fake a tool's version, patch UVToolRunner.get_tool_version, which never reaches the memo.

docs.title: Each test's home directory
docs.text: Every test runs with a home directory of its own. tests/conftest.py points HOME, USERPROFILE, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_STATE_HOME, and XDG_CACHE_HOME at an empty temporary directory for each test, and at another for the whole run before tests are collected, which is where a path that a module computes from the home at import time points. UV_CACHE_DIR stays on the cache uv would use for you, so a test that runs uv does not download again. uv's tool and Python directories follow XDG_DATA_HOME into the test's home on Linux and macOS; on Windows they are under %APPDATA%, which is not moved. The tools ash dependencies install puts in ~/.ash/bin are out of reach too, so the integration tests that need one skip. Set ASH_BIN_PATH to that directory to use them; the run's header says so when the directory has tools. Mark a test @pytest.mark.real_home to give it the values the run started with, and use the developer_home and developer_environment fixtures to read them.

docs.title: Tests that install tools
docs.text: An install by ash dependencies install or the pinned-tool installer writes a receipt under ~/.ash/install-receipts. An autouse fixture sends each receipt that a test writes in the test process to a directory under pytest's base temporary directory instead. A child process does not inherit that, so a second autouse fixture fails a test that starts a tool-installing child, ash dependencies install or a child that calls install_pinned_tool, with the developer's HOME or with no HOME. Give such a child an environment with HOME, and USERPROFILE on Windows, set to a temporary directory.

docs.title: Test module names
docs.text: Every tracked test_*.py file under tests/ must define a test that pytest can collect. A helper or a tool goes in tests/utils/ under a name that does not start with test_; tests/unit/test_test_selection_tool_location.py fails otherwise.

docs.title: Tests need a git checkout
docs.text: The walk guard, the docs checks, and the orphan check list files with git, so the unit suite fails in a directory that is not a git work tree. Run it in a clone.

docs.title: Test an MCP change locally
docs.text:
The MCP server is ash mcp. Its tests are in tests/unit/cli/mcp/ and tests/snapshot/mcp/:

uv run pytest tests/unit/cli/mcp tests/snapshot/mcp

To try the server from a client, have the client start it from your checkout with uv run. Add a server entry like this one to the client's MCP configuration; where that file is depends on the client (see Run the MCP server):

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash-dev": {
      "command": "uv",
      "args": ["run", "--directory", "/path/to/automated-security-helper", "ash", "mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Replace the path with your checkout's. The server runs your working tree's code, so restart it in the client after each change. uv run --directory makes the checkout the server's working directory, so give the scan tools absolute paths: a relative path, and the result tools' default output directory .ash/ash_output, resolve inside the checkout. Do not point the client at a package name instead: the automated-security-helper name on PyPI belongs to an unrelated project.

To check the server without a client, list its tools over stdio with the MCP Python SDK, which the project installs. Save this as a script and run it from your checkout with uv run python, so that ash is the checkout's; in an activated environment, python is enough:

import asyncio

from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client


async def main() -> None:
    server = StdioServerParameters(command="ash", args=["mcp"])
    async with stdio_client(server) as (read, write):
        async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
            await session.initialize()
            tools = await session.list_tools()
            for tool in sorted(tools.tools, key=lambda tool: tool.name):
                print(tool.name)


asyncio.run(main())

It prints the name of every tool the server registers, which the MCP tools reference describes.

If you changed what a client sees (a tool, its description or schema, a resource, or a prompt), regenerate the committed files that record it:

  1. .github/actions/validate-mcp/tool_surface.golden.json pins the server's tool, resource, and prompt lists. tests/unit/cli/mcp/test_mcp_wire_golden_in_process.py compares it with the server on every unit-test leg, and an install job compares it with a live server through the MCP Inspector. Regenerate it with uv run python .github/actions/validate-mcp/compare_tool_surface.py --update, which needs the MCP Inspector's mcp-inspector command on your PATH (CI installs @modelcontextprotocol/inspector version 2.8.0 with npm).
  2. The MCP tool reference, for the agent plugins and for this site, is generated: uv run python scripts/generate_mcp_tool_reference.py.
  3. The agent plugin trees copy that reference: uv run --project ash-agent-plugins/agentic-coding/transpiler agentic-plugins build.

The tool-surface golden and the generated references are golden files, so the commit that changes them needs a Snapshot-Update: trailer (see Snapshot tests).

docs.title: See why a scanner did not run
docs.text:
The scan phase tracks every registered scanner from registration to the final results. Run with --verbose to see each checkpoint in the log: the registered scanners, which are enabled and why each other one is not, the task queue, which scanners completed, and whether every registered scanner is in the results:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress --verbose

In a checkout whose environment is not activated, put uv run in front. The command exits with 2 here because the scan has findings. A registered scanner that is missing from the results at the end is added to them with no findings and the status SKIPPED, MISSING, or ERROR, so a dropped scanner shows in the summary rather than disappearing. An enabled scanner that gets no task in the queue does not run in that scan, and nothing queues it again: the log line Found <n> enabled scanners with no task: <names> names it, and the completeness check reports it with the reason "Scanner was expected to be queued but was not found in task queue". A scanner the scan leaves out is SKIPPED in the results, and the check records it as excluded with the reason it was left out: "Scanner excluded during filtering: not in enabled scanners list" when --scanners does not name it, or "Scanner excluded during filtering: excluded from this run (--exclude-scanners)" when --exclude-scanners does. The tracking is ScannerValidationManager in automated_security_helper/models/scanner_validation.py, called from automated_security_helper/core/phases/scan_phase.py; its tests are tests/unit/models/test_scanner_validation*.py and tests/unit/core/phases/test_scan_phase_validation_*.py.

docs.title: Design, UX, and developer experience review
docs.text:
Review date: October 14, 2026.

Applied skills: high-end-visual-design, animation-vocabulary, ui-ux-pro-max. Scope: every interaction surface in ASH. The surface inventory records the implementation and contract of each interface. The design system is the source of truth for future changes.

docs.title: Direction
docs.text:
Cloudscape sets the colors, typography, containers, controls, and status roles. The requested AWS direction overrides the visual skill's generic font, border, and floating-navigation defaults.

  • Open Sans for the website and HTML reports; native fonts in terminals and GitHub.
  • Neutral surfaces, blue actions, separate severity colors.
  • Flat 16px containers and 8px inputs; shadows on overlays.
  • Text identity without a custom logo.
  • Short labels, commands, factual bullets, and sentence-case headings.
  • Build with <3 at Amazon Web Services in human-facing footers.

The homepage uses Anime.js 4.5.0 (MIT) for local SVG motion. Phosphor icons use MIT; Open Sans uses the SIL Open Font License. Licenses ship with the assets.

docs.title: Navigation architecture
docs.text:
The homepage has four routes: Overview, Documentation, Scanners, and Integrations. Search, theme, and GitHub are separate utilities. At narrower widths, a native navigation dialog supplies the same routes, a close action, and access to the complete documentation drawer.

The handbook groups pages by the reader's task:

Group Reader's question Destination Start here How do I get my first scan? Installation, concepts, language coverage, local execution, migration Scan & triage What ran, what matters, and how do I respond? Configuration, reports, suppressions, scanner and reporter catalogs Integrate ASH Where does this fit in my workflow? CI, pre-commit, AI assistants, MCP, AWS destinations Extend ASH How do I add a capability? Plugin architecture, development, examples, community plugins Reference What is the exact command or interface? CLI, generated options, Python API, glossary Contribute & maintain How do I change ASH safely? Contribution, design, metrics, validation, testing Help How do I recover? FAQ, troubleshooting, uv installation, support

All 78 pages in the previous navigation are retained at their original paths. The MCP tool reference, HTTP transport guide, integration landing page, general troubleshooting guide, and this review are explicitly discoverable. Nested groups are reserved for a real family of tasks; users do not need to know the plugin implementation to find a scan or a report.

The README follows the same journey: first scan, review results, integrate, configure, then discover the complete scanner and tool inventories. Reports navigate between findings, scanner coverage, workspace projects when present, and the scan record. The findings explorer makes the current selection, active filters, and available keyboard actions visible.

docs.title: Animation vocabulary and behavior
docs.text:
These definitions are reproduced verbatim from animation-vocabulary:

Term Definition ASH behavior Purposeful animation Motion should serve a function — orient, give feedback, show relationships — not just decorate. Navigation, feedback, and a labeled example scan Cubic-bezier A custom easing curve you define for precise control. Shared curves; no default linear or ease-in-out browser motion Stagger Animate several items one after another with a small delay between each, creating a cascade. 40ms route offsets in the navigation dialog Orchestration Deliberately timing multiple animations so they feel like one coordinated motion. Example scan steps and their completed state Line drawing An SVG path that draws itself in, like an invisible pen tracing it. File-to-scanner and scanner-to-finding routes Press / Tap feedback A subtle scale-down when an element is clicked, so it feels physical. Brief primary and utility button feedback Morph One shape smoothly turns into another shape, e.g. Dynamic Island. The menu glyph changes from two lines to a close symbol Scroll reveal Elements fade or slide into place as they enter the viewport. Once per section, using IntersectionObserver Origin-aware animation An element animates out of its trigger, like a popover growing from the button that opened it instead of from its own center which is the default in CSS. Menu opens from the upper right, near its trigger Interruptible animation An animation that can be smoothly redirected mid-flight instead of finishing first. Reopening cancels the pending close; state does not depend on animationend Reduced motion Respecting the user's prefers-reduced-motion setting by toning down or removing motion. OS preference, persistent pause control, complete static content Role Timing Behavior Press/copy feedback 160ms Transform or opacity, custom easing Menu entrance 320ms Opacity and transform from its origin Menu exit 180ms Faster dismissal; canceled safely on reopening Route stagger 40ms Small cascade with a bounded total duration Section reveal 240ms Once, with 40ms sibling offsets Vector scan 10s File packets, scanner progress, severity packets, report assembly; plays once

Long-lived motion has a persistent pause control and respects a live OS preference change. Reduced motion and JavaScript-disabled views show complete content immediately. Report actions update state without staged transitions. No scroll handler performs layout work.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
The repeatable workflow is in docs/ui-tests/README.md. Review the gallery after generating the source fixtures and building the site.

Checks cover both themes, narrow and wide screens, keyboard-only paths, search and navigation, rapid modal dismissal, clipboard/storage failure, offline font loading, no JavaScript, printing, empty/suppressed/incomplete/workspace results, the real Textual app, canonical document generation, and packaged report assets. Human reporter snapshots and the existing machine/protocol goldens check the rendered output and consumer contracts.

Automated accessibility results supplement visual and keyboard inspection. The GitHub comment preview approximates GitHub's native styling. Live AWS uploads, model calls, and actual container/Nix execution remain the responsibility of the existing integration jobs.

docs.title: Interface design
docs.text:
Shared theme: Cloudscape colors, Open Sans, flat containers, labeled status, and blue actions.

See the interface review for the surface inventory and the design and UX review for the applied skills, navigation architecture, and motion vocabulary.

docs.title: Visual language
docs.text:
Role Dark Light Background #0f141a #f9f9fa Surface #161d26 #ffffff Text #dedee3 #0f141a Muted text #b4b4bb #424650 Action and focus #42b4ff #006ce0 Critical and error #ff7a7a #db0000 High severity #fe6e73 #ce3311 Medium severity #f89256 #855900 Low severity #f2cd54 #855900 Information #42b4ff #006ce0 Success #2bb534 #00802f

automated_security_helper/utils/ui_theme.py is the terminal palette and theme adapter. The site and offline report styles declare their corresponding CSS variables in the site stylesheet under docs/content/assets/stylesheets/ and in ash-report.css. Check all three surfaces when changing a semantic color.

Open Sans is hosted locally under the SIL Open Font License. Reports embed the font and its license. Terminals use the operator's font; GitHub uses native typography.

Light Phosphor icons and Anime.js 4.5.0 use MIT licenses. The homepage loads a reduced local animation module; other pages and reports do not load it. Run npm run vendor:motion in docs/ui-tests to rebuild the module and its notice.

Use one page title, sentence-case headings, 16px reading text, and labels of at least 12px. Containers use 16px corner radii; inputs use 8px. Reserve shadows for overlays and fixed controls. Use blue for actions and focus. Keep severity colors separate from action colors.

The landing display uses 48/56px on desktop and 32/40px on phones. Documentation and reports use the 24/30px page-heading scale.

Navigation uses a full-width 64px header. The handbook groups tasks into Start here, Scan & triage, Integrate ASH, Extend ASH, Reference, Contribute & maintain, and Help. Preserve page URLs when regrouping content. Long paths, rules, and scanner messages wrap; wide tables and snippets use deliberate scroll regions.

docs.title: Outcome and evidence
docs.text:
State Presentation Next action Actionable findings Review required; severity counts and context Review the highest severity findings Partial coverage Scan incomplete; visible coverage notices Resolve missing scanners, targets, converters, or rules and scan again Stale content database Scan needs attention; database notice Review freshness and refresh the affected scanner No completed scanners No scanners completed Check configuration, dependencies, and execution logs Completed coverage with no actionable findings No actionable findings Review coverage and findings below the gate Suppressed finding Explicit Suppressed label and justification Inspect the recorded decision Filter with no matches No findings match this view Clear the search or reset the filters

Color reinforces these labels. It does not replace them. A zero finding count cannot establish complete coverage.

ReportContentEmitter.get_scan_summary() supplies the factual outcome for human reports. Coverage comes from the existing scan completeness helpers. HTML, Markdown, plain text, console summaries, and Bedrock report introductions show the relevant facts before detailed analysis.

Human finding severity uses the same SARIF resolver as scanner totals and the gate: an explicit issue_severity takes precedence over the SARIF level. Human reports copy the flat presentation data rather than changing the cached flat export.

The existing flat export representation and MCP filtering contracts remain compatible. In particular, MCP's actionable_only excludes suppressed findings; use its severity filter when selecting specific severity levels. This is distinct from the threshold-based Actionable count in human reports.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Use real links for navigation and buttons for actions.
  • Keep installation methods in an ARIA tab list with arrow, Home, and End controls.
  • Keep command text selectable and provide feedback after copying.
  • Provide a visible focus indicator and a skip link.
  • Open search with its button or Ctrl/Command + K. Keep focus in the open dialog, and restore it on Escape.
  • Keep mobile navigation usable with touch and keyboard.
  • Provide a documentation Contents control at tablet widths when the sidebar is hidden.
  • Keep focus in open navigation and contents dialogs; return it to their trigger on Escape.
  • Keep installation commands, navigation, and core content available without JavaScript.

The homepage scan illustration and terminal replay are examples. They do not run scanners or imply that a visitor's project has been scanned.

docs.title: Findings explorer
docs.text:
The table prioritizes severity and the finding. At narrower widths, scanner and location move into the selected finding preview and detail screen. The active selection survives sorting, resizing, and returning from details.

Severity, scanner, suppression, and search filters compose. Escape clears the search input and returns focus to the table. The empty state describes a shortcut that works with the current focus.

Suppressions show the finding, configuration destination, and reason. The reason field receives initial focus. Cancel and Save remain visible outside the scrolling dialog body. Validation and save failures preserve the entered values. Saving gives visible confirmation.

Render scanner-controlled labels with literal Text cells. Escape metadata before putting it in Markdown, and select a code fence longer than any fence in a scanner snippet.

docs.title: Reports and GitHub
docs.text:
HTML reports are self-contained. Finding cards expose context on demand, combine filters, announce result counts, and recover from empty views. All findings remain available without JavaScript. Printing includes findings hidden by a screen filter and expands their details.

Generated GitHub comments and Actions summaries use the Markdown reporter. Lead with the outcome and next action. Keep coverage notices visible in compact mode. Collapse detailed findings and explanations so the first screen remains useful.

The scanner table retains its established ten columns because workflow consumers parse it. Detailed findings are ordered by severity and bounded by the existing report option. Indicate when more findings exist and point to the complete report or findings explorer.

Bedrock summaries show the deterministic scan outcome and coverage before generated analysis. Preserve finding indices so a suggestion can be traced to its evidence. Escape report metadata and protect scanner code fences.

docs.title: CLI and automation
docs.text:
Group help by the decision a user is making: scan scope, reports, exit policy, execution, workspace, CI, containers, configuration, or output. Keep option names, defaults, exit codes, and machine output stable when changing presentation.

Console summaries put the verdict and report locations before the reference guide. Finished progress rows stop their running indicators. Respect NO_COLOR and provide readable monochrome output.

MCP clients stop polling on completed, incomplete, failed, or cancelled. Completed and incomplete scans have readable results. An incomplete scan needs coverage review; failed and cancelled scans need status/error review before retrying.

Edit the canonical editor workflow under ash-agent-plugins/agentic-coding/transpiler/_base/ and rebuild the integrations. Generated copies should never diverge from their source.

docs.title: Motion and resilience
docs.text:
The homepage example connects files, scanners, findings, and report formats. File selection highlights the corresponding tools and evidence. Step buttons allow direct inspection; Play, Pause, and Replay control the timeline.

Use the shared custom easing curves and role-based timings: 160ms feedback, 320ms menu entrance, 180ms exit, 40ms stagger, and 240ms section reveal. Animate opacity and transforms, and use IntersectionObserver for reveals. State changes and focus must succeed independently of transition events. The scan example plays once. It pauses outside the viewport, in hidden tabs, and when keyboard focus enters its controls.

The footer's pause setting persists. Reduced motion and global pause render the complete example. File selection and step controls work with reduced motion. All labels, findings, formats, and installation commands remain available without JavaScript.

Local storage, clipboard access, and JavaScript are enhancements. Their failure should leave the content usable. Clipboard failures offer a manual copying path. Offline reports fetch no external resources.

docs.title: Reviewing a change
docs.text:
The local workflow is documented in docs/ui-tests/README.md. Generate fixture previews, build the documentation strictly, run the browser suite, and inspect the gallery before accepting a visual change.

Review narrow and wide screens, both themes, keyboard focus, long text, empty results, suppressed findings, missing dependencies, incomplete coverage, and printing. Automated accessibility checks help find defects; visual and keyboard review remain necessary.

Rendered output is also covered by tests/snapshot/. Follow the snapshot review and commit trailer policy in DEVELOPMENT.md when intentionally updating those outputs.
