docs.title: Verification and practical limits
docs.text:
The browser matrix checks the homepage at 320, 390, 820, and 1440 pixels in both themes; it checks documentation navigation, indexed search, command copying, keyboard tabs, filters, motion, and no-JavaScript behavior. Report checks cover single-project, workspace, and empty models; responsive layout, both themes, offline operation, filtering, clipboard fallback, printing, and no-JavaScript behavior.

Textual tests use the real app and dialogs. Python coverage also checks reporter compatibility, output escaping, critical threshold detail visibility, incomplete converters/rules, terminal table rendering, progress, configuration flows, report stdout, and JSON-RPC stdout safety.

The snapshot suite reviews CLI help, diagnostics, config prompts, dependency installation, plugins, wrappers, terminal views, every reporter, and MCP results. Golden updates must be reviewed and committed under the repository's Snapshot-Update policy.

The package check builds a wheel, confirms all HTML/CSS/JavaScript report assets are included, and renders a report from the installed artifact.

Automated accessibility checks supplement keyboard and visual review. GitHub's exact native styling belongs to GitHub; the local comment preview is an approximation. Container/Nix execution and live AWS uploads are covered by their existing integration jobs rather than by the local visual preview. The flat export's legacy severity representation is retained for consumer compatibility; a versioned normalization change would require its own migration.

docs.title: Advanced Usage
docs.text: This guide covers advanced features and usage patterns for ASH v3.

docs.title: Execution Modes
docs.text: ASH v3 supports four execution modes:

docs.title: Local Mode
docs.text:
ash --mode local
  • Runs the scan in the local Python process
  • Runs every enabled scanner, using the scanner tools installed on this machine; a scanner whose tool is missing is reported MISSING
  • --python-only limits the scan to the scanners that need nothing but Python
  • Ideal for quick checks during development

docs.title: Tools inside the scanned directory
docs.text:
ASH does not start a scanner or any other tool that it finds inside the directory it is scanning. uv run ash scan --source-dir . puts the repository's .venv/bin first on PATH, and npm run does the same with node_modules/.bin, so under either a scanner installed in the project, such as a bandit or semgrep dependency, is part of the repository being scanned. ASH skips it and uses the next copy on PATH, or the one uv tool installs. If there is none, the scanner is reported as MISSING, with the in-tree path in its missing_reason, in the log, and in the message the incomplete scan exits with.

ASH also never finds a tool through the working directory: not through an empty, . or relative PATH entry, and on Windows not through the working directory that CreateProcess and shutil.which search first. Tools on ordinary absolute PATH entries are found, including Homebrew, nix profiles, uv and pipx shims, asdf and mise shims, conda, Program Files, scoop and Chocolatey. Programs ASH and its scanners start are given a PATH without the scanned directory's entries, unless you allow in-tree tools.

To run tools from inside the scanned directory, pass --allow-in-tree-tools (or set "allow_in_tree_tools": true in a --cli-json-input document), or set ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS to 1, true, yes or on. ASH then uses them and logs a warning naming each one. This also covers the scanner sandbox's own programs (bwrap, firejail, readlink and true). A repository's configuration file cannot turn this on, and ash mcp ignores both: an MCP client's scans never run a tool from inside a scanned or delivered directory, so for MCP use, install scanners outside the repository. See Troubleshoot for the message and the fixes.

docs.title: Container Mode
docs.text:
ash --mode container
  • Builds the ASH container image and runs the whole scan inside it
  • Provides full scanner coverage, because the image has every scanner tool installed
  • Requires a container runtime (Docker, Podman, etc.)
  • Ideal for comprehensive scans

docs.title: Precommit Mode
docs.text:
ash --mode precommit
  • A local scan that runs only bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag and npm-audit, plus any scanners named with --scanners
  • Simplified output and no progress display
  • Scans the whole source directory, not only staged or changed files; add --changed-files-only to report only the findings in changed files (every file is still scanned)
  • In workspace mode it changes only the output; it does not narrow the scanner set
  • Ideal for git hooks and quick CI checks

docs.title: Nix Mode
docs.text:
ash --mode nix
  • Runs the scan inside nix develop, whose shell supplies every scanner at a pinned version
  • Always runs offline
  • Linux and macOS; on Windows, run it in WSL2
  • See Nix mode

docs.title: Where ASH looks for a tool
docs.text:
ASH looks up each program it starts, scanners and uv included, in this order:

  1. The directories on your PATH, in order. ASH uses only absolute entries: an empty entry, ., or a relative directory is skipped, and a command is never found through the current working directory. On Windows, ASH tries the names with .exe, .bat, and .cmd before the bare name.
  2. ASH's bin directory: the directory in ASH_BIN_PATH, or ~/.ash/bin if it is not set or is empty. This is where ash dependencies install puts tools, so you do not need to add it to PATH.
  3. /usr/local/bin, except on Windows.

Only an executable file counts. In each of these directories, a file of the tool's name without the execute bit, or a directory of that name, is skipped and the search goes on; on Windows, the name's suffix decides instead. ASH remembers a path it finds, for the current PATH and ASH_BIN_PATH, and looks again when either changes, or when that file has been removed or has lost its execute bit.

During a scan, a copy found inside the scanned directory is skipped, and the lookup goes on to the next one: see Tools inside the scanned directory.

docs.title: When a scanner shows MISSING
docs.text:
MISSING means the scanner did not run: ASH did not find its tool, found the tool only inside the scanned directory (see Tools inside the scanned directory), the scanner's own dependency check failed, or the sandbox mode was auto and no sandbox backend works on this machine. (Under a backend you name that does not work, or a sandbox refusal of another kind, the scanner is ERROR instead.) The reason is in the scanner's missing_reason in ash_aggregated_results.json. A MISSING scanner makes the scan incomplete, and by default (fail_on_incomplete_scanners) an incomplete scan exits 1.

For most scanners, ash dependencies install installs the tool. To install one scanner's tool, name the scanner, as in ash dependencies install --tool grype. Four scanners need more:

  • detect-secrets ships with ASH as one of its Python dependencies. Reinstall ASH.
  • cdk-nag runs in ASH's own Python and needs Node.js, which ASH does not install. ash dependencies install --tool cdk-nag installs its Python packages.
  • npm-audit needs Node.js and npm, and yarn or pnpm to audit a yarn.lock or a pnpm-lock.yaml. ASH installs none of them.
  • cfn-nag is a Ruby gem. It needs RubyGems and a C compiler (on Windows, a Ruby DevKit) before ash dependencies install --tool cfn-nag can install it.

If you do not need a scanner, leave it out, as in ash --exclude-scanners npm-audit. It is then recorded SKIPPED, which does not make the scan incomplete.

docs.title: Platform limits
docs.text:
• Windows: semgrep and opengrep are off by default. semgrep is SKIPPED even when you turn it on, because it publishes no Windows build. cfn-nag needs a Ruby DevKit. On Windows on arm64, grype, opengrep and trivy publish no build. ASH does not look for tools in /usr/local/bin.
  • macOS: each release binary ASH downloads (actionlint, cfn-guard, gitleaks, grype, opengrep, syft and trivy) has a pinned build for Intel and Apple silicon. cfn-nag needs a C compiler, such as the one in the Xcode Command Line Tools.
  • Linux: each of those release binaries has a pinned build for x86-64 and arm64. ASH downloads opengrep's glibc build on every Linux system, so on a musl-based distribution such as Alpine it may not run.

A SKIPPED scanner does not make the scan incomplete, so on Windows a scan does not fail for lacking semgrep and opengrep, as long as another selected scanner runs.

docs.title: Custom Plugins
docs.text: ASH v3 supports custom plugins for extending functionality:

docs.title: Creating Custom Plugins
docs.text:
1. Create a Python module with your plugins:
# my_ash_plugins/scanners.py
from automated_security_helper.plugins.decorators import ash_scanner_plugin
from automated_security_helper.base.scanner_plugin import (
    ScannerPluginBase,
    ScannerPluginConfigBase,
)
from pydantic import Field
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Literal


class MyCustomScannerConfig(ScannerPluginConfigBase):
    """Configuration for MyCustomScanner"""

    class Options:
        custom_option: str = Field(default="default", description="Custom option")


@ash_scanner_plugin
class MyCustomScanner(ScannerPluginBase):
    """Custom scanner implementation"""

    name = "my-custom-scanner"
    description = "My custom security scanner"
    version = "1.0.0"

    def scan(
        self,
        target: Path,
        target_type: Literal["source", "converted"],
        global_ignore_paths: List = [],
        config=None,
    ):
        # Implement your scanning logic here
        results = self._run_subprocess(["my-scanner", "--target", str(target)])
        return results
  1. Add your module to ASH configuration:
ash_plugin_modules:
  - my_ash_plugins
  1. Use your custom scanner:
ash --ash-plugin-modules my_ash_plugins

docs.title: Offline Mode
docs.text:
For air-gapped environments:

# Build an offline image
ash build-image --offline --offline-semgrep-rulesets p/ci

# Run in offline mode
ash --mode container --offline

# On a host without network access, run the image without rebuilding it
ash --mode container --offline --no-build

Container mode builds the image before every scan unless given --no-build. Without --force, a build upgrades the OS packages and, offline, downloads the databases and rulesets once per UTC day, and is served from the build cache for the rest of that day, so the first build on a new day needs network access. With --force, every build does all of it again.

An offline image's databases are frozen at build time, and ASH fails a scan whose database is past its bound: grype's 5 days (120h) after it was built, the offline semgrep and opengrep rulesets 30 days after they were downloaded. Rebuild the image (ash build-image --offline) at least that often. To scan with an older image anyway, pass --allow-stale-content-db or set content_db_staleness: warn; the scan then passes and every report names the stale database. See What happens when a database is stale.

docs.title: Which scanners run offline
docs.text:
Offline mode is decided when each scanner runs, from these sources in order:

  1. ASH's offline mode: --offline on ash scan, ASH_OFFLINE=true in the environment, or an image built with ash build-image --offline. It applies to every scanner, and no scanner option turns it off.
  2. A scanner's own options.offline: true (checkov, grype, opengrep, semgrep, syft, trivy, trivy-repo). It runs that one scanner offline while the rest of the scan stays online. npm-audit has the option too, and it makes npm-audit MISSING (or SKIPPED without a lockfile) rather than run it offline; see below.

options.offline: false is the default and means "follow ASH's offline mode". It does not put a scanner back online during an --offline scan; ash config init writes offline: false for every scanner that has the option, so a generated config would otherwise undo the flag.

docs.title: What offline mode turns off
docs.text:
Online and offline, trivy, trivy-repo and syft read no config file from the scanned tree, because a trivy.yaml there can turn on a VEX repository download or client/server mode and a .syft.yaml remote license and package lookups. trivy always gets --config, naming the operator's config_file, else TRIVY_CONFIG when that is a file outside the scanned tree, and an empty config ASH ships otherwise; syft runs from outside the tree and is given only a config_file outside it.

Besides the database and rule downloads, offline mode turns off what the scanners do over the network on their own:

  • Every scanner tool process ASH starts, the version probes of its dependency check included, gets environment variables that turn off each tool's update, version and telemetry checks: semgrep's version check and metrics (SEMGREP_ENABLE_VERSION_CHECK=0, SEMGREP_SEND_METRICS=off), checkov's PyPI update check (CKV_SKIP_PACKAGE_UPDATE_CHECK=true), npm's update notifier (npm_config_update_notifier=false), trivy's version check and telemetry (TRIVY_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK, TRIVY_DISABLE_TELEMETRY), and the update checks of syft and grype. They also turn off the lookups a tool's own config file can enable: syft's remote license searches, maven lookups and vcpkg git clones, and grype's external sources. On a Go module syft does not run the Go toolchain (SYFT_GOLANG_USE_PACKAGES_LIB=false), and the toolchain grype runs gets GOPROXY=off and GOTOOLCHAIN=local, so it downloads no module and no toolchain. The full list is in automated_security_helper/utils/offline_tool_env.py. A scanner set offline by its own options.offline: true while ASH runs online gets them too, on its scan and on the version probes of its dependency check.
  • trivy's version check and telemetry are off whatever disable_telemetry says, through TRIVY_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK and TRIVY_DISABLE_TELEMETRY rather than flags, which a trivy too old to know them would refuse.
  • trivy-repo, and trivy when misconfig is in its scanners, do not run trivy's Terraform checks offline. trivy downloads the source of every module block a .tf file names (from the Terraform registry, with the host's git, or over HTTPS), and has no setting that stops it, so ASH passes trivy --misconfig-scanners with trivy's own default list minus terraform. If that list cannot be read from trivy repository --help (trivy fs --help for trivy), trivy's misconfiguration checks are skipped offline. checkov still checks Terraform. Any git a tool runs offline gets GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=file, so it reaches no remote.
  • npm-audit runs no audit, because npm, pnpm and yarn audit only against the package registry's advisory service: offline npm audit --offline reported no advisories for a lockfile with known ones, pnpm audit --offline sent the dependency list to the registry anyway, and yarn npm audit has no offline mode. Every lockfile it would have audited (a package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock or pnpm-lock.yaml beside a package.json) is listed as not scanned, with the reason, in ash_aggregated_results.json (the scanner's inputs_not_scanned), the console summary, and the "Inputs not scanned" section of ash.summary.md and ash.summary.txt. A workspace scan lists every project's, with workspace-relative paths, in each project's inputs_not_scanned entry in the workspace results, the merged summaries and the workspace console summary. When there is a lockfile, npm-audit is MISSING, as snyk-code is, so the scan fails under the default completeness gate (exit code 1). To scan a Node.js project offline without it, pass --exclude-scanners npm-audit. A project with no lockfile has nothing to audit, and npm-audit is SKIPPED.
  • detect-secrets does not verify candidate secrets with their issuers, whatever the scanned repository's .secrets.baseline or any config says. See What each tier may set.

docs.title: Seeding the semgrep and opengrep rule cache
docs.text:
Offline, semgrep and opengrep read their rules only from a local cache: the directory named by SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR or OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR, which must contain at least one .yaml or .yml rule file. If the variable is unset or the directory has no rule files, that scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1. ASH does not fall back to downloading the rules.

For the container, build the image with --offline. The build downloads each ruleset in --offline-semgrep-rulesets (space-separated, default p/ci) into /deps/.semgrep and /deps/.opengrep and sets both variables:

ash build-image --offline --offline-semgrep-rulesets "p/ci p/python"

For a local scan, download the rulesets yourself while online, using the same URL the image build uses, and record the download time in .ash-rules-fetched-at next to them. ASH reads that file to hold the rules to their 30-day bound; without it, it falls back to the oldest rule file's modification time, which a copy resets.

export SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/ash/semgrep"
export OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/.cache/ash/opengrep"
mkdir -p "$SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR" "$OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR"
for ruleset in p/ci; do
  curl -sSf "https://semgrep.dev/c/${ruleset}" -o "$SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR/$(basename "$ruleset").yml"
done
cp "$SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR"/*.yml "$OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR/"
date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ | tee "$SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR/.ash-rules-fetched-at" \
  > "$OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR/.ash-rules-fetched-at"

ash --mode local --offline

Copy the cache directories to the air-gapped host and export the same two variables there. Repeat the download at least every 30 days, or the scan fails as stale.

Under --sandbox, the sandbox mounts the directory each variable names read-only for its scanner, wherever it is, including under $HOME, which the sandbox otherwise hides. Only the variable in ASH's own environment grants it: a rules path in a scanner's options, which the scanned repository can set, is not mounted, and an empty or relative value grants nothing. A variable naming a file, /, $HOME or a directory that holds $HOME is not mounted either, with a warning; point it at the rules directory itself. If semgrep or opengrep still cannot read its rules, it exits 7 and is recorded ERROR, and the scan exits 1.

docs.title: Customizing Scan Phases
docs.text:
ASH v3 executes scans in phases:

# Run only specific phases (give --phases once for each phase)
ash --phases convert --phases scan

# Skip report generation
ash --phases convert --phases scan

# Include inspection phase
ash --phases convert --phases scan --phases report --phases inspect

docs.title: Using Existing Results
docs.text:
You can generate reports from existing scan results:

# Use existing results file
ash --use-existing --output-dir /path/to/results

# Generate a specific report format
ash report --format html --output-dir /path/to/results

docs.title: Interactive Findings Explorer
docs.text:
ASH v3 includes an interactive TUI for exploring findings:

# Launch the findings explorer
ash inspect findings --output-dir /path/to/results

A finding's detail view shows the code snippet its results hold. For a finding with none, it shows the lines around the finding from its file, but only when the results are in the scanned directory's .ash/ash_output (the default output directory), and only from a regular file inside that directory. A hard link inside the tree counts as a file in it, as it does for the scanners. A FIFO, a device, a path outside the directory, a symlink that leads out of it, or results in any other directory show "(source not shown)".

docs.title: Using Alternative Container Runtimes
docs.text:
# Use Podman instead of Docker
ash --mode container --oci-runner podman

# Use Finch
ash --mode container --oci-runner finch

docs.title: Custom Container Images
docs.text:
ASH does not publish a container image to a public registry. Building it yourself and hosting it in your own registry is the recommended posture, so that the provenance and patching cadence of the image that reads your source code belong to you. See Build and host your own image for the reasoning, the rebuild cadence it commits you to, and offline builds.

# Specify a custom container image
export ASH_IMAGE_NAME="my-registry/ash:custom"
ash --mode container

docs.title: Building Custom Images
docs.text:
# Build a custom image
ash build-image --build-target ci --custom-containerfile ./my-dockerfile

docs.title: Advanced Configuration Overrides
docs.text:
# Complex configuration overrides
ash --config-overrides 'scanners.semgrep.options.config=p/owasp-top-ten'
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "build/", "reason": "Generated files"}]'

docs.title: Adding Suppressions via Config Overrides
docs.text:
# Add a suppression rule
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.suppressions+=[{"rule_id": "RULE-123", "path": "src/example.py", "reason": "False positive"}]'

# Add a suppression with line range and expiration
ash --config-overrides 'global_settings.suppressions+=[{"rule_id": "RULE-456", "path": "src/*.js", "line_start": 10, "line_end": 15, "reason": "Known issue", "expiration": "2025-12-31"}]'

docs.title: Inline code suppressions
docs.text:
You can suppress individual findings directly in your source code using special comments. This is useful when a suppression only applies to a single line and you want the context to live next to the code.

Two directives are supported:

Directive Effect # ash-ignore: <rule-id> [reason] Suppresses the finding on the same line as the comment. # ash-ignore-next-line: <rule-id> [reason] Suppresses the finding on the next line.

The directives are case-insensitive. The reason text is optional but recommended.

# Suppress a specific rule on the same line:
password = os.environ[
    "DB_PASS"
]  # ash-ignore: CKV-SEC-001 loaded from env, not hardcoded

# Suppress a specific rule on the next line:
# ash-ignore-next-line: BANDIT-B105 password variable is a placeholder
password = "changeme"

// Languages that use // comments (JS, TS, Java, C#, Go):
const key = process.env.KEY; // ash-ignore: SEC-KEY env var is safe

// Or suppress the next line:
// ash-ignore-next-line: SEC-KEY env var is safe
const key = process.env.KEY;

Both inline and config-file suppressions use Kind1.inSource in the SARIF output. They are distinguishable by their justification prefix: config suppressions start with "(ASH)" while inline suppressions start with "(ASH inline)".

docs.title: Temporarily Ignoring Suppressions
docs.text:
# Run a scan ignoring all suppression rules, ignore_paths included
ash --ignore-suppressions

# Useful for verifying if suppressed issues have been fixed
ash --ignore-suppressions --output-dir ./verification-scan

docs.title: Programmatic Usage
docs.text:
ASH v3 can be used programmatically in Python:

from automated_security_helper.interactions.run_ash_scan import run_ash_scan
from automated_security_helper.core.enums import ExecutionStrategy, RunMode

# Run a scan
results = run_ash_scan(
    source_dir="/path/to/code",
    output_dir="/path/to/output",
    mode=RunMode.local,
    strategy=ExecutionStrategy.PARALLEL,
    scanners=["bandit", "semgrep"],
    config_overrides=["scanners.bandit.enabled=true"],
    # Return the results even when there are actionable findings
    fail_on_findings=False,
)

# Access scan results
stats = results.metadata.summary_stats
print(f"Found {stats.total} findings, {stats.actionable} actionable")

run_ash_scan takes keyword arguments from its signature only. An unknown one, such as a misspelled fail_on_finding, raises TypeError naming it; earlier versions accepted it and ran the scan without it.

The call returns the aggregated results only when the scan's exit code is 0. Otherwise it ends the way ash scan does, by raising SystemExit with that code (see Exit codes): 2 for actionable findings while fail_on_findings is on, which is the default, and 1 for an incomplete scan, for example a selected scanner whose tool is not installed. That exit 1 is a ScanIncompleteExit, a SystemExit subclass whose incompleteness attribute names what was incomplete (the scanners and converters that did not run, and any stale content databases) and whose results attribute holds the results. A run ASH refuses or gives up (3 for a config that does not validate or files git tracks where the scan writes, 5 for a scanner selection that names nothing, 1 for an error during the scan) raises ScanRefusedExit, a SystemExit subclass whose message attribute is the text ash scan prints for it.

docs.title: Logging to your own handler
docs.text:
ASH logs through the ash logger. A handler your application puts on it stays there when a scan sets up ASH's logging, and it gets ASH's records as written: file names and tool output from the scanned repository in them included, such as a line that starts with :: or holds ##vso[, which a CI runner reads as a command. To have your handler write them as ASH's own console and log file do, with control characters as escapes and CI command lines broken, give it CommandSafeFormatter:

import logging

from automated_security_helper.utils.log import CommandSafeFormatter

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(CommandSafeFormatter("%(levelname)s %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger("ash").addHandler(handler)

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text: Tip: The examples below use pinned versions (@main) for reproducibility. You can also use the v3 floating tag (@v3) to always get the latest stable v3.x release, though pinned versions are recommended for CI/CD.

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
name: ASH Security Scan

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  pull_request:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v3
      - name: Set up Python
        uses: actions/setup-python@v4
        with:
          python-version: '3.10'
      - name: Install ASH
        run: pip install git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@main
      - name: Run ASH scan
        run: ash --mode local
      - name: Upload scan results
        # Also when ASH exits non-zero on findings: without a status function
        # GitHub skips this step after any failed step.
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3
        with:
          name: ash-results
          path: |
            .ash/ash_output/reports
            .ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
ash-scan:
  image: python:3.10
  script:
    - pip install git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@main
    - ash --mode local
  artifacts:
    paths:
      - .ash/ash_output/reports
      - .ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json

Both examples keep scanners/ and converted/ out of the artifact: those hold each tool's raw output, which is not masked.

docs.title: Performance Optimization
docs.text:
# Run scanners in parallel (default)
ash --strategy parallel

# Run scanners sequentially
ash --strategy sequential

# Clean up temporary files after scan
ash --cleanup

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
# Enable debug logging
ash --debug

# Enable verbose logging
ash --verbose

# Disable progress display
ash --no-progress

docs.title: Scanner Validation
docs.text:
ASH v3 includes comprehensive scanner validation that monitors scanner registration, enablement, and execution throughout the scan process. When debugging scanner issues:

  • Check logs for validation warnings about missing or disabled scanners
  • Use --debug to see detailed validation checkpoint information
  • Look for specific reasons why scanners might be disabled (dependencies, configuration, etc.)
  • Run the integration verification test: python verify_integration.py (if available in your installation)

The validation system includes result completeness validation that ensures all originally registered scanners appear in the final scan results, even if they failed or were disabled. This provides complete visibility into scan coverage and helps identify any scanners that may have been silently dropped during the scan process.

For detailed information about the scanner validation system, see See why a scanner did not run in the testing guide.

docs.title: ASH GenAI integration guide
docs.text:
This file tells an AI agent how to run ASH (Automated Security Helper), read its results, and propose suppressions without hiding real problems. Give it to your agent as context, for example as a rules file or a steering file. To save a copy in the current directory:

ash get-genai-guide --output ash-genai-guide.md

The guide ships with every installation of ASH (a wheel or sdist, an install from a git URL, a clone of the repository, and the container images ASH builds), so this writes the copy for the installed version without network access. --from-github downloads it from GitHub instead, from main or from the branch or release tag --branch names.

docs.title: Installation for AI Coding Tools
docs.text: The rest of this file is written for the agent.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• Never report a project as clean unless every selected scanner ran and there are zero actionable findings. A scan that ended incomplete, or with exit code 1, did not run every scanner: name the scanners that did not run, and why.
  • Fix before you suppress. Propose a suppression only for a false positive or a risk the user accepts, with a reason the user agrees with, and never to make a scan pass.
  • Do not change what the scan checks to get a passing result: do not disable scanners, raise severity thresholds, set fail_on_findings: false, add broad ignore_paths, or pass --ignore-suppressions, --no-fail-on-findings, or --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners, unless the user asks for that change.
  • Do not set client_supplied in a config. ASH sets it.
  • Do not add sandbox grants or plugin modules to the repository's config to make a scanner work. They are the operator's settings, and ASH ignores sandbox grants from a config inside the scanned repository.
  • When a scanner is MISSING because its tool is installed only inside the project, install the tool outside the project. Do not pass --allow-in-tree-tools or set ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS unless the user asks you to.
  • Do not make .ash, .ash/ash_output, or any directory under it a symbolic link. ASH refuses to write through one.
  • Do not repeat a detected secret's value in your answers. Refer to the file and line.
  • If a tool, option, or field named here does not exist, the installed ASH is older than this guide. Tell the user, and use what the installed version reports (ash --help, the MCP server's tool list).

docs.title: Run a scan with the MCP tools
docs.text:
When the ASH MCP server is connected, a scan takes three steps:

  1. Call run_ash_scan with source_dir set to the absolute path of the project. It returns at once with a scan_id and status running.
  2. Call get_scan_progress with the scan_id about every 5 seconds until is_complete is true. It is true for every final status: completed, incomplete, failed, or cancelled.
  3. When results_available is true, which it is for completed and incomplete, read the results from output_directory, an absolute path in the progress response.
Final status Meaning What to do completed Every selected scanner ran. Read the results. incomplete The scan finished and its results are readable, but a selected scanner did not run or did not finish, or a content database was too old. Read the results, report incomplete_scanners and stale_content_databases, and say the coverage is partial. failed The scan crashed, left no readable results, or ran longer than the server allows. Report error_message. cancelled The scan was canceled. Say so.

After failed or cancelled, results_available is false, so do not report results for that scan. Once ASH has put the previous scan's results back in the output directory, output_holds_previous_results is true, and the results tools refuse that directory with error_category scan_incomplete until another scan finishes there.

The examples in this section call each tool as a function that takes the tool's arguments and returns its response, a dictionary. A response with success false has an error message instead of the keys below. Adapt the calls to your MCP client:

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Before Analyzing Results - Check Tool Availability: 

# Verify jq is available (preferred method)
command -v jq && echo "✓ jq available (recommended)" || echo "✗ jq not found, will use Python fallback"

Default Tool Priority: 1. jq - Fastest and most efficient (ALWAYS TRY FIRST) 2. Python - Reliable fallback (if jq unavailable) 3. grep/awk - Last resort only (limited functionality)

Recommended Approach for GenAI Tools: 1. For most use cases: Use reports/ash.flat.json (simpler structure, smaller size) 2. For complete data: Use ash_aggregated_results.json (but parse efficiently - see warnings below) 3. For dependencies: Use reports/ash.cdx.json (CycloneDX SBOM) 4. For CI/CD integration: Use reports/ash.junit.xml or reports/ash.csv

File Locations: - Primary Results File: ash_aggregated_results.json (complete but large - 1-10MB+) - Simplified Results: reports/ash.flat.json (recommended for most use cases) - Human Reports: HTML, Markdown, Text (NOT for machine parsing) - Dependencies: reports/ash.cdx.json (CycloneDX SBOM) - Configuration: the ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project; a project's existing .ash/.ash.yaml is read first), YAML with a JSON schema - Suppressions: Defined in configuration file under global_settings.suppressions

Tool Requirements: - Preferred: jq (fastest, most efficient for JSON queries - ALWAYS TRY FIRST) - Fallback: Python 3.x (reliable, widely available) - Last Resort: grep, awk (basic text processing, always available)

docs.title: 1. Always Use JSON Formats for Machine Processing
docs.text:
DO: - Read ash_aggregated_results.json for complete scan results (but see file size warnings below) - Use reports/ash.flat.json for simplified finding structure (recommended for most use cases) - Use reports/ash.sarif for SARIF-compliant tooling - Use reports/ash.cdx.json for dependency analysis

DO NOT: - Parse HTML reports (reports/ash.html) - designed for human viewing only - Parse Markdown summaries (reports/ash.summary.md) - may have formatting inconsistencies - Parse Text summaries (reports/ash.summary.txt) - lossy representation

docs.title: 2. Handle Large Files Efficiently
docs.text:
CRITICAL: ASH result files can be very large (1-10MB+). Always: - Check file size before loading into memory - Use streaming parsers for files >5MB - Extract only the data you need - Consider using simpler formats (ash.flat.json, ash.csv) - Provide progress indicators for large file operations

Example - Check before loading: 

import time

# LOW is stricter than the default MEDIUM, so LOW findings count as actionable too.
# Leave severity_threshold out to use the config's threshold.
scan = run_ash_scan(source_dir="/path/to/project", severity_threshold="LOW")
if scan.get("success") is False:
    raise RuntimeError(scan["error"])

if file_size_mb > 5:
    print(f"Large file detected ({file_size_mb:.1f}MB). Using streaming parser...")
    # Use streaming approach
else:
    # Safe to load into memory
    with open(results_file) as f:
        data = json.load(f)

docs.title: 3. Check Tool Availability
docs.text:
IMPORTANT: Always attempt to use jq first for maximum efficiency, but never assume it's installed. Always: - Check if tools are available before using them - Try jq first (fastest and most efficient) - Provide fallback methods (Python, grep, awk) - Use the most reliable method available - Document which tools are required vs optional

Tool Availability Check: 

import shutil

# Check for jq (PREFERRED)
has_jq = shutil.which("jq") is not None

# Check for Python (almost always available)
has_python = shutil.which("python3") is not None or shutil.which("python") is not None

# Use best available method (PREFER jq)
if has_jq:
    # Use jq (PREFERRED - fastest and most efficient)
    pass
elif has_python:
    # Fallback to Python
    pass
else:
    # Last resort: grep/awk
    pass

docs.title: 4. Understanding Suppressed vs Actionable Findings
docs.text:
Key Concepts: - Total Findings: All findings detected by scanners - Suppressed Findings: Findings marked as false positives or accepted risks - Actionable Findings: Total - Suppressed = findings requiring attention

Always Check:

{
  "metadata": {
    "summary_stats": {
      "total": 156,
      "actionable": 61,
      "suppressed": 95
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Important: File Size Considerations
docs.text:
WARNING: The ash_aggregated_results.json file can be very large (often 1-10MB, sometimes larger for big codebases).

Best Practices: 1. DO NOT load the entire file into memory if you only need specific data 2. Use streaming JSON parsers when possible 3. Extract only what you need using command-line tools or streaming libraries 4. Consider using alternative formats for specific use cases: - reports/ash.flat.json - Simplified structure, smaller size - reports/ash.csv - Easy to filter and query - reports/ash.sarif - Industry standard, well-supported

docs.title: Parsing Strategies
docs.text: DEFAULT APPROACH: Always attempt jq first for maximum efficiency. Only use Python or grep if jq is unavailable.

docs.title: Strategy 1: Using jq (PREFERRED - Check Availability First)
docs.text:
Recommended: Use jq for all queries (most Linux/macOS systems have it installed): 

# Extract just summary stats
jq '.metadata.summary_stats' ash_aggregated_results.json

# Get specific scanner results
jq '.scanner_results.bandit' ash_aggregated_results.json

docs.title: Strategy 2: Using Python (FALLBACK - If jq is NOT available)
docs.text:
# Extract summary stats
python3 -c "import json; data=json.load(open('ash_aggregated_results.json')); print(json.dumps(data['metadata']['summary_stats'], indent=2))"

# Get actionable count
python3 -c "import json; print(json.load(open('ash_aggregated_results.json'))['metadata']['summary_stats']['actionable'])"

Alternative: Use grep for simple extractions (always available): 

# Get actionable count (quick and dirty)
grep -o '"actionable": [0-9]*' ash_aggregated_results.json | grep -o '[0-9]*'

# Check for critical findings
grep -o '"critical": [0-9]*' ash_aggregated_results.json | head -1

docs.title: Strategy 3: Streaming JSON Parsers (For Large Files)
docs.text:
Python with ijson (streaming parser, installed separately with pip install ijson): 

import importlib

ijson = importlib.import_module("ijson")  # a third-party package, not part of ASH

# Stream parse - memory efficient
with open("ash_aggregated_results.json", "rb") as f:
    # Extract just summary stats without loading entire file
    parser = ijson.items(f, "metadata.summary_stats")
    summary_stats = next(parser)
    print(f"Actionable findings: {summary_stats['actionable']}")

Python standard library (load specific sections): 

import json

# Load and extract only what you need
with open("ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

# Immediately extract and discard the rest
summary = data["metadata"]["summary_stats"]
del data  # Free memory

print(f"Actionable: {summary['actionable']}")
print(f"Critical: {summary['critical']}")

docs.title: Strategy 4: Use Simpler Formats
docs.text:
For most use cases, use the flat JSON format instead: 

# reports/ash.flat.json is much smaller and easier to parse
import json

with open("reports/ash.flat.json") as f:
    findings = json.load(f)

# Simpler structure, direct access to findings
for finding in findings:
    if finding["severity"] in ["CRITICAL", "HIGH"]:
        print(f"{finding['file_path']}: {finding['message']}")

docs.title: metadata.summary_stats
docs.text:
• total: Total findings detected
  • actionable: Findings that fail the scan: not suppressed, and at or above the severity threshold
  • suppressed: Findings marked as false positives/accepted risks
  • critical, high, medium, low, info: Counts by severity
  • passed: Scanners that completed successfully
  • failed: Scanners that encountered errors
  • duration: Scan duration in seconds

docs.title: scanner_results
docs.text:
Contains one status record per scanner, keyed by scanner name. A record says how the scanner ended and how many findings it produced. It does not hold the findings themselves; those are in sarif, below.

{
  "scanner_results": {
    "bandit": {
      "status": "FAILED",
      "dependencies_satisfied": true,
      "excluded": false,
      "severity_counts": {
        "suppressed": 0,
        "critical": 0,
        "high": 1,
        "medium": 0,
        "low": 1,
        "info": 0
      },
      "finding_count": 2,
      "actionable_finding_count": 1,
      "suppressed_finding_count": 0,
      "exit_code": 0,
      "duration": 1.25,
      "missing_reason": null,
      "skipped_reason": null
    }
  }
}
  • status: PASSED, FAILED (at least one actionable finding), ERROR, MISSING (the tool was not found) or SKIPPED
  • severity_counts, finding_count, actionable_finding_count, suppressed_finding_count: the scanner's findings by severity, in total, actionable, and suppressed
  • duration: seconds the scanner ran
  • exit_code: the scanner tool's exit code, or null when no tool ran
  • missing_reason, skipped_reason: why the scanner did not run, set on a MISSING and a SKIPPED record respectively and null otherwise

docs.title: sarif
docs.text:
The findings are in sarif, a SARIF 2.1.0 report. Each finding is one entry of sarif.runs[].results[]. A file ASH writes has one run that holds every scanner's findings, so loop over all runs rather than reading only the first, and use properties.scanner_name to tell the scanners apart. The fields to read:

  • ruleId: the scanner's rule identifier
  • message.text: what the scanner found
  • locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri: the file path
  • locations[0].physicalLocation.region.startLine: the first line (endLine is the last)
  • level: the SARIF level, error, warning, note or none
  • properties.scanner_name: the scanner that reported the finding, the same name as the key in scanner_results
  • properties.issue_severity: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW or INFO; when a result has none, ASH grades it from its rule's score or its level
  • suppressions: null or empty for an active finding, and one or more entries for a suppressed one

For one record per finding with flat field names, read reports/ash.flat.json instead.

docs.title: Efficient Querying
docs.text: IMPORTANT: Always attempt jq first for maximum efficiency. Check availability and provide fallbacks for compatibility.

docs.title: Recommended: Using jq (Check Availability First)
docs.text:
Get actionable findings count (preferred method): 

jq '.metadata.summary_stats.actionable' ash_aggregated_results.json

Get all critical/high findings (suppressed ones included; the findings are in sarif): 

jq '.sarif.runs[].results[] | select(.properties.issue_severity == "CRITICAL" or .properties.issue_severity == "HIGH") | {scanner: .properties.scanner_name, rule: .ruleId, severity: .properties.issue_severity, file: .locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri, line: .locations[0].physicalLocation.region.startLine, message: .message.text}' ash_aggregated_results.json

Get findings by scanner: 

jq '[.sarif.runs[].results[] | select(.properties.scanner_name == "bandit")]' ash_aggregated_results.json

Get a scanner's status and finding counts: 

jq '.scanner_results.bandit' ash_aggregated_results.json

Get non-suppressed findings: 

jq '.sarif.runs[].results[] | select((.suppressions // []) | length == 0)' ash_aggregated_results.json

Count findings by severity: 

jq '[.sarif.runs[].results[] | .properties.issue_severity] | group_by(.) | map({severity: .[0], count: length})' ash_aggregated_results.json

docs.title: Fallback: Using Python (If jq is unavailable)
docs.text:
Get actionable findings count: 

python3 -c "import json; print(json.load(open('ash_aggregated_results.json'))['metadata']['summary_stats']['actionable'])"

Get all critical/high findings: 

import json

with open("ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

for run in data["sarif"]["runs"]:
    for result in run["results"]:
        properties = result.get("properties") or {}
        if properties.get("issue_severity") in ["CRITICAL", "HIGH"]:
            locations = result.get("locations") or [{}]
            location = locations[0].get("physicalLocation", {})
            uri = location.get("artifactLocation", {}).get("uri")
            line = location.get("region", {}).get("startLine")
            message = result.get("message", {}).get("text")
            print(f"{properties.get('scanner_name')}: {uri}:{line} - {message}")

Get findings by scanner: 

import json

with open("ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

bandit_findings = [
    result
    for run in data["sarif"]["runs"]
    for result in run["results"]
    if (result.get("properties") or {}).get("scanner_name") == "bandit"
]
print(json.dumps(bandit_findings, indent=2))

Count findings by severity: 

import json
from collections import Counter

with open("ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    data = json.load(f)

severities = []
for run in data["sarif"]["runs"]:
    for result in run["results"]:
        severities.append((result.get("properties") or {}).get("issue_severity"))

counts = Counter(severities)
for severity, count in counts.items():
    print(f"{severity}: {count}")

docs.title: Last Resort: Using grep/awk (If neither jq nor Python available)
docs.text:
Get actionable findings count (basic but works): 

grep -o '"actionable": [0-9]*' ash_aggregated_results.json | head -1 | grep -o '[0-9]*'

Check for critical findings: 

grep -c '"issue_severity": "CRITICAL"' ash_aggregated_results.json

List all severity levels found: 

grep -o '"issue_severity": "[A-Z]*"' ash_aggregated_results.json | sort -u

docs.title: Recommended Approach for GenAI Tools
docs.text:
1. Check tool availability first: 

import subprocess
import shutil


def get_actionable_count(results_file):
    """Get actionable findings count using best available method."""

    # Method 1: Try jq (fastest - PREFERRED)
    if shutil.which("jq"):
        try:
            result = subprocess.run(
                ["jq", ".metadata.summary_stats.actionable", results_file],
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
                check=True,
            )
            return int(result.stdout.strip())
        except Exception:
            pass

    # Method 2: Use Python (most reliable fallback)
    try:
        import json

        with open(results_file) as f:
            data = json.load(f)
        return data["metadata"]["summary_stats"]["actionable"]
    except Exception:
        pass

    # Method 3: Fallback to grep (always available)
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            ["grep", "-o", '"actionable": [0-9]*', results_file],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
        )
        return int(result.stdout.strip().split(":")[1].strip())
    except Exception:
        return None

2. Use the flat JSON format when possible: 

# Simpler, smaller, easier to parse
with open("reports/ash.flat.json") as f:
    findings = json.load(f)

actionable = [f for f in findings if not f.get("suppressed", False)]
critical_high = [f for f in actionable if f["severity"] in ["CRITICAL", "HIGH"]]

docs.title: Purpose

docs.title: Querying Dependencies
docs.text: IMPORTANT: CycloneDX files can also be large. Use efficient parsing methods. Always attempt jq first.

docs.title: Recommended: Using jq (Check Availability First)
docs.text:
List all components (preferred method): 

jq '.components[] | {name: .name, version: .version, type: .type}' ash.cdx.json

Find components with vulnerabilities: 

jq '.vulnerabilities[] | .affects[].ref' ash.cdx.json | sort -u

Get high/critical vulnerabilities: 

jq '.vulnerabilities[] | select(.ratings[].severity == "high" or .ratings[].severity == "critical")' ash.cdx.json

List all licenses: 

jq '[.components[].licenses[]?.license.id] | unique' ash.cdx.json

Find dependency tree for a component: 

jq --arg pkg "pkg:pypi/requests@2.31.0" '.dependencies[] | select(.ref == $pkg)' ash.cdx.json

docs.title: Fallback: Using Python (If jq is unavailable)
docs.text:
List all components: 

import json

with open("reports/ash.cdx.json") as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)

for component in sbom.get("components", []):
    print(f"{component['name']} {component['version']} ({component['type']})")

Find components with vulnerabilities: 

import json

with open("reports/ash.cdx.json") as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)

vulnerable_refs = set()
for vuln in sbom.get("vulnerabilities", []):
    for affect in vuln.get("affects", []):
        vulnerable_refs.add(affect["ref"])

for ref in sorted(vulnerable_refs):
    print(ref)

Get high/critical vulnerabilities: 

import json

with open("reports/ash.cdx.json") as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)

for vuln in sbom.get("vulnerabilities", []):
    for rating in vuln.get("ratings", []):
        if rating.get("severity") in ["high", "critical"]:
            print(
                f"{vuln['id']}: {rating['severity']} (score: {rating.get('score', 'N/A')})"
            )
            for affect in vuln.get("affects", []):
                print(f"  Affects: {affect['ref']}")
            break

List all licenses: 

import json

with open("reports/ash.cdx.json") as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)

licenses = set()
for component in sbom.get("components", []):
    for license_info in component.get("licenses", []):
        if "license" in license_info and "id" in license_info["license"]:
            licenses.add(license_info["license"]["id"])

for license_id in sorted(licenses):
    print(license_id)

docs.title: Last Resort: Using grep (If neither jq nor Python available)
docs.text:
Count total components: 

grep -c '"type": "library"' reports/ash.cdx.json

Find if specific package exists: 

grep -i "requests" reports/ash.cdx.json

Count vulnerabilities: 

grep -c '"id": "CVE-' reports/ash.cdx.json

docs.title: Location
docs.text:
• Default: the first config file discovery finds; ash config init creates .ashrc.yaml in the project root
  • Custom: Specify with --config flag or ASH_CONFIG environment variable

docs.title: Schema Structure
docs.text:
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json

project_name: my-project

fail_on_findings: true  # Exit with code 2 if actionable findings exist

global_settings:
  severity_threshold: MEDIUM  # ALL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL

  ignore_paths:
    - path: 'tests/test_data/**'
      reason: 'Test data only'
      expiration: null  # Optional: ISO date string

  suppressions:
    - path: 'src/app.py'
      rule_id: 'B201'
      line_start: 42
      line_end: 42
      reason: 'False positive - debug mode only in development'
      expiration: '2026-12-31'  # Optional: ISO date string

scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    options:
      confidence_level: high  # all, high, medium, low
      ignore_nosec: false
      config_file: .ash/bandit.yaml

  semgrep:
    enabled: true
    options:
      config: auto  # or specific ruleset like 'p/security-audit'

  checkov:
    enabled: true
    options:
      frameworks:
        - all
      severity_threshold: LOW

reporters:
  markdown:
    enabled: true
    options:
      include_detailed_findings: true
      max_detailed_findings: 20

  html:
    enabled: true

  sarif:
    enabled: true

  cyclonedx:
    enabled: true

docs.title: global_settings.severity_threshold
docs.text: The least severe finding that counts as actionable. Findings below it are still detected and reported, but not counted as actionable: they do not fail the scan, and get_scan_results(actionable_only=True) leaves them out.

docs.title: global_settings.suppressions
docs.text:
Array of suppression rules to mark findings as false positives or accepted risks.

Suppression Fields: - path: File path (supports glob patterns like tests/**/*.py) - rule_id: Scanner-specific rule identifier (e.g., B201, SECRET-SECRET-KEYWORD) - line_start: Optional - specific line number - line_end: Optional - end line for multi-line suppressions - reason: Required - explanation for suppression - expiration: Optional - ISO date when suppression expires

docs.title: scanners
docs.text: Configuration for each scanner. Common options: - enabled: Boolean to enable/disable scanner - options: Scanner-specific configuration

docs.title: When to Suppress
docs.text:
• False positives (scanner incorrectly flagged safe code)
  • Accepted risks (security team approved the pattern)
  • Test data (not production code)
  • Third-party code (cannot be modified)

docs.title: Suppression Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Always Provide a Reason:

suppressions:
  - path: 'src/utils.py'
    rule_id: 'B603'
    reason: 'subprocess.call uses list args (no shell=True), validated inputs only'

2. Be Specific with Paths:

# Good - specific file
- path: 'src/auth/login.py'
  rule_id: 'B201'
  reason: 'Debug mode is only enabled in the local development server'

# Good - specific directory
- path: 'tests/**/*.py'
  rule_id: 'B101'
  reason: 'assert is how the tests check results'

# Avoid - too broad
- path: '**/*.py'
  rule_id: 'B201'
  reason: 'Too broad: this hides B201 in every Python file'

3. Use Line Numbers for Precision:

suppressions:
  - path: 'src/app.py'
    rule_id: 'B201'
    line_start: 42
    line_end: 42
    reason: 'Debug mode only enabled in development environment'

4. Set Expiration Dates for Temporary Suppressions:

suppressions:
  - path: 'src/legacy/old_api.py'
    rule_id: 'B501'
    reason: 'Legacy code - will be refactored in Q2 2026'
    expiration: '2026-06-30'

docs.title: Suppression Workflow
docs.text:
1. Identify the Finding:
  2. Check ash_aggregated_results.json for exact details

  3. Note: rule_id, file_path, line_start, line_end

  4. Verify It's a False Positive or Accepted Risk:

  5. Review the code context
  6. Consult security team if needed

  7. Document the decision

  8. Add Suppression to Configuration: 

    global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - path: 'path/from/finding'
      rule_id: 'RULE_ID_FROM_FINDING'
      line_start: 42  # Optional but recommended
      reason: 'Clear explanation of why this is suppressed'

  9. Re-run Scan to Verify: 

    ash --mode local

  10. Confirm Suppression Applied: 

    jq '.metadata.summary_stats.suppressed' .ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json

docs.title: 1. Suppression Not Applied
docs.text:
Issue: Suppression added but finding still shows as actionable

Common Causes: - Path doesn't match exactly (check for leading ./ or trailing /) - Rule ID typo or case mismatch - Line numbers don't match (scanner may report different lines)

Solution: 

# Check exact path and rule_id from results
jq '.sarif.runs[].results[] | select((.suppressions // []) | length == 0) | {file: .locations[0].physicalLocation.artifactLocation.uri, rule: .ruleId, line: .locations[0].physicalLocation.region.startLine}' ash_aggregated_results.json

# Verify suppression in config matches exactly

docs.title: 2. HTML Report Parsing Failures
docs.text:
Issue: Attempting to parse HTML with regex or string matching

Solution: Never parse HTML reports. Use JSON formats: - ash_aggregated_results.json - complete results - reports/ash.flat.json - simplified structure - reports/ash.sarif - SARIF format

docs.title: 3. Missing Scanner Results
docs.text:
Issue: Expected scanner results not in output

Check: 

# Verify scanner was enabled and executed
jq '.metadata.validation_summary' ash_aggregated_results.json

# Check for scanner errors
jq '.scanner_results | to_entries[] | select(.value.status == "FAILED")' ash_aggregated_results.json

docs.title: 4. Dependency Analysis Confusion
docs.text:
Issue: Trying to extract dependencies from scan findings

Solution: Use CycloneDX SBOM: 

# Get all dependencies
jq '.components[] | {name, version, type}' reports/ash.cdx.json

# Get vulnerable dependencies
jq '.vulnerabilities[] | .affects[].ref' reports/ash.cdx.json

docs.title: Pattern 1: CI/CD Pipeline Gate
docs.text:
import json
import sys

# Read results
with open(".ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    results = json.load(f)

stats = results["metadata"]["summary_stats"]

# Fail on actionable critical/high findings
# Note: Use actionable count to exclude suppressed findings (false positives)
if stats["critical"] > 0:
    print(f"FAILED: {stats['critical']} critical actionable findings")
    sys.exit(1)

if stats["high"] > 5:
    print(f"FAILED: {stats['high']} high actionable findings (threshold: 5)")
    sys.exit(1)

print(f"PASSED: {stats['actionable']} actionable findings (within threshold)")
sys.exit(0)

Using MCP Server: 

import sys

# Get only actionable critical/high findings for a CI/CD gate. actionable_only
# adds `findings`, the findings that fail the scan (unsuppressed, at or above its
# severity threshold) and match the filters; the list is in a filter_level="full"
# response only.
result = await get_scan_results(
    output_dir=".ash/ash_output",
    actionable_only=True,
    severities="critical,high",
    filter_level="full",
)

if result["findings_count"] > 0:
    print(f"FAILED: {result['findings_count']} actionable critical/high findings")
    sys.exit(1)

docs.title: Pattern 2: Finding Analysis and Remediation
docs.text:
import json

# Read results
with open(".ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json") as f:
    results = json.load(f)

# Get all actionable high/critical findings
actionable_findings = []
for run in results["sarif"]["runs"]:
    for finding in run["results"]:
        properties = finding.get("properties") or {}
        if finding.get("suppressions"):
            continue
        if properties.get("issue_severity") in ["HIGH", "CRITICAL"]:
            locations = finding.get("locations") or [{}]
            location = locations[0].get("physicalLocation", {})
            actionable_findings.append(
                {
                    "scanner": properties.get("scanner_name"),
                    "rule_id": finding.get("ruleId"),
                    "severity": properties["issue_severity"],
                    "file": location.get("artifactLocation", {}).get("uri"),
                    "line": location.get("region", {}).get("startLine"),
                    "message": finding.get("message", {}).get("text"),
                }
            )

# Sort by severity
actionable_findings.sort(key=lambda x: 0 if x["severity"] == "CRITICAL" else 1)

# Generate remediation plan
for finding in actionable_findings:
    print(f"\n[{finding['severity']}] {finding['file']}:{finding['line']}")
    print(f"  Rule: {finding['rule_id']} ({finding['scanner']})")
    print(f"  Issue: {finding['message']}")
    print(f"  Action: [Suggest remediation based on rule_id]")

Using MCP Server: 

# Get actionable high/critical findings, one entry per finding
results = await get_scan_results(
    output_dir=".ash/ash_output",
    actionable_only=True,
    severities="critical,high",
    filter_level="full",
)

# `findings` holds the findings that fail the scan (unsuppressed, at or above its
# severity threshold) and match the filters. The SARIF they come from is not part
# of the response; read it from the file get_scan_result_paths names if you need
# it, or the findings below the threshold.
for finding in results["findings"]:
    print(
        f"[{finding['severity']}] {finding.get('file_path')}:{finding.get('line_start')} "
        f"{finding['rule_id']} ({finding.get('scanner')}): {finding.get('message')}"
    )

docs.title: Pattern 3: Dependency Vulnerability Report
docs.text:
import json

# Read CycloneDX SBOM
with open(".ash/ash_output/reports/ash.cdx.json") as f:
    sbom = json.load(f)

# Extract vulnerable components
vulnerable_components = {}
for vuln in sbom.get("vulnerabilities", []):
    for affect in vuln.get("affects", []):
        component_ref = affect["ref"]
        if component_ref not in vulnerable_components:
            vulnerable_components[component_ref] = []
        vulnerable_components[component_ref].append(
            {
                "cve": vuln["id"],
                "severity": vuln["ratings"][0]["severity"],
                "score": vuln["ratings"][0].get("score", "N/A"),
            }
        )

# Generate report
print("Vulnerable Dependencies:")
for component, vulns in vulnerable_components.items():
    print(f"\n{component}")
    for vuln in vulns:
        print(f"  - {vuln['cve']} ({vuln['severity']}, CVSS: {vuln['score']})")

docs.title: MCP Server Integration
docs.text: If using ASH via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, follow these guidelines:

docs.title: Available Tools
docs.text:
• run_ash_scan - Start a security scan
  • get_scan_progress - Get current progress and partial results
  • get_scan_results - Get scan results with filtering
  • get_scan_summary - Get lightweight summary
  • get_scan_result_paths - Get file paths for all reports
  • list_active_scans - List running scans
  • cancel_scan - Cancel a running scan and stop it: its running scanner is stopped and no reports are written after the cancel

docs.title: Managing Long-Running Scans
docs.text: CRITICAL: ASH scans can take 30-120+ seconds. MCP connections may timeout if you don't keep them alive.

docs.title: ❌ WRONG: Sleep and Wait (Connection Timeout)
docs.text:
# This will cause connection timeout!
result = run_ash_scan(source_dir="/path/to/project")
scan_id = result["scan_id"]

# Sleeping for 60+ seconds causes MCP connection to close
time.sleep(60)

# This will fail - connection already timed out
summary = get_scan_summary()  # ERROR: Connection closed

docs.title: ✅ CORRECT: Poll Progress (Keep Connection Alive)
docs.text:
import time

# 1. Start scan (returns immediately with scan_id). severity_threshold can make
#    the config's global_settings.severity_threshold stricter for this scan,
#    never looser; omit it to use the config's. LOW also counts LOW findings
#    against the default MEDIUM; a looser value such as HIGH is ignored.
result = run_ash_scan(source_dir="/path/to/project", severity_threshold="LOW")
scan_id = result["scan_id"]

# 2. Poll progress periodically to keep connection alive
while True:
    progress = get_scan_progress(scan_id=scan_id)

    # is_complete is true for every ending: completed, incomplete, failed and
    # cancelled
    if progress.get("is_complete"):
        break
    time.sleep(5)

# 3. Get results if this scan has its own. A completed or incomplete scan does
#    (an incomplete one's findings are real but partial). A failed or cancelled
#    one does not: its output directory holds the previous scan's results.
if progress.get("results_available"):
    # Use filtered queries to reduce data transfer
    results = get_scan_results(
        output_dir=progress["output_directory"], actionable_only=True
    )
else:
    print(f"Scan {progress['status']}: {progress.get('error_message')}")

What to know about the tools:

  • run_ash_scan takes no scanner list. The project's ASH config chooses the scanners and the severity thresholds.
  • Its severity_threshold argument can make the config's global_settings.severity_threshold stricter for that scan, never looser: LOW over a configured MEDIUM makes LOW findings actionable, and CRITICAL over MEDIUM changes nothing. It tightens a scanner's own severity_threshold option the same way, and a scanner without one follows the tightened global threshold. The threshold decides which findings are actionable and whether a scanner reports FAILED, not which findings are reported. get_scan_progress returns the argument as requested_severity_threshold and, once the scan has results, the threshold it was judged by as severity_threshold.
  • Each scan writes .ash/ash_output inside source_dir. Once its options and config are accepted, it sets the previous scan's results there aside, and it deletes them once it has results of its own; a scan that fails or is canceled puts them back, and a scan refused for its scanner selection or its config leaves them as they were. Copy ash_aggregated_results.json before the next scan if you need it for a comparison.
  • cancel_scan stops a running scan: the scanner tool running at the time is stopped, and no further scanner, phase, or reporter starts, so a scan canceled before its report phase writes no reports. A scanner that is already reading its tool's output can still write its own files, but ash_aggregated_results.json is not written after the cancel. Previous results that the output directory held are put back in place of the results the scan wrote; the scan's log, ash.log, stays, and an ash.log.jsonl already there is left as it was. With none to put back, what the scan wrote before it stopped stays, though a cancel during the report phase removes that phase's reports, all but reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md. Its status is cancelled at once. Until the scan has stopped, run_ash_scan refuses another scan of that directory.
  • get_scan_results returns counts and per-scanner summaries. With actionable_only set, a response at the default filter_level, full, also has a findings list of the actionable findings, without their IDs, and its findings_count. Those are the findings that are not suppressed and are at or above the threshold their scanner was judged by, the ones that fail the scan. Findings below it are left out. A summary or minimal response has no list. Read the IDs, and the suppressed findings, from reports/ash.flat.json in the output directory. get_scan_result_paths returns the absolute paths of the main reports and of ash_aggregated_results.json.
  • The server's operator limits how many scans it holds at once, running or waiting (max_concurrent_scans), and how long one may run (scan_timeout_seconds). A scan over the first limit is refused with an error that names it; start it again when another scan has finished. A scan over the second is stopped and ends failed.
  • The server keeps its list of scans in memory. After it restarts, get_scan_progress fails with error_category scan_not_found for older scan IDs; read their results from the output directory.

After a scan, get_scan_progress reports scanner_statuses for every scanner ASH considered and skipped_scanners for the ones that did not run. Use them to tell "ran and found nothing" from "never ran". check_installation reports whether each built-in scanner's tool is installed: ready is false when a scanner that ASH enables by default cannot run and no scan will install its tool, and missing_dependencies names those scanners. It does not read the project's config, and it installs and downloads nothing. When the tool of a scanner that ASH installs with uv is missing, the first scan installs it if the server is online and has uv; such a scanner is listed in installs_on_first_scan and counts toward ready, and otherwise it is in missing_dependencies. Offline, semgrep is also missing when it has no rules cache.

The MCP tools reference lists every tool and its parameters.

docs.title: Stop a scan that runs too long
docs.text:
A canceled scan's status is cancelled at once, so the next poll ends the loop, and results_available is false:

import time


def scan_or_cancel(source_dir):
    scan = run_ash_scan(source_dir=source_dir)
    if scan.get("success") is False:
        return {"error": scan["error"]}
    deadline = time.monotonic() + 20 * 60
    canceled = False
    while True:
        progress = get_scan_progress(scan_id=scan_id)

        # Show status updates
        current_status = progress.get("message", "Running...")
        if current_status != last_status:
            print(f"Status: {current_status}")
            last_status = current_status

        # Check completion: is_complete is true for every ending
        if progress.get("is_complete"):
            break

        # Wait before next poll (keeps connection alive)
        time.sleep(5)

    # A failed or cancelled scan has no results of its own; the files in its
    # output directory are the previous scan's.
    if not progress.get("results_available"):
        reason = progress.get("error_message") or "no results"
        return {"error": f"Scan {progress['status']}: {reason}"}

    # Get filtered results
    output_dir = progress.get("output_directory", f"{source_dir}/.ash/ash_output")
    results = get_scan_results(
        output_dir=output_dir,
        filter_level="summary",
        actionable_only=True,
        severities="critical,high,medium",
    )

docs.title: Pattern 1: fail a build on critical or high findings
docs.text:
Run from the scanned directory after the scan has ended with results:

import sys
from pathlib import Path

# Summary - dashboard data (5-15KB)
summary = await get_scan_results(output_dir=".ash/ash_output", filter_level="summary")

# Full - complete results (50KB-2MB)
results = await get_scan_results(output_dir=".ash/ash_output", filter_level="full")

docs.title: Content Filtering
docs.text:
Filter by scanner, severity, or actionable status:

# Only actionable findings: unsuppressed, at or above the severity threshold
actionable = await get_scan_results(output_dir=".ash/ash_output", actionable_only=True)

# Only critical findings
critical = await get_scan_results(output_dir=".ash/ash_output", severities="critical")

# Actionable critical findings only
actionable_critical = await get_scan_results(
    output_dir=".ash/ash_output", actionable_only=True, severities="critical"
)

# Specific scanners
sast_results = await get_scan_results(
    output_dir=".ash/ash_output", scanners="bandit,semgrep"
)

# Combined filtering - actionable high-priority SAST findings
high_priority_sast = await get_scan_results(
    output_dir=".ash/ash_output",
    filter_level="summary",
    scanners="bandit,semgrep",
    severities="critical,high",
    actionable_only=True,
    severities="critical,high",
)
if results.get("success") is False:
    print(results["error"])
    sys.exit(1)
if results["findings_count"] > 0:
    print(f"{results['findings_count']} actionable critical or high findings")
    sys.exit(1)

The list holds the findings that the scan's own exit code and summary_stats.actionable count, those at or above each scanner's severity threshold, narrowed here to critical and high.

docs.title: Pattern 2: list the findings to fix
docs.text:
from pathlib import Path

results = get_scan_results(
    output_dir=str(Path(".ash/ash_output").resolve()),
    actionable_only=True,
    severities="critical,high",
)
for finding in results["findings"]:
    print(
        finding["severity"],
        finding.get("scanner"),
        finding.get("rule_id"),
        f"{finding.get('file_path')}:{finding.get('line_start')}",
        finding.get("message"),
    )

The list leaves out suppressed findings. reports/ash.flat.json in the output directory has every finding, with is_suppressed.

docs.title: When the server is remote
docs.text: A server on another host cannot read the user's files. Deliver the source first with set_source_git or set_source_zip_chunk and set_source_zip_finalize, then call run_ash_scan without source_dir. A config file inside delivered source is checked against the server's policy: if it sets a field the server does not let clients set, such as fail_on_findings, the scan is refused with error_type config_field_denied and a message naming the field. Remove the field and deliver again. Suppressions and ignore paths in delivered source are applied and marked as client-supplied in the results.

docs.title: Run a scan with the command line
docs.text:
From the project's root directory:

ash --source-dir . --no-progress

ash and ash scan are the same command. The scan runs on this machine and writes its output to .ash/ash_output under the scanned directory unless you pass --output-dir. --scanners runs only the named scanners and --exclude-scanners skips them; use them only when the user asks for a narrower scan. This scan runs detect-secrets alone, without network access:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress
Exit code Meaning 0 No actionable findings, or the config does not fail on findings. 1 The scan is incomplete: a scanner was MISSING or ended in ERROR, a converter failed, a rule could not be evaluated, a content database was too old, or ASH itself failed. 2 Actionable findings. 3 The config is invalid. 4 A workspace definition or workspace policy is invalid. 5 The command line is wrong: an unknown option or argument, a value ASH does not accept, such as a mistyped scanner name, or options that cannot be combined. No scanner ran.

A value ASH does not accept is a usage error, and no scanner runs:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --min-severity urgent --offline --no-progress

To print a summary of the last scan:

ash report --output-dir .ash/ash_output

docs.title: Read the results
docs.text:
The output directory, .ash/ash_output by default, contains:

Path Use it for reports/ash.flat.json Findings, one record each. Start here. ash_aggregated_results.json Each scanner's status and the scan's totals. reports/ash.summary.md A readable summary to show the user. reports/ash.sarif SARIF, for tools that read it. reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json Suppressions that matched no finding, including expired ones. ash.log The scan's log, for errors.

reports/ash.flat.json is an object. Its findings list holds one record per finding with these fields: id, title, description, severity, scanner, rule_id, file_path, line_start, line_end, is_suppressed, code_snippet, and, for suppressed findings, suppression_kind and suppression_justification. Fields with no value are left out, so read them with a default. tags, properties, and raw_data hold JSON encoded as strings.

import json
from pathlib import Path

report = json.loads(Path(".ash/ash_output/reports/ash.flat.json").read_text())
for finding in report["findings"]:
    if finding.get("is_suppressed"):
        continue
    print(
        finding["severity"],
        finding["scanner"],
        finding["rule_id"],
        f"{finding.get('file_path')}:{finding.get('line_start')}",
        finding["id"],
    )

In ash_aggregated_results.json, metadata.summary_stats holds the totals:

  • severity_counts counts findings by severity (critical, high, medium, low, info) and counts suppressed findings separately in suppressed.
  • total is the number of findings that are not suppressed.
  • actionable is the number of findings that are not suppressed and are at or above the severity threshold. The threshold comes from global_settings.severity_threshold in the config, MEDIUM by default, or from a scanner's own severity_threshold option, which replaces it for that scanner.
  • passed, failed, missing, skipped, and error count scanners by status.

The config sets both:

global_settings:
  severity_threshold: MEDIUM  # ALL, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL
scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      severity_threshold: HIGH

import json
from pathlib import Path

results = json.loads(Path(".ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json").read_text())
stats = results["metadata"]["summary_stats"]
print("actionable:", stats["actionable"], stats["severity_counts"])
for name, scanner in results["scanner_results"].items():
    if scanner["status"] in ("MISSING", "ERROR"):
        print(name, scanner["status"], scanner.get("missing_reason"))

scanner_results has one entry per scanner, with its status, finding_count, actionable_finding_count, suppressed_finding_count, and severity_counts. A MISSING scanner also has a missing_reason. The statuses are:

Status Meaning PASSED It ran and found nothing at or above its threshold. FAILED It ran and found something at or above its threshold. This is a result, not an error. MISSING It had files to scan, but its tool is not installed, or was found only inside the scanned tree. It did not run. ERROR It started and failed. SKIPPED It did not run: it is disabled or excluded, or there was nothing for it to scan.

A finding that a scanner reports with no severity of its own, only the SARIF level error, as detect-secrets does, is CRITICAL in ash.flat.json, ash.summary.md, summary_stats, the MCP counts, and the threshold check alike.

docs.title: Explain a finding
docs.text:
Take the finding's id from ash.flat.json and call explain_finding with it and results_path set to the output directory. The answer has the scanner's description, the severity and why it is or is not actionable, CWE and CVE identifiers when the scanner gives them, and the matched code. Without MCP, use the record in ash.flat.json and read the code at file_path and line_start.

An id is the scanner, the rule, and 12 hexadecimal digits of a hash of where the finding is: its file and lines, or the fingerprints its scanner reports. For example, bandit-B602-e1cb79ce5694. Findings at different places have different ids.

docs.title: Suggest a suppression
docs.text:
Call suggest_suppression with the finding's id, results_path set to the ash_aggregated_results.json file (not the directory), and the user's reason as justification. It writes nothing and returns one entry as yaml and json. Its expiration defaults to 90 days from today. Leave out the client_supplied key it includes, and put the entry under global_settings.suppressions in the project's config:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: "SECRET-SECRET-KEYWORD"
      path: "app.py"
      line_start: 3
      line_end: 3
      reason: "Test fixture value, not a real credential"
      expiration: "2027-06-30"
  • path and reason are required. path is relative to the scanned directory and may use glob patterns such as tests/**. Do not start it with ./, which matches nothing.
  • rule_id matches without regard to case and may use glob patterns.
  • line_start and line_end tie the suppression to those lines. Leave them out to match the rule anywhere in the path.
  • Write expiration as a quoted YYYY-MM-DD date. From that date on, the suppression no longer applies and the finding counts again. An expired suppression is listed in reports/ash.unused-suppressions.json, with the ones that matched nothing.
  • ignore_paths entries also need path and reason, and drop every finding in the matching files. Prefer a suppression for one rule.

Edit the config file the scan used, or create .ashrc.yaml in the scanned directory if it has none. ASH uses the first of these it finds in the scanned directory: .ash.yml, .ash.yaml, .ash.json, ash.yml, ash.yaml, ash.json (each in the directory, then in .ash/), then .ashrc.toml, .ashrc.yaml, .ashrc.yml, .ashrc.json, ashrc.toml, ashrc.yaml, ashrc.yml, and ashrc.json in the directory, then the [tool.ash] table of pyproject.toml. If the config has an extends key, its own suppressions list replaces the base config's list instead of adding to it; keep the base's entries by adding yours with a patch operation add at /global_settings/suppressions/-.

Check the edited config before you scan. ash config validate, run in the scanned directory, checks the config a scan there would use the way the scan loads it: it names each field the scan would refuse, such as a suppression without a reason or with a misspelled key, and exits with code 3 when there is one. --config names another file.
