A file with a Resources mapping that ASH cannot model as CloudFormation is reported as a target the scanner could not evaluate, so it counts toward partial coverage instead of disappearing. Templates in the converted target (archives ASH extracted) are scanned too. A template that is a symlink, sits under a symlinked directory, or has more than one hard link is skipped with a warning, because cfn-lint would read it where it points. In the source directory, a link whose target is outside the scanned tree does not get that far: the scan set leaves it out, with the warning Not scanning '<path>': link leaves the scanned tree, and lists it among the inputs not scanned (see What decides the files).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  cfn-lint:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # A .cfnlintrc to use, outside the scanned tree. When unset, ASH gives
      # cfn-lint an empty configuration (see "Configuration files" below).
      config_file: /etc/ash/cfnlintrc
      # Regions to validate against, or [ALL_REGIONS]. When unset, us-east-1 (see
      # "Regions" below).
      regions: [us-east-1, eu-west-1]
      # Rule ids or prefixes to skip everywhere, or to enable (e.g. "I" for
      # informational rules, which cfn-lint does not run by default).
      ignore_checks: [W3005]
      include_checks: [I]
      # Let a template's own Metadata ignore_checks and configure_rules apply
      # (see "Suppressions").
      honor_inline_ignores: false
      # Version constraint for the installed tool.
      tool_version: ">=1.43.3,<2.0.0"
      # Seconds allowed for the uv install of cfn-lint.
      install_timeout: 300
      # Seconds each cfn-lint invocation may run before it is killed (the default;
      # null means no limit).
      scan_timeout: 1800

Region names, rule ids and prefixes are validated when the config is loaded, so a value cannot be passed through to cfn-lint as an option of its own.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: Some of cfn-lint's checks depend on the region, for example whether a resource type exists there (rule E3006). regions names the regions to check against. When it is unset, cfn-lint uses the regions a template names in its own Metadata: cfn-lint: config: regions, then those in the config_file you named, and otherwise us-east-1. On its own, cfn-lint would read AWS_REGION and AWS_DEFAULT_REGION before falling back to us-east-1. ASH does not let it, so a template gives the same findings on every host: an empty AWS_REGION, which a CI job gets from an unset variable, would otherwise make cfn-lint fail on every template.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
Left to itself, cfn-lint reads a .cfnlintrc from the directory it runs in (the scanned repository) and from your home directory. ASH does not let it: unless config_file names a file, ASH passes cfn-lint an empty configuration of its own, which it writes outside the scanned tree and removes when the scan ends, and which stops both lookups. A .cfnlintrc is not passive settings. Its append_rules key names Python files that cfn-lint loads as rules, so a .cfnlintrc in the scanned repository would make cfn-lint import and run a rule module from the scanned tree. Its other keys, such as ignore_checks, would change what cfn-lint reports without appearing in the ASH config, which is where ASH takes ignore_checks, include_checks and regions from instead.

For the same reason config_file is honored only when the operator sets it, through --config-overrides or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written), and only for a file outside the scanned tree. A relative config_file is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). A config_file from the repository's own .ash/.ash.yaml or from an ASH config in any other git checkout, or one naming a file inside the tree, is ignored with a warning and cfn-lint gets ASH's empty configuration, and so is a path inside the tree that leads out of it through a symbolic link there. A config an MCP client delivered that sets config_file is refused, since it is a default denied_paths entry. A file you name this way is used with append_rules included, and one that does not exist fails the scan. cfn-lint resolves the relative paths in it, such as append_rules and custom_rules entries, against its working directory rather than the file's directory. ASH runs cfn-lint in a new, empty directory outside the scanned tree that only your user can enter and that is removed after the scan, so a relative path names nothing: neither a file in the scanned repository nor one in a shared directory such as /tmp. Write those paths as absolute paths: a relative one makes cfn-lint fail on every template. Under --sandbox, a file outside the tree is not mounted unless it is listed in sandbox.extra_read_paths.

tool_version is appended to the package name when ASH installs cfn-lint, so it must be a version constraint such as >=1.43.3,<2.0.0. Anything else, including a direct reference such as @ file:///..., is ignored with a warning and the default constraint is used.

ignore_checks and tool_version are honored only when you set them as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. ignore_checks drops findings before ASH sees them, so they are neither reported nor counted as suppressed, and tool_version chooses the cfn-lint release that is installed. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, each is ignored with a warning and its default is used; a config an MCP client delivered that sets either is refused, since both are default denied_paths entries. To silence a finding in a repository, use an ASH suppression.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
cfn-lint classifies every rule by the first letter of its id. ASH maps that letter to an ASH severity and sets the SARIF level to match, so every report agrees:

cfn-lint rule Meaning ASH severity SARIF level E.... The template is invalid or will fail to deploy MEDIUM warning W.... Best-practice or hygiene problem LOW note I.... Informational (only with include_checks: [I]) INFO none

These sit below the severities of security scanners on purpose. At ASH's default threshold (MEDIUM) an invalid template fails the scan and a warning does not. Raise or lower that per scanner with scanners.cfn-lint.options.severity_threshold. cfn-lint's own class is never lost: it is the first character of the rule id.

E0003 is not reported as a finding. cfn-lint uses it for its own configuration errors, including a template path it could not open, so ASH counts the affected templates as not evaluated.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply to cfn-lint findings by rule_id, path, and line_start/line_end:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: E2533
      path: templates/legacy.yaml
      line_start: 14
      line_end: 14
      reason: The function is pinned to this runtime until it is retired.

Package-scoped suppressions do not apply (cfn-lint reports on templates, not packages), and neither do symbol-scoped ones, which target functions and classes in source code. A template's own ignores, Metadata: cfn-lint: config: ignore_checks on the template or on a resource, do not apply by default, and neither do the rule settings a template gives in Metadata: cfn-lint: config: configure_rules, such as E3031 exceptions or E1029 custom_excludes. cfn-lint would drop what they hide before ASH sees it, so those findings would appear neither as findings nor in ASH's suppressed counts and unused-suppressions report. ASH passes cfn-lint every rule outside your own ignore_checks (and the ignore_checks of the config_file you named) as mandatory, which cfn-lint applies whatever the template says. To let templates ignore or configure away their own findings, set honor_inline_ignores: true as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by an ASH config inside one it is ignored with a warning.

A template's ignore_checks can also reach the template cfn-lint reads after it in the same run. cfn-lint keeps the last template's settings while it reads the next one, and when that one cannot be parsed (duplicate keys, for example) it drops the parse errors (E0000) if the kept ignore_checks cover them, mandatory or not. A list given on the command line replaces a template's, so ASH always passes cfn-lint --ignore-checks: your own ignores, or W0000 when there are none. No rule has that id, and every rule is mandatory then, which cfn-lint ranks above an ignore, so it ignores nothing. With honor_inline_ignores: true ASH passes no placeholder, because it would replace the template-level ignore_checks you let in. It runs cfn-lint once per template instead, so a template's ignores apply to that template only. That costs one cfn-lint start-up per template: with cfn-lint 1.57.2, the 8 CloudFormation templates in ASH's own test data took 3.4 s in one run and 12.0 s in eight.

Rule settings need one more step. cfn-lint takes configure_rules whole from the first place that sets any: the command line, then the template, then the config file. So ASH passes the configure_rules of the config_file you named on the command line, one cfn-lint --configure-rule=RULE:key=value per setting, and when there are none it passes E3012:strict=false, which is E3012's default and changes no finding. Two limits follow from cfn-lint's command-line format. A setting it cannot carry, a list of more than one item or a value containing a comma, a colon or an equals sign, is left out with a warning, and that rule runs with its default; for the built-in rules the default reports at least as much. A config_file that sets merge_configs fails the scan, because cfn-lint would then merge a template's settings into the command line's. So does a config_file that uses a YAML alias: ASH reads the file with aliases refused, as it reads every YAML config, and cfn-lint would read it in full, so ASH could not check what it sets. With honor_inline_ignores: true, ASH passes neither, and cfn-lint reads your config_file as written, a template's configure_rules taking precedence over it.

docs.title: Offline use
docs.text: cfn-lint needs no network to scan. Its resource schemas ship inside the package, and it only downloads updates when asked to (cfn-lint --update-specs and similar), which ASH never does. A scan inside a network namespace with no interfaces produced the same results as one with network access. Installing cfn-lint needs network once; in offline mode (ASH_OFFLINE=true) a cfn-lint that is not already installed is reported as MISSING with the reason.

docs.title: How ASH runs it
docs.text:
cfn-lint --format sarif --output-file=<results> [options] -- <template> ...

in a new, empty directory outside the scanned tree, with every path absolute; ASH reports each location relative to the source directory. Template paths are escaped before they are passed, because cfn-lint expands each filename argument as a glob pattern: a template named a[1].yaml would otherwise not be linted at all. Long template lists are split across several invocations to stay within command-line length limits. With honor_inline_ignores: true each template has an invocation of its own (see "Suppressions").

cfn-lint's exit status is a bitmask of the levels it reported (2 error, 4 warning, 8 informational); any combination of those is a completed run. Other exit statuses, a timeout, missing output, or an E0003 result mark every template in that invocation as not evaluated, so one such template costs the findings of the others in its batch; with honor_inline_ignores: true it costs only its own. The scan then reports partial coverage and exits 1 by default, so nothing is lost silently. The source tree and the converted files are separate targets, and each records the worst exit status of its own invocations.

docs.title: License
docs.text: cfn-lint is MIT-0 (MIT No Attribution). It is installed as a separate tool and is not bundled into ASH's Python package.

docs.title: cfn-guard
docs.text: AWS CloudFormation Guard (cfn-guard) evaluates CloudFormation templates against policy-as-code rules written in the Guard DSL. cfn-guard ships no rules of its own, so ASH pins a rule source, the AWS Guard Rules Registry, and lets you add or substitute your own rules.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ash dependencies install --tool cfn-guard

installs two pinned artifacts, each verified against a SHA256 recorded in ASH's source (automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py):

  • the cfn-guard 3.2.1 release binary for your platform (Linux, macOS and Windows, amd64 and arm64), into ASH_BIN_PATH;
  • the AWS Guard Rules Registry release 1.0.2 rules archive. Its output/*.guard files are extracted into aws-guard-rules-registry-1.0.2/ under $ASH_CFN_GUARD_RULES_DIR, or under <ASH_BIN_PATH>/../share/cfn-guard-rules when that is unset. ASH's source also pins what the archive extracts to: one SHA256 over the names and digests of all 50 rule files. The extracted files are checked against it before they are moved into place. A .ash-rules-manifest.json beside them records what was installed; no check relies on it.

A download whose bytes do not match the pinned digest is refused. The ASH container image ships both, installed read-only for the scan user: the rules are in /usr/share/ash/cfn-guard-rules, which the image checks at build time is owned by root, as is every directory above it. nixpkgs has no cfn-guard package, so the nix flake packages the same pinned release binary (nix/cfn-guard.nix), and the nix shell installs the rules bundle into ASH_CFN_GUARD_RULES_DIR on first entry, and again on any entry where the bundle there is not the pinned one: after an ASH upgrade that changes the pin, or when the rule files there no longer match the pinned contents.

ash dependencies install keeps a bundle that is already in place only when its rule files match the pinned contents; otherwise it downloads and installs the pinned archive again. Without network access that download fails, and the install stops with a message that names the directory, says its rules do not match the pinned contents, and says that network access, or the ASH container image, is needed. The rules already there are left as they were.

Before every scan ASH checks the installed rule files against the pinned contents in the same way. A rule file that was edited, removed, renamed or added, or is not a regular file, makes the scanner MISSING with the reinstall command rather than scanning with it. Files in that directory without the .guard suffix are not part of the bundle and are not read.

docs.title: Rule sets
docs.text:
The registry release contains 50 rule-set files: one per compliance framework (CIS AWS Benchmark, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, HIPAA and others), a Well-Architected Security Pillar set, a Well-Architected Reliability Pillar set, and guard-rules-registry-all-rules.

The default is wa-Security-Pillar, the registry's mapping of the AWS Well-Architected Security Pillar (45 rules: public access, encryption, logging, TLS, IAM and similar). guard-rules-registry-all-rules (67 rules) was considered and not chosen: it adds 22 reliability and operations rules, such as backup plans, Multi-AZ, deletion protection, S3 replication and object lock, and Lambda concurrency, which are not security findings and would fail templates for reasons a security scan should not. The compliance-framework sets are a choice for your own context rather than a default.

scanners:
  cfn-guard:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # Bundled registry rule sets, by file name without ".guard".
      rule_sets:
        - wa-Security-Pillar
        - cis-aws-benchmark-level-1
      # Your own .guard files or directories. A relative path is taken from the
      # directory of this config file (from the working directory for
      # --config-overrides). Evaluated in addition to rule_sets; set
      # rule_sets: [] to use only these.
      rules_paths:
        - policy/guard
      # Seconds each per-template cfn-guard run may take.
      scan_timeout: 1800

A rule-set name with a .guard extension or characters outside letters, digits, ., _ and - fails config validation. A well-formed name that is not in the bundle makes the scanner MISSING, with the list of available names.

rule_sets is honored only when you set it as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. A narrower set drops findings before ASH sees them: wa-Reliability-Pillar alone turns the 24 findings on ASH's test template into 9, losing every public-access, encryption and logging finding. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or by an MCP client, it is ignored with a warning and wa-Security-Pillar is evaluated.

rules_paths is honored only when you set it as the operator, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; a path the operator names may be inside the scanned tree. A relative entry is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides (rules_paths=[...] or rules_paths+=<path>), not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). The scanned repository decides what is at such a path, so one that leads out of the tree through a symbolic link in it, to a file or a directory, makes the scanner MISSING and is not read. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or by an MCP client, it is ignored with a warning, and if rule_sets is empty as well, cfn-guard evaluates the default wa-Security-Pillar set instead of nothing. cfn-guard prints a rules file it cannot parse, all of it, in its error, so a path the scanned repository chose could otherwise put any file the scan can read into the report.

For a directory, ASH collects the files cfn-guard would read from it: .guard and .ruleset files at any depth, case-sensitively, not entering symlinked subdirectories. cfn-guard follows a symlinked rules file, so one that resolves outside the directory you named is refused with a warning; a link that stays inside it is read. ASH reads each file itself and gives cfn-guard a copy, written in a directory of that scanner run's own outside the scanned tree, made with mode 0700 and removed when the run ends, which is also why rules_paths needs no sandbox grant: under --sandbox, cfn-guard can read that directory and cannot write to it. A directory with no rules files selects nothing, and when nothing else is selected the scanner is MISSING ("no cfn-guard rules are selected"): cfn-guard given such a directory would report a clean run. A rules_paths entry that does not exist, a named file that is not a regular file, or a subdirectory that cannot be listed also makes the scanner MISSING.

docs.title: Why the rules are not age-checked
docs.text: ASH holds downloaded content databases (grype's and trivy's vulnerability databases, the offline semgrep and opengrep rulesets) to a maximum age, because those are fetched at build or scan time and can go stale silently. The Guard rules are not declared there. They are a fixed release archive pinned by digest, like the policies inside the pinned checkov package: they change only when ASH changes the pin, and an age bound would measure how recently the same bytes were copied rather than how current the rules are. Release 1.0.2 is the newest the registry has published.

docs.title: Which files it scans
docs.text: The same files cfn-nag and cfn-lint scan: every .json, .yaml and .yml file in the scan set that parses as YAML or JSON and has a top-level Resources mapping. A file with a Resources mapping that ASH cannot model as CloudFormation is counted as not evaluated.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
Every failed cfn-guard rule is reported as HIGH with SARIF level error.

cfn-guard marks every failure error and the registry's rules carry no severity of their own, so there is nothing per rule to map from. Every finding is HIGH because a template that violates a rule of the compliance set you chose has failed that control; the default set checks security configuration (public access blocks, encryption, logging, TLS). That includes rules that are less severe in isolation, such as a missing access log: to keep those out, choose a narrower rule set with options.rule_sets, or suppress the rule by id. ASH sets issue_severity on each result as well as the SARIF level, so the summary, the exit-code gate and every reporter all read HIGH. Adjust what fails the scan with scanners.cfn-guard.options.severity_threshold. cfn-guard reports one result per failing clause, so one rule can appear more than once for the same resource. Many rules are in more than one of the registry's rule sets, and cfn-guard reports such a rule's results once for each selected set that holds it; ASH reports each identical result once.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply by rule_id, path, and line_start/line_end. Each result is located at the line cfn-guard reports, usually the resource's Properties, so a line-scoped suppression names that line:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: S3_BUCKET_LOGGING_ENABLED
      path: templates/logging-bucket.yaml
      reason: This bucket is the access-log destination.

Package-scoped and symbol-scoped suppressions do not apply to templates. The registry's rules also honor cfn-guard's own in-template suppression, which never reaches ASH:

Resources:
  LogBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Metadata:
      guard:
        SuppressedRules:
          - S3_BUCKET_LOGGING_ENABLED

docs.title: Offline use
docs.text: cfn-guard needs no network to scan: the binary is static and the rules are local files. A scan inside a network namespace with no interfaces produced the same results. If the binary or the rules are missing in an air-gapped environment, the scanner is MISSING with the reason; nothing is fetched at scan time.

docs.title: How ASH runs it
docs.text:
Once per template:

cfn-guard validate --rules=<rules file>... --data=<template> \
  --output-format=sarif --structured --show-summary=none

One template at a time because one unparseable data file makes cfn-guard exit 255 with no output for the whole invocation, and because cfn-guard writes result locations as absolute paths, which ASH replaces with the repository-relative path of the template it ran. Exit 0 means every rule passed or was skipped and 19 means at least one failed; any other status, a timeout, or a 19 with no results marks that template as not evaluated. As for cfn-lint, the source tree and the converted files each record the worst exit status of their own runs.

docs.title: Licenses
docs.text: cfn-guard and the AWS Guard Rules Registry are both Apache-2.0. Neither is bundled into ASH's Python package; both are downloaded by ash dependencies install or shipped in the container image as separate artifacts.

docs.title: Gitleaks scanner
docs.text:
gitleaks finds credentials (API keys, tokens, private keys) by matching its rule set against file contents. ASH runs it as gitleaks dir over the files in the scan target. It does not scan git history.

detect-secrets stays on by default and is unaffected; the two can run side by side. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so a secret both of them find is reported twice, once under each scanner's name and rule id; suppress it for each scanner, or enable only one.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
Gitleaks is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.gitleaks.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If the tool is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

gitleaks is a native binary, so --python-only does not run it.

docs.title: Installing gitleaks
docs.text:
• Container image: included. The image installs the pinned release (currently v8.30.1) whether or not you enable the scanner.
  • Local mode: ash dependencies install downloads the pinned release asset from GitHub and checks it against the SHA256 recorded in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py before installing it. A download that does not match is refused.
  • Nix mode: the flake supplies nixpkgs' gitleaks.
  • A gitleaks already on PATH is used as is. ASH is tested against the pinned version.

gitleaks makes no network calls while scanning, so it works offline and in air-gapped environments with no extra setup.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  gitleaks:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # A gitleaks TOML config; a relative path is taken from where it is set.
      config_file: null
      # A gitleaks JSON report whose findings gitleaks ignores (--baseline-path).
      baseline_path: null
      # Honor gitleaks:allow comments in the scanned tree. Off by default.
      honor_inline_ignores: false
      # Skip files larger than this many megabytes. Operator-only.
      max_target_megabytes: null
      # Seconds before the gitleaks process is killed. Inherited by every scanner.
      scan_timeout: 1800
      # This scanner's override of the global severity threshold. Every gitleaks
      # finding is CRITICAL, so any threshold still fails on them.
      severity_threshold: null

docs.title: Which gitleaks config is used
docs.text:
The scanned repository's own gitleaks configuration is not used. A .gitleaks.toml can replace gitleaks' rules or allowlist every path, and a .gitleaksignore drops findings by fingerprint, before ASH sees the report: what they hide is neither reported nor counted as suppressed. Tune findings with ASH suppressions, which are both.

  1. options.config_file, when the operator set it: from --config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written). A path that does not exist fails the scan rather than falling back to gitleaks' default rules.
  2. Otherwise, if GITLEAKS_CONFIG or GITLEAKS_CONFIG_TOML is set in the environment, gitleaks resolves the config from it. Under --sandbox those variables are not passed in, and step 3 applies.
  3. Otherwise gitleaks' default rules, through a config ASH writes that extends them and adds nothing. It is passed as gitleaks --config, so gitleaks does not fall back to a .gitleaks.toml in the scanned tree. ASH writes it outside the scanned tree, with the empty directory it passes as gitleaks --gitleaks-ignore-path, and removes both when the scan ends.

config_file, baseline_path, max_target_megabytes or honor_inline_ignores set by an ASH config inside any git checkout or the scanned directory (such as .ash/.ash.yaml), or by an MCP client, is ignored with a warning, and a .gitleaks.toml or .ash/.gitleaks.toml in the tree is noted at INFO. The operator's files may be absolute paths or point outside the source directory. A relative config_file or baseline_path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). A file the operator names may also be inside the scanned tree, unless that path leads out of the tree through a symlink: the scanned repository decides what is there, so such a path stops the scanner with an error and gitleaks is not run.

gitleaks always reads .gitleaksignore at the root of the path it scans, whatever gitleaks --gitleaks-ignore-path says, and has no flag to turn that off. When the scan root has one, ASH copies the files it names into a directory of its own, at the same paths, runs gitleaks once more over the copies (there is no .gitleaksignore there), and reports the findings the first run dropped. That directory is outside the scanned tree, in a directory of the scanner run's own made with mode 0700, and under --sandbox gitleaks can read it and cannot write to it. ASH reads .gitleaksignore the way gitleaks does (a line ends at a newline only, surrounding whitespace is trimmed as Go trims it, and a backslash in a path is a slash), so it re-scans the files gitleaks matched. Files the first run does not read are not copied: files under .git or another directory gitleaks' allowlists skip, files reached through a symlink, and anything that is not a regular file. A failed re-run fails the scan, and the copies are deleted when it ends. The re-run copies at most 10,000 files and runs within one scan_timeout; when the file names more, the rest are not re-scanned, a warning gives their number, and the scan exits 1 as incomplete, because a finding the file hides in them would not be reported.

A .gitleaksignore at the scan root that is a symlink, a FIFO or another file that is not a regular file, or one with a second hard link, stops the scanner with an error before gitleaks runs: gitleaks would open whatever the name points to and copy lines of it into its log.

gitleaks' options are described by the JSON schema (automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json) and listed above.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text: gitleaks reports no severity of its own. ASH rates every gitleaks finding CRITICAL, in the summaries and in every report: the SARIF result has level: error and the finding carries CRITICAL as its own severity, which ash.flat.json and the CSV report read. A detect-secrets finding carries only level: error, so the summaries rate it CRITICAL too, while ash.flat.json and the CSV report read HIGH for it; the same credential found by both scanners can therefore read differently in those two reports. gitleaks has no per-rule confidence to grade on: each rule says "a credential of this kind is present".

docs.title: Secret values never reach ASH's output
docs.text:
ASH always runs gitleaks --redact=100, so gitleaks writes REDACTED in place of each secret in its report and its log. ASH also overwrites any report snippet that is not REDACTED before the result is stored, so the value cannot appear in ash_aggregated_results.json, the SARIF, or any other report.

gitleaks is a secrets scanner (tool type SECRETS), so a gitleaks finding is a secret finding: in ASH's reports the line it reports reads [masked: a secret finding reports this line] in every snippet, its own included (see "Secret values in reports" in the output formats page), and the Bedrock summary reporter counts gitleaks findings rather than sending them to the model. gitleaks' own report under scanners/gitleaks/ keeps its REDACTED.

gitleaks' log repeats each line of a .gitleaksignore it cannot parse. ASH cuts those lines short in the log it keeps (GitleaksScanner.stderr.log), and does not quote gitleaks' log in error messages; an error names the log file instead.

docs.title: Suppressing findings
docs.text:
Use ASH suppressions: they are recorded in the reports and counted. gitleaks' own mechanisms drop findings before ASH sees the report, so only these still apply:

  • A gitleaks:allow comment on the line with the secret, only when the operator sets options.honor_inline_ignores: true with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory. By default ASH runs gitleaks --ignore-gitleaks-allow, so the comment hides nothing; set from a config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, the option is ignored with a warning.
  • [[allowlists]] in an operator's config_file (paths, regexes, stopwords, per-rule).
  • An operator's baseline_path: a previous gitleaks JSON report whose findings are ignored.

The scanned repository's .gitleaks.toml and .gitleaksignore do not apply (see above).

ASH suppressions use the gitleaks rule id (for example github-pat, aws-access-token) and the path relative to the source directory:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: github-pat
      path: tests/fixtures/settings.py
      line_start: 12
      line_end: 12
      reason: Fabricated token used by the test suite

Rule, path and line suppressions apply. A symbol suppression (the enclosing function or class) applies to a finding in a source language ASH can parse. Package-scoped suppressions do not apply: a gitleaks finding is about a file, not a dependency. global_settings.ignore_paths removes gitleaks findings under those paths, and findings inside ASH's own output directory are removed, except in the files ASH extracted from archives and notebooks, and in files the repository committed there. In a git checkout, a file git tracks in that directory is the repository's and keeps its findings; outside a checkout nothing tells the repository's files from ASH's, and every finding there is removed.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: ASH runs gitleaks --exit-code=2, because gitleaks otherwise exits 1 both when it finds leaks and when it fails. 0 (nothing found) and 2 (leaks found) are success; any other code, including 1 for an unreadable config or path, makes the scanner report an error and the scan exit 1.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• Working tree only. Secrets that were committed and later removed are not reported; run gitleaks git separately if you need history.
  • gitleaks reads ASH's output directory when it sits inside the source tree (the default .ash/ash_output), because it has no option to skip a directory. ASH discards the findings there, except those in files the repository committed to that directory, but the files are still read. That directory holds the files ASH extracts from archives and notebooks; gitleaks scans those copies separately, so a secret in an archive is reported once, at its extracted path.
  • The SARIF semanticVersion that gitleaks 8.30.1 writes is wrong (v8.0.0), so ASH removes it; the real version comes from gitleaks --version.

docs.title: Trivy filesystem scanner (trivy)
docs.text: trivy matches the packages in your dependency manifests and lockfiles against its vulnerability database. ASH runs it as trivy fs over each scan target.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text:
The trivy scanner is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.trivy.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If the tool is not installed, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

trivy is a native binary, so --python-only does not run it.

docs.title: Installing trivy
docs.text:
• Container image: included. The image installs the pinned release (currently v0.75.0).
  • Local mode: ash dependencies install downloads the pinned release asset from GitHub and checks it against the SHA256 recorded in automated_security_helper/utils/tool_downloads.py before installing it. trivy publishes no Windows arm64 asset, so there it has to be installed another way.
  • Nix mode: the flake supplies nixpkgs' trivy, and the nix shell keeps its vulnerability database in TRIVY_CACHE_DIR (default ~/.cache/ash/trivy), updating it on every entry; trivy returns at once when the database is current. Nix mode scans offline, so when the shell had no network and nothing is cached, trivy is reported MISSING with the reason; see Offline and air-gapped use.
  • A trivy already on PATH is used as is. ASH is tested against the pinned version.

docs.title: What it scans by default, and why
docs.text:
trivy has four scanners. This scanner runs one of them unless you, as the operator, ask for more:

trivy scanner Enabled Why vuln on Known vulnerabilities in dependencies, from trivy's own database. grype answers the same question from a different database; a second database is the reason to enable trivy. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so a vulnerability both find is reported by each, trivy usually under the CVE id and grype under the GHSA id, and one suppression by rule_id does not cover both. secret off detect-secrets runs by default. Both would report the same credential under different rule ids, and a suppression for one does not cover the other. misconfig off checkov, cfn-nag and cdk-nag cover IaC by default. license off License findings are a compliance question and depend on a license policy ASH does not hold. 
scanners:
  trivy:
    enabled: true
    options:
      # Any of vuln, secret, misconfig, license. At least one. Honored only from
      # the operator (--config-overrides or a config file outside every git
      # checkout and the scanned directory); set by a config inside one, it is
      # ignored with a warning.
      scanners: ["vuln"]
      # Report only vulnerabilities with a fixed version. Off: an unfixed
      # vulnerability is still a vulnerability. ASH logs a warning when it is on.
      ignore_unfixed: false
      # Look for licenses in source headers too. Only used with `license`.
      license_full: false
      # Only the operator sets it to false (--config-overrides or a config file
      # outside every git checkout and the scanned directory); any config may set
      # it to true. Offline, trivy sends nothing whatever this says.
      disable_telemetry: true
      # A trivy.yaml (from the operator), a .trivyignore and a trivy-secret.yaml,
      # each outside the scanned tree. Unset, the ones in the scanned repository
      # are NOT read; see below.
      config_file: null
      ignore_file: null
      secret_config_file: null
      # false follows ASH (--offline / ASH_OFFLINE); true forces trivy offline.
      offline: false
      # Gates the verdict, as for every scanner. Findings below it are still
      # reported. ASH does not pass it as trivy --severity.
      severity_threshold: null
      # Seconds before the trivy process is killed; also passed as trivy --timeout.
      # null leaves both unbounded: ASH passes trivy --timeout=2562047h (about 292
      # years), since it reads 0s as a deadline already passed. Its default is 5m.
      scan_timeout: 1800

docs.title: trivy configuration in the scanned repository
docs.text:
trivy reads trivy.yaml, .trivyignore and, for the secret scanner, trivy-secret.yaml from its working directory, which is the repository being scanned. Any of them can remove findings without the report saying so: a severity: [CRITICAL] or scan.skip-files entry in trivy.yaml removes every lower-rated or skipped finding, an ignore-policy it names (a Rego file) drops whatever the policy matches, each .trivyignore line removes an advisory, and trivy-secret.yaml can disable secret rules. A trivy.yaml can also point trivy at a directory of WASM modules (module.dir) and enable them, which runs them during the scan, and turn on a VEX repository download or client/server mode, which reach the network. So the builtin scanner passes trivy --config, trivy --ignorefile and trivy --secret-config pointing at files that set nothing (the empty config ASH ships, and an empty ignore file and secret config ASH writes outside the scanned tree), and a repository's own files are not read. It also passes trivy --module-dir naming an empty directory ASH makes outside the scanned tree for each run, so trivy loads no WASM module, from ~/.trivy/modules or a config's module.dir; unlike trivy-repo, the builtin scanner has no module_dir option. trivy reads no other file from a default location: trivy --ignore-policy has no default.

To use your own:

  • config_file: set it as the operator, through --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written), for a file outside the scanned tree. Set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, or naming a file inside the tree, it is ignored with a warning, and an MCP client cannot set it at all: /scanners/trivy/** is denied to every client, as for each scanner that can send data off the host. So is a path inside the tree that leads out of it through a symbolic link there: the link chose the file, not the operator. A relative path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings). Unset or ignored, trivy gets TRIVY_CONFIG from the environment, for a file outside the scanned tree (a relative path in it is taken from the working directory ASH runs in, not from the source directory), and otherwise ASH's empty config.
  • ignore_file and secret_config_file: under the same rule as config_file, a relative path included. Otherwise TRIVY_IGNOREFILE and TRIVY_SECRET_CONFIG from the environment, for a file outside the scanned tree; a relative path in either is taken from the working directory ASH runs in. A file inside the tree is ignored with a warning, and trivy gets ASH's empty one, which ASH writes outside the scanned tree and removes when the scan ends. trivy-repo takes all three the same way.
ash scan --config-overrides 'scanners.trivy.options.ignore_file=/etc/ash/trivyignore'

A configured file that does not exist fails the scan rather than running without it.

ASH always passes trivy --exit-code=0, which outranks TRIVY_EXIT_CODE and an exit-code set in your config_file. trivy then exits nonzero only when it fails, and its report is read whatever it found. trivy-repo gets the same flag.

To accept a finding, prefer an ASH suppression, which is recorded in the reports and counted. The community trivy-repo plugin passes its own config file, modules directory, ignore file and secret config the same way; see its config_file, module_dir, ignore_file and secret_config_file options.

docs.title: Severity
docs.text:
Each finding is reported at trivy's own severity for it (CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW), not at a band of its CVSS score, so a finding trivy rates HIGH is reported HIGH whatever its score. A finding trivy rates UNKNOWN falls back to ASH's usual SARIF mapping: the rule's CVSS score (security-severity), then the SARIF level.

severity_threshold works as for every other scanner: ASH applies it after the scan, to that severity, so a finding below it is still reported and does not fail the scan. ASH does not pass it as trivy --severity, which would drop those findings before ASH saw them.

The severity is read per finding, from the Severity: line trivy writes in each result's message, not from the result's SARIF rule. trivy writes one rule per advisory, and one advisory can be rated differently for two packages in the same scan (Debian, for example, rates some binutils advisories CRITICAL for binutils and LOW for gdb); the rule carries only one of those ratings.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
ASH suppressions apply as for any scanner:

  • rule_id is the advisory id (CVE-2021-23337, GHSA-...), or the check id (DS-0002) for misconfiguration findings.
  • path and line_start/line_end match the manifest and the line trivy reports for the package.
  • package_name, package_version and package_path match one package copy. For npm lockfiles, a result covering two installed copies of the same version is split into one result per copy, so a suppression can cover one copy and not the other.

Symbol-scoped suppressions (function or class) do not apply: a dependency finding points at a manifest entry, not at code.

docs.title: Vulnerability database and staleness
docs.text:
The database is declared as trivy-db in automated_security_helper/utils/content_databases.py, with a 24h bound measured from its UpdatedAt, which is trivy's own rule for its published database. After the scan, ASH reads UpdatedAt from trivy version --format json and fails the scan when the database is older than that (content_db_staleness: warn or --allow-stale-content-db turns the failure into a warning carried in every report). This is the same check grype's database gets. In an image built with OFFLINE=YES the stale database warns instead of failing; see Offline and air-gapped use.

  • Online, ASH updates the database once per scan before trivy and trivy-repo run (trivy image --download-db-only, outside the scanner sandbox and under a lock in trivy's cache, so the two never write it at the same time), and fails the scan if it cannot download one. The update runs from a directory outside the scanned tree with an explicit trivy --config: your config file when the scan uses one (config_file, or TRIVY_CONFIG), so a database mirror it names applies, and otherwise the empty one ASH ships. Both scanners then run with trivy --skip-db-update --skip-java-db-update, trivy --skip-check-update when misconfig is on, and trivy --cache-dir naming the cache the update wrote, so the scan only reads the cache. fs and repository scans never read the Java database.
  • If you turn trivy's own update off, with TRIVY_SKIP_DB_UPDATE=true or db.skip-update: true in your config file, ASH does not run its update either: trivy refuses to download a database under that setting, and you set it to keep trivy off the database registry, for example in CI that restores a cached database. ASH logs a warning naming the setting, and trivy and trivy-repo read the database already in the cache. The post-scan check still holds it to the 24h bound, so a cache you do not keep current fails the scan (or warns, under content_db_staleness: warn).
  • Offline, ASH passes trivy --skip-db-update --skip-java-db-update --skip-check-update, so trivy uses whatever database is in its cache (named with trivy --cache-dir, as below), and the post-scan check holds it to the bound.
  • Online or offline, trivy scans never contact package registries: ASH passes trivy --offline-scan on every scan, and the database refresh is the separate step above. trivy then resolves Maven dependencies from the pom.xml files in the scanned tree and the local Maven repository (~/.m2/repository), not from the repositories a pom.xml declares or Maven Central. trivy does not check for new versions or announcements either: online every scan gets trivy --skip-version-check, and offline TRIVY_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=true in trivy's environment turns the same check off (see What offline mode turns off), since a trivy too old to know the flag refuses the command over it and ignores the variable. trivy-repo gets the same.
  • Where the database is kept: where trivy itself keeps it on the host. That is TRIVY_CACHE_DIR when it is set, else $XDG_CACHE_HOME/trivy on Linux when that is set, else ~/.cache/trivy (~/Library/Caches/trivy on macOS, %LocalAppData%\trivy on Windows). ASH names that directory to the update, to every scan (trivy --cache-dir), online and offline, and to the post-scan check, so all three read one database, sandboxed or not: the sandbox does not pass XDG_CACHE_HOME, and trivy left to its own default there would read another cache. A cache.dir in a trivy.yaml does not move it; set TRIVY_CACHE_DIR instead.

The database is only read by the vuln scanner; with vuln off nothing is measured.

docs.title: Offline and air-gapped use
docs.text:
trivy needs a database in its cache to scan offline. With none, ASH reports trivy MISSING with the reason and the scan exits 1; trivy is not run. To provide one, on a machine with network access:

TRIVY_CACHE_DIR=/path/to/cache trivy image --download-db-only

and point the offline scan at the same TRIVY_CACHE_DIR.

With misconfig added to scanners, trivy's Terraform checks do not run offline: trivy downloads the source of every module block a .tf file names (from the Terraform registry, with the host's git, or over HTTPS) whatever offline flags it is given. ASH passes trivy --misconfig-scanners with the installed trivy's own default list minus terraform, read from trivy fs --help, and logs a warning; when that list cannot be read, misconfig is left out of the offline scan. checkov still checks Terraform. trivy-repo does the same. In nix mode, export TRIVY_CACHE_DIR before running ash scan --mode nix; the variable is passed through to the scan. The container image built with --offline ships a trivy database (in /deps/.trivy, its TRIVY_CACHE_DIR), downloaded at build time; the build fails if that download fails or leaves the cache empty. Once that database is older than the 24h bound, scans in that image still pass: the image holds trivy-db to warn rather than fail, so every report records the stale database and its age. Its findings still lack advisories published since the build, so refresh it anyway: rebuild the image, or mount a fresher cache as TRIVY_CACHE_DIR. To make the stale database fail the scan instead, set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false (see Stale content databases). This default follows ASH_OFFLINE_AT_BUILD_TIME=YES, which the offline image sets; without it, a stale database in a TRIVY_CACHE_DIR you provide is held to content_db_staleness.

docs.title: Running it alongside the trivy-repo community plugin
docs.text:
The community trivy-repo plugin (enabled through ash_plugin_modules) keeps its name and its defaults (all four trivy scanners, unfixed vulnerabilities dropped, license_full: true), and has a module_dir option trivy does not. It names its own config file and modules directory, so a trivy.yaml in the scanned repository is not loaded, and settings that file made no longer apply. The two share their implementation (the database update, the cache and the treatment of trivy's input files) but are separate scanners. trivy-repo keeps its own scan path: it gets no trivy --timeout (trivy's 5-minute default applies), no trivy --skip-dirs for ASH's output directory, no offline check for a missing database, and its findings are rated by ASH's usual SARIF mapping rather than at trivy's own severity (see Severity), so one finding can carry different ASH severities in the two scanners.

trivy is on by default, so listing the Trivy plugin for trivy-repo runs trivy twice, and each finding is reported once per scanner, under that scanner's name. Both read the same database, which is measured once for each: a stale database is reported, and fails the scan, under each scanner's name. The rule ids are the same, so one suppression by rule_id and path covers both. To avoid the duplicate, keep one: set scanners.trivy.enabled: false, or stop listing the plugin.

docs.title: zizmor (GitHub Actions)
docs.text:
zizmor is a static analyzer for GitHub Actions. ASH runs it over a repository's workflows and composite actions and reports template injection, dangerous triggers, credential persistence, unpinned actions, excessive permissions and the rest of zizmor's audits.

actionlint, also a builtin scanner, flags template injection from untrusted event data too. ASH does not deduplicate across scanners, so with both enabled such a step is reported by each, under its own rule id.

docs.title: Enabling it
docs.text: zizmor is a builtin scanner, enabled by default: a default scan runs it. scanners.zizmor.enabled: false in the ASH config turns it off, and --scanners and --exclude-scanners select it as they select any scanner. If no zizmor satisfying tool_version is found, ASH installs one with uv tool install (online only). If that fails, the scanner is reported MISSING and the scan exits 1 (the incomplete-scan gate), as for every builtin scanner; ash dependencies install and the container image provide it.

docs.title: What gets scanned
docs.text:
ASH passes zizmor two kinds of file, taken from its scan set so .gitignore, .ignore and global_settings.ignore_paths apply (the ignore files only while honor_ignore_files is on, the default):

  • workflows: *.yml and *.yaml directly inside a .github/workflows directory (the only place GitHub runs a workflow from; subdirectories are not scanned), including when the source directory is itself .github or .github/workflows;
  • composite actions: every action.yml and action.yaml.

Files under directories named node_modules, .venv or venv are skipped, and so is a file that is a symlink resolving outside the scan root, with a warning: zizmor would read it where it points. In the source directory, such a link is left out by the scan set before zizmor's check sees it, with the warning Not scanning '<path>': link leaves the scanned tree, and is listed among the inputs not scanned (see What decides the files). A broken symlink (its target is missing, or links loop) is skipped with a warning too, since zizmor would fail the whole run on it. A repository with neither kind of file does not start zizmor; the scanner reports SKIPPED with zero findings, the same as cfn-nag on a repository with no templates.

zizmor is a Python package ASH runs through uv, so --python-only runs it.

A file named action.yml that is not a GitHub Actions definition is not counted. A workflow or action that zizmor cannot load (a YAML syntax error, or a file in .github/workflows that is not a valid workflow) is counted as a target that failed, which --fail-on-incomplete-scanners reports.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  zizmor:
    enabled: true
    options:
      persona: regular        # regular, pedantic or auditor
      config_file: null       # zizmor config; relative to where it is set, or absolute
      online_audits: false    # see "Network access and tokens"
      honor_inline_ignores: false  # see "Suppressions"
      tool_version: ">=1.29.0,<2.0.0"
      install_timeout: 300
      scan_timeout: 1800
      severity_threshold: null
  • persona: zizmor's persona. regular has the fewest false positives, pedantic adds code-smell findings, and auditor reports everything.
  • config_file: passed as zizmor --config, when the operator set it: from --config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (one that is not repository-written). A relative path is taken from the directory of the ASH config file that sets it, or from the working directory for --config-overrides, not from the source directory (see Relative paths in the operator's settings); an absolute path is used as given. Without it, ASH runs zizmor --no-config, so a zizmor.yml or .github/zizmor.yml in the scanned repository is not read: a config there can disable audits or ignore findings, which zizmor then never reports, so they would be neither in ASH's results nor counted as suppressed. config_file set by an ASH config inside a git checkout or the scanned directory is ignored with a warning, and an MCP client cannot set it at all (see online_audits below). A configured file that does not exist fails the scan rather than being ignored. The file may be inside the scanned tree, but the scanned repository decides what is at such a path, so one there that leads out of the tree through a symbolic link fails the scan with ERROR and zizmor is not run. zizmor quotes the offending text of a config it cannot parse in its error, and that error reaches ASH's log and the scanner's stderr log, so do not point this at a file holding anything else.
  • honor_inline_ignores: when true, zizmor applies its own # zizmor: ignore[...] comments and the ignore rules of an operator's config_file. Off by default; see "Suppressions". Honored only when the operator sets it.
  • tool_version: the pip-style constraint for installing zizmor. A value that is not a valid constraint is ignored with a warning and the default is used. It decides which zizmor is installed and which one on PATH is accepted, so a value other than the default is honored only when the operator sets it (--config-overrides, or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory); set by an ASH config inside one, it is ignored with a warning.
  • install_timeout: seconds allowed for uv tool install of zizmor.
  • scan_timeout: seconds zizmor may run; past it zizmor is killed and the scanner reports ERROR.
  • severity_threshold: this scanner's override of the global severity threshold.

docs.title: Network access and tokens
docs.text:
ASH always runs zizmor --offline unless online_audits: true. Offline is the default because zizmor reads a GitHub token from GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN by itself, and a token that happens to be in a CI job's environment is not permission to use it. While offline, ASH removes those three variables from zizmor's environment.

online_audits: true drops zizmor --offline and lets those variables reach zizmor unchanged, which enables the audits that query the GitHub API (for example known-vulnerable actions and impostor commits). It is honored only when the operator sets it, with --config-overrides or an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by a config inside one, it is ignored with a warning and zizmor runs offline without the tokens. An MCP client cannot configure zizmor at all: its whole section, /scanners/zizmor/**, is denied to a client whatever a profile's denied_paths says, as for every scanner that can send data off the host. ASH never reads, copies or logs the token and never puts it on zizmor's command line. ASH's own offline mode (ASH_OFFLINE=true or ash scan --offline) overrides online_audits. Under --sandbox, zizmor never gets the token: the sandbox passes no GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, so online audits cannot authenticate. It gets a network only when the operator lists zizmor in sandbox.network_scanners, and never when the scan is offline.

ZIZMOR_CONFIG, ZIZMOR_OFFLINE and ZIZMOR_NO_ONLINE_AUDITS are always removed from zizmor's environment, so a scan's result depends on the repository and the ASH config rather than on the shell it ran in. Use config_file instead of ZIZMOR_CONFIG.

docs.title: Severity mapping
docs.text:
zizmor rates each finding with a severity and a confidence. ASH combines them:

zizmor severity confidence Medium or High confidence Low High HIGH MEDIUM Medium MEDIUM LOW Low LOW INFO Informational INFO INFO

zizmor's scale stops at High, so no zizmor finding is CRITICAL. A low-confidence finding is one zizmor expects to be wrong some of the time, so it is reported one band lower. The SARIF level is set to match (HIGH error, MEDIUM warning, LOW note, INFO none), and zizmor's own values stay on the result as properties["zizmor/severity"] and properties["zizmor/confidence"]. A finding missing either value keeps zizmor's own level.

With the default MEDIUM threshold, the low-confidence artipacked finding (Medium, Low) is reported LOW and does not fail the scan on its own.

docs.title: Suppressions
docs.text:
Rule IDs are zizmor's audit names with a zizmor/ prefix, for example zizmor/template-injection. ASH suppressions by rule, path and line all apply:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: zizmor/dangerous-triggers
      path: .github/workflows/release.yml
      line_start: 3
      reason: "Runs only on tags pushed by maintainers"

zizmor's own ignore comments (# zizmor: ignore[template-injection]) are not honored by default. Such a comment makes zizmor drop the finding before ASH sees it, so it would be neither reported nor counted as suppressed; ASH runs zizmor --no-ignores, which also turns off the ignore rules of an operator's config_file (its other settings still apply). To honor both, the operator sets honor_inline_ignores: true with --config-overrides or in an ASH config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory; set by an ASH config inside one, it is ignored with a warning. A zizmor.yml in the scanned repository is never read. Package-scoped and symbol-scoped suppressions do not apply: zizmor reports no packages, and a workflow has no functions or classes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ash dependencies install installs zizmor with uv tool install, the newest release within tool_version, and the ASH container image ships zizmor 1.30.1. ASH also uses any zizmor already on PATH whose zizmor --version satisfies tool_version, which covers the nix flake (nixpkgs supplies zizmor), Homebrew, and cargo install. Offline, ASH does not try to install zizmor; install it first.

zizmor is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Community Plugins
docs.text: This section is dedicated to community-developed plugins for ASH. Community plugins extend ASH's functionality with additional scanners, reporters, converters, and event handlers developed by the community.

docs.title: Security Scanners
docs.text:
• Ferret Scan Plugin - Integrates Ferret Scan for comprehensive sensitive data detection (credit cards, passports, SSNs, API keys, secrets, and more)
  • Snyk Code Plugin - Integrates Snyk Code for static application security testing (SAST) of source code vulnerabilities
  • Trivy Plugin - Integrates Aquasec's Trivy for vulnerability, misconfiguration, secret, and license scanning

These three ship inside ASH. Each takes part in a scan only when that scan names its plugin module in ash_plugin_modules or --ash-plugin-modules, as its page shows. The MCP list_scanners tool reports them either way; listing one does not add it to any scan.

docs.title: Contributing a Community Plugin
docs.text:
We encourage the community to develop and share plugins that extend ASH's capabilities.

To contribute a community plugin:

  1. Develop your plugin following the Plugin Development Guide
  2. Host your plugin in a public repository
  3. Open a pull request to add your plugin to this documentation
  4. Include the following information in your PR:
  5. Plugin name and description
  6. Link to the repository
  7. Installation instructions
  8. Configuration options
  9. Example usage

docs.title: Plugin Submission Guidelines
docs.text:
To ensure quality and security, community plugins should:

  • Be open source with a compatible license
  • Include comprehensive documentation
  • Follow ASH's plugin development best practices
  • Include tests and examples
  • Be actively maintained

docs.title: Plugin Review Process
docs.text:
When you submit a PR to add your plugin to this documentation, the ASH team will:

  1. Review the plugin code for security and quality
  2. Test the plugin functionality
  3. Provide feedback on any necessary changes
  4. Merge the documentation PR once the plugin meets the guidelines

docs.title: Example Plugin Documentation Template
docs.text:
Replace <my-plugin-package-name> with the actual name of the plugin package you are creating.

## Plugin Name

**Description**: Brief description of what the plugin does and its key features.
\*Description\*\*: Brief description of what the plugin does and its key features.

**Repository**: [Link to GitHub/GitLab/etc. repository](https://github.com/username/plugin-repo)

**Author**: Your Name or Organization

**License**: License type (e.g., Apache 2.0, MIT)

### Installation

```bash
# Installation instructions
pip install <my-plugin-package-name>
```

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
# Example configuration in your ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project)
plugins:
  my-plugin:
    enabled: true
    options:
      option1: value1
      option2: value2

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Feature 1: Description
  • Feature 2: Description

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
# Example command line usage
ash scan --ash-plugin-modules my_plugin

[!CAUTION] > Community Plugin Security: The community plugins listed above ship with ASH, in automated_security_helper/plugin_modules, and need no separate package. ash scan loads one only when its module is listed in ash_plugin_modules or passed with --ash-plugin-modules. Each runs an external tool: the container image includes trivy, and you install the Snyk CLI and ferret-scan yourself, so check where each tool comes from. A plugin published outside ASH is a third-party package you install separately (for example with pip install), and ASH imports it into its own process, so verify its source and trustworthiness before installing it.

docs.title: ASH Ferret Scan Plugin
docs.text: This plugin integrates Ferret Scan with the Automated Security Helper (ASH) to provide comprehensive sensitive data detection for source code and documents.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Ferret Scan plugin enables ASH to leverage Ferret's powerful sensitive data detection capabilities for:

  • Credit Card Detection: 15+ card brands with mathematical validation (Luhn algorithm)
  • Passport Numbers: Multi-country formats including US, UK, Canada, EU, and MRZ
  • Social Security Numbers: Domain-aware validation with HR/Tax/Healthcare context
  • API Keys & Secrets: 40+ patterns including AWS, GitHub, Google Cloud, Stripe, and more
  • Email Addresses: RFC-compliant with domain validation
  • Phone Numbers: International and domestic formats
  • IP Addresses: IPv4 and IPv6 with network context
  • Social Media Profiles: LinkedIn, Twitter/X, Facebook, GitHub, Instagram, TikTok
  • Intellectual Property: Patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets
  • Document Metadata: EXIF and document metadata extraction

docs.title: ASH Convention Compliance
docs.text: This plugin follows ASH conventions for consistent behavior across all scanners:

docs.title: Hardcoded by Plugin (Do NOT configure at plugin level)
docs.text: Feature ASH Convention Notes Output Format Always SARIF Required by ASH for result aggregation Color Output Always --no-color ASH handles formatting

docs.title: Ferret-Scan Log Controls
docs.text:
Option Description ferret_debug: true Enables ferret-scan's own debug output (preprocessing/validation flow) ferret_verbose: true Enables ferret-scan's own verbose output (detailed finding info)

Note: Bare debug and verbose are blocked to avoid confusion with ASH's --debug/--verbose flags.

docs.title: Managed by ASH Framework
docs.text: Feature ASH Convention Notes Output Directory .ash/ash_output/scanners/ferret-scan/ Follows ASH conventions Offline Mode ASH_OFFLINE=true Respects ASH offline mode Suppressions global_settings.suppressions in the ASH config file Managed centrally by ASH

docs.title: Unsupported Options
docs.text:
The following ferret-scan CLI options are NOT supported and will raise an error:

Option Reason format, output_format ASH requires SARIF format debug, verbose Use ferret_debug/ferret_verbose instead (avoids confusion with ASH flags) web, port Web server mode not applicable enable_redaction, redaction_*, memory_scrub Post-processing, not scanning generate_suppressions, show_suppressed, suppressions_file ASH manages suppressions extract_text Utility mode, not scanning preprocess_only, pre_commit_mode, list_profiles Utility/pre-commit modes — produce no SARIF scan results

docs.title: Version Compatibility
docs.text:
This plugin is tested and compatible with specific ferret-scan versions. Using versions outside the supported range may result in unexpected behavior.

Supported Versions: 2.4.5 to 2.6.0 (exclusive)

Plugin Version ferret-scan Version Notes Current 2.4.5 - 2.6.0 (exclusive) 2.4.5 and 2.5.2 verified end to end; 2.5.2 is the recommended version

docs.title: Install Ferret Scan
docs.text:
The plugin runs the ferret-scan command. ASH finds it on PATH, or beside the Python interpreter that runs ASH, which is where ash dependencies install puts it.

ASH (Recommended) — installs the version the plugin is tested against into the Python environment that runs ASH, with pip or uv, whichever owns that environment (a uv tool, uvx or uv venv install has no pip):

ash dependencies install --config .ash/.ash_community_plugins.yaml

pip: pass the supported range. A bare pip install ferret-scan resolves to the newest release, which may sit outside the range in the table above — that is how a release published partway through a CI run once failed every open pull request without a source change.

pip install 'ferret-scan>=2.4.5,<2.6.0'

Build from Source:

git clone https://github.com/awslabs/ferret-scan.git
cd ferret-scan
make build

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
ferret-scan --version
ferret-scan --help

docs.title: Enable the Plugin
docs.text: The ferret-scan plugin is a community plugin that must be explicitly enabled. There are two ways to do this:

docs.title: Option 1: Add to ASH Configuration File (Recommended)
docs.text:
Include the plugin module in your ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project):

ash_plugin_modules:
  - automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins

scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Option 2: Command Line Flag
docs.text:
Use the --ash-plugin-modules flag when running ASH:

uv run ash scan --source-dir /path/to/code \
    --ash-plugin-modules automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins

docs.title: Verify Plugin is Loaded
docs.text:
# With config file
uv run ash plugin list | grep -i ferret

# Or with command line flag
uv run ash plugin list --ash-plugin-modules automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins | grep -i ferret

You should see ferret-scan in the list of scanners.

docs.title: Basic Configuration
docs.text:
Add scanner configuration to your ASH config file (.ashrc.yaml in a new project):

scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true

docs.title: Run Ferret Scan
docs.text:
# Scan current directory
uv run ash --scanners ferret-scan

# Scan specific directory
uv run ash --source-dir /path/to/project --scanners ferret-scan

# Run with ferret-scan's own debug output
uv run ash --scanners ferret-scan -o ferret_debug=true

# Run with ferret-scan's own verbose output
uv run ash --scanners ferret-scan -o ferret_verbose=true

docs.title: Run Without Configuration File
docs.text:
If you want to run Ferret Scan without saving a configuration file:

# Scan current directory only with ferret-scan
uv run ash --scanners ferret-scan \
  --ash-plugin-modules automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins

# Scan with all available scanners (including ferret-scan)
uv run ash --ash-plugin-modules automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins

docs.title: Basic Options
docs.text:
scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true
    options:
      confidence_levels: "all"    # high, medium, low, or combinations
      checks: "all"               # Specific checks to run
      recursive: true             # Recursively scan directories

docs.title: Configuration Options Reference
docs.text: Option Type Default Description confidence_levels string "all" Confidence levels: high, medium, low, or combinations like high,medium checks string "all" Specific checks to run (comma-separated) recursive bool true Recursively scan directories config_file string null Path to custom Ferret YAML config file use_default_config bool true Use the default config bundled with this plugin. Set by the operator only; see Using profiles profile string null Profile name from config file. Set by the operator only; see Using profiles exclude_patterns list [] Glob patterns to exclude. ASH also excludes its own output directories inside the scanned directory, except one whose path holds a comma, which ferret-scan's comma-separated ferret-scan --exclude cannot hold; ferret-scan then reads it, ASH logs a warning naming it, and the findings ferret-scan reports there are dropped. The files global_settings.ignore_paths ignores are excluded too, each by its full path, as ASH matches the ignore paths: an ignore path ASH matches to no file, such as a bare api (write api/ for the directory), excludes nothing. show_match bool false Display matched text in ferret-scan's own output (see show_match below) enable_preprocessors bool true Enable text extraction from documents (PDF, Office) finding_limit int 0 Max findings ferret-scan emits (ferret-scan --limit). 0 = unlimited. ASH defaults to 0 because ferret-scan's own default of 200 silently truncates large scans. fail_on_incomplete bool false Pass ferret-scan --fail-on-incomplete so ferret-scan exits 3 when a file could not be fully scanned; ASH still reports the partial findings, counts the target as failed, and records the scanner ERROR, so the completeness gate fails the scan. respect_gitignore bool false Pass ferret-scan --respect-gitignore to honor .gitignore. Off by default, because .gitignore often hides high-value files (.env, *.pem) a sensitive-data scan should see. disable_ip_types string null Comma-separated INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY sub-types to skip (ferret-scan --disable-ip-types): copyright,patent,trademark,trade_secret,internal_url. explain bool false Pass ferret-scan --explain for an offline per-finding rationale + verdict + drafted suppression reason. No data leaves the host. validator_budget string null Per-validator time budget (ferret-scan --validator-budget), e.g. SSN=500ms,all=2m. Over-budget validators stop and mark the scan incomplete. max_live_bytes string null Cap on extracted content held in memory (ferret-scan --max-live-bytes), e.g. 256MB/1GB. Bounds peak memory on constrained hosts. ferret_debug bool false Enable ferret-scan's own debug logging (preprocessing/validation flow) ferret_verbose bool false Enable ferret-scan's own verbose output (detailed finding info) tool_version string null Version constraint for ferret-scan (e.g., >=2.4.5,<2.6.0, ==2.5.2) skip_version_check bool false Skip version compatibility check (use with caution)

docs.title: Options NOT Supported (Will Raise Error)
docs.text:
The following options are not supported because they conflict with ASH conventions. Setting one stops the scan with exit code 3 when ASH loads the plugins, before anything is converted or scanned. The error names the option's location and gives the message in the table, for example:

Configuration validation failed: scanners.ferret-scan.options (scanner 'ferret-scan'): Value error, Unsupported option 'debug' in ferret-scan plugin configuration. Use 'ferret_debug: true' instead. Bare 'debug' is blocked to avoid confusion with ASH's --debug flag.

Any other option the plugin does not declare is refused the same way, as Unknown key '<option>' with the accepted options listed. ash config validate and ash config lint do not import the plugin, so they do not catch either kind; both say its section is not checked there, and a scan checks it.

Option Error Message format, output_format "ASH requires SARIF format for result aggregation" debug "Use 'ferret_debug: true' instead. Bare 'debug' is blocked to avoid confusion with ASH's --debug flag." verbose "Use 'ferret_verbose: true' instead. Bare 'verbose' is blocked to avoid confusion with ASH's --verbose flag." web, port "Web server mode is not supported in ASH integration" enable_redaction, redaction_output_dir, redaction_strategy, redaction_audit_log, memory_scrub "Redaction is not supported in ASH integration" generate_suppressions, show_suppressed, suppressions_file "ASH manages suppressions centrally" extract_text "Text extraction mode is not supported" preprocess_only "Outputs extracted text and exits — produces no SARIF results" pre_commit_mode "ASH manages output formatting and exit codes; use ASH's own pre-commit hook" list_profiles "Only prints available profiles and exits — produces no scan results"

docs.title: show_match
docs.text:
With show_match on, ferret-scan writes each matched value (card numbers, national IDs, keys) into its own output: the result message (Matched text: '...') and the SARIF snippets. ASH masks those values before it writes ash_aggregated_results.json or any report, so they do not reach ASH's reports, the Bedrock summary or MCP responses (see "Secret values in reports" in the output formats page). They do stay in ferret-scan's own results file under scanners/ferret-scan/, and in its log output.

show_match is off by default, and every profile in the bundled ferret-config.yaml sets it to false, including debug, comprehensive, json-api, person-name, enhanced-metadata and social-media, which turned it on before. Turn it on only where the scanner's own output directory is protected.

docs.title: Available Checks
docs.text:
The authoritative list for your installed version is ferret-scan --help checks — do not hardcode it, as ferret-scan adds detectors between releases. As of v2.4.5 through v2.5.2:

  • BANK_ACCOUNT - Bank account / IBAN / routing numbers
  • CLOUD_RESOURCES - Cloud resource identifiers (AWS ARNs, Azure/GCP/OCI/IBM/Alibaba IDs)
  • CREDIT_CARD - Credit card numbers (Visa, MasterCard, Amex, etc.)
  • DATE_OF_BIRTH - Dates of birth
  • DRIVERS_LICENSE - Driver's license numbers (state formats)
  • EMAIL - Email addresses
  • INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY - Patents, trademarks, copyrights (internal-URL detection requires config)
  • IP_ADDRESS - IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
  • MEDICAL_ID - Medical / health identifiers (PHI)
  • METADATA - Document, image, audio, and video metadata
  • OTP - One-time-passcode / two-factor secrets
  • PASSPORT - Passport numbers (multi-country)
  • PERSON_NAME - Person names
  • PHONE - Phone numbers
  • PHYSICAL_ADDRESS - Physical / postal addresses
  • SECRETS - API keys, tokens, passwords
  • SOCIAL_MEDIA - Social media profiles
  • SSN - Social Security Numbers
  • VIN - Vehicle Identification Numbers

docs.title: Note: API_KEY_OR_SECRET false positives (SECRETS check)
docs.text:
The SECRETS check includes a generic API_KEY_OR_SECRET detector that matches on the name of an assignment when the name is a secret keyword (session, token, secret, password, api_key, …) — regardless of the value. So typed code and config such as a session field on a generated model, a session local, or a Terraform local named manage_auth_secret can be flagged at HIGH confidence even though no credential is present.

This detector cannot be disabled in ferret-scan's config (the tool honors disabled_types only for the INTELLECTUAL_PROPERTY check, not SECRETS). The plugin keeps it enabled so real secrets are still found, and expects you to manage false positives with ASH's own controls — a path-scoped suppression:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - path: path/to/generated_or_test_file.py
      rule_id: API_KEY_OR_SECRET
      reason: "False positive — variable/field name matches the secret-keyword heuristic, not a credential"

or the plugin's exclude_patterns, or scoping the checks option to omit SECRETS.

docs.title: Advanced Configuration
docs.text:
scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true
    options:
      confidence_levels: "high,medium"
      checks: "CREDIT_CARD,SECRETS,SSN,PASSPORT"
      recursive: true
      profile: "security-audit"
      config_file: "/etc/ash/ferret-config.yaml"  # outside the scanned tree
      # show_match: false  # Keep disabled to avoid logging sensitive data
      enable_preprocessors: true  # Extract text from PDFs, Office docs
      exclude_patterns:
        - "*.log"
        - "node_modules/**"
        - "vendor/**"
        - ".git/**"

profile, use_default_config and config_file take effect only from the operator: profile and use_default_config from --config-overrides or a config file outside the scanned tree, and config_file only when the file it names is outside the tree.

Note: Do NOT configure bare debug, verbose, format, or suppression options at the plugin level. Use ferret_debug/ferret_verbose for ferret-scan's own log output. Other options are managed by ASH globally.

docs.title: Version Pinning
docs.text:
Pin to a specific ferret-scan version for reproducible builds:

scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: "==2.5.2"  # Exact version

Or use a version range:

scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true
    options:
      tool_version: ">=2.4.5,<2.6.0"  # Compatible range
