To hold repositories to a gate that their own pull requests cannot change, see Roll out ASH across repositories. Set the gate covers every option.

docs.title: 4. Upload results to code scanning
docs.text:
Add a second job under jobs:, at the same indentation as ash:

  sarif:
    needs: ash
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.ash.outputs.artifact-id != '' }}
    uses: awslabs/automated-security-helper/.github/workflows/upload-ash-sarif.yml@v3.7.0
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write

Pin its uses: line to the same commit as the first one, with the same # v3.7.0 comment.

This job downloads the ash_output artifact and uploads ash.ghas.sarif to code scanning. It needs security-events: write, which the scan job cannot hold: a called workflow can only narrow the permissions its caller grants, and the scan workflow does not ask for this one. The scan sets its artifact-id output once it has uploaded its reports, which it does when it fails on findings too, so the if: uploads after such a scan and skips the upload after a scan that stopped before ASH wrote its reports. Without !cancelled() in it, GitHub skips the job whenever the scan job fails.

Push the change, then merge the pull request. The merge starts the workflow on main, and when that run finishes, the repository's Security and quality tab lists ASH's findings under Code scanning, with the tool name ASH - Automated Security Helper. That analysis of main is what code scanning compares later pull requests with.

docs.title: 5. See a finding on a pull request
docs.text:
Create a new branch from main and add a file with a known problem, for example ash_demo.py:

import subprocess


def run(command):
    return subprocess.call(command, shell=True)

Push it and open a pull request. This time:

  • The scan job fails with exit code 2: bandit reports the subprocess call with shell=True.
  • The pull request comment shows bandit as FAILED, with its findings counted by severity.
  • The ASH Scan JUnit Test Report check is red and names the finding.
  • The Code scanning results check annotates the line in Files changed. Code scanning shows a pull request only the alerts on lines that the pull request changes.

Delete the file and push again, and the checks pass, provided main itself had no actionable findings.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Run ASH in GitHub Actions: every input of the reusable workflow, writing the steps yourself, caching, and changed-files scans.
  • Read scan results: what each report file is for.
  • Choose scanners: turn scanners on and off.
  • Scale to large repositories: split a scan across runners.

docs.title: Run your first scan
docs.text:
In this tutorial you install ASH and its scanner tools, scan a small Python project, read the results, suppress a false positive, and fix a real issue. It takes about 15 minutes, most of it spent on downloads.

The commands are for a POSIX shell on Linux, macOS, or Windows Subsystem for Linux. For native Windows, see Install ASH.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need:

  • curl and git
  • Node.js, which npm-audit and cdk-nag use
  • Ruby with a C compiler, to install cfn-nag
  • network access: the first install and the first scan download scanner tools, rules, and vulnerability databases

ASH runs without Node.js or Ruby. The scanners that need them are cdk-nag, cfn-nag, and npm-audit, and this tutorial's project has nothing for them to scan, so they show as SKIPPED either way; ash dependencies install in step 3 still exits 1 and names them. In a project with CloudFormation templates or a lockfile beside a package.json, those scanners show as MISSING without their tools, and the scan exits 1. Step 5 shows what to do then.

docs.title: 1. Install uv
docs.text:
ASH installs and runs with uv. Install it with the official installer:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

Open a new terminal so that uv's directory is on your PATH. uv --version then prints a version number.

docs.title: 2. Install ASH
docs.text:
uv tool install --python 3.12 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0'

This installs ASH v3.7.0 from GitHub, with the cdk extra that the cdk-nag scanner needs, into its own environment. --python 3.12 keeps uv from choosing a Python newer than ASH's dependencies support; uv downloads 3.12 if you do not have it. ASH is not published on PyPI: the PyPI project named automated-security-helper is not published by this project, so never install ASH by that name. Install ASH covers the other install methods and pins.

Check the install:

ash --version

awslabs/automated-security-helper v3.7.0

docs.title: 3. Install the scanner tools
docs.text:
ASH runs other projects' scanners. Install the ones it can install for you:

ash dependencies install

It prints a table with one row per scanner and ends with a box like this:

╭─────────────────────────── Installation Complete ────────────────────────────╮
│ Commands run: 15 (0 failed)                                                  │
│ Tools verified on PATH: 17 -- actionlint, bandit, cdk-nag, cfn-guard,        │
│ cfn-lint, cfn-nag, checkov, detect-secrets, gitleaks, grype, jupyter,        │
│ npm-audit, opengrep, semgrep, syft, trivy, zizmor                            │
│ No install path on this platform: cdk-nag, detect-secrets, npm-audit         │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

The "No install path" line is expected: cdk-nag comes from the cdk extra, detect-secrets is part of ASH, and npm-audit uses the npm that comes with Node.js. When a tool that a scan would use is still missing afterwards, the box reads "Installation Incomplete", its last line names the tool, and the command exits 1. ASH still installs every tool it can. Without Ruby, a warning near the top says cfn-nag cannot be installed here and the last line is needed tool(s) still absent after install: cfn-nag. Without Node.js, it names cdk-nag (node) and npm-audit. This tutorial's project has nothing for those scanners, so the scans below show them as SKIPPED.

Manage scanner tools explains where each tool goes and how ASH finds it.

docs.title: 4. Create a project to scan
docs.text:
Create a directory with one Python file that has two problems in it, and a .gitignore that keeps ASH's output out of version control:

mkdir ash-tutorial
cd ash-tutorial
echo '.ash/ash_output/' > .gitignore
cat > app.py <<'EOF'
import hashlib
import subprocess


def cache_key(data: bytes) -> str:
    """Name a cache entry after its contents. Not used for security."""
    return hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()


def archive(directory: str) -> None:
    subprocess.run(f"tar -czf backup.tgz {directory}", shell=True, check=True)
EOF

cache_key uses MD5, which scanners flag as a weak hash, but here it only names cache entries. archive passes its argument to a shell, so a directory name such as x; touch injected would run a second command.

Do the same in your own projects before you scan them: the scan results can contain the values of secrets that scanners detect, so .ash/ash_output/ must not be committed. Add it to .gitignore, or run ash config init, which writes a .gitignore inside .ash/.

docs.title: 5. Run the scan
docs.text:
Run ash with no arguments. It scans the current directory with every scanner:

ash
echo "exit code: $?"

The same scan limited to bandit and detect-secrets gives the same result on every machine that has those two tools, without the network:

ash --scanners bandit,detect-secrets

│ bandit         │ 0 │ 0 │ 2 │ 0 │ 1 │ 0 │ 637ms │ 2      │ FAILED  │ MED (g) │
...
│ detect-secrets │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 1.7s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
...
ERROR (2) Exiting due to 2 actionable findings found in ASH scan

The rows of the other scanners show SKIPPED, because --scanners leaves them out.

The full scan takes a minute or two the first time, most of it grype downloading its vulnerability database. Later scans of this project take about 20 seconds. The scan prints a summary table, then where it wrote the results:

                           ASH Scan Results Summary
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━┳━━━┳━━━┳━━━┳━━━┳━━━┳━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Scanner        ┃ S ┃ C ┃ H ┃ M ┃ L ┃ I ┃ Time  ┃ Action ┃ Result  ┃ Thresh  ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━╇━━━╇━━━╇━━━╇━━━╇━━━╇━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━┩
│ actionlint     │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 25ms  │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ bandit         │ 0 │ 0 │ 2 │ 0 │ 1 │ 0 │ 468ms │ 2      │ FAILED  │ MED (g) │
│ cdk-nag        │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 25ms  │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ cfn-guard      │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 72ms  │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ cfn-lint       │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 171ms │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ cfn-nag        │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 30ms  │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ checkov        │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 3.8s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ detect-secrets │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 373ms │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ gitleaks       │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 594ms │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ grype          │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 3.0s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ npm-audit      │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 160ms │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
│ opengrep       │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 5.1s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ semgrep        │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 4.7s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ syft           │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 1.4s  │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ trivy          │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 458ms │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
│ zizmor         │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ <1ms  │ 0      │ SKIPPED │ MED (g) │
└────────────────┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───────┴────────┴─────────┴─────────┘
                                source-dir: '.'
                         output-dir: '.ash/ash_output'
...
ERROR (2) Exiting due to 2 actionable findings found in ASH scan
exit code: 2

Each row is one scanner:

  • S is the number of suppressed findings, and C, H, M, L, and I count the rest by severity: critical, high, medium, low, and informational.
  • Thresh is the lowest severity that counts against the scan. MED (g) means MEDIUM, set globally, which is the default.
  • Action counts the findings at or above that threshold. bandit found two HIGH findings and one LOW one, so Action is 2.
  • Result is PASSED, FAILED (actionable findings), SKIPPED (the scanner did not run: here, because this project has nothing for it, such as no GitHub workflows, CloudFormation templates, or lockfiles), MISSING (its tool is not available), or ERROR (it ran and failed).

The exit code is the scan's verdict: 0 when nothing is actionable, 2 when something is, and 1 when the scan is incomplete or ASH hit an error. An incomplete scan exits 1 even when it also has findings. See Exit codes.

The results are in .ash/ash_output/. The reports/ directory there holds an HTML report, Markdown and text summaries, SARIF, and other formats.

docs.title: If a scanner shows MISSING
docs.text:
A MISSING scanner makes the scan exit 1 and print which scanners did not run, and why. If ash dependencies install could not download grype, for example, the scan ends with:

ERROR (1) Exiting because the scan was incomplete: 1 selected scanner(s) did not
evaluate everything they were given
  grype: MISSING
    its tool grype was not found on PATH or in ...; install it with
`ash dependencies install` or exclude grype with --exclude-scanners

Install the tool the scanner needs (Troubleshoot lists the fix for each), or leave out the scanners you cannot run:

ash --exclude-scanners grype

An excluded scanner shows as SKIPPED and does not fail the scan. Add the same --exclude-scanners option to the scans in the rest of this tutorial.

docs.title: 6. Look at a finding
docs.text:
ash report prints the latest results in the terminal. After the scan details, a legend, the scanner table, and the files with the most findings, it prints one block per actionable finding:

ash report

...
Finding 1: B324

 • Severity: HIGH
 • Scanner: bandit
 • Rule ID: B324
 • Location: app.py:7

Description: Use of weak MD5 hash for security. Consider usedforsecurity=False

Code Snippet:

 """Name a cache entry after its contents. Not used for security."""
     return hashlib.md5(data).hexdigest()

Piped to another program, or with --no-color, it prints the same report as Markdown:

ash report --no-color

...
### Finding 1: B324

- **Severity**: HIGH
- **Scanner**: bandit
- **Rule ID**: B324
- **Location**: app.py:7

**Description**:
Use of weak MD5 hash for security. Consider usedforsecurity=False
...

Finding 2 is B602, subprocess call with shell=True, at app.py:11. The Rule ID is what a suppression names in the next step. To browse the findings interactively, run ash inspect findings, which shows the same value in its Rule ID column, or open .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.html in a browser.

docs.title: 7. Suppress the false positive
docs.text:
B324 is a false positive here, because the hash only names cache entries. In ash-tutorial, create a file named .ashrc.yaml with this content:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - rule_id: B324
      path: app.py
      reason: MD5 only names cache entries here. It is not used for security.
      expiration: "2027-04-30"

rule_id and path select the findings to suppress. reason is required. expiration is optional: from that date the suppression stops applying and the finding counts again, so set it to a date a few months from today, when you want to look at the decision again. Keep the date in quotes: unquoted, YAML reads it as a date rather than text, and ASH rejects the whole file with exit code 3. A date in the past is accepted, and the suppression then does nothing. Suppress findings covers line ranges, symbols, and inline suppressions.

docs.title: 8. Scan again
docs.text:
ash
echo "exit code: $?"

bandit now shows the B324 finding as suppressed (S is 1), and one actionable finding remains:

│ bandit         │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │ 0 │ 428ms │ 1      │ FAILED  │ MED (g) │
...
ERROR (2) Exiting due to 1 actionable findings found in ASH scan
exit code: 2

docs.title: 9. Fix the real issue
docs.text:
In app.py, replace the archive function with this version, which passes its arguments as a list and starts no shell:

def archive(directory: str) -> None:
    subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", "backup.tgz", directory], check=True)

Scan once more:

ash
echo "exit code: $?"

│ bandit         │ 1 │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ 3 │ 0 │ 429ms │ 0      │ PASSED  │ MED (g) │
...
exit code: 0

The three LOW findings are below the MEDIUM threshold, so they do not fail the scan. They are still listed in the SARIF and HTML reports.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Suppress findings in other ways, and ignore paths.
  • Set the gate: choose which findings fail a scan.
  • Run ASH with pre-commit before each commit.
  • Add ASH to a GitHub Actions pipeline.
  • Read scan results: what each output file is for.
  • Troubleshoot a scan that does not do what you expect.

docs.title: Roll out ASH across repositories
docs.text: This tutorial is for a security or platform team that runs ASH for many repositories. By the end you have an ASH image in your own registry, one operator config that every scan uses and no repository can change, a plan for keeping vulnerability databases current, and results going where your team reads them.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need ASH installed (Install ASH), docker or another container runtime, and a registry you can push to. Steps 2 and 3 run on any machine with ASH, and step 3 creates a small repository to test the gate on.

docs.title: 1. Build the image and push it to your registry
docs.text:
ASH publishes no prebuilt image. Build one from v3.7.0, name it for your registry, and push it:

export ASH_IMAGE_NAME=registry.example.com/security/ash:3.7.0
ash build-image --no-run --oci-runner docker --ash-revision-to-install v3.7.0 \
  --container-uid 1001 --container-gid 1001
docker push "$ASH_IMAGE_NAME"

You should see Building image registry.example.com/security/ash:3.7.0, a few minutes of build output, and then the push. --oci-runner docker builds with the runtime you push with; without it, ASH uses finch when finch is installed. The image holds every scanner tool and runs as a non-root user with the UID and GID you passed; use the ones your CI jobs run as. A build host that runs as root needs --build-target ci, because ASH refuses to build the non-root image as UID 0; see Root and non-root images.

docs.title: 2. Write the operator config
docs.text:
The operator config is the one file whose settings apply to every scan. Keep it where only your team can change it, outside the directories you scan and outside every git checkout, including an operations repository and a home directory or /etc kept in git. ASH treats a config file inside any git checkout, or inside the directory it scans, as written by a repository, even when you name it with --config, and ignores the settings in it that only an operator may make, such as sandbox grants and the AWS reporters' destinations and credentials. Such a config can turn on plugin modules that are already installed outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, such as in site-packages. It can't load plugin code from the repository or any other checkout, load ash_aws_plugins or ash_snyk_plugins unless an operator source names them, or turn on a reporter that sends findings off the host. It logs that only to ash.log, and the warning says how to keep the setting: put it in a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, or pass it with --config-overrides (Configuration trust model). This tutorial uses $HOME/ash-operator/ash.yaml; on shared runners, a path such as /etc/ash/ash.yaml is a better choice.

OPERATOR_CONFIG="$HOME/ash-operator/ash.yaml"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$OPERATOR_CONFIG")"
cat > "$OPERATOR_CONFIG" <<'EOF'
fail_on_findings: true
fail_on_incomplete_scanners: true
content_db_staleness: fail
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: MEDIUM
EOF
if git -C "$(dirname "$OPERATOR_CONFIG")" rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  echo "The operator config is inside a git checkout; move it." >&2
  exit 1
fi

The last three lines check that the file is in no git checkout: git rev-parse must fail there. That is the rule ASH applies to config files, and the check catches a file it would treat as a repository's before any scan warns about it, for example under a home directory kept in git. The four settings are the gate: fail on findings at MEDIUM or above, fail when a scanner was MISSING or ended in ERROR, and fail when a vulnerability database or offline ruleset is past its age bound. They are also ASH's defaults, and writing them down still matters: with this file in use, ASH does not read a repository's config file, so the repository cannot change them. Add your organization's suppressions, scanner options, and reporters to the same file; Configure ASH shows how.

docs.title: 3. Check that a repository cannot change the gate
docs.text:
Create a repository with one hardcoded password in it:

mkdir ash-gate-demo
cd ash-gate-demo
git init --quiet
printf 'DATABASE_PASSWORD = "correct-horse-battery-staple-1234"\n' > app.py

Scan it with the operator config:

ash scan --config "$OPERATOR_CONFIG" --scanners detect-secrets

--scanners detect-secrets keeps the check fast: detect-secrets ships with ASH, so it needs no other tools. The scan ends with ERROR (2) Exiting due to 1 actionable findings found in ASH scan. Once the scan has loaded a config file, .ash/ash_output/ash.log names it in a Using ASH configuration from line. A file you name with --config appears as you named it:

grep -F "Using ASH configuration from $OPERATOR_CONFIG" .ash/ash_output/ash.log

Now give the repository a config file that turns the gate off, and scan without your config:

printf 'fail_on_findings: false\n' > .ashrc.yaml
ash scan --scanners detect-secrets

ash.log now names the repository's file. A file ASH finds on its own appears by its resolved path, with every symbolic link followed, so the check uses pwd -P:

grep -F "Using ASH configuration from $(pwd -P)/.ashrc.yaml" .ash/ash_output/ash.log

The scan exits 0 although the finding is still there. Scan again with your config:

ash scan --config "$OPERATOR_CONFIG" --scanners detect-secrets

The scan exits 2 again, because ASH read only your file.

In a scan of one directory, when you pass --config or set ASH_CONFIG, ASH does not read the repository's config file at all, so a repository cannot turn off the gate, raise the threshold, disable scanners, or add suppressions through it. In workspace mode, your --config is layered over each project's own config: every setting your file makes is final for every project, and a project's config fills only the settings yours leaves out (Scan a multi-project workspace). That holds for the settings only an operator may make, such as sandbox grants and the AWS reporters' destinations, only while your file is outside every git checkout; inside one, the plugin modules it may add are limited the same way as a repository's.

The repository can still affect results in other ways:

  • Inline ash-ignore comments, which ASH honors and marks (ASH inline) in the SARIF report.
  • The scanners' own inline suppressions, such as bandit's # nosec and detect-secrets' # pragma: allowlist secret. To have bandit report # nosec lines too, set scanners.bandit.options.ignore_nosec: true in your file.
  • Its .gitignore and .ignore files, which decide which files ASH scans, committed files included.
  • The tool config files some scanners read from the repository, such as detect-secrets' .secrets.baseline, whose plugin and filter settings apply unless your file sets scanners.detect-secrets.options.scan_settings.plugins_used. What the trust model does not protect lists the scanners whose own config files ASH keeps from being read, semgrep's and opengrep's .semgrepignore included.

When you let ASH read a repository's config file instead, that file can change the verdict, but it cannot load ASH's plugin packages that send data off the machine, choose reporter destinations or credentials, grant sandbox access, or set the scanner options in Options only the operator can set. Configuration trust model has the complete rules.

docs.title: 4. Run the scan in CI
docs.text:
In CI, run ASH inside your image, mount the repository and the operator config, and point ASH_CONFIG at the config:

test -f /etc/ash/ash.yaml
mkdir -p "$PWD/../ash-results"
docker run --rm \
  --mount type=bind,source="$PWD",destination=/src,readonly \
  --mount type=bind,source="$PWD/../ash-results",destination=/out \
  --mount type=bind,source=/etc/ash/ash.yaml,destination=/etc/ash/ash.yaml,readonly \
  --env ASH_CONFIG=/etc/ash/ash.yaml \
  registry.example.com/security/ash:3.7.0 \
  ash scan --source-dir /src --output-dir /out

The test -f line stops the job before docker run when the operator config is missing. ASH inside the container refuses an ASH_CONFIG that names no file too, with exit code 3, instead of scanning with the defaults. The repository is mounted read-only, and the results go to a directory outside it. The job fails with exit code 2 on findings and 1 on an incomplete scan; Exit codes lists them all.

ash scan --mode container --no-build, with ASH_IMAGE_NAME naming your image, works too. Container mode mounts your --config file read-only for the scan inside the container (The config file). The CI guides show the same setup for each service: Run ASH in GitHub Actions, Run ASH in GitLab CI, and Run ASH in Jenkins, CodeBuild, Azure Pipelines, CircleCI, and other CI systems.

docs.title: 5. Plan content database refresh
docs.text:
grype and trivy check code against vulnerability databases, and ASH fails a scan when a database is past its age bound. An image that scans online refreshes the trivy database during each scan, and grype updates its own database, so the hosts need outbound access to the databases' download sites. An offline image carries the databases it downloaded at build time. trivy's bound is the shortest, a day, and it counts from when the database was built upstream, which is before your image build. An offline image holds trivy's database to warn, so its trivy scans keep passing after that day and the reports record the stale database. grype's bound is five days, and past it the scan fails.

An offline image cannot run npm-audit, because npm, yarn, and pnpm audit a lockfile by asking the registry. A scan with it reports npm-audit MISSING, and exits 1, for a project with a lockfile beside its package.json. Add --exclude-scanners npm-audit to the scan command for those projects, or scan them with an online image.

An offline build downloads current databases once per UTC day even without --force, but only --force keeps the build from reusing the cached layers that hold the old tools, so rebuild the image on a schedule with it:

ash build-image --no-run --force --oci-runner docker --ash-revision-to-install v3.7.0 \
  --container-uid 1001 --container-gid 1001
docker push "$ASH_IMAGE_NAME"

If the rebuild runs in a CI job that runs as root, as AWS CodeBuild and container-based GitLab and Jenkins jobs do, pass --build-target ci: ASH refuses to build the non-root image as UID 0. Rebuild offline images more often than every five days, because grype's bound also counts from the database's upstream build, and more often still to keep trivy's findings current. Rebuild online images at least weekly, so the scanner tools get their fixes. Keep content_db_staleness: fail in the operator config; a repository cannot relax it while you pass --config. To hold trivy's database to its bound in an offline image too, also set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false. Run ASH offline covers air-gapped hosts, and Content databases lists every bound.

docs.title: 6. Send findings where your team reads them
docs.text:
Every scan writes its reports to reports/ in the output directory. Send each to the place your team works:

  • GitHub code scanning: upload ash.ghas.sarif (Export reports).
  • GitLab security dashboards: publish ash.gl-sast-report.json as a SAST report from a job that succeeds, because GitLab ingests security findings only from successful jobs (Run ASH in GitLab CI).

  • A central store or SIEM: copy a findings file, such as ash.ocsf.json or ash.sarif, with your own tooling:

    aws s3 cp ../ash-results/reports/ash.ocsf.json \
  "s3://example-security-scan-results/$REPOSITORY_NAME/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).ocsf.json"

  • AWS services: ASH's AWS reporters are loaded by the operator only. The S3 and CloudWatch Logs reporters send the scan summary and configuration, not individual findings; read AWS reporters for what each one sends before you turn it on.

Next, set the threshold and failure rules for your organization in Set the gate.

docs.title: Install the ASH plugin for your agent
docs.text:
The repository ships a generated integration for each of several agent platforms, under ash-agent-plugins/agentic-coding/plugins/. Each one registers ASH's MCP server with the agent and adds instructions that tell the agent how to use the tools: a skill, rules, commands, or an agent definition, depending on what the platform supports. If you would rather add the server yourself, follow Connect an AI agent to ASH.

Every MCP configuration in these files starts the server the same way:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--from=git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper@v3.7.0",
        "ash",
        "mcp"
      ]
    }
  }
}

uvx installs ASH v3.7.0 from GitHub the first time the agent starts the server, and reuses that copy afterward. The plugin does not need ASH installed separately.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• uv, with uvx on the PATH that the agent uses. On Linux and macOS, uv's installer is:

    curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

    Desktop apps often do not see your shell's PATH. If the agent cannot start the server, replace uvx in its config with the absolute path that command -v uvx prints. - git, and network access to GitHub the first time the server starts. - The scanner tools. Install them once for your user:

    uvx --python 3.12 --from=git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper@v3.7.0 ash dependencies install

    Without them the scans still run, but a scan ends with status incomplete when a scanner that has files to scan has no tool, and lists those scanners. - The plugin files, from a clone of the repository:

    git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git
cd automated-security-helper/ash-agent-plugins/agentic-coding/plugins

The paths below are relative to that plugins directory.

docs.title: Pin the Python version
docs.text:
The generated configs let uv choose the Python version. Releases up to 3.7.x fail to install under Python 3.15, which uv picks on a machine where it is the newest Python. Add "--python", "3.12" at the start of the config's arguments; uv downloads Python 3.12 if it is not installed:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": [
        "--python",
        "3.12",
        "--from=git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper@v3.7.0",
        "ash",
        "mcp"
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Directories the server refuses
docs.text: The plugins do not set ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS, so a project in a directory the server refuses by default, such as /root, needs it added to the config's environment; see step 5 of the tutorial.

docs.title: Choose your platform
docs.text:
Platform Directory What it adds Notes Claude Code claude/ MCP server, the ash-mcp skill, scan and results commands, and a security-scanner agent Codex CLI codex/ MCP server, the ash-mcp skill Kiro kiro/ A power: MCP server and instructions GitHub Copilot in VS Code copilot/ .vscode/mcp.json, Copilot instructions, scan and results prompts, and an agent OpenCode opencode/ MCP server, skill, commands, and agent Cursor cursor/ MCP server and a rule Windsurf windsurf/ A rule, and an install.sh that adds the ash server to your global MCP config Cline cline/ Rules, and an install.sh that adds the ash server to your global MCP settings macOS and Linux only. Continue continue/ MCP server and a rule Gemini CLI gemini/ An extension: MCP server and instructions Goose goose/ An extension and AGENTS.md Claude Desktop mcpb/ An MCP bundle, ash.mcpb Roo Code roo/ MCP server, rules, and a custom mode Roo Code's maintainers announced its shutdown for 2026-05-15. Amazon Q Developer CLI amazonq/ An agent definition Amazon Q Developer CLI is now Kiro CLI. The script writes the Amazon Q Developer CLI agent location. Aider aider/ Conventions only Aider does not support MCP, so it cannot call ASH's tools. Any Agent Skills client generic-skill/, and skills/ at the repository root The ash-mcp skill only, with no MCP server See Agent Skills.

AGENTS.md in the plugins directory holds the same instructions as a plain file, for agents that read an AGENTS.md at the root of your repository.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Start Claude Code with the plugin loaded:

claude --plugin-dir claude

claude --plugin-dir loads the plugin for that session only.

docs.title: Codex CLI
docs.text:
Add the directory as a plugin marketplace:

codex plugin marketplace add ./codex

docs.title: Kiro
docs.text: Add kiro/ as a power from its GitHub directory. Kiro reads POWER.md for the instructions and mcp.json for the server.

docs.title: GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Cursor, Continue, and Roo Code
docs.text:
Copy the platform's files into the root of the repository you want to scan:

Platform Copy GitHub Copilot in VS Code copilot/.github/ and copilot/.vscode/ OpenCode opencode/opencode.json and opencode/.opencode/ Cursor cursor/.cursor/, and cursor/AGENTS.md if you want it Continue continue/.continue/ Roo Code roo/.roo/, roo/.roomodes, and roo/AGENTS.md

If the repository already has one of these files, such as .vscode/mcp.json, add the ash entry to it instead of replacing it. VS Code's mcp.json names its servers under servers, not mcpServers.

docs.title: Windsurf and Cline
docs.text:
Copy the rules into your repository: windsurf/.windsurf/ for Windsurf, cline/.clinerules/ for Cline. Then run the platform's install.sh. It adds the ash entry under mcpServers in the global MCP file and keeps every other server and setting there: ~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json for Windsurf, and cline_mcp_settings.json in VS Code's global storage for the Cline extension.

  • Before it changes the file, it saves the old one beside it as <file>.ash-backup-<UTC time>, with the file's own permissions. Running it again changes nothing while the ash entry is the one the script writes. An ash entry you changed, for example to add ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS to its env, is replaced with the script's, after the backup.
  • It needs python3. Without it, or when the file is not plain JSON (a comment or a trailing comma is enough) or cannot be written, it changes nothing, prints the entry to add by hand, and exits with code 1.
  • The Cline script supports macOS and Linux. On other systems it exits with code 1 and names the file to edit. It also exits with code 1 when it does not find the Cline extension's settings in VS Code's user directory, as with VS Code Insiders or VSCodium.

docs.title: Gemini CLI
docs.text:
Install the directory as an extension:

gemini extensions install ./gemini

gemini/install.sh is the alternative. It adds the ash entry to ~/.gemini/settings.json the way the Windsurf and Cline scripts do, keeping the rest of the file and saving a backup.

docs.title: Goose
docs.text: goose/install.sh appends extension.yaml to ~/.config/goose/config.yaml when that file has no extensions: section, after saving the old file, if there is one, beside it as config.yaml.ash-backup-<UTC time>. When the section already lists the same ASH, the script changes nothing and exits 0. When it lists another ASH version, the script names that version and the uvx --from argument to change it to; when it has no ASH entry, it prints the entry to merge by hand. Both exit with code 1 and change nothing. A commented-out line does not count as listing an ASH. The script does not install AGENTS.md; copy it into your repository if you want Goose to read it.

docs.title: Claude Desktop
docs.text: Open mcpb/ash.mcpb with Claude Desktop. The bundle contains only a manifest that starts the server with uvx, so uvx must be on the PATH that Claude Desktop sees.

docs.title: Amazon Q Developer CLI
docs.text: amazonq/install.sh copies agent.json to ~/.aws/amazonq/cli-agents/ash.json. Start the agent with q --agent ash.

docs.title: Aider
docs.text: Copy aider/CONVENTIONS.md and aider/.aider.conf.yml into your repository. Aider then reads the conventions in every session. It has no MCP support, so it cannot run ASH's tools.

docs.title: Agent Skills
docs.text:
The ash-mcp skill follows the Agent Skills format: SKILL.md and two reference files, tool-reference.md and troubleshooting.md. The same skill is in skills/ash-mcp/ at the repository root and in generic-skill/skills/ash-mcp/.

Install it with the skills command-line tool, which reads skills/ at the root of the repository:

npx skills add awslabs/automated-security-helper

Or copy skills/ash-mcp/ into your agent's skills directory. The skill contains no MCP configuration, so also add the server as in step 3 of the tutorial.

docs.title: Change the ASH version a plugin uses
docs.text:
Each file pins ASH v3.7.0, the release this repository's files were generated for. To use another release, change the tag in the uvx --from argument of the installed MCP configuration, for example in .mcp.json, .cursor/mcp.json, or .vscode/mcp.json. Older releases have fewer MCP tools than the MCP tools reference lists.

To use an ASH you installed yourself instead, replace uvx and its arguments:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "ash",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Regenerate the plugins
docs.text: The plugin files are generated from ash-agent-plugins/agentic-coding/transpiler/_base/. Edit the files there, never the generated copies, and rebuild and check them as the transpiler README describes. CI fails when the generated files differ from what the transpiler produces. The version pin comes from the version in [tool.commitizen] of pyproject.toml, and the release bump rewrites it in _base/.

docs.title: Choose scanners
docs.text: ASH runs every enabled scanner it has, and all 16 built-in scanners are enabled by default (on Windows, semgrep and opengrep are off by default). This page shows how to see which scanners a scan will run, turn some off, add community scanners, and set a scanner's options. The scanner reference lists each scanner with its tool and options.

docs.title: See which scanners will run
docs.text:
ash plugin list

ash plugin list prints the scanners, reporters, and converters, with an Enabled column that applies the config ASH finds in the current directory. Add --show-versions to see which scanner tools are installed on this machine.

A scanner whose tool is not installed is recorded MISSING, and the scan exits 1, because fail_on_incomplete_scanners is on by default. Install the tools with ash dependencies install (see Manage scanner tools), run the scan in the container image, or turn the scanner off. Set the gate explains the incomplete-scan rule.

A scanner that has nothing to scan in the source is the exception: it is recorded SKIPPED, whether or not its tool is installed, and the scanner's skipped_reason in ash_aggregated_results.json says why. cdk-nag, cfn-nag, cfn-guard, and cfn-lint have nothing to scan when no scanned file is a CloudFormation template; actionlint when there is no GitHub Actions workflow; zizmor when there is no workflow or composite action; and npm-audit when no package.json has a lockfile (package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, or pnpm-lock.yaml) beside it. When a scanner's tool is not installed, ASH counts a .json, .yaml, or .yml file that does not parse as a template, and records the scanner MISSING, when the file's text has AWSTemplateFormatVersion or a Type: AWS:: resource type, as a damaged template does. With the tool installed, the scanner passes over such a file and is SKIPPED.

In a repository with no CloudFormation template and one detect-secrets finding, cfn-nag is SKIPPED, so this scan exits 2 for the finding rather than 1, also on a machine without cfn-nag's tool:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets,cfn-nag --offline --no-progress

docs.title: Turn scanners off
docs.text:
To turn a scanner off for every scan of a repository, set enabled: false in its config section:

scanners:
  cfn-guard:
    enabled: false
  trivy:
    enabled: false

Use the hyphenated names that ash plugin list shows (detect-secrets, cdk-nag, and npm-audit). A misspelled name is ignored without a warning, so the scanner keeps running.

To choose scanners for one run, use --scanners to run only the ones you name, or --exclude-scanners to run all but those:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

ash --source-dir . --exclude-scanners trivy,grype

Both options take a comma-separated list or can be repeated, and the ASH_SCANNERS and ASH_EXCLUDED_SCANNERS environment variables set them too. How they combine with the config:

  • A scanner runs only when it is enabled in the config, named by --scanners (when given), and not named by --exclude-scanners.
  • --scanners cannot run a scanner the config disables. To turn one back on for a run, override the config: --config-overrides scanners.bandit.enabled=true.
  • A name in both lists is excluded. If every scanner --scanners names is also excluded, ASH refuses the run with exit 5, the code for a usage error.
  • An unknown name in --scanners gets a warning when another name matches; when none matches, ASH refuses the run with exit 5. When some match, the scan runs those, and the results record the names that matched nothing in metadata.requested_scanners_not_run (Output files); the console summary lists them after the scanner table, as in Requested but not run: trivyy (no registered scanner has this name). An unknown name in --exclude-scanners excludes nothing, and a warning names it; the scan still runs, and the results do not record the name.

A scanner that is turned off, not selected, or excluded is recorded SKIPPED and does not affect the exit code. If every selected scanner is SKIPPED, including when none of them has a file to scan, the scan exits 1 (with fail_on_incomplete_scanners on, the default).

docs.title: Run only Python-based scanners
docs.text: --python-only keeps the scanners that need nothing but Python: bandit, cfn-lint, checkov, detect-secrets, semgrep, and zizmor. ASH applies it before it checks the scanners' tools, so every other scanner is recorded SKIPPED whether or not its tool is installed, and does not affect the exit code. When the run selects no Python-only scanner, as with --python-only --scanners grype, no scanner runs and the scan exits 1.

docs.title: Add community scanners
docs.text:
Community scanners ship with ASH in plugin modules that load only when you name them. Add the module to ash_plugin_modules:

ash_plugin_modules:
  - automated_security_helper.plugin_modules.ash_ferret_plugins
scanners:
  ferret-scan:
    enabled: true

You can also load a module for one run with --ash-plugin-modules or the ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES environment variable. The modules and their scanners are listed in Community plugins. Two modules send data off the host, ash_snyk_plugins (the scanned source) and ash_aws_plugins (findings), and ASH loads them only from an operator source: --ash-plugin-modules, ASH_PLUGIN_MODULES, --config-overrides, or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory (Configuration trust model). From any other config file they are ignored with a warning.

docs.title: Set a scanner's options
docs.text:
Each scanner's options go under scanners.<name>.options:

scanners:
  bandit:
    options:
      confidence_level: high
      severity_threshold: HIGH
      scan_timeout: 600

Every scanner has severity_threshold, which overrides the global threshold for that scanner (Set the gate), and scan_timeout, in seconds (default 1800; null for none). The other options are per scanner and listed in the scanner reference. An option the scanner does not have makes the config invalid (exit 3), also for a scanner the run does not select. When a declared option is close to the unknown one, the error names it:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress \
  --config-overrides scanners.bandit.options.severity_level=HIGH

Unknown key 'severity_level' (did you mean 'severity_threshold'?) in these plugin options.

An option belongs under options, not beside enabled. ASH refuses a config that sets one directly in the scanner's section (exit 3), and the error says to move the key under options:

cat > section-key.yaml <<'EOF'
project_name: payments-api
scanners:
  bandit:
    enabled: true
    severity_threshold: HIGH
EOF
ash config validate --config section-key.yaml

docs.title: Keep one scanner of an overlapping pair
docs.text:
Some default scanners cover the same ground, and ASH does not deduplicate their findings: the same problem reported by two scanners is two findings, each with its own rule ID (How ASH works).

Scanners What they both do semgrep and opengrep Run the same p/ci ruleset by default grype and trivy Report known vulnerabilities in dependencies detect-secrets and gitleaks Find secrets in the source

The community scanner trivy-repo runs trivy as well. To keep one of each pair, turn the other off:

scanners:
  opengrep:
    enabled: false
  trivy:
    enabled: false
  gitleaks:
    enabled: false

Keeping both reports more and costs scan time. A suppression matches findings by rule ID, so a suppression for one scanner's rule leaves the other scanner's finding in place.

docs.title: Options only the operator can set
docs.text:
Some scanner options name a file, a rule directory, or a program for the scanner's tool to use, or choose which part of a tool's own config applies, whether the tool sends usage data to its vendor, or which release of the tool runs. For the scanners in this table, ASH honors these options only from an operator source: --config-overrides, or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, named with --config or ASH_CONFIG (The scanned tree). A config in an ops checkout of its own is not an operator source here. A config file that an MCP client delivered is limited the same way, and under the MCP server's default policy one that sets these options is refused (What a delivered config cannot set).

Scanner Operator-only options Path may be inside the scanned repository actionlint config_file yes actionlint shellcheck, pyflakes: a repository may set only the plain names shellcheck and pyflakes, or leave them empty; a path is operator-only no bandit config_file yes cfn-guard rules_paths yes cfn-lint config_file no checkov config_file no detect-secrets baseline_file no gitleaks config_file, baseline_path yes grype config_file yes opengrep config, patterns, and metrics other than off yes semgrep config, and metrics other than off yes syft config_file yes trivy config_file, ignore_file, secret_config_file no zizmor config_file yes zizmor online_audits not a path ferret-scan (community) config_file no ferret-scan (community) profile, use_default_config not a path snyk-code (community) honor_tree_exclusions not a path trivy-repo (community) config_file, ignore_file, secret_config_file, module_dir no trivy-repo (community) disable_telemetry set to false not a path

tool_version, in the section of every scanner and converter, is operator-only too: it chooses which release of the tool ASH installs and accepts.

When a repository config sets one of these to a value other than the operator's, ASH ignores the value, logs a warning that names the option and says how to keep it, and runs the scanner with the operator's value or its default (for trivy's ignore_file and secret_config_file, with the file the matching TRIVY_IGNOREFILE or TRIVY_SECRET_CONFIG environment variable names, if you set one). When an operator source names a path that does not exist, the scanner fails (ERROR; MISSING for actionlint's shellcheck and pyflakes), and the scan exits 1. bandit, grype, and syft are the exception: they run with an empty config, and bandit logs a warning.

ash --source-dir . --config-overrides scanners.gitleaks.options.config_file=/etc/ash/gitleaks.toml

These scanners do not read the repository's own config files for their tools, such as .gitleaks.toml, .gitleaksignore, zizmor.yml, actionlint.yaml, .bandit, bandit.yaml, bandit.toml, .grype.yaml, .syft.yaml, trivy.yaml, .trivyignore, or .cfnlintrc. To use one, point the option at it from an operator source.

The options in this table are the only scanner options ASH limits this way. Other scanners' options apply from any repository config, and detect-secrets still reads a .secrets.baseline it finds in the scanned directory. semgrep and opengrep do not read a .semgrepignore there. When you scan a repository you do not control, set scanner options from an operator source and pass your config with --config, so the repository config is not read; Configuration trust model lists what that does not cover.

docs.title: Configure ASH
docs.text: ASH runs without a config file. Add one when you want to change a default: the gate, which scanners run, suppressions, or a scanner's options. This page covers creating the file, where ASH looks for it, overriding settings for one run, and checking a file before you rely on it. Every key is listed in the configuration reference.

docs.title: Create a config file
docs.text:
Run this in the root of the repository you scan:

ash config init

ash config init writes .ashrc.yaml in the current directory, with project_name set to the directory's name and every other setting at its default value, and .ash/.gitignore, which keeps ASH's output directory .ash/ash_output out of git. It exits 1 if the file already exists; pass --force to overwrite it. It also exits 1 when the directory already has another config source, such as .ash/.ash.yaml or a [tool.ash] table, because ASH never merges sources, and --force does not change that. With --config, or ASH_CONFIG set, it writes to that path instead, and a path that ends in .json gets a JSON file. It then does not look for another config source, so a file it writes next to an existing .ash/.ash.yaml is one a scan does not read. project_name is then the name of the directory that holds the file, and .ash/.gitignore is written only when the file is in .ash/ or has one of the names ASH looks for.

You can delete every key you don't change. A key you keep holds its value when a later ASH release changes the default, and a key you delete follows the new default. A short file also has less to review:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json
project_name: payments-api
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: HIGH
scanners:
  cfn-guard:
    enabled: false

project_name names the project in the reports. Without it, ASH uses the ASH_PROJECT_NAME environment variable, else ash-scan.

A config file inside the repository you scan, including the .ashrc.yaml that ASH finds on its own, is a repository config: whoever can commit to the repository controls it, so ASH ignores the few settings in it that grant sandbox access, load ASH's plugins that send data off the host, turn on the reporters that send findings off the host, choose where findings are sent, relax the stale content database check, choose which release of a scanner's tool runs, let trivy send usage data to its vendor, or point the scanners listed in Options only the operator can set at their tool files. Command-line flags, and a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory that you name with --config, are operator sources and may set everything. A config in a separate ops or dotfiles checkout is held to the same limits as a repository config; Configuration trust model has the details.

docs.title: Where ASH looks for its config
docs.text:
ash scan looks in its source directory (--source-dir, by default the current directory), and so do ash config get, ash config validate, ash config lint, and ash config validate-plugin-dependencies, which take --source-dir too. ash config init, ash config update, and ash config wizard look in the current directory. ASH uses the first source it finds, in this order:

  1. .ash.yml, .ash.yaml, .ash.json, ash.yml, ash.yaml, ash.json. ASH tries each name in the directory and then in its .ash/ subdirectory before it moves to the next name, so .ash/.ash.yml wins over .ash.yaml.
  2. .ashrc.toml, .ashrc.yaml, .ashrc.yml, .ashrc.json, ashrc.toml, ashrc.yaml, ashrc.yml, and ashrc.json, in the directory only.
  3. The [tool.ash] table of pyproject.toml.

ASH never merges sources and does not look in parent directories. Every other source it finds is ignored, with a warning that names it. The configuration reference lists all 21 locations in order.

When a file from the first group is used while an ashrc file or a [tool.ash] table also exists, the warning adds that the first group's names are deprecated in favor of the other two. The file from the first group is still the one ASH uses. ash config init writes .ashrc.yaml, and these pages use that name.

The commands that edit a config file (ash config update, ash config wizard, and ash inspect findings) write YAML, and JSON into a file whose name ends in .json. They refuse TOML files, and update and wizard also refuse a file that uses extends or patch or reads values from the environment, because a rewrite would store what the references resolve to. With no config file, wizard and inspect findings create .ashrc.yaml. ash config update --set takes the same key.path=value form as --config-overrides, including JSON values and +=. update and wizard exit 3 and leave the file unchanged when a scan refuses it, and update also when a --set leaves a config a scan would refuse. Neither checks the options of plugins loaded from ash_plugin_modules, so a scan can still refuse a file they wrote. They write every setting, defaults included, keep top-level keys ASH does not know (a JSON $schema, for example), and keep no comment other than the schema line.

In pyproject.toml, the same settings go under [tool.ash]:

[tool.ash]
project_name = "payments-api"

[tool.ash.global_settings]
severity_threshold = "HIGH"

docs.title: Use a specific file
docs.text:
--config (-c) or the ASH_CONFIG environment variable names the file to use. In a scan of one directory, ASH then skips discovery, so it does not read the repository's own config at all. In workspace mode, the file is layered over each project's own config instead: every setting it makes is final for every project, a project's own config fills only the settings it leaves out, and a project with no config uses the file alone. ASH refuses such a file inside the workspace's tree (exit 3), and one inside another git checkout cannot make the operator-only settings final (Scan a multi-project workspace). --config-overrides applies to every project as well. A relative path is resolved against the current directory, not the source directory.

ash --source-dir . --config ~/ash/ci.yaml

A scan uses the default configuration only when there is no config file at all. A config file that --config or ASH_CONFIG names, or that discovery finds, stops the scan with exit 3 before anything is scanned when it does not exist, is not a regular file, cannot be read, is not UTF-8, does not parse, or fails validation, and so does an extends base that is missing or does not parse. Check a config shows how to catch these before a scan.

A scan that names a file that does not exist is refused:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress --config no-such-config.yaml

So is one whose ASH_CONFIG names such a file, also when --config names a file that loads:

ASH_CONFIG=no-such-config.yaml ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress

docs.title: Share settings with extends
docs.text:
A config file can build on other files. extends names one base file or a list of them, relative to the file that names it:

extends: config/ash-base.yaml
project_name: payments-api
scanners:
  trivy:
    enabled: false
patch:
  - op: add
    path: /global_settings/suppressions/-
    value:
      path: app.py
      rule_id: SECRET-SECRET-KEYWORD
      reason: Fixture value, not a real password

ASH merges the bases in order and then the file itself. Mappings merge key by key; a list or a single value from the later file replaces the base's. To add to a base's list instead of replacing it, use patch, a list of JSON Patch operations (add, remove, replace, and test) applied after the merge.

A plugin's section is found by the plugin's name with case, punctuation, and the words Scanner, Reporter, and Converter ignored, so CSV, CsvReporter, and csv name one reporter, and DetectSecretsScanner names detect-secrets. A child's spelling of a section the base writes another way is that section: the merged config holds it under a built-in plugin's own name (csv), and otherwise under the child's spelling. A file that writes two such spellings, such as detect-secrets and DETECT_SECRETS, is refused with exit 3 by a scan and by ash config validate, which name both spellings and none of their values. A config that a results file recorded is read, not refused, by ash report and ash merge: of two such spellings in it, they read the one that the scan which recorded it read, and when the spelling not read sets a value the read one does not, a warning names the spellings and the one read, never a value.

patch works on what the files set, not on ASH's defaults. add at /global_settings/suppressions/- appends to a list that a file in the chain set; when none did, the operation fails with exit 3, and you add the whole list instead (path: /global_settings/suppressions with a list as the value), which in turn needs a file in the chain to set global_settings. replace also fails on a key that no file set; use add for those. The error for an operation that fails names the file, the entry's place in patch, its op, and its path, and not its value. In a patch path, a key spelled with - and the same key spelled with _ are one key, and a plugin's section is matched as its name is: /reporters/CSV/enabled and /scanners/detect_secrets/enabled reach the csv and detect-secrets sections.

A base must be inside the scanned directory. For a config file outside the scanned directory, its bases must be in that file's own directory or below it (for a file in .ash/, the directory that holds .ash/). URLs are refused, and so are cycles, chains more than 10 levels deep, and chains of more than 50 files.

docs.title: Override settings for one run
docs.text:
--config-overrides sets one key for one run, on top of the config file. Repeat it to set several; when two set the same key, the later one wins.

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress \
  --config-overrides fail_on_findings=false \
  --config-overrides global_settings.severity_threshold=HIGH

The form is key.path=value:

  • The key is a dotted path into the config, such as scanners.bandit.options.confidence_level. Plugin names use their hyphenated config names (detect-secrets, cdk-nag), and a key reaches a plugin's section by that name, so reporters.csv.enabled sets the csv section's. There is no list indexing.
  • The value is split from the key at the first =. true, false, null, and none, in any case, become booleans and null; numbers become numbers; and a value wrapped in [...] or {...} is read as JSON (a [...] that is not valid JSON is split at its commas). Anything else is a string. Threshold values are case-sensitive, so HIGH is a threshold and high is an error.
  • key.path+=value appends to an existing list instead of replacing it: --config-overrides 'global_settings.ignore_paths+=[{"path": "vendor/**", "reason": "Third-party code"}]'. On a key that is not a list yet, it sets the value.

ASH applies the overrides after loading the config file and validates the result again. An override that does not parse or does not validate stops the scan with exit 3, and so does an unknown key in a plugin's options or a plugin option set beside enabled instead of under options. An override of a key the model ignores, such as an unknown top-level key or an unknown plugin name under scanners, reporters, or converters, is accepted and has no effect. Overrides are an operator source, so they can set the settings a repository config cannot.

docs.title: Read values from the environment
docs.text:
A config value written as ${NAME} or ${NAME:default} is replaced by the environment variable NAME. With a default, default applies when the variable is not set:

project_name: ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME:payments-api}
global_settings:
  severity_threshold: ${ASH_GATE_THRESHOLD:HIGH}
  • Write the reference at the start of the value. In YAML, an unquoted value that starts with ${ is replaced, and a quoted one only when it is tagged !ENV (!ENV '${NAME}'). In TOML, every string value that starts with ${ is replaced. A JSON config file is never read this way.
  • Only names that start with ASH_, and AWS_REGION, AWS_DEFAULT_REGION, and AWS_PROFILE, are read. Any other name is left in the value as written, with a warning.
  • In container mode, the scan inside the container gets from the host only the variables that your own config files read and that are set, not those a config in the scanned directory or a git checkout reads (The config file).
  • ${NAME} without a default needs the variable: when it is not set, ASH refuses the config with exit 3 and names the variable. For a variable that may be unset, write a default. ${NAME:} and ${NAME:None} resolve to nothing (null), and so does a variable that is set to an empty string, with or without a default.
  • Text after the reference is kept when it contains no }: ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME:payments}-api resolves to the variable's value, or payments, followed by -api. When the text after the reference does contain a }, ASH reads that text as part of the reference. With a default, as in ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME:payments}/{run}, the default becomes payments}/{run, and the whole value is replaced by the variable when it is set. Without a default, as in ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME}/{run}, the value is left as written. A reference after other text is not replaced, and neither is a second reference in the same value.
  • The result is a string. That works for string and threshold values, but a boolean or number key such as fail_on_findings fails validation (exit 3).
  • The scan runs with the values. What ASH records of the config holds each reference as the file wrote it instead: the ash_config in the scan's results (ash_aggregated_results.json) and in the merged results, the results' metadata where it names a config value (a scanners key in expected_scanners), what an off-host reporter sends, and what ash config get prints. A reference whose variable is not set is recorded as the default the file wrote, and one that resolves to nothing as null. Debug and info lines name a section's keys, not its values, apart from the plugin modules a scan loads and the settings a scanner, reporter, or converter reports while it runs. In ASH's own log lines, a value that a reference read from the environment is shown as <value>, unless the value has no letter or digit, such as .; a value the file writes itself is shown as written. Report files are not log lines and keep the values, as the next point says, and output a scanner's tool writes is kept as the tool wrote it.
  • The reports the scan writes are built from the values, and the record does not cover them: the reports a scan writes itself, such as ash.html, show the values. So do not read secrets into the config.
  • ash merge and ash report read the recorded config and do not read the environment for a reference in it. A text field such as project_name keeps the reference as its value. A field that takes a fixed choice, a boolean, or a number, such as severity_threshold, cannot hold one: the command warns that the field reads as its default, then exits 3 naming the field and the reference, until you supply the field with --config-overrides or in the file --config names.
  • A config file under the ASH MCP server's workspace root, where delivered source is kept, may not use a reference at all: ASH refuses it, on the CLI too, with exit code 3. Under ash mcp, neither may a config file an MCP client names outside the directories ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names, and the MCP tools refuse it with config_env_not_resolved (What a delivered config cannot set).
  • An editor that checks the file against ASH's schema marks a reference in a field with fixed values, such as severity_threshold, as an error. ASH accepts it.

ash config get loads the file with the variable read, and prints the reference, not the value:

cat > env-example.yaml <<'EOF'
project_name: ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME}
EOF
ASH_SERVICE_NAME=payments-api ash config get --config env-example.yaml

project_name: ${ASH_SERVICE_NAME}

Without the variable, the same file is refused:

ash config validate --config env-example.yaml

docs.title: Relative paths in the operator's settings
docs.text:
A relative path in one of the operator's settings is taken from where it was set, not from the source directory being scanned:

  • In a config file outside the tree (--config, ASH_CONFIG, a workspace's --config, an MCP profile), from that file's directory. In an extends base, from the base's directory. In a patch operation, from the directory of the file that holds it.
  • In --config-overrides, in a CLI flag, and in TRIVY_IGNOREFILE, TRIVY_SECRET_CONFIG or TRIVY_CONFIG, from the working directory ASH runs in.

This covers config_file of actionlint, bandit, cfn-lint, checkov, ferret-scan, gitleaks, grype, syft, trivy, trivy-repo and zizmor, gitleaks' baseline_path, each entry of cfn-guard's rules_paths, detect-secrets' baseline_file and the file:// entries of its scan_settings, trivy's and trivy-repo's ignore_file and secret_config_file, trivy-repo's module_dir, opengrep's and semgrep's config when a file or directory is there (otherwise it is a registry entry such as p/ci), and sandbox.extra_read_paths. It does not cover actionlint's shellcheck and pyflakes, which name a program: a bare name there is looked up on PATH, and a relative path is taken from the source directory. A path that starts with ~, or is absolute, is used as written. In TRIVY_IGNOREFILE, TRIVY_SECRET_CONFIG and TRIVY_CONFIG, any other value is taken from the working directory exactly as written, a $ or :// in it included, and a .. after a symbolic link goes up from where the link points.

A config file inside the scanned tree does not set these options (How a file's tier is decided). To name a file in the scanned repository, give its absolute path, or a path relative to where you run ASH with --config-overrides.

docs.title: Get completion in your editor
docs.text:
The first line ash config init writes points editors that use the YAML language server (VS Code with the Red Hat YAML extension, for example) at ASH's JSON schema:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper/refs/heads/main/automated_security_helper/schemas/AshConfig.json

The editor then completes keys and checks values as you type. ASH itself treats the line as a comment. The URL follows the main branch, not the ASH version you have installed, so the schema can list keys your version does not have. The schema flags an unknown key only where ASH itself refuses one (the unknown-key rows of the table in Which mistakes ASH catches that end in exit 3, plus build and mcp-resource-management), and it does not include the community plugins' sections.

docs.title: Check a config
docs.text:
Three commands check a config file. ash config validate and ash config lint give the verdict a scan would give: they load the file with the loader and model ash scan uses, and exit 3 when a scan would refuse it. The one exception is the options of plugins loaded from ash_plugin_modules, which only a scan checks. Each of the three takes --config to check a file other than the one ASH finds, and --source-dir (or ASH_SOURCE_DIR; by default the current directory) for the directory a scan would scan. An ASH_CONFIG that names a file that does not exist makes each of them exit 3, also beside a --config file that loads, as it stops a scan. Each finds the config there and holds its extends chain to the bounds a scan of that directory sets (Share settings with extends), and validate and lint match ignore and suppression paths against it. validate and get also take --config-overrides and check the config with them applied, as a scan given the same overrides does. An override does not make a file that a scan refuses valid: the file is checked on its own before the overrides apply.

Command What it checks What it misses ash config validate Loads the file the way a scan does: it parses, its extends chain and its environment references resolve, and ASH's config model accepts every key and value, with any --config-overrides you pass applied, and a scan accepts the module names in ash_plugin_modules. It also warns, without failing, about what a scan accepts but is probably a mistake: an unknown or repeated top-level key, a missing project_name, the internal build section and a plugin section's internal fields (such as name and extension). An ignore path that names an existing directory with neither a trailing / nor **, and a suppression path that names one without **, are warnings too, since a scan accepts them; the warning gives the pattern for every file inside, <dir>/ for an ignore path and <dir>/**/* for a suppression path. So is a path that matches nothing because it starts with ./ (./src is src/) or is empty or ., and the warning says what to write instead. A path that matches the tree only in another case (tests/** against Tests/) gets a warning that names the tree's spelling and says that patterns match case-sensitively The options of plugins loaded from ash_plugin_modules, which only a scan checks (a note names those sections), and keys the model accepts and never reads (see below) ash config lint Everything validate checks, marking each problem that makes a scan refuse the file [blocks the scan], plus suppressions (line_start without line_end, expired entries, multi-line reasons, and symbol values), expired ignore paths (also in bandit excluded_paths, checkov skip_path, and syft exclude), and snake_case plugin names. --fix repairs what it can; --fix-unused comments out suppressions the last scan's unused-suppressions report lists The same as validate ash config get Loads the file the same way and prints the resolved config, with each value read from the environment shown as the reference the file wrote. Exits 3 on any value or key the model refuses The same as validate. It does not print validate's warnings.

Run ash config validate and ash config lint from the repository root before you commit a change. ash config get prints the resolved config, so you can see what ASH read from the file:

ash config validate
ash config lint
ash config get

A missing project_name and an unknown top-level key are warnings, which leave the exit code at 0: a scan takes the project's name from the ASH_PROJECT_NAME environment variable, else ash-scan, and it ignores the unknown key, so a config written for another ASH version still loads. A file that does not parse is invalid for validate and lint (exit 3), and a scan refuses it the same way.

In the messages of the ash config commands, and of a scan that refuses a config, a value that a reference read from the environment is shown as <value> where the message quotes it, however short the value is, so the commands do not print what the variable holds. A value that a field taking a fixed choice, a boolean, or a number refuses is not quoted at all: the message names the field and what it takes. ash config get prints a valid config with each reference as the file wrote it.

docs.title: Which mistakes ASH catches
docs.text:
A scan refuses a misspelled key in most of the config. It ignores an unknown top-level key and an unknown plugin name, so a misspelling there does nothing at all, with no error:

Mistake Example What a scan does Unknown top-level key fail_on_finding: false Ignores it. validate and lint warn about it. Unknown key in global_settings, sandbox, workspace, or a content_db_staleness_overrides entry severity_treshold: HIGH Refuses the config, exit 3 Unknown key in a suppression or an ignore path ruleId: B602, expiry: "2027-01-31" Refuses the config, exit 3 Unknown key directly under a plugin's options confidance_level: high Refuses the config, exit 3. A key inside an option's value, such as an entry of cdk-nag's nag_packs, is not checked. Wrong value severity_threshold: high, or an unquoted expiration: 2027-01-31 Refuses the config, exit 3 Missing required field a suppression without reason Refuses the config, exit 3 A plugin option written directly in the plugin's section, beside enabled severity_threshold: HIGH beside enabled: true under scanners.bandit Refuses the config, exit 3. The error says to move the key under options. Misspelled scanner, reporter, or converter name detect_secret: Ignores the section

When a known key is close to the unknown one, the error names it. This suppression is refused:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - path: src/deploy.py
      ruleId: B602
      reason: The command is a constant; no user input reaches it

Invalid value at 'global_settings.suppressions[0]': Value error, Unknown key 'ruleId' (did you mean 'rule_id'?) in a suppression. Accepted keys: expiration, line_end, line_start, package_name, package_path, package_version, path, reason, rule_id, symbol.

ash config validate, ash config lint, and ash config get catch every mistake that ends in exit 3, with one exception: they do not load the plugins named in ash_plugin_modules, so only a scan checks those plugins' options, once it has loaded them. validate and lint also warn about the unknown top-level key. No command catches the last mistake. For that one, compare your keys with the configuration reference and the scanner reference, and look for the value you meant to set in the output of ash config get.

docs.title: Deploy ASH on AWS
docs.text:
The repository's deploy/ directory has infrastructure as code for running ASH as a service in your own AWS account: an MCP server for agents, a pull request gate, and a sharded pipeline for large repositories. Each target comes as a CDK stack, with its synthesized CloudFormation template committed, and as a Terraform module.

ASH publishes no container image, so every deployment builds the ASH image into an ECR repository in your account, with a CodeBuild project that clones ASH from GitHub and rebuilds the image on a schedule.

docs.title: What deploy/ provides
docs.text:
Target What it deploys CDK template Terraform module Image pipeline ECR repositories and scheduled CodeBuild builds of the ASH image AshImagePipeline ash-image-pipeline AgentCore ASH's MCP server on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime AshAgentCore agentcore Fargate ASH's MCP server on ECS Fargate behind an internal Application Load Balancer AshFargate fargate CodeCommit gate A container Lambda function that scans a CodeCommit pull request and comments on it AshCodeCommitGate codecommit-gate Distributed pipeline A CodePipeline that splits one scan across CodeBuild shards and merges the results into one verdict AshDistributedPipeline codepipeline-executor
  • deploy/cdk is a CDK app in TypeScript. Its templates are in deploy/cdk/templates, and you can launch them from the CloudFormation console without running CDK. Each target template includes its own image build.
  • deploy/terraform has one module per target. Every target module uses the image that the ash-image-pipeline module builds, and you start its first build yourself after terraform apply.
  • deploy/cdk-constructs has ASHScanStep, a construct that adds an ASH scan to a CDK Pipelines pipeline. It is not published to npm or any other registry; you build it from the repository to use it.

deploy/README.md lists the parameters the targets share and how the CDK and Terraform names map.

Prerequisites:

  • An AWS account, and credentials that can create IAM roles, an ECR repository, a privileged CodeBuild project (it builds a container image), and the services of the target you choose.
  • Outbound internet access for the image build. CodeBuild clones ASH from GitHub, pulls the Python base image from Amazon ECR Public, and downloads the scanner tools.
  • For a console launch, nothing else. To deploy from source, Node.js and npm for CDK, or Terraform with access to the Terraform registry for terraform init.

docs.title: Before you deploy
docs.text:
• AshVersion, the git ref the image is built from, defaults in the CloudFormation templates to the ASH release they ship in. The Terraform ash_version variable has no default, and the Terraform examples pin the same release. Both accept a tag, a branch, or a full commit SHA. The targets need options that no release up to 3.7.1 has: stateless MCP (ash mcp --stateless-http), and ash merge with the shard options for the distributed pipeline. Set AshVersion to an ASH that has them, for example the commit SHA you deploy from. With one that lacks them, the Fargate MCP container exits at startup, the AgentCore server starts in stateful mode and logs a warning, and the distributed pipeline cannot run its shard and merge commands. Each target's README lists what it needs.
  • The image is only as current as its last build. The build runs on the RebuildSchedule you set, and rebuilding the image does not update a running service on its own; each target's README says how to roll it out.
  • Deleting a stack leaves the ECR repository and artifact buckets in place on purpose.
  • The image the targets build has neither bubblewrap nor firejail. When a client's config or a scanned repository's config sets sandbox.mode to bwrap or firejail, every scanner that mode would wrap is MISSING and the scan is incomplete: an MCP scan ends with status incomplete, and ash exits with code 1.

docs.title: Network defaults
docs.text:
The CloudFormation templates set these defaults. The Terraform modules have defaults of their own: for example, the fargate module can terminate TLS with a certificate and lets its tasks send to any address. Each module's README lists them, and each README explains how to change them.

  • Fargate: the load balancer is internal, listens on HTTP port 80, and has no ingress rule until you set McpIngressCidr, which rejects 0.0.0.0/0. With it empty, nothing can reach the endpoint. The tasks can send only TCP 443.
  • AgentCore: the runtime uses AgentCore's PUBLIC network mode, and callers reach it through the IAM-authorized InvokeAgentRuntime API.
  • Both MCP targets: the server checks a shared header only when you set McpAuthHeaderName and McpAuthHeaderValue. Both are empty by default, which leaves the network rules (and, on AgentCore, IAM) as the only control on who can call it.

docs.title: Target READMEs
docs.text:
Each module's README covers its inputs, outputs, verified behavior, and known limitations:

  • ash-image-pipeline
  • agentcore
  • fargate
  • codecommit-gate
  • codepipeline-executor

For the CDK stacks, see deploy/cdk/README.md. To run ASH's MCP server yourself instead, see Run the MCP server.

docs.title: Export reports
docs.text:
Every scan writes its reports to reports/ in the output directory (.ash/ash_output/reports/ by default). Thirteen reporters are on by default, and each writes its own file (unused-suppressions writes two), so the usual way to export is to pick the file your destination reads:

Destination File in reports/ GitHub code scanning ash.ghas.sarif Other SARIF consumers (IDEs, code review tools) ash.sarif GitLab security reports ash.gl-sast-report.json, ash.gl-dependency-scanning-report.cdx.json CI test results ash.junit.xml SBOM tools ash.cdx.json (CycloneDX), ash.spdx.json (SPDX, off by default) Security data lakes, SIEMs ash.ocsf.json Spreadsheets ash.csv A person ash.html, ash.summary.md, ash.summary.txt Your own scripts ash.flat.json

Reporters reference lists every reporter with its options, and Output files describes the rest of the output directory.

docs.title: Choose which reports to write
docs.text:
To write fewer files, pass --output-formats (or -f) with a comma-separated list:

ash scan --scanners detect-secrets --output-formats sarif,junitxml

When detect-secrets finds a secret, the scan exits 2, and reports/ holds only the two files you asked for:

ls .ash/ash_output/reports

ash.junit.xml
ash.sarif

The option works like this:
