  • It accepts the name of every reporter ASH ships, including github-ghas, gitlab-sast, gitlab-cyclonedx, and unused-suppressions, and the names of the AWS reporters, which write a report only when an operator loads their plugin module. It also accepts aggregated, dict, asff, and custom, which no reporter writes. Reporters left out of the list do not run. A reporter from your own plugin module cannot be named; it runs only when no list is given.
  • An unknown name stops the scan with a usage error before scanning, and exits 5.
  • The list narrows the enabled reporters and does not turn on a disabled one. yaml and spdx are disabled by default. Naming one writes nothing until you enable its reporter; ASH logs an error in ash.log that names the setting.

To make the same choice for every scan, list the names under output_formats in your ASH config file. It also takes one name, or names separated by commas, as --output-formats does, and a name it does not accept makes the configuration invalid (exit 3). --output-formats replaces the configured list for one scan, and with neither, every enabled reporter writes its report. In a workspace scan, a project's output_formats applies to that project's reports, and the combined reports follow --output-formats only:

cat > .ashrc.yaml <<'EOF'
output_formats:
  - sarif
EOF
ash scan --scanners detect-secrets

ls .ash/ash_output/reports

ash.sarif

To control reporters from configuration, turn each one on or off. This adds SPDX to the default set and drops HTML:

reporters:
  spdx:
    enabled: true
  html:
    enabled: false

On the command line, the same settings are --config-overrides reporters.spdx.enabled=true --config-overrides reporters.html.enabled=false.

To produce one more format after a scan, render it from the saved results with ash report. It runs any loaded reporter, including reporters that are disabled, apart from the AWS reporters, which run only when --config-overrides turns them on (Rendering a reporter from saved results), and it prints the report alone to standard output:

ash report --format gitlab-sast > gl-sast-report.json

docs.title: GitHub code scanning
docs.text:
Upload ash.ghas.sarif. It is SARIF 2.1.0 in which every rule a scanner declares gets a security-severity, the scanner's own or one from its most severe finding (see How ASH counts findings), so GitHub shows those findings as Critical, High, Medium, or Low. A scanner that declares no rules, such as detect-secrets, gives results with no rule entry, and GitHub shows those by their SARIF level. The file leaves out suppressed findings (exclude_suppressed, default true), because GitHub has its own dismissal workflow. The job needs security-events: write, and the upload step has to run when the scan step fails, because a scan with findings exits 2:

- name: Upload SARIF to code scanning
  if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
  uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@9b3254085494b55a0f7c4c2b3d2d52cc712ce370 # v4.39.1
  with:
    sarif_file: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.ghas.sarif
    category: ash

Run ASH in GitHub Actions has the complete workflow, including the reusable workflows ASH ships.

docs.title: GitLab
docs.text:
GitLab reads three of the files, each under its own artifacts:reports keyword:

File in reports/ Keyword ash.gl-sast-report.json (GitLab SAST report, schema 15.2.2) sast ash.gl-dependency-scanning-report.cdx.json (CycloneDX) cyclonedx ash.junit.xml junit

GitLab uploads report artifacts whatever the job's result, but it ingests the findings of a security report such as sast only when the job that produced it succeeds. A scan with findings exits 2, so the job that runs ASH has to succeed and leave the verdict to a later job. Run ASH in GitLab CI has the two jobs that do this.

The SAST report keeps suppressed findings at severity Info with the reason in their solution field. Set reporters.gitlab-sast.options.exclude_suppressed: true to leave them out.

docs.title: JUnit
docs.text: ash.junit.xml has one test suite per scanner and one test case per finding. Suppressed findings and findings below the severity threshold are written as skipped test cases, so a CI test view shows the same verdict as the scan. Actionable findings are written as <error> elements. To report those below the threshold as errors too, set reporters.junitxml.options.respect_severity_threshold: false.

docs.title: CycloneDX and SPDX
docs.text:
ash.cdx.json is the software bill of materials that syft produces. When no SBOM scanner ran, for example because syft is not installed or --scanners left it out, the file is still a valid CycloneDX document. Its components list is empty, and a compositions entry with aggregate set to unknown tells a consumer that the inventory's completeness is not known, rather than that the project has no dependencies:

{"bomFormat":"CycloneDX","specVersion":"1.6","version":1,"components":[],"compositions":[{"aggregate":"unknown"}]}

ash.gl-dependency-scanning-report.cdx.json then has an empty component list in GitLab's format. ash.spdx.json converts the same SBOM to SPDX 2.3 and is written only when you enable the spdx reporter.

docs.title: CSV, HTML, and the summaries
docs.text:
• ash.csv has one row per finding, with suppression status and justification columns.
  • ash.html is a single page with inline styles, suitable for an artifact viewer.
  • ash.summary.md is a Markdown summary for pull request comments. --compact-report shortens it.
  • ash.summary.txt is plain text for logs.

docs.title: Before you share a report
docs.text:
• Reports can contain source text. ASH masks secrets in finding messages, but a scanner that includes the matching source lines in its result passes them through to the SARIF, CSV, flat JSON, GitLab SAST, and YAML reports. Treat report files as you treat the code.
  • Findings in files that ASH extracted from archives or converted from notebooks carry absolute paths from the machine that ran the scan.
  • A reporter that fails does not change the exit code. ASH logs the error and the file is missing, so check that the file you upload exists.
  • The AWS reporters send data off the machine. They are operator-only and off unless loaded; see AWS reporters.

docs.title: Install ASH
docs.text:
ASH is a Python command-line tool that you install from its GitHub repository. It is not published on PyPI. The PyPI project named automated-security-helper is not published by this project, so installing or running ASH by that name from PyPI gets that project's package, not ASH. Always install from the GitHub URL, as on this page.

Installing ASH gives you the ash command. The scanners it runs are separate tools: after installing, run ash dependencies install, described in Manage scanner tools.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 to 3.14. uv and pipx can fetch a matching Python for you.
  • git, which the installer uses to fetch the repository.
  • Linux (x86-64 or arm64), macOS, or Windows (x86-64). CI installs ASH with pip and pipx on Python 3.10 to 3.14 and with uvx on 3.12, on Ubuntu (x86-64 and arm64), macOS on Apple silicon, and Windows. Intel Macs and Windows on arm64 are not tested.

Some scanner tools are not available on every platform: see Platform limits.

Always pass a Python version to uv and pipx, as the commands below do. The v3.7.x releases accept any Python 3 version from 3.10 up, so on a machine with no suitable Python, uv picks the newest release, 3.15, and the install fails while building a dependency that does not support 3.15.

Every install on this page includes the cdk extra, which the cdk-nag scanner needs. Without it, cdk-nag shows as MISSING in a project with CloudFormation templates, and the scan exits 1. See Extras.

docs.title: Choose an install method
docs.text: Method Use it when Status uv tool install you want ash on your PATH in its own environment recommended uvx you want to run ASH without installing it supported pipx you already use pipx supported pip in a virtual environment you manage Python environments yourself supported Container image you want every scanner without installing them build it yourself Nix mode you use Nix not in any release; install from main or use a source checkout Homebrew you install your tools with Homebrew, on macOS or Linux supported pre-commit you want a scan on every commit see Run ASH with pre-commit From a clone you are changing ASH see Contribute to ASH

docs.title: Install with uv
docs.text:
Install uv:

Linux and macOSWindows

The installer needs curl:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

In PowerShell:

powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Open a new terminal so that uv's directory is on your PATH, then install ASH. The command is the same in a POSIX shell and in PowerShell:

uv tool install --python 3.12 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0'
ash --version

awslabs/automated-security-helper v3.7.0

The install provides three names for the same program: ash, ashv3, and automated-security-helper. On Windows, Git Bash and MSYS2 ship an unrelated shell named ash that can come first on your PATH. Use ashv3 there.

To move to another version, run the same command with the new tag and add --force.

docs.title: Run without installing: uvx
docs.text:
uvx --python 3.12 --from 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0' ash --version

uvx builds the environment once and reuses it, so later runs start quickly. Every command needs the full uvx --from specification, so you may want a shell alias:

alias ash="uvx --python 3.12 --from 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0' ash"

docs.title: Install with pipx
docs.text:
pipx install --python python3.12 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0'

Install pipx itself from your package manager, for example apt install pipx on Ubuntu, or with uv tool install pipx. On systems whose Python is marked as externally managed, such as Ubuntu 24.04, pip refuses to install pipx outside a virtual environment. pipx needs the named Python on your PATH.

ASH installs bandit, checkov, and semgrep with uv. It uses the uv that pipx installs into ASH's environment, so a pipx install needs no separate uv.

docs.title: Install with pip
docs.text:
Create a virtual environment outside the projects you will scan, activate it, and install into it. Use any Python 3.10 to 3.14 in place of 3.12. On systems whose Python is marked as externally managed, such as Ubuntu 24.04, pip installs only into a virtual environment.

Linux and macOSWindows 

python3.12 -m venv ~/.venvs/ash
. ~/.venvs/ash/bin/activate
pip install 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0'
ash --version

In PowerShell:

py -3.12 -m venv $HOME\.venvs\ash
& $HOME\.venvs\ash\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0'
ash --version

Activate the environment in each new shell before you run ash, or run the environment's ash by its path. Either way, ASH installs bandit, checkov, and semgrep with the environment's own uv.

Keep the environment outside the scanned directory. During a scan ASH does not run tools that it finds inside the directory it is scanning, so scanners installed into a virtual environment inside the project show as MISSING. See Tools inside the scanned directory.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
Extra Adds Needed for cdk aws-cdk-lib, cdk-nag, constructs the cdk-nag scanner, which also needs Node.js symbols tree-sitter grammars for Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, and Java symbol in suppressions; see Suppress findings

To install an extra from git, use the direct-reference form name[extra] @ URL, as the commands on this page do. List several extras with commas, as in [cdk,symbols].

You can also add the cdk packages later: ash dependencies install --tool cdk-nag installs them into ASH's environment, whichever way you installed ASH. A later uv tool upgrade or uv tool install --force rebuilds a uv tool environment without them, so installing the extra with ASH is simpler.

The symbols extra is in main and not in releases up to 3.7.x. Its tree-sitter packages publish no wheels for Linux on arm64 with musl (Alpine), so on that platform the install needs a C compiler.

docs.title: Choose a version to pin
docs.text:
Reference What you get @v3.7.0 That release. The release process creates each version tag once and moves only the v3 tag. a full commit SHA That commit. The only reference that cannot change. @v3 The latest 3.x release. It moves with each release. @main The current development state.

Release tags are lightweight and unsigned, and releases have no signed artifacts. If you need a reference that cannot change, pin a commit SHA.

The v3 tag moves to each new 3.x release, and a release is not always made from main: v3.7.1 is a backport made on a separate branch, outside main's history. While v3 points at a release like that, it lacks features of main that these docs describe. A 3.x release can also include breaking changes, so read the release notes before upgrading a v3 or <4 pin.

docs.title: Install from main
docs.text:
To use a feature that is on main before a release includes it, install from main:

uv tool install --python 3.12 'automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@main'

main reports the same version number as the latest release until the next release is made, so ash --version does not tell the two apart. Pin a commit SHA instead of @main when you need to know which code you ran.

docs.title: Container image
docs.text: No ASH image is published. ash --mode container builds an image with every scanner on your machine and scans inside it; it rebuilds the image on every run unless you pass --no-build. ash build-image builds one to push to your own registry. See Run ASH in a container.

docs.title: Nix mode
docs.text:
ash --mode nix runs the scan inside a Nix shell whose scanner tools come from ASH's flake.nix. It needs Nix with flakes enabled, on Linux or macOS (on Windows, inside WSL2). It does not install ASH itself: the scan inside the shell runs the same ASH you started, so install ASH with one of the methods above first.

The Nix shell supplies the tools of every built-in scanner except cdk-nag, which runs on the Python environment ASH is installed in, so install ASH with the cdk extra for it. It does not supply ferret-scan or the Snyk CLI, which two community plugins run.

The scan inside the shell gets your environment, so it reads the file ASH_CONFIG names first, as a local scan does, and then the file --config names. With no --config, the file ASH_CONFIG names is the config too, and with neither, the scan uses the config file it discovers. In a scan of one directory, ASH resolves that config on the host before the shell starts. A file that is missing, cannot be read, does not parse, or is not a valid config stops the scan with exit code 3 before the previous run's output is cleared, and that includes the file ASH_CONFIG names when --config names a valid one.

Nix mode is not in any release: v3.7.x rejects --mode nix. Use it from a source checkout or from an install of main:

  • From a source checkout, ASH uses that checkout's flake.nix.
  • An install of main looks for the flake at the release tag that matches its version number. Until a release contains flake.nix, that fails with an error saying flake.nix does not exist. Set ASH_NIX_FLAKE_REF to a flake reference that has it: a checkout, written path: followed by its absolute path, or a branch or commit, such as github:awslabs/automated-security-helper/main.

docs.title: Homebrew
docs.text:
The repository is a Homebrew tap: its formula is Formula/ash.rb. Add the tap and install the formula by its full name:

brew tap awslabs/automated-security-helper https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git
brew install awslabs/automated-security-helper/ash
ash --version

Naming the formula in full installs it from a tap you have not trusted, and Homebrew trusts that one formula as it installs it. To install it by its short name, brew install ash, first run brew trust awslabs/automated-security-helper: Homebrew refuses to load a formula by its short name from a tap you have not trusted. A Homebrew release without brew trust has no such check.

The formula installs the release named on its url line, which is the latest release; it cannot install main. It builds ASH on Homebrew's Python 3.12, with the cdk extra, and installs the dependency versions locked in that release's uv.lock, each checked against the sha256 the lock records. ASH's own build requirements, hatchling and the packages it needs, are resolved from PyPI by version range and are not checked against a hash. The formula downloads all of them during the install, so the install needs network access, and building with HOMEBREW_FORMULA_BUILD_NETWORK=deny is not supported. The formula also installs Node.js, which cdk-nag and npm-audit run on; a node already on your PATH comes first. It does not install the scanners that are separate programs, such as grype, syft, opengrep, and cfn-nag, so run ash dependencies install as with the other methods.

In container mode, a Homebrew install builds its image from the commit the formula built. When Homebrew built ASH from a source tarball with no git metadata, it builds the release tag of ASH's version instead and logs a warning that this is a guess.

CI installs the formula, built from the commit under test, with Homebrew on Ubuntu (x86-64) and on macOS on Apple silicon, then runs brew test and scans with the installed ash. Homebrew is not available on Windows, and Linux on arm64 is not tested.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text:
Remove ASH with the tool that installed it:

uv tool uninstall automated-security-helper
pipx uninstall automated-security-helper
brew uninstall ash

For a pip install, delete the virtual environment. After brew uninstall, remove the tap with brew untap awslabs/automated-security-helper.

The scanner tools and data that ASH installed stay behind. To remove them too:

  • ~/.ash/, which holds the binaries from ash dependencies install, their install records, and the cfn-guard rules. If you installed with --bin-path or ASH_BIN_PATH, the binaries are in that directory instead, and the cfn-guard rules are in share/cfn-guard-rules next to it.
  • The scanners installed as uv tools. Name the ones uv tool list shows, because uv tool uninstall fails for a name that is not installed: uv tool uninstall bandit checkov semgrep nbconvert. Earlier ASH releases also installed cfn-lint and zizmor as uv tools, so add whichever of them uv tool list still shows.
  • The cfn-nag gem: gem uninstall cfn-nag. The gems it depends on stay installed.
  • The scanners' own caches, such as ~/.cache/grype and ~/.cache/trivy.
  • The .ash/ash_output/ directory that each scan writes in the project it scanned.

docs.title: Run the MCP server
docs.text: ash mcp starts ASH's Model Context Protocol server. An agent or IDE on your machine usually starts it for you over stdio, as in Connect an AI agent to ASH. This page is for running the server yourself: choosing a transport, limiting what clients can reach, serving it over HTTP, and cleaning up after clients. Every option is listed in the CLI reference, and every tool in the MCP tools reference.

docs.title: How the server runs scans
docs.text:
• Scans run inside the server process, in local mode, with the scanner tools installed for the user that runs the server. Install them as that user with ash dependencies install. Nothing runs in a container.
  • A scan writes its output to .ash/ash_output inside the directory it scans, so the server needs write access there. When the scan starts, it moves the previous scan's results into .ash/ash_output/.ash_previous_results, and it deletes them once it has results of its own. If the scan fails or is canceled, it puts them back in place of what it wrote, and get_scan_progress then reports output_holds_previous_results true; a first scan, with nothing to put back, leaves what it wrote. A call that run_ash_scan refuses leaves the previous results as they were. With clean_output false, the scan's own set-up moves the previous results a moment later instead.
  • A scan uses the config ASH discovers in the scanned directory, or the file a client names with config_path. When there is neither, it uses the file ASH_CONFIG names in the server's environment, or the built-in defaults.
  • If .ash or .ash/ash_output in the scanned directory is a symbolic link, run_ash_scan refuses before the scan starts, with error_type output_dir_not_permitted. A link deeper in the output directory, such as reports or ash.log, fails the scan, and get_scan_progress names the link in error_message and says to replace it in .ash/ash_output with a directory. run_ash_workspace_scan refuses an output_dir that is a link, or that has a link where ASH writes in it, including projects and projects/<project>, and asks for a directory that is not a link. Output files lists every path ASH checks.
  • run_ash_scan also refuses before the scan starts when source_dir is a file, with error_type source_dir_not_usable, and when .ash/ash_output in it is a file or a directory the server cannot write, with error_type output_dir_not_usable. run_ash_workspace_scan refuses such an output_dir the same way. Each refusal has exit_code 5 and a message that names the case, such as Output directory cannot be written: <path> (Permission denied), and nothing is created.
  • A path that holds a NUL character is refused before the server looks it up, with exit_code 5: a source_dir is refused with source_dir_not_usable, and the output_dir of run_ash_workspace_scan, get_scan_results, get_scan_summary or get_scan_result_paths is refused with output_dir_not_usable. The workspace tools refuse a workspace_file or workspace_config that holds one with exit_code 4 and the message Workspace definition is not a valid path: <path> or Workspace policy is not a valid path: <path>. Each message shows the NUL as \x00, and nothing is created.
  • MCP scans never run a tool found inside a scanned or delivered tree, whatever ASH_ALLOW_IN_TREE_TOOLS says, and ash mcp has no option to allow it. A scanner installed only inside the project, for example in its .venv, is reported as MISSING. See Tools inside the scanned directory.

ash mcp exits with code 5 for an unknown option, a value of the wrong type, options that cannot be combined, or an ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT that names no transport, and with code 3 when a --profile file does not load or an HTTP transport cannot listen on its address. It also exits with code 3 when ASH_CONFIG names no config file it can load. It exits with code 1 when the MCP package is missing or the server fails, and prints the error to standard error even with --quiet. Ctrl-C stops the server, and ash mcp exits with code 130 on every transport. A stdio server exits with code 0 when the client closes the connection, and, on Linux and macOS, when it gets SIGTERM or SIGHUP. An HTTP server that gets SIGTERM ends with the signal, which a shell reports as code 143. SIGHUP stops an HTTP server the way SIGTERM does, and ash mcp then exits with code 0.

docs.title: Choose a transport
docs.text:
Transport Use it for Clients connect to stdio, the default An agent or IDE on the same machine, which starts the server as a child process. The server's standard input and output. streamable-http A client that cannot start a local process, or a server on another host. http://HOST:PORT/mcp sse A client that supports only the older SSE transport, which the MCP SDK deprecates. http://HOST:PORT/sse

Use stdio whenever the client can start the server. The server is designed to serve one trusted client. It does not keep clients apart, so do not share one server between users or tools you would not trust with each other's source and results: run one server per user.

docs.title: Run over stdio
docs.text:
Clients start the server with this command and arguments:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "ash",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

On stdio the server's standard output carries the protocol, so ASH writes every message and log line to standard error, and so do the scans and the tools they run. --quiet hides the startup messages. --log-level, --verbose, and --debug set the HTTP server's log level and have no effect on stdio, and --color has no effect on any transport.

A stdio server lives as long as its client. When the client closes the connection, or, on Linux and macOS, the server gets SIGTERM, SIGHUP, or Ctrl-C, it cancels every running scan as cancel_scan would, except that each scanner's tool gets half a second after SIGTERM instead of ten, waits up to 1.5 seconds for the scans to stop, and exits. SIGHUP comes from a closed terminal or from a supervisor. SIGTERM, SIGHUP, and Ctrl-C stop the server this way even while the client keeps the connection open, and it exits with code 0 for SIGTERM and SIGHUP and 130 for Ctrl-C. A scan that stops in time leaves its output directory as cancel_scan does: previous results are put back, and with none, what the scan wrote before it stopped stays. Its log, ash.log, stays either way, and an ash.log.jsonl already there is left as it was. A scan still busy after the 1.5 seconds is left to the process exit, and its previous results stay in .ash/ash_output/.ash_previous_results, where the next MCP scan of that directory takes them back.

On Windows the server sets up no SIGTERM handling: a client or supervisor that ends the process ends it at once, with the exit code that the ending process sets, and the running scans are not stopped first. Their previous results stay in .ash_previous_results the same way. Ctrl-C there does not reach the scanners' tools, which run in process groups of their own, but the server stops its scans as it does when the client leaves. It exits, with code 130, only once the client has closed the connection, because the MCP SDK reads standard input on a thread that Ctrl-C cannot interrupt.

On every transport, a server started with SIGINT ignored, as a non-interactive shell starts a background job, keeps ignoring it, so a Ctrl-C meant for the job in the foreground does not stop it. A server started with SIGHUP ignored, as nohup starts one, keeps ignoring that too, and outlives the terminal it was started from. SIGTERM still stops either.

Over HTTP, a scan keeps running when its client disconnects, until it finishes or the server stops. Use streamable HTTP when scans must outlive a client's connection.

docs.title: Limit what a local agent can scan
docs.text:
On stdio, with ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS unset, an agent can scan, and read results from, any directory the server's user can read, except the filesystem root, the workspaces of other sessions, and a short list of system directories: /boot, /dev, /etc, /proc, /root, and /sys, or on Windows the Windows, Program Files, and ProgramData directories. A project inside one of them, such as /root when you work as root in a container, is refused until you name it in the variable. To limit scan targets and result paths to the directories you name and their subdirectories, set the variable in the server's environment:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ash": {
      "command": "ash",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": {
        "ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS": "/home/me/src"
      }
    }
  }
}

Separate several directories with :, or with ; on Windows. On stdio this does not limit which config files a client can name with config_path: those are refused only in the directories above. A file a client names counts as the client's, wherever it is, unless it is in a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names and no client delivered it (see What a delivered config cannot set).

docs.title: Run over streamable HTTP
docs.text:
The supported setup is one trusted client per server, an auth header on every request, and a server that is reachable only on the loopback interface or through a proxy you control.

  1. Choose a token:

    TOKEN="$(python3 -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"

  2. Set the environment and start the server:

    export ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT=streamable-http
export ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS="$HOME/src"
ash mcp --transport streamable-http --auth-header-name X-ASH-Token --auth-header-value "$TOKEN"

    The server prints Streamable-HTTP MCP server listening on http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp to standard error. --host, --port, and --mount-path change the address, which defaults to 127.0.0.1, port 8000, path /mcp.

  3. Point the client at the URL and give it the header. In Claude Code, for example:

    claude mcp add --transport http ash http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp --header "X-ASH-Token: $TOKEN"

--auth-header-name and --auth-header-value must be given together; one without the other is a usage error, and ash mcp exits with code 5 before it starts:

ash mcp --transport streamable-http --auth-header-name X-ASH-Token

The header name is matched without regard to case, and every request, on every path and method, must carry the exact value. A request without it gets 401 Unauthorized. The auth header is the server's only access control. The value is passed on the command line, so anyone who can list the host's processes can read it: run the server where other users cannot read its command line. ASH writes no access log; log requests at your proxy if you need a record.

Always set ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT to the transport you serve, streamable-http or sse. ASH ignores the value's case and surrounding whitespace. A value that names no transport, one other than stdio, streamable-http, or sse, makes ash mcp exit with code 5 before it starts:

ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT=http ash mcp

ash mcp does not set the variable for you. With it set, ASH applies its rules for remote clients to every call:

  • A client can scan, and read results from, only the directories in ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS and source delivered over MCP. With the variable unset, it can scan only delivered source.
  • A client can name config files (config_path, every base an extends chain names, and workspace files) only in ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS, the scan roots, and its session's config/ directory. The workspace tools use a workspace policy file only from ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS, on every transport (Workspace scans over MCP).

These rules limit what the server's client can reach. They do not keep clients apart, so serve one trusted client per server.

Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP stops an HTTP server: it stops its running scans and their scanners' tools, and ash mcp exits with code 130 for Ctrl-C and 0 for SIGHUP, or ends by SIGTERM, which a shell reports as code 143. Before it stops the scans, the server waits for the requests clients still hold open, for at most 5 seconds, and then cancels them. The wait is bounded so that the whole stop fits inside the grace period a service manager gives before it sends SIGKILL, such as the 10 seconds docker stop waits by default: a SIGKILL of the server leaves the scanners' tools running. A second Ctrl-C during the wait ends the server at once, with code 130. It kills the scanners' tools without waiting for the scans, and previous results a scan had not put back stay in .ash_previous_results, where the next MCP scan of that directory takes them back.

docs.title: Serve clients on another host
docs.text:
ASH serves plain HTTP. Put a proxy you control in front of it for TLS, and keep the server on the loopback interface when the proxy runs on the same host. If the proxy forwards the client's Host header, pass --allowed-host with that name even when the server listens on loopback. If the server must listen on another address, name every Host header value it should accept:

ash mcp --transport streamable-http --host 0.0.0.0 --allowed-host ash.example.com \
  --auth-header-name X-ASH-Token --auth-header-value "$TOKEN"

Always pass --allowed-host with a non-loopback --host. It names the Host header values the server accepts, which protects against DNS rebinding. The option can be repeated. Each value must match the Host header exactly, including case and any port the client sends. A value ending in :* matches that name with any port, but not the name without one; list both if clients send either. Once you pass the option, the loopback names are accepted only if you list them too. ASH does not support browser-based clients. Limit who can reach the port with your firewall or network rules as well.

ASH enforces this. With a non-loopback --host and neither --allowed-host nor --trust-upstream-host-check, ash mcp refuses to start, because the server would answer any Host and any Origin header. With --allowed-host, the server refuses every request that carries an Origin header. On a loopback --host without --allowed-host, it accepts only its own address as Host: 127.0.0.1, localhost, or [::1] with the port it listens on, and on port 80 also without the port. It accepts the same names as http:// origins.

--trust-upstream-host-check is for a proxy or platform in front of ASH that checks the Host and Origin headers itself. With it, ASH accepts any Host and any Origin, so the protection against DNS rebinding is only what that proxy or platform provides. It applies only to the HTTP transports with a non-loopback --host, and it cannot be combined with --allowed-host. On stdio, with a loopback --host, or with --allowed-host, ash mcp refuses to start:

ash mcp --transport streamable-http --trust-upstream-host-check

docs.title: Behind a load balancer or a managed runtime
docs.text:
By default the server keeps one session per client: it issues an Mcp-Session-Id when a client connects and refuses session IDs it did not issue. --stateless-http handles every request on its own instead. It is for load balancers that may send consecutive requests to different replicas, and for runtimes that set their own Mcp-Session-Id. It is accepted only with --transport streamable-http; with another transport, the default stdio included, it is a usage error, and ash mcp exits with code 5 before it starts:

ash mcp --stateless-http

In stateless mode the server issues no session IDs. Use it only where the platform requires it, and keep to one trusted client per server with ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT set.

A stateless server identifies no session by itself, so the tools that keep state for a session refuse every call with error_type session_identity_required: run_ash_scan, get_scan_progress, list_active_scans, cancel_scan, set_source_git, set_source_zip_chunk, set_source_zip_finalize, clear_source, and select_profile. run_ash_workspace_scan returns its results in its response and needs no session. The session is never what a client claims: on a stateful server an Mcp-Session-Id the server did not issue names no session, and on SSE the session is the one the server issued for the event stream.

When a platform in front of ASH issues and authenticates Mcp-Session-Id, start the server with --trust-upstream-session-id as well. The header then names the caller's session, so two callers are kept apart only as well as the platform keeps their headers apart. ASH checks only that the value can name one directory: letters, digits, and ., _, -, ~, +, and =, and not . or ... It refuses any other value instead of rewriting it, with error_type invalid_session_id. The option applies only to --transport streamable-http --stateless-http; anywhere else, ash mcp refuses to start:

ash mcp --transport streamable-http --trust-upstream-session-id

The templates in deploy/ run the server for you on AWS: see Deploy ASH on AWS.

docs.title: SSE
docs.text: --transport sse serves the SSE transport at /sse, unless you pass --mount-path with a path other than /mcp. It takes the same host, port, and auth options as streamable HTTP, and not --stateless-http. Use it only for a client that cannot use streamable HTTP, with ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT=sse set and one trusted client.

docs.title: Environment variables the server reads
docs.text:
Variable When unset Effect ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT Not set by ash mcp. Set it to streamable-http or sse, in any case, to apply the remote-client rules above to every call. A value that names no transport stops ash mcp from starting, with exit code 5. ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS Local clients: everything outside the system directories, the filesystem root, and other sessions' workspaces. Remote clients: only delivered source. Directories, and their subdirectories, that clients may scan and read results from. ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS A remote client may read config only from the scan roots and its session's config/ directory. Extra directories remote clients may read config files from, such as a shared policy file. A config file a client names there counts as yours, not the client's, unless a client delivered it. ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS No host: set_source_git clones from nowhere. The hosts set_source_git may clone from, separated by spaces or commas, matched without regard to case. See Deliver source to the server. ASH_MCP_WORKSPACE_ROOT $XDG_CACHE_HOME/ash-mcp, or ~/.cache/ash-mcp Where each session's workspace lives: delivered source, uploads, and session configs. ASH_CONFIG The built-in defaults. The server's own config. Its global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides section is the policy that delivered configs are checked against, and its mcp-resource-management section limits the scans. When it names a path that is not a file, a file the server cannot read, or a config that does not load or validate, ash mcp refuses to start, on every transport, with exit code 3. An empty value counts as unset. Keep it outside every git checkout and the directories clients scan: inside one, its sandbox grants and plugin modules do not count (Configuration trust model).

A missing ASH_CONFIG file stops the server before it serves anything, with an error that names the variable and the path:

ASH_CONFIG=/nonexistent ash mcp

The environment variable reference lists every variable ASH reads.

docs.title: Limit how many scans run and for how long
docs.text:
The server enforces two limits from the mcp-resource-management section of its own config, the file ASH_CONFIG names in the environment of the ash mcp process. A scanned repository's config and a config a client delivers cannot change them. Without ASH_CONFIG, the defaults apply. The server reads the section again for each scan.

max_concurrent_scans: 3
scan_timeout_seconds: 1800
  • max_concurrent_scans, 3 by default and at most 100, is the most scans the server holds at once, across every session: running, waiting for another scan of their session, or canceled and still stopping. run_ash_scan beyond the limit is refused with error_type scan_start_failure and an error that names the limit; the client starts the scan again once one has finished or been canceled.
  • scan_timeout_seconds, 1800 by default, is the longest one scan may run, from 60 to 86400 seconds. The clock starts when the scan starts running, so the time it waits for another scan of its session does not count. A scan still running then is stopped the way cancel_scan stops one, and ends failed with an error_message that names the limit.

0 or null turns either limit off. A workspace scan, run_ash_workspace_scan, takes one slot for all of its projects and is refused like any other scan when no slot is free. scan_timeout_seconds covers the whole workspace scan: past it, every project still running is stopped and ends failed, and the call returns success false with error_category operation_timeout and the scan_ids. A workspace scan stopped this way writes no combined results file and no workspace reports, unless it was stopped while writing them. cancel_scan with one project's scan id stops that project, which ends failed, and the other projects carry on. The section's other keys are accepted so that existing configs keep validating, and nothing reads them.

docs.title: Deliver source to the server
docs.text:
A client that does not share a filesystem with the server sends the source over MCP, then calls run_ash_scan without source_dir to scan it. Each session's source lands in <workspace root>/<session ID>/source.

set_source_git clones a repository with git, so the server's host needs git. The clone is shallow: depth is the number of commits it fetches, a positive whole number, 1 by default. Any other value, 0 included, is refused before anything is created, with error_type invalid_clone_depth.

It refuses these before it creates or clones anything:

  • A URL or ref that begins with -, and URLs that use the ext:: transport, with error_type clone_url_not_permitted or clone_ref_not_permitted.
  • A local path or file:// URL, with error_type local_clone_source_refused, whatever the scan roots allow. To scan a directory on the server's host, the client names it as run_ash_scan's source_dir.
  • A URL with a scheme other than https or ssh, with error_type clone_url_not_permitted.
  • A host that ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS does not list, with error_type clone_host_not_permitted. The variable is empty unless you set it, so the server clones from no host until you name the ones clients may clone from, separated by spaces or commas.
  • Any ssh_key_id, with error_type ssh_key_not_registered. The server registers no SSH keys, and it never accepts a private key over MCP.

git then runs without the server's credentials or git configuration:

  • Its environment keeps only PATH, the locale, the temporary directories, and the TLS trust settings GIT_SSL_CAINFO, GIT_SSL_CAPATH, SSL_CERT_FILE, and SSL_CERT_DIR, with HOME set to the session's directory. Tokens, proxy settings, SSH agent sockets, and GIT_* variables in the server's environment do not reach it, so a clone that needs a proxy fails.
  • System and global git configuration are off, no credential helper or askpass program runs, and git starts no hook and no fsmonitor command.
  • Only the https and ssh protocols are allowed, for submodules too, and git follows no HTTP redirect, so an allowed host cannot send it to another one.
  • ssh runs with no configuration file, identity file, or agent, never prompts, and checks the host key against the system-wide known hosts file only.

Each git command, the clone and, for a ref, the fetch and the checkout, may run for 10 minutes. One that runs longer is stopped with every process it started, nothing it cloned is kept, and the call fails with error_type clone_timed_out. A git command that runs and fails gives git_clone_failed or git_checkout_failed, with git's own message in error.

  • It deletes the session's previous tree before it clones, so a failed clone leaves the session with nothing to scan until the client delivers again.
  • What git can reach over the network is what the server's host can reach. Restrict the host's outbound network to the hosts in ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

set_source_zip_chunk and set_source_zip_finalize take a zipped tree in base64 chunks.

  • Chunks arrive in order, each at most 1 MiB once decoded.
  • The finished zip must match the SHA-256 the client gives, and may be at most 100 MiB, with at most 500 MiB and 50,000 entries once extracted.
  • A zip with an entry that has an absolute path, a .. component, or a symbolic link is refused as a whole, before anything is extracted.
  • A new zip is extracted beside the old tree and replaces it only when extraction succeeds.

While a scan of a session runs, clear_source, set_source_git, and set_source_zip_finalize are refused with error_type source_delivery_busy, because each would remove or replace the tree the scan is reading. Call them again once the scan has finished. A run_ash_workspace_scan over a workspace in the session's delivered tree holds the tree the same way for the whole workspace scan. The other way round, run_ash_scan and run_ash_workspace_scan are refused with the same error_type while one of those calls is changing the session's tree. Chunks are still accepted, because they land beside the tree. set_source_zip_chunk and select_profile are refused with error_type session_workspace_busy while an HTTP server removes the session's workspace for being unused longer than --session-workspace-ttl. The upload and the bound profile go with the workspace, so the client selects the profile again and sends the upload again from chunk 0. ASH sets no quota on uploads per session or in total. The server's config limits how many scans run and for how long; see Limit how many scans run and for how long.

docs.title: What a delivered config cannot set
docs.text:
A config file inside delivered source is an MCP-client file. So is a config file a client names as config_path to run_ash_scan, get_config, or validate_config, wherever it is, unless it is in a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names or in its session's config/ directory, which only the server writes: a config in another checkout the server may scan is that checkout's, not yours. ASH judges a config path a client names by where it sits as well as by the file it reaches, so a symbolic link a client names is the client's wherever it points. A config file that ASH finds by itself in a directory the server scans in place is a repository config, trusted the way the CLI trusts it; see Configuration trust model.

ASH checks every MCP-client file in a config chain against the server's policy, the global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides section of the server's own config, whether or not runtime_overrides.enabled is set. Only what the file writes counts: a value equal to the server's at the same key is accepted. Every operation in the file's patch is checked as written, and one that targets a denied field is refused even when it writes the server's value. The policy's denied_value_patterns apply to delivered files too.

With the default policy, a delivered config is refused as a whole, with error_type config_field_denied and a message naming each field, if it sets any of these to a value other than the server's own:

  • the gate: fail_on_findings, fail_on_incomplete_scanners, content_db_staleness, content_db_staleness_overrides, and content_db_staleness_offline_image_default
  • scanner options that drop findings by rule ID, by a baseline, or by a whole category, such as exclude_rule, config, and severity of opengrep and semgrep, checkov's frameworks, cfn-lint's ignore_checks, detect-secrets' baseline_file and scan_settings, and trivy's scanners and ignore_unfixed
  • options that limit how much a scanner reads or reports, or that turn on its own network calls, such as ferret-scan's finding_limit and recursive, gitleaks' max_target_megabytes, and zizmor's online_audits
  • any scanner's offline option
  • options that name a scanner's own config file or another file or program its tool reads: every scanner's config_file, and others such as trivy's ignore_file, gitleaks' baseline_path, and actionlint's shellcheck and pyflakes
  • which version of a tool runs: any scanner's or the jupyter converter's tool_version, and opengrep's version and sha256
  • any setting of the reporters that send findings off the host, aws-security-hub, bedrock-summary-reporter, cloudwatch-logs, and s3, their enabled included
  • the gitlab-sast reporter's exclude_suppressed, which leaves suppressed findings out of its report

ash config init writes the full default list into the config it creates, and the configuration reference shows it. validate_config reports each such field as an error of type denied_by_runtime_policy; for config_content, only when a remote client calls it. A delivered workspace whose project config sets one fails to resolve. To scan, the client removes those fields and delivers the config again.

A delivered config cannot turn a reporter that sends findings off the host on or off. Its enabled: false for one of the four is not refused, but it has no effect: each runs as the server's config says, or by the reporter's own default where that config sets nothing. The same holds for a reporter a plugin module adds that declares destination options, and a delivered value for one of those options is replaced by the server's instead of refused, because the module is loaded only when the scan runs. A delivered config can still turn the reporters that write only local files, such as html, sarif, and yaml, on or off and set their options, apart from gitlab-sast's exclude_suppressed.

If the policy itself cannot be loaded, because the file ASH_CONFIG names exists but does not load, or has two sections that ASH reads as the same plugin, a config with an MCP-client file is refused with config_policy_unreadable. A file that does not load stops the server when it starts, so a call meets that case only when the file changed after the server started. A scan that reads no such file is unaffected.

Under the default denied_paths, a delivered config's sandbox settings and plugin modules may restrict the server's own but not widen them. A file whose own sandbox section or ash_plugin_modules list asks for more in one of these ways is refused with config_field_denied, naming the setting; an equal or tighter value scans:

  • sandbox.network_scanners may list only scanners the server's settings give a network. A shorter list takes the network away from the scanners it leaves out.
  • sandbox.extra_read_paths may list only paths the server's settings grant.
  • sandbox.mode can turn the sandbox on when the server's mode is off, and otherwise must equal the server's mode. The images that deploy/ builds have neither bubblewrap nor firejail, so there a bwrap or firejail mode leaves the scanners it would wrap MISSING; see Deploy ASH on AWS.
  • ash_plugin_modules may add only ASH's own plugin modules and modules installed outside every git checkout and the scanned directory, and never the AWS or Snyk plugin modules, or a module inside either.

Any other sandbox grant or plugin module a delivered file asks for, such as a read_path_scanners or env_scanners entry, is dropped with a warning, as for a repository's config.

The server's settings are the ones in the file ASH_CONFIG names, and that file grants nothing when it is inside a git checkout, or inside the directory a scan covers, so keep it outside every checkout. A delivered config's global_settings.mcp section has no effect.

An MCP-client file reads no environment variables, since the environment it would read is the server's. A file in which a plain value starts with a ${VAR} or ${VAR:default} reference, or that uses an !ENV tag, is refused: run_ash_scan and get_config, with or without raw, return error_type config_env_not_resolved, and run_ash_scan does not start the scan; validate_config reports an error of that type. The rule follows where the file is, so a CLI scan of a delivered tree refuses such a config too, with exit code 3. The refusal covers the file a client names as config_path and every file a client delivered. A file in a directory ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names keeps its references.

get_config never returns a value that a config read from the environment, since the server's environment is not the client's. The resolved config shows such a value as <from ${VAR}>, and with raw the reference appears as the file wrote it. For how a scan's results record such a value, see Read values from the environment.

Suppressions and ignore paths in a delivered config are applied, and marked as coming from the client:

  • Each entry from a delivered config file that the operator did not also supply has client_supplied: true in the results' copy of the config.
  • In SARIF, the suppression justification starts with (ASH, client-supplied config) and the suppression carries properties.clientSupplied: true.
  • Files under a delivered ignore path are still scanned. Their findings are kept and marked suppressed instead of being dropped.
  • Path exclusions in scanner options, such as bandit's excluded_paths, are taken out of the options and handled the same way, and a delivered scanners.trivy-repo.options.ignore_file becomes marked suppressions instead of being passed to trivy. Configuration trust model says how each is matched.

Suppressions, ignore paths, and scanner exclusions explains how suppressed findings affect the exit code and each report.

docs.title: Refuse delivered suppressions too
docs.text:
To refuse delivered suppressions and ignore paths, give the server's config a denied_paths list of its own: the full default list, as ash config init writes it, followed by these two entries, which say so explicitly:

- /global_settings/suppressions/**
- /global_settings/ignore_paths/**

A list of your own replaces the default list and is applied exactly as written, so keep every default entry, start each one with /, and compare your list with the default again after you upgrade ASH. A list equal to a default that ASH has shipped, such as the one an earlier ash config init wrote, still counts as the default, and gets every entry of the current default list. Any other list is your own, even the default list with one entry added or removed, and every entry in it applies as written. While it keeps the default's /global_settings/suppressions and /global_settings/ignore_paths entries, delivered suppressions and ignore paths are refused. While it keeps the /sandbox and /ash_plugin_modules entries, a delivered config that sets either to any value other than the server's is refused, even a tighter one. If your list leaves the /sandbox and /ash_plugin_modules entries out, ASH does not refuse a delivered file that asks for more: it drops the grants and modules instead, as it does for a repository's config.

An entry matches a key spelled with - or _. Under /scanners, /reporters, and /converters, an entry for a plugin's section also matches every spelling ASH reads as that plugin. A glob in the plugin segment matches every key it matches as written, and also the other spellings of the plugins that ship with ASH and of the plugins your server config configures, so /scanners/trivy-*/options/ignore_file also covers /scanners/TrivyRepo/options/ignore_file; to cover another plugin under every spelling, write its name.

docs.title: Config profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a named ASH config that clients can choose. Register profiles when you start the server, with --profile NAME=path/to/ash.yaml once per profile, on any transport:

ash mcp --profile strict=/etc/ash/strict.yaml --profile default=/etc/ash/default.yaml

The server loads and validates every profile when it starts. A spec without =, a missing file, or a file that does not load, including one with an unknown top-level key, stops it with exit code 3. The server reads each file once, so an edit takes effect when it restarts. A client cannot add a profile.

  • list_profiles returns each profile's name and path_sha256, a SHA-256 of the file's absolute path, sorted by name. It never returns the path or the file's contents.
  • select_profile binds a profile to the calling session. A later run_ash_scan in that session that names no config_path scans under the profile, instead of the config ASH would find in the scanned directory. The workspace tools use it for each project that has no config of its own, and their profile argument names a profile for one call instead.
  • select_profile with patch_ops or override_yaml changes the profile for that session, and the workspace tools' config_overrides argument changes the config for one call. Each change must be allowed by the global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides section of the profile, or of the defaults when the session has no profile. Runtime overrides are off by default, so without a profile that turns them on, every change a client asks for is refused. A change that is refused, or that does not apply, is reported without its value: by its op and path, or, when an override_yaml does not parse or validate or a config_overrides entry leaves the config invalid, by the problem and where it is (the parser's position, the field, or the key).
  • Such a change cannot turn a reporter that sends findings off the host on or off either. Turning one on, removing its section, or setting any of its options is refused. Its enabled: false for one of the four is not refused, but it has no effect: each runs as the profile says, and sends where the profile says.
  • The copy of a profile the server writes into a session's workspace holds each value the profile read from the environment as the profile's file wrote it, not the value. A scan under the profile still uses the value from the server's environment, also when the client changed the profile.
  • No op sees a value or key the profile read from the environment. A test at one fails whatever value it gives, a path through such a key names nothing, and an add of a key beside one is refused. A value an op or override_yaml writes is the client's text: the session's copy holds it, and get_config shows it, as the client wrote it, even where it equals what the profile read. A value the profile read keeps its reference wherever the ops move its list entry. A profile in which such a value is part of a longer string, such as a relative path that ASH takes from the profile's directory (${VAR}/bandit.yaml), can't be written to a session with its reference, so select_profile, and a workspace scan's profile, refuse it without naming the value. Set the variable to an absolute path, or to the whole string.

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
• clear_source deletes the calling session's workspace, <workspace root>/<session ID>.
  • An HTTP server removes a session's workspace, with its delivered source, uploads, and bound profile, when it sees the session end: a stateful session's DELETE, a session the MCP SDK discarded, an SSE event stream that closes, and every session it issued when it shuts down.
  • It also removes a workspace nobody used for --session-workspace-ttl seconds, 86400 (24 hours) by default, which covers sessions whose end it cannot see, such as every stateless one. Each request that names a session counts as a use. A workspace whose scan is running, or whose tree is being changed, is kept, and so is anything under the workspace root that ASH did not create as a session workspace. A set_source_zip_chunk or select_profile call holds its session from the moment the tool starts, so a sweep that runs while the call writes keeps the session.
  • Servers that share one workspace root take a lock under the root before a sweep removes a session. A sweep that cannot take that lock within about a second, because another server holds it, removes nothing more and leaves the remaining sessions to its next sweep, so another server cannot hold up a stop signal.

  • --session-workspace-ttl takes a positive number of seconds and applies only to the HTTP transports. On stdio, ash mcp refuses to start with it:

    ash mcp --session-workspace-ttl 3600

  • The stdio session's workspace is removed when the last stdio server that uses that workspace root exits.

  • Scan output stays in each scanned directory's .ash/ash_output. If the server is killed during a scan, the previous results stay in .ash/ash_output/.ash_previous_results, and the next MCP scan of that directory takes them back.
  • The server keeps its list of scans in memory. After a restart, get_scan_progress no longer knows earlier scan IDs, and their results are still readable from the output directory with get_scan_results.

docs.title: Checklist for an HTTP server
docs.text:
• Prefer stdio for an agent on the same machine.
  • Serve one trusted client per server, and run one server per user.
  • Keep the default stateful streamable HTTP; use --stateless-http or SSE only where the platform requires it.
  • Always set --auth-header-name and --auth-header-value, and run the server where other users cannot read its command line.
  • Bind to loopback, or put a proxy you control in front. Pass --allowed-host behind any proxy that forwards the Host header, and with any non-loopback --host.
  • Set ASH_MCP_TRANSPORT to streamable-http or sse.
  • Set ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS, and ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS if clients need shared config, to the directories the client needs and nothing more.
  • Set ASH_MCP_GIT_ALLOWED_HOSTS only if clients clone with set_source_git, and only to the hosts they clone from.
  • Set max_concurrent_scans and scan_timeout_seconds in the server's config to what the host can run.
  • Run the server as a dedicated user without credentials the client should not use, and limit its network access.
  • Lower --session-workspace-ttl if delivered source should not stay on the host for up to 24 hours after its client stops using it.

Scanning untrusted code describes what protects the host when the source a client sends is hostile. To scan a VS Code workspace over MCP, see Scale to large repositories.

docs.title: Migrate from v2
docs.text:
ASH v3 is a rewrite. v2 was a shell script that ran every scanner in a container. v3 is a Python program that runs scanners on your machine by default, reads a configuration file, writes different output files, and uses exit codes with fixed meanings. This page lists what changes for a v2 user and what to do about each.

v2 v3 Install clone the repository and add it to PATH install from GitHub with uv, pipx, pip, or Homebrew (Install ASH) Where scanners run always in a container built on each run on your machine, or in a container with ash --mode container Configuration none a config file, .ashrc.yaml in a new project, with ignore paths, suppressions, thresholds, and scanner settings Output ash_output/aggregated_results.txt .ash/ash_output/, with a JSON results file and a reports/ directory Exit code the highest exit code of any scanner 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5, each with one meaning Requirements a container runtime Python 3.10 to 3.14, plus scanner tools or a container runtime

docs.title: Install v3
docs.text:
1. Remove the v2 clone from your PATH. The v3 repository still has an ash script at its root, so a clone on your PATH can shadow the ash command you install.
  2. Install v3 as described in Install ASH.
  3. Choose where the scanners run:
  4. To run them on your machine, as v3 does by default, install them with ash dependencies install. See Manage scanner tools.
  5. To keep v2's behavior of running everything in a container, run ash --mode container. See Run ASH in a container.

docs.title: Command-line options
docs.text:
v2's options were parsed by its shell scripts. In v3, ash with no subcommand is the same as ash scan.

v2 option v3 --source-dir --source-dir, unchanged --output-dir --output-dir. The default is now .ash/ash_output inside the source directory, instead of ash_output. --ext, -extension removed. Choose scanners with --scanners and --exclude-scanners, or turn them on and off in the configuration. --format text, --format json changed. --format is now an alias of --output-formats, which takes reporter names such as sarif or html. json is not one of them, so a v2 --format json exits 5, a usage error, with 'json' is not a valid format. text is the text reporter, so a v2 --format text keeps only ash.summary.txt in reports/. v3 always writes its JSON results file. --offline --offline. In local mode the scanners then need their databases and rules already on the machine; see Run ASH offline. --offline-semgrep-rulesets --offline-semgrep-rulesets, changed. In v2 it also turned on offline mode. In v3 it only chooses the rulesets an offline container image is built with, and does nothing in local mode; pass --offline as well. --build-target, --no-build, --no-run, --force unchanged, for container mode --no-cleanup accepted. v3 keeps its working files by default; --cleanup removes them. -c, --no-color --no-color. -c now means --config. -s, --single-process ash --strategy sequential -o, --oci-runner --oci-runner and -o, unchanged. The OCI_RUNNER variable also works. -p, --preserve-report removed. Use a different --output-dir for each run. -p now means --progress. -d, --debug --debug and -d, unchanged -q, --quiet --quiet only -v, --version --version only. -v now means --verbose. -h, --help --help only --container-uid -u, --container-gid --container-uid (-u) and --container-gid (-g) --finch, -f removed; use ash --mode container --oci-runner finch. -f now means --output-formats.

Remove v2 options from your scripts. ash and ash scan reject an option they do not know, or a value an option does not accept, with a usage error, exit code 5, so a stale command line fails before it scans. A v2 --format json fails this way:

ash --format json

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
v2 had no configuration file. It skipped files matched by .gitignore and .ignore files, and in a git repository it scanned a clone, so only committed files were scanned.

v3 also honors .gitignore and .ignore, but it scans the working tree, so uncommitted and untracked files that are not ignored are scanned too. Expect findings in files v2 never saw. Neither version reads a .ashignore file.

Everything else is set in a configuration file. ash config init writes a starting file, .ashrc.yaml, in the current directory:

ash config init
head -n 3 .ashrc.yaml

In it you can:

  • skip paths, each with a reason, under global_settings.ignore_paths;
  • suppress findings, each with a reason and an optional expiration date, under global_settings.suppressions;
  • set the severity that fails a scan, global_settings.severity_threshold;
  • turn scanners on and off, and set their options, under scanners.

See Configure ASH and Suppress findings. The scanners' own inline comments, such as bandit's # nosec, still work.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
v2 wrote one text file, ash_output/aggregated_results.txt, made by joining each scanner's text output. v3 writes .ash/ash_output/ in the scanned directory:

  • ash_aggregated_results.json: every scanner's status and findings.
  • reports/: the same results in several formats. ash.summary.txt and ash.summary.md are the closest to v2's file; there are also ash.html, ash.sarif, ash.junit.xml, ash.csv, and others.
  • scanners/: each scanner's raw output.
  • ash.log: the scan's log.

ash report prints a summary of the latest results in the terminal. See Output files.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
v2 exited with the highest exit code that any scanner returned, so any finding or any error gave a nonzero code. v3 uses fixed codes:

Code Meaning 0 nothing actionable 1 the scan is incomplete, for example a scanner is MISSING, or ASH hit an error 2 actionable findings at or above the severity threshold 3 a configuration ASH cannot use, or an input it refuses before scanning, such as a linked output directory 4 workspace error 5 a usage error, such as an option ASH does not know

Two defaults affect CI jobs that you move from v2:

  • Only findings at or above MEDIUM severity fail the scan. Low-severity findings that failed a v2 scan pass in v3. To fail on them too, set global_settings.severity_threshold to LOW.
  • A scanner that has files to scan but whose tool is missing fails the scan with code 1, even when nothing else is wrong. Install the tools, use container mode, or exclude the scanners you do not run.

See Set the gate and Exit codes.

docs.title: Scanners
docs.text:
v2 ran git-secrets, bandit, semgrep, checkov, cfn_nag, cdk-nag, npm audit, grype, and syft, choosing them by the file types it found. v3 runs actionlint, bandit, cdk-nag, cfn-guard, cfn-lint, cfn-nag, checkov, detect-secrets, gitleaks, grype, npm-audit, opengrep, semgrep, syft, trivy, and zizmor. A scanner shows as SKIPPED when the project has nothing for it to scan, whether or not its tool is installed: for example cdk-nag and cfn-nag in a project without CloudFormation templates.

  • git-secrets is gone. detect-secrets and gitleaks look for secrets.
  • semgrep runs the p/ci ruleset by default. v2 ran --config=auto.
  • More scanners can report the same problem, because v3 does not merge findings from different scanners.

See Scanners reference.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
v2 always ran in a container. v3 has four modes, chosen with --mode:

  • local, the default: scanners run on your machine.
  • container: ASH builds its image on your machine and scans inside it. It looks for finch, docker, nerdctl, and podman in that order, as v2 did.
  • precommit: a faster scan with a smaller set of scanners, for pre-commit hooks.
  • nix: scanners come from ASH's Nix flake. Releases up to v3.7.x reject it; see Install ASH.

docs.title: pre-commit and CI
docs.text:
The ash pre-commit hook ID still exists. In v3 it runs a local scan in precommit mode instead of a full container scan; the ash-full-scan hook builds ASH's image and scans in it. Set rev: to a v3 release tag. See Run ASH with pre-commit.

v2's CI examples cloned the repository and ran its script. In v3, install ASH from its GitHub URL with a pinned version in the job, or call the reusable GitHub Actions workflow. See Add ASH to a GitHub Actions pipeline.

docs.title: Run ASH with pre-commit
docs.text:
ASH's repository defines hooks for the pre-commit framework. This page sets up the ash hook, says what it scans, and what it costs per commit.

Prerequisites:

  • pre-commit, running on Python 3.10 to 3.14, or a language_version as shown below.
  • A git repository with a .pre-commit-config.yaml.
  • Network access to GitHub and PyPI the first time the hook runs.

docs.title: Add the hook
docs.text:
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper
    rev: v3.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: ash

Then install the git hook and run it once on every file:

pre-commit install
pre-commit run ash --all-files

The first run builds the hook's environment, with ASH's cdk extra, and installs bandit and checkov, so it takes longer than later runs. When the hook finds something, pre-commit prints Failed with ASH's summary and - exit code: 2, and the commit stops. Exit code 1 means the scan did not complete, for example because a scanner was MISSING; Exit codes lists every cause.

Ignore ASH's output directory in git, so the reports are not committed. ASH leaves its own files there out of the scan whether or not .gitignore lists them, but it scans a file committed there like any other. ash config init writes a .ash/.gitignore that ignores it, or add the line yourself:

.ash/ash_output/

Do not ignore all of .ash/: an ASH config file can live there, as .ash/.ash.yaml.

docs.title: What the hook runs
docs.text:
The ash hook runs ashv3 --mode=precommit with your args. Precommit mode:

  • runs five scanners: bandit, detect-secrets, checkov, cdk-nag, and npm-audit. --scanners can add others but cannot remove these; --exclude-scanners removes them.
  • scans the whole repository on every run, not only the staged files. A commit that touches one file is still blocked by a finding in a file committed earlier.
  • prints simplified output and writes the usual reports to .ash/ash_output/.

The hook's environment includes the cdk extra that cdk-nag needs. cdk-nag and npm-audit also need Node.js and npm on PATH, but only when the repository has files they scan: CloudFormation templates for cdk-nag, including the *.template.json files cdk synth writes to cdk.out even when .gitignore lists cdk.out, and a package.json with an npm, yarn, or pnpm lockfile beside it for npm-audit. In a repository with neither, both are SKIPPED and the hook runs without Node.js. In one that has them, Node.js and npm must be on PATH, or ASH reports the scanner that has files to scan as MISSING and the hook fails with exit code 1 on every commit. To run without Node.js there, exclude the two scanners:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper
    rev: v3.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: ash
        args: [--exclude-scanners, cdk-nag, --exclude-scanners, npm-audit]

They are then SKIPPED, and the hook passes or fails on the other three. ash-simple-scan is the same hook under another name.

Do not add --no-fail-on-incomplete-scanners to the hook: with it, a commit passes when a scanner did not run, and the output says only Passed.

docs.title: Add Python packages to the hook
docs.text: additional_dependencies in your configuration replaces the hook's own list rather than adding to it. The ash hook's list is .[cdk], which installs the cdk extra from the hook's clone of ASH, so a list of your own has to include .[cdk] as well. Without it, cdk-nag is MISSING in a repository with CloudFormation templates.

docs.title: When the hook runs
docs.text:
The hook has no stages setting, so it runs on every commit. To run it less often, set one:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper
    rev: v3.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: ash
        stages: [pre-push]

With stages: [pre-push], install that hook type with pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push, and a failing scan blocks git push. With stages: [manual], the hook runs only when you ask: pre-commit run --hook-stage manual ash.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text:
Measured on a repository of three files:

Run Time First run, with the hook environment and scanner installs 65 to 150 seconds Later runs 11 to 15 seconds

checkov is the slowest scanner. Scan time grows with the size of the repository, because every run scans all of it. The hook environment takes about 650 MB under ~/.cache/pre-commit, and bandit and checkov about 240 MB under ~/.local/share/uv.

docs.title: Use an ASH you already installed
docs.text:
If ASH is installed with uv tool install or in a virtual environment outside the repository, a local hook runs that installation instead of building one per repository:

repos:
  - repo: local
    hooks:
      - id: ash
        name: ASH
        entry: ash --mode precommit
        language: system
        pass_filenames: false

ash must be on PATH when git runs the hook. ASH installs bandit and checkov with the uv installed with it, or with a uv on PATH. pass_filenames: false is required. Without it, pre-commit appends the staged file names, and ASH rejects the first one as an unknown command, a usage error, with exit code 5.

This hook uses the extras and tools of that installation. When the repository has CloudFormation templates, cdk-nag needs the cdk extra in that installation and Node.js on PATH; when it has npm lockfiles, npm-audit needs npm on PATH. A scanner that lacks them is MISSING and every commit fails with exit code 1. Add --exclude-scanners cdk-nag --exclude-scanners npm-audit to entry to leave the two out.

docs.title: Pre-commit on another Python
docs.text:
pre-commit builds a Python hook's environment with the interpreter it runs under, and ASH installs on Python 3.10 to 3.14 only. If pre-commit itself runs on another version, building the hook environment fails; on Python 3.9 the error is No matching distribution found for hatchling>=1.32.4. Install pre-commit on a supported interpreter:

uv tool install --python 3.12 pre-commit

Or point the hook at a newer Python that is on your PATH:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper
    rev: v3.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: ash
        language_version: python3.12

default_language_version at the top of the file does the same for every Python hook.

docs.title: A frozen rev is flagged as a secret
docs.text:
pre-commit autoupdate --freeze replaces the tag with a 40-character commit SHA, and detect-secrets reports that line of .pre-commit-config.yaml as a high-entropy string, which fails the hook with exit code 2. Suppress that finding for that file, with the reason:

global_settings:
  suppressions:
    - path: .pre-commit-config.yaml
      rule_id: SECRET-HEX-HIGH-ENTROPY-STRING
      reason: pre-commit autoupdate --freeze pins hooks to commit SHAs

Put it in your ASH config file, or, if the repository has none, in a new .ashrc.yaml at its root. Suppress findings covers expiration dates and narrower matches.

docs.title: The ash-full-scan hook
docs.text:
.pre-commit-hooks.yaml also defines ash-full-scan, which runs ashv3 --mode=container --simple. It builds ASH's container image from the source that pre-commit installed, then scans the repository inside it with every scanner the image carries. It needs a container runtime on the host: finch, docker, nerdctl, or podman, found in that order. The first run builds the image and takes several minutes, so give the hook stages: [pre-push] or stages: [manual]:

repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper
    rev: v3.7.0
    hooks:
      - id: ash-full-scan
        stages: [manual]

pre-commit run --hook-stage manual ash-full-scan --all-files

Run ASH in a container covers container mode.

docs.title: Read scan results
docs.text: A scan that runs to the end prints a summary table and writes its results to an output directory. This page shows where the results go, how to read the table, and which file to open for each task. Output files describes every file in detail.

docs.title: Where results land
docs.text:
ASH writes to .ash/ash_output under the directory it scans. Run from your project root, that is .ash/ash_output in the current directory:

ash --scanners detect-secrets --no-progress

ls .ash/ash_output

analysis
ash-ignore-report.txt
ash-scan-set-files-list.txt
ash.log
ash_aggregated_results.json
converted
reports
scanners

With --source-dir, the default moves with it: ash --source-dir ../service writes to ../service/.ash/ash_output. To write somewhere else, pass --output-dir, or set ASH_OUTPUT_DIR. If you give the source directory itself as the output directory, ASH writes to .ash/ash_output inside it instead.

ash --scanners detect-secrets --no-progress --output-dir build/ash-results

Things to know about the output directory:

  • Each scan replaces the previous results. ASH empties reports/, scanners/, converted/, and analysis/, and removes the top-level results files, before it writes. Copy anything you want to keep. In local mode it does this only once it has accepted the command line and the configuration, so a scan refused with exit 5 or 3 leaves the earlier results in place (Output files).
  • The default location is inside the scanned tree. Keep it out of version control: ash config init writes a .ash/.gitignore that ignores ash_output*.
  • ASH refuses an output directory that is itself a symbolic link or a Windows junction, that is reached through one below the scanned directory (such as a linked .ash), or that has one at reports/, scanners/, converted/, analysis/, or a file ASH writes there, such as ash.log. The scan stops with exit code 3 before it writes anything. See Output files.
  • Reports contain source text. ASH masks secrets in finding messages, but the code snippets attached to findings are copied as they are, secrets included. Treat the output directory like the code it came from.

docs.title: Read the summary table
docs.text:
After the scan, ASH prints one row per scanner. This scan of a small project ran with --scanners bandit,cdk-nag,detect-secrets,grype on a machine without grype: bandit found an actionable finding, grype's tool was missing, cdk-nag had no CloudFormation template to read, and semgrep was not selected (trimmed to four rows):

                                                 ASH Scan Results Summary
┏━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━┳━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
