┃ Scanner        ┃ Suppressed ┃ Critical ┃ High ┃ Medium ┃ Low ┃ Info ┃ Duration ┃ Actionable ┃ Result  ┃ Threshold       ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━╇━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ bandit         │ 0          │ 0        │ 1    │ 0      │ 2   │ 0    │ 889ms    │ 1          │ FAILED  │ MEDIUM (global) │
│ cdk-nag        │ 0          │ 0        │ 0    │ 0      │ 0   │ 0    │ <1ms     │ 0          │ SKIPPED │ MEDIUM (global) │
│ grype          │ 0          │ 0        │ 0    │ 0      │ 0   │ 0    │ <1ms     │ 0          │ MISSING │ MEDIUM (global) │
│ semgrep        │ 0          │ 0        │ 0    │ 0      │ 0   │ 0    │ <1ms     │ 0          │ SKIPPED │ MEDIUM (global) │
└────────────────┴────────────┴──────────┴──────┴────────┴─────┴──────┴──────────┴────────────┴─────────┴─────────────────┘
                                                      source-dir: '.'
                                               output-dir: '.ash/ash_output'

Scan incomplete: grype (MISSING)

When the terminal is narrower than 100 columns, or the output is not a terminal (as when you redirect it to a file), the headers are shortened to S, C, H, M, L, I, Time, Action, Result, and Thresh, and the threshold reads MED (g).

Column Meaning Suppressed Findings a suppression matched. They are not in the severity columns and never count as actionable. Critical to Info Unsuppressed findings at each severity (see How ASH counts findings). Duration How long the scanner ran. Actionable Unsuppressed findings at or above the scanner's threshold. These decide whether the scan fails. Result The scanner's status, below. Threshold The threshold and where it came from: global is global_settings.severity_threshold (default MEDIUM), config is the scanner's own scanners.<name>.options.severity_threshold.

The Result column has five values. A row takes the first one that applies, in this order: ERROR; FAILED; SKIPPED because the scanner was not selected or its platform is not supported; MISSING; SKIPPED because it had nothing to read; PASSED.

Result What happened What to do ERROR The scanner produced no usable result for a target: its tool failed, or never started as asked, recorded with the start-failure code 127 (a sandbox the configuration asks for that ASH cannot provide, for example). One good target does not outweigh another, so the row is ERROR when any target failed or was never evaluated. On Linux and macOS, a tool ended by a signal ASH did not send, such as an out-of-memory kill, is ERROR whatever exit codes the scanner accepts, with an error that names the signal and an exit code of 128 plus the signal's number. How a sandbox backend's own exit code is read back is the note under the table. Read the error in the scan output or in ash.log; the full record is in scanners/<name>/source/ASH.ScanResults.json. FAILED The scanner ran and reported at least one actionable finding. It says nothing about the tool crashing. Fix or suppress the findings. SKIPPED (not selected) The scanner was not selected (--scanners, --exclude-scanners, enabled: false, or --python-only), or its platform is not supported. Nothing, unless you expected it to run. MISSING The scanner never ran: its tool was not found, or was found only inside the scanned directory. Install the tool (ash dependencies install), or see Troubleshoot. SKIPPED (nothing to read) The scanner had nothing to read, such as cdk-nag with no CloudFormation template, npm-audit with no lockfile beside a package.json, or actionlint with no workflows. These are SKIPPED whether or not their tools are installed. Nothing, unless you expected it to find files. PASSED The scanner ran and nothing reached its threshold. Findings below the threshold still show in the severity columns. Nothing.

Under a sandbox backend that reports a signal death as its own exit (bwrap and firejail; ASH knows which backends report this way), a scanner exit of 128+N is read back as a likely death by signal N: the scanner's row is ERROR with a reason that says 'likely' and names the exit code it came from, and the run's exit reflects it. This is an inference from the shell convention. A scanner that declares its tool's exit code a count of findings (cfn_nag) opts out, and such an exit grades by the findings the tool rendered; a native signal death still reads as one for every scanner. Unsandboxed runs and backends without the behavior keep such an exit as the tool's own answer.

The read-back takes only exits 129 through 192 (N of 1 to 64); 128, 255 and codes above the range stay the tool's own answer. Its fail-closed direction is deliberate: a tool that itself exits with such a code under such a backend reads as a signal death, which errs toward never reporting a killed scan as passed. The count opt-out trades that direction away for its scanner: under such a backend a count-declaring scanner's death by signal arrives only as the backend's own 128+N exit, indistinguishable by the exit code alone from a count, so it grades by the findings the tool rendered.

Lines under the table add what the status cannot say: Incomplete coverage names a scanner that could not read some of its inputs, Scan incomplete lists the scanners that did not finish, and a stale content database is reported there too.

The exit code follows the table. By default an ERROR or MISSING row, a scan where every scanner was SKIPPED, including one in which no selected scanner had a file to scan, or a file a converter could not convert makes the scan exit 1, and an actionable finding makes it exit 2. Set the gate changes these rules, and Exit codes lists them all.

The Markdown, text, and HTML reports carry the same table, and ash.flat.json has the same counts under scanner_metrics.

docs.title: How ASH counts findings
docs.text:
The counts come from the aggregated SARIF after suppressions are applied, so the table, the reports, and the exit code agree on which findings are actionable.

A finding counts as suppressed when its SARIF result carries a suppression: one ASH applied from a global_settings.suppressions entry or an inline ash-ignore comment, or one the scanner recorded itself. A finding under global_settings.ignore_paths is removed, not counted. See Suppress findings.

ASH gives each unsuppressed finding one severity, from the first of these that exists:

  1. The severity the scanner integration assigned (the result's issue_severity property: CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, or INFO).
  2. The rule's CVSS base score (its security-severity property): 9 or more is critical, 7 or more high, 4 or more medium, above 0 low. A score of 0, or one that is not a number from 0 to 10, counts as no score.
  3. The SARIF level: error is critical, warning medium, note low, and none info. A result that states no level takes none when its kind is not fail, else its rule's defaultConfiguration.level, else warning. A level that is not one of the four also counts as warning.

So a rule's CVSS score wins over the scanner's level, in either direction: an error advisory with a score of 5.0 counts as medium.

A finding is actionable when its severity is at or above the threshold; Severity thresholds lists the severities each threshold includes.

The table, the exit code, ash inspect findings, and every report except ash.ghas.sarif give a finding this same severity. Formats with a scale of their own carry it in that scale: GitLab SAST as Critical to Info, and OCSF as severity_id 5 to 1.

ash.ghas.sarif gives each rule one security-severity score, which GitHub code scanning reads as the severity of that rule's alerts. The score is the first of these that exists:

  1. The score the rule's scanner gives it, unchanged.
  2. The score for the most severe of the rule's findings, suppressed findings included, from the table below. A finding's severity here is its issue_severity, else its SARIF level, as in the list above.
  3. The score for the rule's defaultConfiguration.level, read the same way.
  4. 6.0.
ASH severity security-severity GitHub shows CRITICAL 9.5 Critical HIGH 8.0 High MEDIUM 6.0 Medium LOW 3.0 Low INFO 1.0 Low

So every alert from one rule shows the same severity, and a rule that its scanner scores can show a severity other than ASH's: a finding with issue_severity HIGH under a rule scored 5.0 is high for ASH and medium on GitHub. GitHub reads a score of 0.0, or one outside 0.1 to 10.0, as no security severity.

ASH does not merge findings across scanners. When two scanners report the same issue, such as grype and trivy finding one vulnerable package, it is counted twice. See How ASH works.

docs.title: Pick the file to open
docs.text:
All paths are relative to the output directory.

To Open Read the findings in a browser reports/ash.html Paste a summary into a pull request reports/ash.summary.md (--compact-report shortens it) Read a plain-text summary reports/ash.summary.txt Upload to GitHub code scanning or another SARIF tool reports/ash.ghas.sarif or reports/ash.sarif; see Export reports Open the findings in a spreadsheet reports/ash.csv Process the results in a script ash_aggregated_results.json, or reports/ash.flat.json for one record per finding Find out why a scanner is ERROR or MISSING the scan output, ash.log, and scanners/<name>/source/ASH.ScanResults.json See a scanner's own output scanners/<name>/source/ Check which files were selected for scanning ash-scan-set-files-list.txt, and ash-ignore-report.txt for the ignore rules Clean up stale suppressions reports/ash.unused-suppressions.md

In ash_aggregated_results.json, a scanner's row says why it did not run. missing_reason on a MISSING row gives the reason: the tool that was not found and where ASH looked, what the scanner's own check reported (semgrep offline with no rule cache, for example), or that the tool was found only inside the scanned directory. skipped_reason on a SKIPPED row names the option that left the scanner out, or what it had nothing to scan, as in no CloudFormation template in the scanned files. The row's exit_code is the tool's exit code, the highest over its targets, the start-failure code 127 for a tool that could not start as asked, or null when no tool ran.

To read the results from a script:

import json
from pathlib import Path

results = json.loads(
    Path(".ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
)
for name, row in sorted(results["scanner_results"].items()):
    if row["status"] != "SKIPPED":
        print(name, row["status"], row["actionable_finding_count"])

detect-secrets FAILED 1

docs.title: Print a report in the terminal with ash report
docs.text:
ash report renders a report of the last scan and prints it to standard output. It reads ash_aggregated_results.json only from .ash/ash_output under the current directory, and does not write a report file:

ash report

The default format is markdown. --format takes any reporter name, including reporters a scan does not run by default, such as yaml:

ash report --format text

To read another output directory, pass --output-dir, or set ASH_OUTPUT_DIR. ASH looks for the results file in .ash/ash_output and ash_output under that directory, and in the directory itself, and reports on the one it finds:

ash report --output-dir build/ash-results --format sarif > build/ash-report.sarif

When more than one of the three holds a results file, ASH prints More than one scan results file found: with each path, reports on none, and exits 5. Point --output-dir at the directory that holds the one to report on.

ash report writes its log to standard error, so standard output holds the report alone. To get the report exactly as the reporter wrote it, command lines included, redirect standard output to a file, as in the command above: ASH then writes the reporter's output unchanged, so the command above writes a SARIF file.

On a pipe, ASH changes every line of the report that a CI system (GitHub Actions, Azure Pipelines, or TeamCity) would read as a command, so that none of them runs, whether or not a CI variable is set. A JSON report has the # of a ##name[ form written as JSON's own escape for it, so it parses to the same document. On a terminal it changes those lines when GITHUB_ACTIONS, TF_BUILD, or TEAMCITY_VERSION is set. Apart from that, the output on a pipe is the reporter's output as the reporter wrote it, not wrapped or styled. On a terminal with color, JSON is indented and Markdown is rendered. On a terminal, with or without color, no character a terminal acts on is written as it is: it is shown as an escape, such as \x1b for an escape character in a file name, or in a JSON report as JSON's own escape, such as \u001b. Rendered Markdown leaves such characters out. ASH's own messages, such as a refusal that quotes a path, have their CI command lines changed the same way even when they go to a file; only the report itself is written to a file as is.

A missing results file prints No scan results found: with the paths it checked, and exits 5. With --output-dir or ASH_OUTPUT_DIR the message names the three paths ASH looked in (none of … exists); otherwise it names .ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json under the current directory, in full (… does not exist). ash report creates nothing then, and an output directory under a directory it cannot search counts as missing. An output directory that exists but cannot be entered is refused with exit 5, Output directory cannot be entered: and the path as given. So is an output directory that is a file, Output directory is not a directory:, and a path the system cannot look up, such as one holding a NUL character, Output directory is not a valid path:. None of these refusals creates anything. An unknown format is refused before the results are read: ASH prints Error: Reporter plugin '<name>' not found. and the reporter names, and exits 5.

ash report --format nosuch

The reporters are listed in Reporters.

docs.title: Explore findings with ash inspect findings
docs.text:
ash inspect findings opens an interactive browser of the findings in the terminal. It reads ash_aggregated_results.json from .ash/ash_output, or from --output-dir:

ash inspect findings --output-dir build/ash-results
Press To j, k Move to the next or previous finding v Show the selected finding, with its code snippet when the scanner gave one s or / Search; Escape leaves the search f Show or hide the filters h Show or hide suppressed findings (hidden at start) x Suppress the selected finding q Quit

The Severity column uses the same severity as the summary table (see How ASH counts findings).

x asks for a reason and an optional expiration date, then adds a suppression for that rule, file, and line to a config file: the one --config or ASH_CONFIG names, else the config file a scan of the current directory would use, else .ashrc.yaml in the current directory. It writes YAML, or JSON to a .json file. It refuses a TOML file, and a file that extends another and has no suppressions list of its own, because writing one there would replace the base file's list. If the file already has the same suppression, x writes nothing; one that differs, such as another line range for the same rule and file, is added. The suppression applies from the next scan. See Suppress findings before you suppress from here.

docs.title: Check which SARIF fields survive with ash inspect sarif-fields
docs.text:
ash inspect sarif-fields is for plugin authors and for debugging a scanner integration. It reads every scanner's own SARIF under scanners/ and the reports' SARIF under reports/, and shows which fields each scanner fills in and whether they reach the aggregated report:

ash inspect sarif-fields --sarif-dir .ash/ash_output --output-dir build/sarif-fields

It prints a summary and writes sarif_fields.json, sarif_fields.csv, sarif_excluded_fields.json, sarif_excluded_fields.csv, and sarif_validation_report.html to the output directory, which defaults to .ash/ash_output/inspect under the current directory. It exits 1 when it finds no SARIF files.

ash scan --inspect runs the same analysis at the end of a scan, on that scan's output directory, and writes the files to its analysis/ directory.

docs.title: Run ASH in a container
docs.text:
Container mode runs the scan inside ASH's container image, which carries every scanner tool, so the host needs ASH and a container runtime and nothing else. ASH publishes no prebuilt image: the first container-mode scan on a machine builds one, and later scans reuse it.

Prerequisites:

  • ASH installed on the host (Install ASH).
  • One of finch, docker, nerdctl, or podman on PATH.
  • Network access while the image builds. The build pulls the Python base image from Amazon ECR Public, clones ASH from GitHub unless it builds a local source tree, and downloads the scanner tools.

docs.title: Scan in container mode
docs.text:
Run container-mode scans from a directory that is not the repository you scan and holds no Dockerfile of its own. Name the repository with --source-dir, and keep the source and the output in separate directory trees:

cd ~/work
ash scan --mode container --source-dir src/my-app --output-dir ash-output/my-app

ASH builds the image (several minutes the first time; later builds reuse the layer cache), runs the scan inside it, reads the results back from the output directory, and exits with the same exit codes as a local scan. A container that fails to start, and a build that fails, exit with the runtime's own status instead.

These ash scan options control the image:

Option Effect --no-build Run the existing image instead of building it. --force Rebuild without the layer cache. --no-run Build the image and stop. --build-target ci Build the root image instead of the non-root one.

ash build-image builds the image and then scans the current directory with it, writing to .ash/ash_output there. Add --no-run to build only. It takes no --source-dir, --output-dir, or other scan option: an argument its help does not list stops it with exit code 5 before anything is built, so use ash scan --mode container to choose the directories. Every option of both commands is in the CLI reference.

Spell options out in full: the short flags differ between the two commands. On ash scan, -o is --oci-runner and -r is --run; on ash build-image, -r is --oci-runner.

docs.title: Choose the container runtime
docs.text:
ASH uses the first of finch, docker, nerdctl, and podman that it finds on PATH. To pick one, pass --oci-runner podman or set OCI_RUNNER=podman. To prefix every runtime call with another command, such as sudo, set OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER=sudo.

Each of these takes a command name or an absolute path, and so does the oci_runner of a --cli-json-input document, which ASH reads as if you had typed it as --oci-runner. A ~ or ~user at the start is expanded, so ~/bin/docker names $HOME/bin/docker; in OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER that applies to the first word. A $ in the document's value is not expanded, so $HOME/bin/docker there is a relative path. With no usable home directory (HOME empty or relative, or unset with no absolute home in the passwd entry), a value that starts with ~/ is not used: ASH logs a warning about HOME and picks a runtime as if none were named, or, for the wrapper, starts the runtime without one. A relative path with a directory part, such as bin/docker, is read against the directory you run ASH in when you pass it to --oci-runner or give it in the document. In OCI_RUNNER it is not run: ASH logs a warning and picks a runtime as if none were named. As the first word of OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER it is not used either, and the runtime starts without a wrapper, with a warning.

docs.title: Root and non-root images
docs.text:
The Dockerfile has two final stages:

  • non-root, the default, runs as ash-user. ash build-image and container-mode scans give that user the UID and GID of the user running ASH, so the scan can write to the mounted output directory. Pass --container-uid and --container-gid to choose other values.
  • ci runs as root.

--build-target chooses the stage (-BuildTarget for Invoke-ASH). Without it, ASH builds non-root, or ci on Windows, where the non-root user cannot write the mounted output directory. --custom-containerfile always builds on ci. The CI variables CI, IsCI, ISCI, and CODEBUILD_BUILD_ID do not change the stage.

The non-root user cannot have UID 0 or GID 0, which are root's. A non-root build that would give it either stops with exit code 3 before anything is built. That happens when ASH runs as root, as it does in many CI jobs, such as AWS CodeBuild and container-based GitLab and Jenkins jobs, and when you pass --container-uid 0 or --container-gid 0. Pass --build-target ci there to build the image that runs as root. Other --container-uid and --container-gid values work only when that user can write the output directory.

The image is tagged automated-security-helper:non-root or automated-security-helper:ci. Set ASH_IMAGE_NAME to build and run an image under another name.

docs.title: Which ASH goes into the image
docs.text:
The image installs ASH from source, chosen from how ASH was installed on the host:

Host install Source of the image From a git URL with a tag, such as @v3.7.0 That tag, cloned from GitHub when the image builds. From a git URL with a branch, such as @main The tip of that branch when the image builds, which can differ from the commit installed on the host. From a git URL with no ref The installed commit, fetched from GitHub by its commit ID. A clone of the ASH repository, an editable install of one, or pip install <directory> That source tree, built with its own Dockerfile, so the image holds the same ASH as the host. Any other install, such as Homebrew, a wheel or sdist file, or an archive URL The commit the package was built from, fetched by its commit ID. A package built outside a git checkout of ASH, such as from a source tarball, records no commit: the image then installs the release tag of the installed version, such as v3.7.0, and ASH logs a warning that this is a guess. A development or pre-release version has no release tag, so the build stops before it starts and asks for --ash-revision-to-install.

--ash-revision-to-install overrides the table with a tag, a branch, or a full 40-character commit ID. It accepts letters, digits, dots, hyphens, underscores, and slashes. Run from the top directory of a checkout of ASH, ash build-image and container-mode scans build that checkout whatever the revision says; to build another revision, run them from another directory.

A branch, or the floating v3 tag, is cloned again on every build, because it can have moved since the last one. A release tag or a commit ID is cloned once, and later builds take that clone from the build cache.

docs.title: Mounts and network
docs.text:
The container sees two host directories: the source directory at /src and the output directory at /out. Keep the two in separate directory trees, such as ~/work/src/my-app and ~/work/ash-output/my-app, as in the example above; ASH then mounts the source read-only. The default output directory, .ash/ash_output, is inside the scanned directory.

Every path ASH mounts has to be UTF-8: the source and output directories, the config file and each file it extends, the file ASH_CONFIG names and each file it extends, and a workspace policy. A path holding a byte that is not UTF-8 stops the scan with exit code 3 before the container runtime runs. The error names the path with each such byte written as \udcNN, as in caf\udce9. A scan of one directory is refused before it creates the output directory, and the previous run's ash.log is left as it was. ./ash refuses the same source directory, output directory, and config file, with the same exit code.

A source or output directory that a local scan refuses, such as a source directory that does not exist or an output directory that cannot be created, stops ash scan --mode container with exit code 5, also with --no-run, and with the line a local scan prints (Exit codes). ./ash refuses them as well: it prints the line after ERROR: and exits 5.

An output directory that is a symlink, or that a symlink below the source directory leads to, such as a committed .ash link for the default .ash/ash_output, stops ash scan --mode container and ash build-image with exit code 3 (Exit codes), because the scan inside the container would write wherever the link points. The refusal comes before a container runtime is looked up, with --no-run too, so nothing is built, created, or mounted. ./ash and Invoke-ASH refuse the same output directory.

Inside the container ASH runs a local-mode scan of /src. Some things do not carry over:

  • Environment variables. The container gets only the variables ASH sets for it and the ones the operator's config files read (The config file), so AWS credentials and other settings in the host environment are not passed in, and neither are the host's AWS credential files.
  • The scanner sandbox. Container mode never sandboxes the scanners inside the image; the container is the boundary (The scanner sandbox).
  • --changed-files-only. The scan stops with exit code 5 before anything is built or run, also when ASH_CHANGED_FILES_ONLY sets it. Scan with --mode local to report only the findings in changed files.
  • Third-party plugin modules. --ash-plugin-modules is passed in, but only modules installed in the image load. Add packages with --custom-containerfile.

--ignore-suppressions reaches the scan inside and works there as in a local scan: it lifts suppressions and ignore paths for every scanner, and ASH's own output directory stays out of the results (See every finding).

The container uses the runtime's default bridge network. --offline runs it with no network and builds an offline image (Run ASH offline). ash build-image --container-network takes another network mode, such as none or a named network.

docs.title: The config file
docs.text:
--config names the config file, or ASH_CONFIG when no --config is given. With neither, the scan inside the container finds the repository's own config file under /src the way a local scan does. ASH checks a file you name on the host before it builds or runs anything, in ash scan --mode container, ash --mode container, ./ash, and Invoke-ASH. A path that names no file stops the scan with exit code 3:

ash scan --mode container --config missing.yaml

Config file not found: missing.yaml. ...

A file ASH cannot read stops it the same way. With --no-run nothing is scanned, and the config is not checked.

Beside a --config, the file ASH_CONFIG names is still the trusted base, as in a local scan: ASH reads it first, and when the config is a repository's, takes from it the settings a repository may not choose (Configuration trust model). ash scan --mode container and ash --mode container mount that file, and each file it extends, read-only under /ash-env-config, and the scan inside reads it as its ASH_CONFIG. A file of that chain the host counts as written by a repository is marked for the scan inside, file by file. An ASH_CONFIG file that is missing, cannot be read, does not parse, or is not a valid config stops the scan with exit code 3 on the host, before anything is built, run, mounted, or cleared, even when --config names a valid file.

A relative path is taken from the directory you run ASH in, not from --source-dir. The scan inside is given the file's path in the container:

  • A file inside --source-dir is read through the source mount, at /src/<path>, and so is every file it extends, which has to be inside --source-dir too, as in a local scan.
  • Any other file is mounted read-only under /ash-config: ~/ash/ash.yaml is /ash-config/ash.yaml. Container mode also mounts each file of its extends chain, at its place relative to the config, and no other file. ./ash and Invoke-ASH mount the config alone, so they refuse a config outside the source directory that has an extends entry, with exit code 3.

ASH refuses these with exit code 3 before anything runs, because each would let the repository being scanned choose a host file to mount:

  • A config named inside the scanned tree, the outermost git checkout at or above --source-dir, that is a symbolic link, or is reached through one, to a file outside that tree. A link that stays inside the tree is followed.
  • A config outside --source-dir whose extends chain includes a file inside --source-dir, or in which a file of the scanned checkout extends a file outside that checkout.
  • In workspace mode, a workspace policy (ash-workspace.yaml or --workspace-config) that is a symbolic link, or is reached through one, out of the workspace's tree. A policy outside the workspace root is mounted read-only under /ash-workspace-config.

ash scan --mode container and ash --mode container also refuse, with exit code 3, a chain they cannot place in the container where the host reads it, such as an extends entry that names its base by an absolute path. Write each base relative to the file that extends it.

A config the host counts as written by a repository, one inside any git checkout or inside --source-dir, keeps a repository config's limits inside the container, so the host and the container give the same file the same tier (Configuration trust model). A file under /src is in the scanned directory there. For a file mounted from a git checkout, ASH tells the scan inside that a repository wrote it. It marks each file of the chain on its own, so a config outside every checkout that extends a base in a git checkout keeps its own settings, as on the host, and the scan inside drops the same settings with the same warnings as a local scan.

A workspace scan does the same with a --config from another git checkout, such as an operations repository beside the workspace. The workspace scan inside limits that file, and every file it extends, for every project and for the plan, with the same settings dropped and the same warnings as a workspace scan in local mode. A --config outside every checkout is the operator's. A --config in the workspace's tree, the git checkout around the workspace root, or the workspace root itself when it is in no checkout, is refused with exit code 3 before anything is built or mounted, as in a local workspace scan (Scan a multi-project workspace). That covers a file inside the workspace root, a file in the checkout outside the root, and a path that is a link, or is reached through one, into that tree or out of it. The error names each file, says to move the config and every base it extends outside the checkout, or outside the workspace root when it is in no checkout, and ends To keep a setting, move the file outside every git checkout, or pass the setting with --config-overrides. A file inside the scanned directory has to move out of it as well.

The scan inside the container reads the host's environment only for the variables the operator's own config files read. Those files are the --config file and the file ASH_CONFIG names, with the files each extends, when they are outside the scanned directory and every git checkout. A --config inside one of those makes every file it extends the repository's too, while the files of the ASH_CONFIG file's chain are judged one by one. ASH passes in each variable such a file reads (Read values from the environment) that is set on the host. It passes each one by name, so the value is not on the runner's command line. Through OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER, it writes the values to an env file that only you can read, in a new directory outside the scanned and output directories, passes the file with the runtime's own env-file option, and removes it when the run ends, also after an error, Ctrl-C, or SIGTERM. A variable that a config in the scanned directory or in a git checkout reads is not passed in, so the scan inside reads that file as though the variable were not set.

A config file that reads a variable ASH sets in the container, or reads as one of its own settings, such as ASH_DEBUG or ASH_BIN_PATH, stops the scan with exit code 3 before anything is built or run, when that variable is set. The error names the file, the variable, and the field, and says to write the value in the file or pass it with --config-overrides. Through OCI_RUNNER_WRAPPER, the scan also stops with exit code 3, before the container runs, when the runner is not docker, finch, nerdctl, or podman, when a value holds a line break or a NUL, or when the temporary directory is inside the scanned or output directory. None of these errors prints a value.

docs.title: The scanner sandbox
docs.text:
Container mode never sandboxes the scanners inside the image: the container is the boundary, and every scanner in it shares the container's access. So --sandbox with any mode but off stops the scan with exit code 5 before anything is built or run:

ash scan --mode container --sandbox bwrap

--sandbox bwrap cannot be used with --mode container: ...

To sandbox each scanner, scan with --mode local --sandbox <mode>. ./ash refuses --sandbox the same way, and Invoke-ASH sets $LASTEXITCODE to 5 and throws.

A sandbox.mode from a config file or --config-overrides is not refused, so one config file serves local and container scans. The scan inside the container gets sandbox.mode=off as its last override, and ash scan --mode container logs a warning that names the mode, such as The scanner sandbox (bwrap, from sandbox.mode in a config file, --config-overrides or the operator's config) is not applied in container mode. The mode can come from --config-overrides, the config file, a workspace project's config, or a trusted config whose mode applies under a repository's own: an operator --config under a workspace project's config, or ASH_CONFIG under an in-tree --config. When the host cannot resolve the config, ASH still warns about a mode that --config-overrides or the operator's config asks for. With no sandbox asked for, or with --no-run, it logs no warning. ./ash and Invoke-ASH also give the scan inside sandbox.mode=off as its last override, and log no warning about it.

docs.title: Build and host your own image
docs.text:
Build the image once, push it to a registry your organization controls, and run that image in CI instead of building per run. With ASH_IMAGE_NAME set, ash build-image tags the image with your registry's name:

export ASH_IMAGE_NAME=registry.example.com/security/ash:3.7.0
ash build-image --no-run --oci-runner docker --ash-revision-to-install v3.7.0 \
  --container-uid 1001 --container-gid 1001
docker push "$ASH_IMAGE_NAME"

Set the UID and GID to the user your CI jobs run as. Hosts that have ASH_IMAGE_NAME set run that image with ash scan --mode container --no-build, and the runtime pulls it when it is not present.

To build without ASH installed, build the Dockerfile from a clone. The clone is the build context, so the image contains exactly the ref it cloned:

git clone --depth 1 --branch v3.7.0 https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git
cd automated-security-helper
docker build --target non-root --build-arg UID=1001 --build-arg GID=1001 \
  --tag registry.example.com/security/ash:3.7.0 .

Build arguments:

Argument Default Effect BASE_IMAGE public.ecr.aws/docker/library/python:3.12-slim-bookworm Base image for every stage. Point it at a mirror of the same image. INSTALL_ASH_REVISION LOCAL LOCAL builds the build context. Any other value is a tag or branch cloned from GitHub, or a full commit ID fetched from it, unless the build context is ASH's own source tree, which is then built instead. OFFLINE NO YES downloads the grype and trivy databases and the semgrep and opengrep rulesets into the image, and makes every scan in it offline. BUILD_DATE_EPOCH -1 A new value makes an offline build download the databases and rulesets again; with the same value, that step comes from the build cache. ASH passes UTC midnight of the current day, in epoch seconds, for offline builds. OFFLINE_SEMGREP_RULESETS p/ci Space-separated semgrep registry rulesets an offline image downloads. UID, GID 500, 100 UID and GID of the non-root user.

Scanner tool versions are pinned in tool_downloads.py, and the build checks each tool against its pin.

To add tools, write a Dockerfile that builds on the ASH image and pass it with --custom-containerfile; ASH passes the base image's name to that build as a build argument, named in the option's help. ASH then builds its base image from the root ci target and tags the result automated-security-helper:custom. The final image runs as root unless your Dockerfile sets another user, so secure it yourself.

To run your image in CI with your own configuration, run ASH inside it in local mode and mount the files it needs. Roll out ASH across repositories shows the full setup.

Rebuild on a schedule. The image holds the scanner tools and, for an offline image, the vulnerability databases, so it ages; see Run ASH offline. A rebuild whose inputs did not change comes from the build cache, so pass --force, which rebuilds every layer, to install current scanner tools. Without --force, an offline build downloads current databases and rulesets once per UTC day; with --force, on every build. The same holds for ./ash --offline and Invoke-ASH -Offline.

docs.title: Third-party license files
docs.text:
The image carries license and notice files for these third-party components, taken from the release it carries, in /usr/share/doc/ash/third-party/<tool>/: actionlint, cfn-guard and the AWS Guard Rules Registry rules it reads, gitleaks, grype, opengrep, syft, trivy, and uv; and the scanners installed from PyPI, bandit, checkov, cfn-lint, semgrep, and zizmor.

Beside each program's files, a SOURCE file names the upstream repository, release tag, and commit. For the copyleft components, opengrep and semgrep (LGPL-2.1-only), SOURCE also gives the git commands that check out the corresponding source. index.json in /usr/share/doc/ash/third-party lists each of these components with its version, license, repository, commit, and files. The build writes it only after checking each entry against the built image.

Other Python packages in the image, such as the scanners' dependencies and nbconvert, keep their license files in their .dist-info directories, and Debian packages keep theirs in /usr/share/doc/<package>/. cfn-nag and the Ruby gems it depends on, and the yarn and pnpm that corepack prepares, have no entry in this directory. The licenses of libraries built into the bundled programs, such as the modules statically linked into the Go and Rust programs, are not reproduced.

docs.title: Windows and macOS
docs.text:
ASH's own CI tests container mode on Linux only, with docker, podman, finch, and nerdctl.

  • On Windows, ash build-image always builds the root ci image, because the non-root user cannot write to the bind-mounted output directory there. ash scan --mode container does not force it. If ash runs a different program, such as the ash shell that ships with Git for Windows, run ashv3, which is the same command.
  • On macOS, the image builds for the host's architecture; the Dockerfile supports amd64 and arm64.

docs.title: Run ASH offline
docs.text: In offline mode ASH installs nothing and runs every scanner in its offline mode, apart from npm-audit, which cannot run offline. Scanners that need vulnerability data read it from a local cache, and ASH fails the scan when a cache is past its age bound: a clean result from a stale database is not evidence of a clean target. Offline mode does not remove the network itself, and detect-secrets can still make requests (see What each scanner does offline); only the sandbox, or container mode with --offline, takes the network away. Content databases explains the bounds; this page is about preparing for them.

docs.title: Turn on offline mode
docs.text:
Pass --offline to a scan:

ash scan --offline --scanners detect-secrets

This scan runs offline as usual; in a repository with a hardcoded password it exits 2. The log also shows a warning for each scanner whose offline cache is not set up, such as Grype offline mode: GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR not set.

The other ways to turn it on:

How Scope ASH_OFFLINE=YES (also TRUE or 1) in the environment Every ASH run that inherits it. --offline in local mode sets it for one scan and restores it afterward. ash scan --mode container --offline Builds an offline image and runs it with no network. See the offline image. --mode nix Always offline. scanners.<name>.options.offline: true That scanner only. false, the default, follows ASH and cannot give a scanner network while ASH is offline. npm-audit's option does not run it offline: it makes npm-audit MISSING, or SKIPPED in a project without a lockfile, as below.

There is no config key for offline mode. build.build_mode exists in the config schema but has no effect.

docs.title: What each scanner does offline
docs.text:
Scanner Offline behavior grype Reads its cached database with updates and grype's own age check off. ASH fails the scan when the database is past its age bound (Refresh cadence). trivy, trivy-repo Read the cached trivy database with its updates off. ASH fails the scan when the database is past its age bound, except in the offline image, where it warns (Refresh cadence). With no database, trivy is MISSING. Every trivy scan gets trivy --offline-scan and trivy --skip-version-check, so trivy contacts no package registry and does not check for a newer release. semgrep, opengrep Run the rulesets in SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR or OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR plus ASH's bundled rules, instead of the configured registry rulesets. MISSING when the directory is unset or empty. ASH fails the scan when the rulesets are past their age bound. detect-secrets Runs as usual. If its settings turn on detect-secrets' verification filter, it still sends each candidate secret to the service that issued it, to check whether it is live; under the sandbox, leave detect-secrets out of sandbox.network_scanners to stop that. checkov Uses the policies in the installed package and skips platform downloads. npm-audit Does not run: npm, yarn, and pnpm audit a lockfile by asking the registry. MISSING for a project with a package-lock.json, npm-shrinkwrap.json, yarn.lock, or pnpm-lock.yaml beside a package.json, which fails the scan, and SKIPPED for a project with none. syft Skips its update check. zizmor Runs offline, as it does by default. snyk-code Does not run. bandit, cdk-nag, cfn-nag, cfn-lint, cfn-guard, actionlint, gitleaks No change, once installed.

Offline, ASH also skips every tool install. A scanner whose tool is not already on the machine is MISSING, and a MISSING scanner fails the scan by default.

An offline scan of a project with a lockfile reports npm-audit MISSING and exits 1:

mkdir -p js-app
printf '{"name": "js-app", "version": "1.0.0"}\n' > js-app/package.json
printf '{"name": "js-app", "version": "1.0.0", "lockfileVersion": 3, "packages": {}}\n' > js-app/package-lock.json
ash scan --offline --scanners npm-audit --source-dir js-app --output-dir js-app-results

To scan such a project offline, leave npm-audit out with --exclude-scanners npm-audit.

docs.title: Prepare a host for offline scans
docs.text:
Do this while the host still has network access:

  1. Install the scanner tools with ash dependencies install. It puts grype and trivy in ~/.ash/bin (or the directory ASH_BIN_PATH names), which ASH searches but which is not on your PATH.

  2. Download each database into the cache the scan will read. Set the cache variables the same way for the download and for every scan; when they are unset, grype and trivy use their platform defaults (for example ~/.cache/grype/db and ~/.cache/trivy on Linux):

    export GRYPE_DB_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/ash-cache/grype" TRIVY_CACHE_DIR="$HOME/ash-cache/trivy"
"${ASH_BIN_PATH:-$HOME/.ash/bin}/grype" db update
"${ASH_BIN_PATH:-$HOME/.ash/bin}/trivy" image --download-db-only --cache-dir "$TRIVY_CACHE_DIR"

  3. For semgrep and opengrep, download the rulesets into SEMGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR and OPENGREP_RULES_CACHE_DIR and record the download time, as described in Seeding the semgrep and opengrep rule cache. Without a recorded time, ASH takes the age of the oldest rules file.

If you also run scanners in the sandbox (Enable the scanner sandbox), semgrep and opengrep can read only the directories the sandbox mounts. Keep the rules cache under a system directory such as /opt, or add it to sandbox.extra_read_paths in a config file outside every git checkout (Who may grant) or with --config-overrides. Then check that a sandboxed offline scan of a file with a known finding reports it.

docs.title: The offline image
docs.text:
ash build-image --offline and ash scan --mode container --offline build the image with OFFLINE=YES. The build needs network access: it downloads the grype database, the trivy database, and the semgrep rulesets named by --offline-semgrep-rulesets (default p/ci), copies the rulesets for opengrep, and fails if any of them is empty. The image has ASH_OFFLINE set, so every scan in it runs offline. npm-audit cannot run in it; see What each scanner does offline.

Without --force, an offline build downloads the databases and rulesets once per UTC day: later offline builds that day come from the build cache, and the first one on a new day downloads again and re-runs the install steps that follow the download, so it needs network access. With --force, which builds without the layer cache, every build downloads them. The same holds for ./ash --offline and Invoke-ASH -Offline. Container mode builds the image before every scan unless you pass --no-build, so on a host without network access, scan with the image you moved there:

ash scan --mode container --offline --no-build

The image has to carry the name ASH runs, automated-security-helper:<target>, or the one ASH_IMAGE_NAME names.

Offline and online builds share one tag, automated-security-helper:<target>, so building one replaces the other. Set ASH_IMAGE_NAME to keep both. --offline-semgrep-rulesets only affects the image build; it does nothing in local mode.

docs.title: Refresh cadence
docs.text:
ASH measures the grype and trivy databases from the time they were built upstream, which is before you download them, and the rulesets from the time they were downloaded:

Database Name in the config Bound Refresh grype grype-db 120 hours grype db update, or rebuild the offline image trivy trivy-db 24 hours trivy image --download-db-only, or rebuild the offline image semgrep rulesets semgrep-offline-rules 30 days Download again, or rebuild the offline image opengrep rulesets opengrep-offline-rules 30 days Download again, or rebuild the offline image

The trivy bound is the shortest. On an offline host, refresh the trivy cache more than once a day, or exclude trivy with --exclude-scanners trivy. An offline image holds trivy-db to warn by default, so its trivy scans keep passing after the first day and the reports record the stale database; rebuild the image as often as you want trivy's findings current, and more often than every 5 days for grype, whose bound also counts from before the image build. A second rebuild on the same UTC day reuses that day's databases unless you pass --force. The bounds are fixed in the code; no setting changes them. When ASH cannot read a database's age at all, it counts the database as stale.

Under fail, a stale database fails the scan with exit code 1 and a message that names the database, its build time, its age, and the bound. The findings are kept in the reports.

docs.title: Allow a stale database
docs.text:
content_db_staleness: warn lets a scan pass against a stale database and records the warning in the reports. In the offline image, trivy-db is already held to warn; set content_db_staleness_offline_image_default: false to make a stale trivy database fail the scan there too (Content databases). To relax one database for a limited time, add an entry with an expiration date and a reason:

content_db_staleness: fail
content_db_staleness_overrides:
  - database: trivy-db
    policy: warn
    expiration: "2027-06-30"
    reason: Air-gapped runners get a new image weekly until the mirror is ready.

The entry applies until 00:00 UTC on its expiration date, then ASH ignores it and logs a warning. Quote the date: an unquoted date makes the whole config invalid.

For one scan, --allow-stale-content-db sets warn and --no-allow-stale-content-db sets fail. Either form also clears every content_db_staleness_overrides entry for that scan and turns the offline image's trivy-db default off.

Who can relax the policy depends on where the setting comes from:

  • A config file inside a git checkout or the scanned directory, such as a repository's own, cannot relax it: ASH keeps content_db_staleness: warn or a policy: warn entry from such a file only when it equals yours, drops any other, and says so in a warning. It keeps a stricter fail. Relax the policy with --allow-stale-content-db, --config-overrides, or a config file outside every git checkout and the scanned directory.
  • A config file that an MCP client delivers cannot set either key under the server's default policy.

Set the gate covers the other settings that decide the exit code.

docs.title: Scale to large repositories
docs.text:
Three features help when one scan of one tree is too slow or too coarse:

  • Changed-files scans gate a pull request on the files it changed.
  • Sharding splits the scanners of one scan across several runners, and ash merge recombines the results.
  • Workspace scans scan the folders of a .code-workspace file as separate projects in one run, from the command line or over MCP.

None of them splits the files of a scan between runners. Each section ends with what the feature does not do.

docs.title: Gate on the files a change touches
docs.text:
--changed-files-only keeps only the findings in files that changed between --base-ref (default origin/main) and HEAD. The environment variables ASH_CHANGED_FILES_ONLY and ASH_BASE_REF set the same options.

These examples use a git repository whose app.py has a detect-secrets finding and whose notes.txt has none. Change only notes.txt on a branch:

git switch -c edit-notes
echo "More notes." >> notes.txt
git commit -q -am "Edit the notes"
ash scan --scanners detect-secrets --changed-files-only --base-ref main

The scan exits 0. detect-secrets still scanned app.py, and its finding was dropped because app.py is not in the change. The finding is gone from every report:

import json

for name in ("ash.sarif", "ash.ghas.sarif"):
    with open(f".ash/ash_output/reports/{name}") as report:
        runs = json.load(report)["runs"]
    print(name, sum(len(run.get("results", [])) for run in runs))

ash.sarif 0
ash.ghas.sarif 0

How the change is computed and applied:

  • The changed files are git diff --name-only <base-ref>...HEAD: files changed in commits since the merge base. Staged, modified, and untracked files that are not committed are not included. A renamed file counts under its new name. When the change moves a submodule to another commit, git diff lists only the submodule's path, and every file inside the submodule counts as changed.
  • Every scanner scans the whole tree, so the option does not make a scan faster.
  • After the scan, ASH removes the findings whose file is not in the changed set before it writes any report, so they are gone from every report, from the summary table, and from ash_aggregated_results.json, and the exit code counts only what is left. Findings with no file location are kept. Each scanner's own output under scanners/ still has them.
  • metadata.changed_files_only in ash_aggregated_results.json is true when the findings were filtered this way, and false on a full scan, including the fallback below, so a reader can tell a filtered result from a full one.
  • When the changed set is empty, every finding with a file location is discarded and the scan exits 0. If that discarded any findings, ASH logs a warning that the result is not evidence of a clean tree.

ASH falls back to reporting every finding, with a warning and the full scan's exit code, when the base ref does not exist (in a shallow clone, for example), when there is no merge base, when the directory is not in a git repository or git is not installed, and in container mode. The warning says which, such as --changed-files-only was requested but git is not installed or not on PATH. CI clones are often shallow, so fetch the base branch's history first; the Run ASH in GitHub Actions and Run ASH in GitLab CI show how.

The option is not available over MCP.

docs.title: Split a scan across runners
docs.text:
--shard-index and --shard-count (or ASH_SHARD_INDEX and ASH_SHARD_COUNT) give each runner a share of the scanners. Every runner scans the whole tree with its share; ash merge then combines the shards' results into one set of reports and one exit code.

ASH sorts the names of every registered scanner and deals them out in turn, so shard i of n gets the scanners at positions i, i + n, and so on. Counts above about four save little time: a scan is never faster than its slowest scanner, and the split balances the number of scanners, not their run time.

Split the scan in two, writing each shard's output outside the repository so that the second shard does not scan the first one's reports. The shards run with --no-fail-on-findings, as they do in CI, so each exits 0 and the merge gives the verdict:

ash scan --scanners detect-secrets --shard-index 0 --shard-count 2 --output-dir ../shard-0 --no-fail-on-findings

ash scan --scanners detect-secrets --shard-index 1 --shard-count 2 --output-dir ../shard-1 --no-fail-on-findings

--scanners narrows what a shard runs, not how the scanners are split, so detect-secrets runs only on the shard it is dealt to, and the other shard runs no scanner. Each shard records its share in metadata.shard:

import json

for index in (0, 1):
    path = f"../shard-{index}/ash_aggregated_results.json"
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as results:
        shard = json.load(results)["metadata"]["shard"]
    print(f"shard {index}:", ", ".join(shard["selected_scanners"]) or "no scanner")

shard 0: no scanner
shard 1: detect-secrets

Which shard is dealt detect-secrets depends on the scanner list of the ASH you run. Merge the shards. The merge exits 2 for the finding in app.py, whichever shard found it:

ash merge --fail-on-findings --results ../shard-0 --results ../shard-1 --output-dir ../merged

Scanners: 16 | Findings: 1 | Actionable: 1 | Suppressed: 0

--results takes a shard's ash_aggregated_results.json or its output directory, once per shard. ash merge writes ash_aggregated_results.json and every report the shards' configuration enables, including ash.ghas.sarif and ash.gl-sast-report.json, unless --output-formats, or else the output_formats setting in the shards' configuration, narrows them. It reads the fail-on-findings setting, the incomplete-scan setting, the severity thresholds, and the suppressions from the configuration recorded in the lowest-numbered shard; --fail-on-findings and --fail-on-incomplete-scanners on the command line override the first two. A value the shards' configuration read from the environment is recorded as its reference, and ash merge does not read the environment for it: a field that takes a fixed choice, a boolean, or a number, such as severity_threshold, cannot hold the reference, so the merge exits 3 naming the field until you supply it with --config-overrides or in the file --config names (Read values from the environment). The AWS reporters send the merged findings only with their enabled and destination options in ash merge's --config-overrides, not from a config file (AWS reporters). Name their package for the merge too, with --config or --config-overrides, and leave out --output-formats, which stops them. It combines each converter's results across the shards, failed inputs included, so a notebook or archive that one shard could not convert makes the merged scan incomplete.

Its exit codes:

Exit code When 0 Every shard is present and nothing actionable was found. 1 It refused to merge, a scanner in some shard was MISSING or failed, or a converter in some shard failed. 2 Actionable findings. 3 A fixed-choice, boolean, or number field the shards' configuration read from the environment, which the command line does not supply. Nothing was merged. 3 Two reporters that the merge loads have the same name or names that read as one (Exit codes). Nothing was merged. 5 A usage error, such as a missing --results, a --results path that does not exist, or an output directory that is not a directory, cannot be created, entered, or written, or is not a valid path because it holds a NUL character, which a --cli-json-input document can carry (Exit codes). Nothing was merged.

It refuses to merge, and exits 1, when a shard index is missing or repeated, the shards disagree about the count, two shards ran the same scanner, the shards split different sets of scanners, a results file is not from a sharded scan, a --results directory holds no results file, or a shard owned scanners and completed none of them. A shard that owned only scanners that --scanners or --exclude-scanners left out counts as complete. It warns, without refusing, when a scanner ran on no shard although a shard's selection asked for it: the jobs of the matrix were given different --scanners, --exclude-scanners, or configuration, and the shard that owned the scanner did not select it.

docs.title: Sharding in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
One matrix job per shard, then a job that merges and uploads:

name: ASH sharded
on:
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
env:
  INSTALL_SPEC: "automated-security-helper[cdk] @ git+https://github.com/awslabs/automated-security-helper.git@v3.7.0"
jobs:
  shard:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shard: [0, 1, 2, 3]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@18d369b23da25a81e9458561248e1aafff6a70fa # v10.3.1
        with:
          version: latest
      - uses: ruby/setup-ruby@b1da4809b005e0178fe08a1d57317bffc00b7b4c # v1.332.0
        with:
          ruby-version: "3.3"
      - name: Install ASH and the scanner tools
        run: |
          token="$(od -An -N16 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"
          if [ "${#token}" -ne 32 ]; then
            echo "::error::no random token could be read for stop-commands, so the command did not run"
            exit 1
          fi
          printf '::stop-commands::%s\n' "${token}"
          status=0
          {
            uv tool install "${INSTALL_SPEC}" &&
              uv tool dir --bin >> "${GITHUB_PATH}" &&
              cd "${RUNNER_TEMP}" &&
              "$(uv tool dir --bin)/ash" dependencies install \
                --tool grype --tool syft --tool opengrep --tool cfn-nag \
                --tool actionlint --tool cfn-guard --tool gitleaks --tool trivy
          } 2>&1 || status=$?
          printf '\n::%s::\n' "${token}"
          exit "${status}"
      - name: Scan one shard
        env:
          SHARD: ${{ matrix.shard }}
        run: |
          token="$(od -An -N16 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"
          if [ "${#token}" -ne 32 ]; then
            echo "::error::no random token could be read for stop-commands, so the command did not run"
            exit 1
          fi
          printf '::stop-commands::%s\n' "${token}"
          status=0
          ash scan --mode local --no-progress --no-fail-on-findings --no-allow-stale-content-db \
            --shard-index "${SHARD}" --shard-count 4 \
            2>&1 || status=$?
          printf '\n::%s::\n' "${token}"
          exit "${status}"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@043fb46d1a93c77aae656e7c1c64a875d1fc6a0a # v7.0.1
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        with:
          name: ash-shard-${{ matrix.shard }}
          # Not the whole output directory: scanners/ and converted/ hold each
          # tool's raw output, which is not masked. `ash merge` reads each
          # shard's ash_aggregated_results.json.
          path: |
            .ash/ash_output/reports
            .ash/ash_output/ash_aggregated_results.json
  merge:
    needs: shard
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
      actions: read # private repositories only
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@18d369b23da25a81e9458561248e1aafff6a70fa # v10.3.1
        with:
          version: latest
      - name: Install ASH
        run: |
          token="$(od -An -N16 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"
          if [ "${#token}" -ne 32 ]; then
            echo "::error::no random token could be read for stop-commands, so the command did not run"
            exit 1
          fi
          printf '::stop-commands::%s\n' "${token}"
          status=0
          {
            uv tool install "${INSTALL_SPEC}" &&
              uv tool dir --bin >> "${GITHUB_PATH}"
          } 2>&1 || status=$?
          printf '\n::%s::\n' "${token}"
          exit "${status}"
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@9000827ccba6bdab643e8b6fd33ac0654aef8333 # v8.0.2
        with:
          pattern: ash-shard-*
          path: shards
      - name: Merge the shards
        run: |
          token="$(od -An -N16 -tx1 /dev/urandom | tr -d ' \n')"
          if [ "${#token}" -ne 32 ]; then
            echo "::error::no random token could be read for stop-commands, so the command did not run"
            exit 1
          fi
          printf '::stop-commands::%s\n' "${token}"
          status=0
          ash merge --fail-on-findings --fail-on-incomplete-scanners --output-dir .ash/ash_output \
            --results shards/ash-shard-0 --results shards/ash-shard-1 \
            --results shards/ash-shard-2 --results shards/ash-shard-3 \
            2>&1 || status=$?
          printf '\n::%s::\n' "${token}"
          exit "${status}"
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@9b3254085494b55a0f7c4c2b3d2d52cc712ce370 # v4.39.1
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        with:
          sarif_file: .ash/ash_output/reports/ash.ghas.sarif
          category: ash

Each step that runs uv or ash stops workflow commands around it, as the steps in Write the steps yourself do.

The shards run with --no-fail-on-findings, so a shard job fails only when one of its scanners did not run, and the merge job gives the verdict. The merge reads its gate settings from the configuration that the shards recorded, which on a pull request is the branch's own, so it passes --fail-on-findings and --fail-on-incomplete-scanners, and the shards pass --no-allow-stale-content-db. The thresholds and suppressions still come from the branch; to keep those yours, run the shards with --config and a file outside the checkout. Each shard installs every tool, because which scanners land on which shard depends on the scanner list of the ASH it installs. Every shard must load the same plugin modules, or the merge refuses them. Run ash merge with the ASH version the shards ran: an older ash merge refuses the results of a newer ASH's shards.

What sharding does not do:

  • It does not split files. Each shard scans the whole tree.
  • It does not balance by run time.
  • It does not combine with workspace scans (the scan exits 1) and is not available over MCP.
  • ash merge does not remove duplicate findings that two scanners report for the same problem, and keeps the software bill of materials of one shard only.

docs.title: Scan a multi-project workspace
docs.text:
--workspace takes a VS Code .code-workspace file and scans each of its folders as a separate project, with that project's own configuration, in one run. Pass --workspace auto to use the only .code-workspace file in the current directory.

Make two projects from that repository and a workspace file that names them:

mkdir -p services/api services/web
git mv app.py services/api/app.py
printf 'def handler():\n    return "ok"\n' > services/web/main.py
cat > services.code-workspace <<'EOF'
{
  "folders": [
    {"path": "services/api"},
    {"path": "services/web"}
  ]
}
EOF
ash scan --workspace services.code-workspace --dry-run

--dry-run prints the plan, one entry per project with its path, configuration, threshold, and scanners, and scans nothing. Before it prints the plan, it imports the plugin modules the run loads (--ash-plugin-modules and each project's ash_plugin_modules) and refuses what the run refuses before any project starts, with the run's exit 3 and message and no plan: a module outside the plugin namespace, a module that does not import, and two plugins of one type whose names are the same or that the config lookup reads as one, such as csv_ beside csv. Scan it:

ash scan --workspace services.code-workspace --scanners detect-secrets

  FAIL     services-api -- 1 actionable of 1 at threshold MEDIUM (1.7s)
  pass     services-web -- 0 actionable of 0 at threshold MEDIUM (1.7s)

The workspace file:

  • ASH reads only folders[].path. The file must be plain JSON: a comment in it is an error.
  • Paths are relative to the workspace file. A folder outside the workspace file's directory, a path with .., a symbolic link, the directory itself (.), and overlapping or repeated folders are refused. The VS Code layout that lists sibling repositories as ../name does not work; put the workspace file in the parent directory instead.
  • A missing project fails the run, so a typo cannot pass as a clean scan. --allow-missing-projects skips missing projects and records them in the plan.

Each project uses its own ASH config file, with the file --config (or ASH_CONFIG) names layered over it: every setting your file makes is final for every project, and a project's own config fills only the settings yours leaves out. A project that has no config uses your file alone, or ASH's defaults with no --config. --config-overrides, the command-line flags, and the workspace policy apply after both. --dry-run prints an operator: line under each project your file is layered over, and the threshold it prints is the layered result. The config file beside the workspace file is not a fallback for the projects. Keep your file outside every git checkout: ASH treats a file inside one as written by a repository, so the settings only an operator may make, such as sandbox grants and the AWS reporters' destinations, are not final from it, and the plugin modules it may add are limited the same way as a repository's (Configuration trust model). Container mode gives your file the same tier: the host mounts a file from another git checkout and tells the workspace scan inside that a repository wrote it, and that scan limits the file, and every file it extends, for every project and for the plan, with the same warnings (The config file).

Your file, and every base it extends, must be outside the workspace's tree: the outermost git checkout around the workspace, or the workspace directory itself when it is in no checkout. ASH cannot tell a file there from one the repository committed, so a --config inside that tree, beside the workspace in the same checkout included, or under the MCP workspace root, is refused with exit code 3 and the file named, before any project is resolved. Container mode refuses it the same way, with the same error, before anything is built or mounted, a file under the workspace root included. ash dependencies install reads only the configuration of the directory it runs in, so name the tools the projects need with --tool, or run it in each project's directory.

The output directory, .ash/ash_output next to the workspace file by default, holds:

  • combined reports for the workspace in reports/;
  • each project's full output, as from a single scan, in projects/<project>/. GitHub code scanning, GitLab SAST, and CycloneDX reports exist only there, one per project, because each describes one repository. A project's output_formats setting narrows its own reports; the combined reports follow --output-formats only;
  • the combined ash_aggregated_results.json, whose workspace member lists each project with its status, its finding counts, incomplete_scanners, and incomplete_converters, which names each converter that lost coverage and why.

A link at projects or .workspace-spool stops the whole run, and a link at projects/<project> fails that project; see Links are refused.

A workspace policy file applies to every project: a severity threshold that projects can tighten but not relax, suppressions and ignore paths for every project, and extra scanners. ASH finds ash-workspace.yaml, .yml, or .json, with or without a leading dot, in the workspace directory or its .ash directory, or takes the path from --workspace-config; the configuration reference lists its keys. Its suppressions and ignore paths are written relative to the workspace and rebased into each project, keeping a trailing slash: api/vendor/ is vendor/ in project api. A pattern with no exact form inside a project, such as **/vendor/** or **/vendor/, refuses the workspace with exit code 4.

The exit code is the most severe of the projects' results, ranked 3, then 2, then 1, then 0, so a workspace with findings in one project and a missing scanner in another exits 2. Codes 4 and 5 are not part of that ranking: ASH gives them when it refuses the workspace before any project runs. Exit code 4 means the workspace itself is wrong: the workspace file or policy file cannot be used, a project is missing, or the projects need different plugin modules or incompatible scanner versions. --workspace and --source-dir together also exit 4. Exit code 5 is a usage error, such as a --scanners list that names no scanner or that --exclude-scanners cancels:

ash scan --workspace services.code-workspace --scanners detect-secret

--changed-files-only works per project, against that project's own git repository. A project with no changes is skipped, and a project that is not in a git repository is scanned in full, with a warning. Each project's reports are filtered as a single scan's are. --mode precommit changes only the output in a workspace: it does not narrow the scanners or select changed files.

docs.title: Workspace scans over MCP
docs.text:
ash mcp offers the same scans to an MCP client through two tools:

  • resolve_ash_workspace returns the plan, like --dry-run, except that it does not check plugin names: it runs in the server and scans nothing, so it imports no project's plugin module, and its response says plugin_names_checked false. run_ash_workspace_scan refuses two plugins whose names read as one before it scans anything, as --dry-run does.
  • run_ash_workspace_scan runs it and returns the exit code, the output directory, the path of the combined results, and a scan ID per project. To read one project's findings, pass that project's output directory to get_scan_results.

Both tools return exit_code, the code the CLI would exit with, and exit_code_meaning, its description. When run_ash_workspace_scan returns success true, exit_code is the workspace's verdict, ranked as above; success says only that the call completed. The codes go to different people:

exit_code Meaning Who acts 0 Success: the plan resolved, or the scan ran and no project has actionable findings. No one 1 A project failed or is incomplete; the server stopped the scan because it was cancelled or ran past scan_timeout_seconds; or an error inside ASH. An unexpected error is reported as 1, not 4, so that it does not send you to a workspace file that is correct. The owner of the incomplete project; for an error inside ASH, report it as a bug in ASH 2 Actionable findings at or above a project's threshold. The scan ran. The owners of the projects listed with exceeds_threshold true 3 A project's own config is invalid, or a config an MCP client delivered sets a field the server's policy denies; also a profile the server has not registered, or config_overrides the server's allowlist does not allow. That project's owner, or the caller for profile and config_overrides 4 The workspace file or policy file cannot be used; the workspace file, the policy file, output_dir, or a project folder is outside the roots the server allows (see below); an MCP client delivered the policy file; an enabled reporter cannot write a workspace report; or no project could be scanned. Whoever owns the workspace file or the server's allowed roots 5 A usage error: a scanners selection that matches no scanner, or one that excluded_scanners cancels. Only run_ash_workspace_scan takes these. The caller

To stop one project, pass its scan ID to cancel_scan: the other projects carry on, and the response reports that project as failed. The server's max_concurrent_scans and scan_timeout_seconds treat a workspace scan as one scan; see Limit how many scans run and for how long.

The scan tool refuses the whole workspace, with exit code 4, when any project folder resolves outside the roots the server allows (ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS); see Run the MCP server. Both tools use a workspace policy file only when it is in a directory that ASH_MCP_ALLOWED_CONFIG_ROOTS names, whether workspace_config names it or ASH finds it in the workspace file's directory or its .ash directory. Any other policy file refuses the workspace with exit code 4. A policy file an MCP client delivered that also sets a field the server's policy denies is refused first, with exit code 3. In a workspace inside source an MCP client delivered, each project's config file is a delivered config: if one sets a field the server's policy denies, both tools fail with exit code 3, with error_type ASHConfigValidationError and a message that names the project (see What a delivered config cannot set). Over MCP there are no changed-files, sharding, or fail-gate parameters.

Config profiles come from the operator. ash mcp --profile NAME=path/to/ash.yaml, which can be repeated, registers one; the server loads and validates each file when it starts, and a file that does not load stops it with exit code 3. Clients see the names with the list_profiles tool. A workspace call's profile names one for that call; without it, the call uses the profile the session bound with select_profile, if any. The profile is the configuration of each project that has none of its own, and an unknown name is refused with exit code 3. config_overrides applies only what the server's global_settings.mcp.runtime_overrides allowlist allows, and that allowlist is off by default, so a call it denies is refused with exit code 3.

What workspace scans do not do:

  • They do not run projects on separate machines, and cannot be sharded.
  • They do not accept .. paths or a workspace file with comments.
  • They do not write a workspace-level GitHub code scanning or GitLab SAST report.

docs.title: Set the gate
docs.text: A scan's exit code is its verdict: 0 passes, 2 means findings failed it, 1 means the scan did not produce a result you can rely on, and 3 means the config is invalid. 5 is a usage error: the command line was wrong, as with an unknown option or a --scanners list that names no scanner. This page shows which settings decide the verdict, in what order ASH checks them, and how to set them for CI. Every code, for every command, is in Exit codes.

docs.title: What decides the exit code
docs.text:
ASH decides the exit code from these conditions, in order, and stops at the first one that holds. A usage error (5) comes before all of them, except a --scanners list that names no scanner, which ASH refuses after the config check, when the scan phase starts; Exit codes gives the whole order:

Order Condition Exit Controlled by 1 The config does not validate 3 The config itself; ASH stops before scanning 2 A selected scanner did not complete (ERROR, MISSING, or some targets not scanned), no scanner ran, or a converter failed 1 fail_on_incomplete_scanners, on by default 3 A rule could not be evaluated, such as a cdk-nag rule that raised an error on a template 1 Always checked 4 A content database is past its age bound 1 content_db_staleness, fail by default 5 fail_on_findings is off 0 fail_on_findings, on by default 6 An unsuppressed finding is at or above its scanner's severity threshold, and an unsuppressed finding is at or above --min-severity 2 The thresholds and --min-severity 7 None of the above 0

Two consequences of the order: a scan with findings and a MISSING scanner exits 1, not 2, and turning off fail_on_findings does not hide an incomplete scan or a stale database.

Suppressed findings and findings under an ignore path never count in row 6. See Suppress findings.

docs.title: Severity thresholds
docs.text:
The threshold names the least severe finding that still fails the scan. A higher threshold is a looser gate:

Threshold Findings that fail the scan ALL CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW, and INFO LOW CRITICAL, HIGH, MEDIUM, and LOW MEDIUM (default) CRITICAL, HIGH, and MEDIUM HIGH CRITICAL and HIGH CRITICAL CRITICAL

Set it for the whole scan in global_settings, and for one scanner in its options. A scanner's own threshold replaces the global one for that scanner, in either direction; null (the default) uses the global one.

global_settings:
  severity_threshold: HIGH
scanners:
  detect-secrets:
    options:
      severity_threshold: ALL
  grype:
    options:
      severity_threshold: CRITICAL

The values are uppercase and case-sensitive. high, INFO, and NONE are not thresholds, and a config that uses them is refused:

ash --source-dir . --scanners detect-secrets --offline --no-progress \
  --config-overrides global_settings.severity_threshold=high

When no config sets the global threshold, the ASH_DEFAULT_SEVERITY_LEVEL environment variable does. It takes the same five names in any case (high works there), and an unrecognized value falls back to MEDIUM with a warning.

A finding's severity is the one its scanner reports. A finding with none is graded from its rule's security-severity score when the rule has one (9 and above is CRITICAL, 7 HIGH, 4 MEDIUM, and above 0 LOW), and otherwise from its SARIF level: error is CRITICAL, warning is MEDIUM, and note is LOW. detect-secrets and gitleaks findings are graded CRITICAL this way, in the gate and in every report that carries ASH's severity, so a CRITICAL threshold fails on them. ash.ghas.sarif scores rules rather than findings, so GitHub can show these alerts at another severity; Read the results explains how.

ASH does not pass a threshold to trivy, so trivy reports every finding it makes, for the built-in trivy scanner and for trivy-repo alike. ASH applies the threshold after the scan, as for every scanner, to the severity trivy gave each finding: a finding below it stays in the reports and in the summary table's severity columns, is not counted as actionable, and does not fail the scan.

docs.title: --min-severity
docs.text: --min-severity (critical, high, medium, low, or none, in any case; default low) is a second, scan-wide condition on the command line. A scan that fails its thresholds exits 2 only when at least one unsuppressed finding is at or above this severity; otherwise it exits 0. critical and high are equivalent, and none turns the condition off. Any other value is a usage error (exit 5).

docs.title: Report findings without failing
docs.text:
fail_on_findings: false in the config, or --no-fail-on-findings on the command line, makes findings never fail the scan:
